TMP-0003.text: Accessibility Macmillan Learning is committed to the goal of providing equal access to all products regardless of an individual’s age, ability, or situation and embraces the opportunity to develop services and information technologies that are accessible and usable by all individuals. Accessibility at Macmillan Learning is about extending the power of education to all users. In addition to addressing product compatibility with assistive technologies such as screen reader software, alternative keyboard devices, and voice recognition products, we are working to ensure that the content and platforms we provide are fully accessible. Our E-books Macmillan Learning became the first education solutions company to become Global Certified Accessible™ , providing “born accessible” digital learning (e-book) options for

TMP-0004.text: students with disabilities. Books that are born accessible are developed to ensure that all students, no matter their ability, have the same access to information. This is increasingly important for students and instructors, as more than one out of every ten students who attends college has a disability. To become Global Certified Accessible, Benetech evaluated Macmillan Learning’s workflow for creating accessible books, as well as many samples of content across the disciplines they publish in, and certified conformance to the accessible EPUB creation guidelines, which are based on WCAG 2.0 AA+ standards put in place by the international standards organizations and the publishing community. Using a collaborative process, Benetech evaluated and provided feedback on more than one hundred accessibility features. The certification applies to all books created using Macmillan Learning’s updated process, which includes all e-books with a 2019 copyright and beyond. Extended Descriptions In this book, extended descriptions are present for complex images and graphs that may be helpful to understanding content. These extended descriptions can be accessed

TMP-0005.text: via this icon, either as a link or a dropdown starting with the text “Extended description for”: Alternative Text When an image provides important pedagogical information, alternative text (which is also known as alt text) is provided for the image. This text is not visible on the page but can be accessed and read with screen reader technology and other assistive technologies. Our alt text is written and reviewed by subject matter experts. Color Contrast All of our book designs and illustrations are checked to ensure that they meet contrast requirements for WCAG 2.0 AA . Meeting these standards ensures ease of use for users with low vision and color blindness, and can create a more supportive learning environment for users with learning disabilities.

TMP-0006.text: Navigation E-book navigation is designed to make it easy for users, with or without assistive technology, to discover and learn from content within the textbook. Text reflows when resized so there is no horizontal scrolling on the page, and page numbers are embedded in the book so that students can always find where they are compared to classmates using the print equivalent. Heading structures are clearly marked up so it’s easy to see where you are within the book as you work your way through. Accessibility Help If you have any questions about the accessibility of this e-book or other Macmillan Learning e-books, please reach out to us at webaccessibility@macmillan.com . For student resources, visit our knowledge base .

TMP-0045.text: About the Authors David A. Anderson David A. Anderson, PhD, has been involved in AP ® programs and leadership since 1994, including service on the National Advisory Board for AP ® Business with Personal Finance and as the Chief Reader for AP ® Economics or AP ® Microeconomics for five years. An experienced instructor of business principles and entrepreneurship, Anderson is the Paul G. Blazer Professor of Business and Economics at Centre College. He has won Courtesy David Anderson awards for excellence and innovation in the classroom. He received his BA from the University of Michigan and his MA and PhD from Duke University. He earned a graduate certificate in innovation and entrepreneurship from the Harvard Extension School and

TMP-0046.text: an MBA from the University of the People. He also has experience in retail management and banking. Anderson has authored or coauthored dozens of scholarly articles and 18 books, including Economics for the AP ® Course, Environmental Economics and Natural Resource Management, and The Light in the Library Basement: A Personal Finance Mystery Story. His research topics include stock markets, wages, unemployment compensation, pedagogy, and the cost of crime. His favorite hobby is long-distance running. He resides with his family in Danville, Kentucky. Heidi M. Neck Heidi Neck, PhD, is the Jeffry Timmons Professor of Entrepreneurial Studies at Babson College, where she also serves as the Academic Director of the Babson Academy. In this role, she helps to shape the future of entrepreneurship education, influencing universities worldwide to rethink and innovate their approaches to teaching entrepreneurship. The Babson Academy, under Neck’s Courtesy Sage Publications, Inc.

TMP-0047.text: leadership, serves as a catalyst for this transformation, expanding access to high-quality entrepreneurship education and fostering a global community of educators dedicated to advancing the field. She also founded the Babson Collaborative, which connects institutions globally to grow entrepreneurship ecosystems. Neck holds a BS in Marketing from Louisiana State University and an MBA and PhD in Strategic Management and Entrepreneurship from the University of Colorado at Boulder. When she’s not inspiring the next generation of entrepreneurs or shaping the future of entrepreneurship education, Neck enjoys engaging in one of her newest passions: pickleball. Whether on the court or in the classroom, she continues to embody the entrepreneurial spirit, pushing boundaries and challenging conventional wisdom to drive innovation in education and beyond. Christopher P. Neck Christopher P. Neck, PhD, is currently a professor of management at Arizona State University, where he held the title “University Master Teacher.” From 1994 to 2009, he was part of the Pamplin College of Business faculty at Virginia Tech, where he received numerous teaching honors, including the 2002 Wine Award for Teaching Excellence and

TMP-0048.text: ten “Students’ Choice Teacher of the Year” awards, voted on by students across the university. Dr. Neck’s research specialties include employee/executive fitness, self-leadership, leadership, group decision-making processes, and self-managing teams. He has over 200 publications in the form of books, chapters, and articles in various journals. Dr. Neck earned his PhD in Management from Courtesy Sage Publications, Inc. Arizona State University and his MBA from Louisiana State University. Dr. Neck is also an avid runner. He has run the marathon distance over 100 times including the Boston Marathon, New York City Marathon, and the San Diego Marathon. In fact, his personal record for a single long-distance run is a 48-mile run. Emma L. Murray Emma L. Murray, BA, Hdip, completed a bachelor of arts degree in English and Spanish at University College Dublin (UCD) in County Dublin, Ireland, followed by a higher diploma (Hdip) in business studies and information technology at the Michael Smurfit Graduate School of Business in County Dublin, Ireland. Following her studies,

TMP-0049.text: Murray spent nearly a decade in investment banking before becoming a full-time writer and author. Murray has worked on numerous texts, including business and economics, self-help, and psychology. She lives in London, UK, with her husband and two children. Courtesy Sage Publications, Inc.

TMP-0050.text: Content Advisory Board Luiz Bravim Luiz Bravim has taught in Korea, China, and all over the United States. He has consulted for AP ® World History, AP ® European History, and AP ® Business with Personal Finance. A long-time AP ® Exam Reader who has presented at hundreds of conferences, Luiz believes that every student should have access to rigorous college-level curriculum. He has a BA from the University of Central Luiz Bravim Florida and an MBA from the Huizenga School of Business at Nova Southeastern University. He serves as Director of Instruction at Cardinal Gibbons High School in sunny Ft. Lauderdale, where he has taught for over a decade. Luiz enjoys spending time

TMP-0051.text: with his wife, Jennifer, and daughter, Avery. In his spare time, Luiz is an avid Toastmaster and the author of multiple books. Alex Lamon Alex Lamon has taught AP ® Economics, personal finance, and business courses in New Jersey since 2014. He is the Lead Teacher of Livingston High School’s Business Education department, the state’s largest business program among comprehensive high schools. Alex has served as an AP ® Reader, Mentor, and contractor during the development of the AP ® Business with Personal Finance course. Alex Lamon He has received educator awards from the University of Chicago and the Council for Economic Education, published resource books for AP ® teachers, and contributed as a test writer for New Jersey’s business teacher certification exam. In higher education, Alex teaches future business educators as an adjunct professor and student teacher supervisor at Rider University. He also leads professional development for teachers nationwide and serves as Executive Director of the New Jersey Council for Economic Education.

TMP-0052.text: Roland Lewin Roland Lewin taught high school economics and math for 30 years, including 20 years teaching AP ® Microeconomics and AP ® Macroeconomics. Overlapped with his high school teaching, he taught Environmental Economics and Policy at the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) for eight years and is currently teaching economics at Santa Barbara City College for the fourteenth year. He has a BA in Business Economics and a Master’s degree in Economics from UCSB, and a Master’s degree in Education from UCLA. Roland Lewin Roland served three years on the College Board’s Social Sciences Academic Advisory Board and was an AP® Reader for several years. Roland is a past recipient of the Excellence in Economics Education Award (1998) from the national Council on Economic Education and the Adam’s Apple Award (2007) for outstanding service in economics education from the California Council on Economic Education. He has coached numerous winning high school teams in the Econ Challenge, Capital Markets Contest, and the Financial Advisors Contest.

TMP-0054.text: BUSINESS WITH PERSONAL FINANCE for the AP® Course Laying the Foundation for Your Future No matter your path after high school—college, career, or both— Business with Personal Finance helps you prepare. It’s real-world learning designed to support your goals—academic, professional, and personal. Turn the page to get started!

TMP-0061.text: Extended description for Organization (continued) The text at the top of the third screenshot's page reads, It Takes Money to Make Money. The mother-daughter team of Cassandra and India Ayala started a restaurant business called The Bumbling Bee. Their concept was plant-based “vegan junk food” that would satisfy people’s cravings for items like shakes and burgers in a healthy way. They tested their concept on a small-scale with a food truck in 2019. That was a big hit, so they followed up with a brick-and-mortar restaurant the same year, and a second food truck and restaurant in 2020. Despite sales of 324,000 dollars in 2020, the company needed more money to pay for its operating expenses and growth. Cassandra and India appeared on the television show Shark Tank, on which a panel of successful entrepreneurs hears sales pitches from fledgling entrepreneurs who are seeking financial support. The panel decided that The Bumbling Bee had not differentiated itself enough from competing eateries to warrant their investments, and denied the company any funding. The Bumbling Bee received new customers thanks to the television appearance, but the short-lived increase in business was not enough to carry it through the doldrums of the COVID-19 pandemic. With many customers feeling safer eating at home, restaurant revenues were down sharply nationwide, and The Bumbling Bee was reduced to just one food truck and no restaurants. In 2023, the Ayalas invested another 10,000 dollars to bring the food truck to the College of William and Mary, but the revenue was insufficient to maintain that operation.

TMP-0062.text: Extended description for Organization (continued) They decided to pivot to a new business concept they felt might have greater appeal. In 2024, they turned The Bumbling Bee food truck into a business called Solana Street Food, with a new menu featuring Puerto Rican flavors with carnivore, vegetarian, vegan, and gluten-free options. That business is still serving tacos, nachos, and empanadas as of this writing. In their entrepreneurial adventures, the Ayalas found that financial shortfalls drove key decisions about their food-truck business. Money fuels business opportunities and growth, but it doesn’t come easily. Individuals face related challenges, even if they never go into business. Money creates opportunities for education, homes, cars, and healthcare, among other critical needs and wants. And, as for businesses like this one, the need for money often comes long before the availability of money. In the modules ahead, we’ll learn how businesses and individuals can navigate financial challenges by planning well, limiting spending, saving when possible, borrowing when necessary, keeping good records, and managing finances responsibly. Learning Goals What are the ways businesses can get their products to customers? • The 4 Ps of the marketing mix include place, which is the channel for making the product available and distributing it to consumers. Decisions about place involve the location where customers encounter the product as well as the broader distribution strategy that makes products available to customers. • A distribution channel (also known as a marketing channel) is the way the finished product reaches customers. A direct distribution channel is a way for a company to sell goods or services directly to consumers without the use of intermediaries such as wholesalers or retailers. An indirect distribution channel is a way to sell goods or services using intermediaries.

TMP-0078.text: Extended description for Module-Ending A P Practice (continued) • Business-to-business (B2B) companies sell their goods and services primarily to other businesses. Business-to-consumer (B2C) companies sell their goods and services primarily to consumers for personal use. B2B marketing targets committees and business professionals with information-based appeals. B2C marketing targets individual consumers who make relatively emotional, impulsive purchasing decisions. How does a business evaluate and choose the most effective distribution channel for its product? • The advantages of a direct distribution channel include higher profits, increased control, and a closer connection to customers. The disadvantages include higher operational costs, responsibility for order fulfillment, and limited market reach. • The advantages of an indirect distribution channel include the ability to reach a broader market, fewer responsibilities for supply-chain logistics, and the ability to draw on the expertise of intermediaries. The disadvantages include less control over decisions and a broader sharing of profits. Text accompanying the screenshot reads, Review the Module. Mark Cuban’s success shows how strong leadership can turn problems into business opportunities. He worked his way through college teaching disco dancing lessons and selling stamps door to door. He co-founded video portal Broadcast.com and sold it to Yahoo for 5.7 billion dollars. He gained considerable fame as a “shark” on Shark Tank, a reality television show that features entrepreneurs pitching their product ideas. But this businessman wasn’t done with his entrepreneurial adventures, because he continued to identify problems and opportunities too important to ignore. One of those was an opportunity to help people with health issues and financial needs. The solution, as he saw it, was the Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company. A photo accompanying the text shows Mark Cuban on stage, projected onto a large screen for an audience. The photo caption reads, Mark Cuban brought his successful leadership style to the Cost Plus Drug Company to disrupt the pharmaceutical industry.

TMP-0082.text: Extended description for Module-Ending A P Practice (continued) The second page of the screenshot continues the case study. The top of the page reads, Practice Your A P (trademark) Skills continued. People across the United States face health problems that are treatable with medication—if they can afford it. Customers also face uncertainty about how drug prices are determined and whether that price is reasonable. Cost Plus’s mission is to dramatically reduce the cost of drugs and add transparency to drug pricing. Cost Plus sets prices by taking its own cost for the drug and adding 15 percent, plus the 5.00 dollars cost of having a pharmacy prepare and provide the prescription. For example, it can cost over 200 dollars for a bottle of difluprednate eye drops to treat pain and swelling after eye surgery. Cost Plus pays 44.10 dollars for a bottle of difluprednate. Adding 15 percent plus 5.00 dollars, the price to customers becomes 55.72 dollars plus tax and shipping. The problem of high drug prices has existed in the United States for a long time. The opportunity to offer lower prices has been there too, but it took the right business leader to bring the solution to the masses. Mark Cuban’s leadership style fits Cost Plus well. He is passionate about achieving goals and helping people in need, and he keeps employees focused on that mission. Cuban’s leadership style includes direct communication and generous compensation packages that often provide bonuses for loyal, successful employees. The transparent prices at Cost Plus mirror the transparency he prefers in the workplace; according to Cuban, “Open offices keep everyone in tune with what is going on and keep the energy up.”

TMP-0083.text: Extended description for Module-Ending A P Practice (continued) Cuban also likes to disrupt industries with radical change. His disruption of the drug industry by changing the pricing model is consistent with his leadership practices elsewhere. He disrupted the media industry as the co-founder of Broadcast.com, the technology industry as the co-founder of Micro-Solutions, and the professional sports industry as the owner of the Dallas Mavericks basketball team. Cuban’s new approaches in these industries challenged established businesses to evolve for the sake of survival. For example, Broadcast.com was one of the first platforms to bring streaming audio and video to the internet. Micro Solutions gave small businesses access to advanced computing systems before that was common. And after buying the Dallas Mavericks, Cuban created a winning culture by treating players like partners, investing heavily in skill development programs, and providing top-quality training and recovery facilities. If you watch Shark Tank reruns, you might notice Cuban’s embrace of up-and-coming businesses intent on disrupting industries in their own ways. You will also see strong communication skills on display as he negotiates deals with budding entrepreneurs. Cuban understands the value of hard work and notes that success is “not about money or connections—it’s the willingness to outwork and outlearn everyone.” Inc. Magazine calls Cuban “one of today’s most inspiring and successful entrepreneurs.” His success across multiple industries demonstrates how strong management skills are transferable, and that purposeful leadership can spark innovation and change.

You will find five A P (trademark) Skills Workshops in this text—one at the end of each of the five units, with each workshop addressing one of the Course Skills. In this workshop, we will focus on Concept Application. Identify Concept Application

TMP-0094.text: Extended description for A P Skill Building Tools (continued) It is essential to recognize the unique terms and concepts used in the world of business, so that you can begin to think like a business owner and entrepreneur. Concept application is the process of taking what you’ve learned in these modules and thinking about how it shows up or could be used in real-life situations. Applying concepts helps to make them more meaningful and memorable. Understand Concept Application Understanding how to apply these terms and ideas in real-world scenarios will be required for success in this course and on the A P (trademark) Exam. Concept application may be tested in the multiple-choice section as well as the free-response section of the exam. In this A P (trademark) Skills Workshop, we will work to ensure that you understand the concept of competitive advantage. Let’s start with a self-test: • Describe the concept of competitive advantage within a business context. • Answer: A competitive advantage is a firm’s position of superiority over its competitors. That superiority enables the firm to create more value for its customers, which leads to greater sales, market share, and profit for the firm. Identifying a firm’s competitive advantage is key to understanding what companies have to offer in the marketplace. Buyers have many choices when it

TMP-0095.text: Extended description for A P Skill Building Tools (continued) comes to the types of products and services they support with their money. A competitive advantage gives buyers a reason to select one product over its competitors. To put concept application into action, let’s consider a real-world example. Children have long enjoyed playing with water, particularly during warmer months. In 1989, NASA engineer Lonnie Johnson invented a toy he called the Power Drencher. The first model was produced and sold by Larami Corporation in 1990, which later rebranded it as the Super Soaker. Unlike previous toy squirt guns, which had low pressure and could spray only very small quantities of water a short distance, the Super Soaker featured an air pressure chamber and a water reservoir. This allowed the toy to blast water 25 to 50 feet away with accuracy. Kids could play different games with friends that would have been impossible with older models. The toy became so popular that Larami, the corporate owner of the product, was purchased by toy and entertainment giant Hasbro. Let’s test your knowledge again: • Explain the competitive advantage of Johnson’s product. • Answer: Johnson’s competitive advantage was that his toy outperformed old water pistols in nearly every way. It could squirt water farther, featured a stronger spray, and could hold much more water due to the attached reservoir. Another important business concept that is key to this example is that of the target demographic. The target demographic is a set of common characteristics of a group of people that a firm seeks to reach with its

TMP-0113.text: MODULES 1.1 What Is a Business? 1.2 Markets and Competitive Advantage 1.3 PESTEL Factors and the Business Environment 1.4 How Do Business Ideas Originate? 1.5 Vision 1.6 Business Ethics 1.7 Organization, Roles, and Responsibilities 1.8 Supply Chains Meeting Customer Needs and Wants: Cotopaxi Davis Smith was born in Utah, but he spent his childhood in Latin America. There, he witnessed extreme poverty and unequal opportunities firsthand. In college, Smith was inspired by a couple who had sold their business and devoted their lives to helping people lift themselves out of poverty by teaching them entrepreneurial skills. In the years that followed, Smith continued to see business as a positive force for change. After dabbling in several other business ventures, he launched Cotopaxi in 2014 as an outdoor gear company that could be that needed uplifting force. Headquartered in Salt Lake City,

headings.text: Meeting Customer Needs and Wants: Cotopaxi

TMP-0114.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0114.navLabel: Meeting Customer Needs and Wants: Cotopaxi
TMP-0114.text: Utah, Cotopaxi’s mission is to create “outdoor products and experiences that help alleviate poverty, move people to do good, and inspire adventure.” 1 To promote his company and its llama logo, Smith bought two llamas and used them to attract attention on college campuses. Students loved taking selfies with his mascots. Smith also held festivals called Questivals, where teams competed in a series of quests designed to help them “do good” and discover the great outdoors. Examples of the quests included making someone’s day, bonding over a campfire, or catching a lizard. The photos from these events lit up social media and boosted brand awareness for Cotopaxi. While promoting his brand image, Smith created a line of outdoor products that matched his good intentions. Cotopaxi backpacks and apparel are produced almost entirely of responsibly made, recycled, or remnant materials. All Cotopaxi headwear comes from the first Fair Trade Certified factory in China, meaning it complies with strict standards for the treatment of workers, fair pay, and environmental stewardship. When a Cotopaxi product is sold, 1% of the revenue goes to support healthcare, education, and opportunity in Latin America. Smith’s approach led to success for Cotopaxi, which now generates over $100 million in annual revenue.

TMP-0115.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0115.navLabel: Meeting Customer Needs and Wants: Cotopaxi
TMP-0115.text: Other businesses thrive by serving the needs and wants of society as well. Seeing a problem with healthcare or transportation or boredom, an entrepreneur can endeavor to provide better solutions in the form of medicine or ridesharing or entertainment. Beyond that, customers tend to appreciate an ethical business and the opportunity to make a difference with their purchase. By combining innovative products, ambitious marketing, and a mission to give society what it needs, companies like Cotopaxi can do well by doing good. In this unit, you will learn more about how entrepreneurs like Davis Smith align their ideas, business goals, and ethics to create value by offering products that meet customers’ needs and wants. TMP-0119.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0119.text: Businesses Meet Needs and Solve Problems LG What is a business, and what does it do? AP ® students have the ambition required to make a difference in this world. We want you to know that the world needs you. Today’s society values people who can solve problems and fill gaps. Among them are people who can think and act like entrepreneurs by channeling needs into business opportunities, innovating, and leading organizations. This book will help you learn how to do exactly that. This module examines how businesses create value for customers and capture some of that value for themselves. We’ll begin by introducing some business-related terms. An organization is an entity formed to work toward a common goal. A business is an organization regularly engaged in the production or purchase and distribution of goods

TMP-0120.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0120.text: or services. Businesses generally seek profit by selling their products for more than the cost of obtaining them. In Module 1.5 , we will discuss nonprofit organizations and social enterprises that have goals beyond profit. organization A structured group of people formed to achieve common goals. business An organization that produces or purchases goods or services and then sells them; most businesses seek profit by selling their products for more than the cost of obtaining them. Businesses come in all shapes and sizes and serve customers, face-to-face or virtually, at every scale from local to global. A food cart with one employee can serve customers from a small section of a city. A multinational corporation operates in multiple countries. For example, McDonald’s has restaurants in over 100 countries and employs more than 150,000 workers. An e-commerce business such as Etsy exists primarily online and its customers can be anywhere with internet access.

TMP-0121.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0121.text: Left to right: Phillip Bond/Alamy Stock Photo; Sundry Photography/Alamy Stock Photo; GREG BAKER/Getty Images Extended description for Businesses The first photo shows a woman seated at a parked pedal ice-cream cart named WALL'S. An open umbrella shades her from the sun. The second photo shows the large, single-story storefront for an ACE Hardware. The third photo shows a skyscraper with a colorful Google sign on the sidewalk in front of the building. Businesses come in all shapes and sizes.

TMP-0122.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0122.text: Customers and Consumers For a business to be successful, it needs customers. Although we tend to use the terms customer and consumer interchangeably, they do not mean the same thing. A customer is the buyer of a good or service. A consumer , on the other hand, is the user of a good or service. Both customers and consumers can be individuals, businesses, governments, or groups of any kind. Often, the customer and the consumer are the same person. If you buy yourself a sandwich, you are both the customer and the consumer. customer The buyer of a good or service. consumer The user of a good or service. In many cases, the consumer of a product is not the customer who bought it. For example, someone else in your household may have purchased the food you ate for breakfast. If so, that makes you the consumer but not the customer for those products. Other examples include hospitals buying products for their patients, businesses buying products for their employees, and schools buying products for their students. The distinction between customers and consumers can be important when a business

TMP-0123.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0123.text: decides how to pitch a product. The focus on vitamins, fiber, and whole grain in Kellogg’s cereal advertising is a good indication that the company knows exactly who is doing the grocery shopping.

TMP-0124.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas

TMP-0125.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0125.text: Extended description for Kellogg's Froot Loops Text on the box reads, Kellogg's FROOT LOOPS ; Good source of FIBER and made with WHOLE GRAIN ; Sweetened multi-grain cereal; Natural fruit flavors. A series of labels in the upper-right corner list nutrients. The mentions of fiber and whole grain on packages of children’s cereal may appeal more to the customers than the consumers. The Problem-Solution Fit Business opportunities arise out of customer problems, needs, and wants. It might be more fun to open a business that sells your own favorite thing, but if customers aren’t looking to buy it, the fun will end when it comes time to pay the business’s bills. A

TMP-0126.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0126.text: successful business seeks problem-solution fit , which is a close match between its product and the problems of intended customers. To solve customers’ problems, a business must understand its customers well. For that reason, in Module 1.4 , we’ll see that the journey to problem-solution fit begins with careful attention to the goods and services that would satisfy customers’ needs but are currently hard to find. problem-solution fit The match between a business’s product and the problems of intended customers. Searches for problems turn up many, ranging from illnesses without cures to inadequate computing power to a hankering for Thai food. A business clearly cannot satisfy all of its potential customers’ problems. The necessary selection of which needs to address is informed by several considerations: How severe is the problem? How many people share the problem? Can this business address the problem better than other businesses? Are customers willing to pay more than the cost of providing the solution? How difficult it is to reach the intended customers?

TMP-0127.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0127.text: Answers to these questions help a business decide which potential customers to serve and which problems, needs, and wants to address. Consider Rent The Chicken, a business that caters to customers who want to quickly and easily try backyard egg production without a long-term commitment. The company provides hens, a chicken coop, food, and supplies for seven months, with the option to adopt the chickens after the rental. There are many needs and wants out there, but for several reasons it makes sense for these entrepreneurs to serve the large number of egg lovers. Egg prices are often high. The entrepreneurs are experts at raising chickens. Other businesses that can do this better are scarce. Many customers are willing to pay at least $500 for a rental package. And with locations nationwide, it is not difficult for this business to reach its intended customers. Careful analysis of the costs and egg-spenses convinced the owners that they could create value by renting out chickens.

TMP-0130.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0130.text: Businesses Create Value LG How do businesses create value, and how is that value captured? While businesses contribute to the economy by creating jobs and paying taxes, their central role is to create value by providing goods and services that improve consumers’ lives. The value of a product is the worth customers assign to it based on how well it serves their needs and wants. A common measure of the value a customer places on a product is the highest price the customer would be willing to pay for it. This value increases as the problem-solution fit improves. That is, customers place a higher value on—and thus are willing to pay more for—products that better address their needs and wants. value The worth assigned to a good or service based on its perceived fit with customers’ needs and wants; businesses create value by offering products that solve customers’ problems or satisfy their interests.

TMP-0131.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0131.text: For example, suppose things aren’t going your way and you want a funny movie to cheer you up. You would be willing to pay more to watch a comedy that is a fitting solution to your problem than to watch a drama that is a poor remedy for your bad day. Likewise, you would gain more value from, and be willing to pay more for, a medicine that is a good fit for your health problems, a college that is a good fit for your educational goals, and a meal that is a good fit for your appetite or nutritional needs. Value creation occurs when a business offers a product that solves customers’ problems or satisfies their needs and wants. Businesses have a direct incentive to create value because they can capture some of that value. Value capture occurs when a business can charge customers a price that exceeds the cost of providing the product. value creation Occurs when a business offers a product that solves customers’ problems or satisfies their needs and wants. value capture Occurs when a business can charge customers a price that exceeds the cost of providing the product. Figure 1.1-1 illustrates how value capture works. The height of the bar represents the value of a product to a customer. When a customer pays the price for the product, the

TMP-0132.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0132.text: money received in exchange for the product is called revenue , as shown by the striped segment of the bar. Some of the revenue is spent by the business in the process of making or purchasing the product, as shown by the orange segment of the bar. The remaining portion of revenue, shown in blue, is the value captured by the business. That value is called profit , which is the revenue received minus the cost of making the product and operating the business. revenue The money received in exchange for goods or services. profit Revenue minus the cost of making the product and operating the business. AP ® Exam TIP Questions about easily confused terms may appear on the AP ® Exam because a correct answer distinguishes a strong student. The terms customer and consumer are examples, as are value creation and value capture . Can you explain the differences? In most cases, consumers hold on to a portion of the product’s value as well. Perhaps you would be willing to pay far more than the price for your favorite clothing, food, or electronic device. The difference between the value of a product and its price is the

TMP-0133.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0133.text: value you hold onto. A simple term for your share of the value is consumer surplus . The exception to you receiving some value is if your willingness to pay equals the price. If you value a cup of coffee at $3 and its price is $3, you don’t hold onto any of the coffee’s value. In that case, you would be paying an amount equal to the coffee’s value and you would be indifferent between buying it or not. (See A Deeper Dive for a closer look at value and consumer surplus .) A DEEPER DIVE Determining Value Recall the Cotopaxi example discussed in the Unit 1 opener. That company creates value for consumers by making outdoor gear that satisfies consumers’ needs and wants. Cotopaxi can sell winter jackets for $100 only if that product provides at least $100 worth of value to consumers. If Cotopaxi sells a winter jacket for $100, that sale creates $100 in revenue. Suppose the costs of the materials, labor, and electricity used to make the jacket, along with the appropriate share of indirect costs such as rent and advertising, amount to $80. The profit from selling that jacket would be $100 minus $80, which is $20. That $20 portion of the value of the product is captured by the business. The consumer retains some of the value of a jacket if the price paid is less than the value the consumer places on the jacket. Suppose a consumer would be willing to pay $130 for the jacket that Cotopaxi sells for $100. Figure 1.1-1 illustrates this situation. The value of the jacket is $130, not $100, because the jacket’s value is the most the buyer would be willing to pay for it. After paying the

TMP-0134.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0134.text: $100 price, the consumer retains $130 – $100 = $30 of the value. The $30 in value that the consumer receives over and above the purchase price is consumer surplus.

TMP-0135.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0135.text: Value held by consumer = $30 Value captured by business = $20 Value = $130 Price = $100 Cost to business = $80 Revenue = $100 Copyright © BFW Publishers Extended description for Figure 1.1-1 The Value Created by a Jacket The breakdown of the graph reads as follows: • Value equals 130 dollars • Value held by consumer equals 30 dollars • Price equals 100 dollars

TMP-0136.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0136.text: • Value captured by business equals 20 dollars • Cost to business equals 80 dollars • Revenue equals 100 dollars Figure 1.1-1 The Value Created by a Jacket If you pay $100 for a jacket that is worth $130 to you, you hold on to $30 of the jacket’s value. If the jacket costs $80 to make and the seller receives a price of $100, the seller captures $20 of the jacket’s value. In this example, the jacket is worth $130 to the consumer, the seller earned $20 of that value as profit, and the buyer received $30 as consumer surplus. We’ve only accounted for $50 of the $130 value of the jacket. Where did the rest of the value go? With the purchase of $80 worth of materials, labor, electricity, rent, advertising, and other things needed to operate its business, Cotopaxi sent that $80 portion of the value out to other participants in the economy.

TMP-0137.text: Module 1.1 Review Learning Goals LG What is a business, and what does it do? Businesses and other organizations arise to solve problems or address unmet needs. An organization is a structured group of people formed to achieve common goals. A business is an organization that produces or purchases goods or services and then sells them. Most businesses seek profit by selling their products for more than the cost of obtaining them. The buyer of a good or service is called a customer , while the user of that good or service is called a consumer . A successful business seeks problem- solution fit , which is a close match between its product and the problems of intended customers.

TMP-0138.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0138.text: LG How do businesses create value, and how is that value captured? • Businesses create value by offering products that solve customers’ problems or satisfy their interests. • The value of a good or service to customers is the worth they assign to it based on its perceived fit with their needs and wants. Value creation occurs when a business offers a product that solves customers’ problems or satisfies their needs and wants. Businesses have a direct incentive to create value because they can capture some of that value. Value capture occurs when a business can charge customers a price that exceeds the cost of providing the product. • Revenue is the money received in exchange for goods or services. Profit is revenue minus the cost of making the product and operating the business. Customers capture value when the price they pay is below the most they are willing to pay.
