TMP-0141.text: CASE STUDY Imperfect Foods Richard Levine/Alamy Stock Photo Extended description for Imperfect Foods The advertisement on the van shows a bunch of tomatoes with text that reads, Imperfect , hashtag van on a mission; Fight food waste. Save money. w w w dot imperfect dot com.

TMP-0142.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0142.text: Imperfect Foods is a business that solves two problems at once, as its advertising reminds us. Ben Simon gained experience with problem-solution fit even before he started a business. As a student at the University of Maryland, Ben was shocked to see how much food was being wasted in the school cafeteria. He recalls, “I was shocked to see someone buy a full sandwich, eat half of it, and throw the other half out. It was not the values I grew up with.” 2 To address this problem, he and three classmates started the Food Recovery Network (FRN) in 2011. They recovered good dining hall food at the end of the night and provided free meals to homeless shelters. By the end of the school year, they had recovered 30,000 meals for Washington, D.C.-area organizations working to solve the problem of hunger. The following year, the second chapter of FRN was started at Brown University. In 2013, the Sodexo Foundation provided FRN with funds to hire full-time staff. Today, FRN has 195 chapters in 45 states. After their early success with FRN, Ben and his colleague Ben Chesler realized that the same goals that drove their charitable organization could form the basis of

TMP-0143.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0143.text: a profitable business. The origin of Imperfect Foods was a reaction to daunting waste statistics. Approximately 10 million pounds of produce on farms go to waste every year simply because “ugly” or “imperfect” produce does not match the beauty standards of grocery stores in the United States. 3 These aesthetic standards require fruits and vegetables to be fairly uniform in size, symmetric, and free from unattractive blemishes and scars. As a result, farmers are unable to sell a large portion of their crops—anywhere from 5% to 30%. This wasted food represents wasted resources, such as the labor, land, and water used to grow the unsalable produce. While farmers struggled with cosmetically imperfect produce, customers wanted lower grocery prices. Ben and Ben had a solution that fit these problems. In 2015, they founded Imperfect Produce, a seller of affordable, high-quality fruits and vegetables that would otherwise be trashed due to their appearance. Initially, the founders wanted to sell their produce through grocery stores, but they quickly learned that grocery stores had little interest given their beauty standards. So, the business model changed, and Imperfect Produce became an online store, selling its

TMP-0144.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0144.text: not-so-pretty produce at a 30% reduced cost directly to customers using a subscription model. Seeing consumer interest in a broader assortment of discounted foods, in 2019, Imperfect Produce changed its name to Imperfect Foods and expanded its offerings. In 2022, Imperfect Foods was acquired by Misfits Market, another online grocer addressing the dual problems of food waste and food cost. Together, Imperfect Foods and Misfits Market deliver food to every zip code in the continental United States. They source their produce from hundreds of local producers across the country and offer dozens of produce items, along with hundreds of grocery items, to their customers. APPLY YOUR AP ® SKILLS 1. Are the Food Recovery Network and Imperfect Foods both businesses? Explain your answer. 2. Many food customers seek beautiful food, which Imperfect Foods does not offer. Identify two factors that could influence the buying decisions of

TMP-0145.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0145.text: Imperfect Foods’ customers enough to make up for any issues they may have with ugly food. 3. How does a business like Imperfect Foods capture value? 4. What is one aspect of the business model at Imperfect Foods that is likely to help the company capture value despite charging low prices?

TMP-0146.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0146.text: MODULE 1.2 Markets and Competitive Advantage LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 1.2.A Explain how markets create value for buyers and sellers and establish prices 1.2.B Evaluate whether a business plan will give a company competitive advantage

TMP-0147.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0147.text: Paul Christian Gordon/Alamy Stock Photo Pike Place Market in Seattle, Washington, attracts customers with the spectacle of flying fish. It’s just one example of how markets bring sellers and buyers together.

TMP-0148.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0148.text: What Markets Do LG What happens in markets? You are part of a market whenever you make a purchase. The market for a good or service is made up of buyers and sellers interacting in person or virtually. Some markets are local, such as Pike Place Market in Seattle, Washington. For almost 100 years, fish market participants have met there on the water’s edge to buy and sell freshly caught seafood. However, most markets are much larger than any one place. For example, U.S. buyers and sellers of education, real estate, cellphone service, Japanese food, and construction work are spread across the country. Some markets are global, such as the oil market. Even so, smartphones and computers can bring the markets for most goods almost anywhere by allowing buyers and sellers to connect remotely. market A place, real or virtual, where buyers and sellers can exchange goods and services.

TMP-0149.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0149.text: In Module 1.1, we discussed how a business creates value by satisfying customers’ needs or wants. Recall that when a buyer pays less for a good than they think it is worth, they receive some of that value. The seller captures some of that value as profit if the price exceeds the cost of providing the good. And some of the value is distributed elsewhere in the economy when the buyer and seller pay taxes and the seller pays for labor, rent, utilities, and other inputs. Markets help the economy create value by bringing buyers and sellers together for the voluntary exchange of money for goods and services. The amount of value created, and the distribution of that value, depends on the number and characteristics of buyers and sellers in the market. Most economies are made up of markets with varying degrees of competition among the sellers of goods and services. For convenience, it is common to refer to those business organizations as firms . In the next two sections, we will explore the implications of having many firms in a market—and having very few. Highly Competitive Markets Markets differ in important ways. You will find a wide variety of offerings in the market for basketball shoes, whereas every seller offers pretty much the same thing in

TMP-0150.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0150.text: the market for Spanish peanuts. Market structure refers to the characteristics of a market, such as the number of firms, the similarity of the products being sold, and the ease of entrance by firms into the market. At one extreme are perfectly competitive markets , which have plentiful firms and are particularly effective at creating value. A perfectly competitive market is a market in which: there are many buyers and sellers. the firms sell exactly the same product. buyers and sellers are fully informed about the product and its price. it is easy for firms to enter and exit the market. No market is perfectly competitive in every respect, but many markets come close. Examples include the markets for agricultural goods such as rice, bananas, and cotton; the markets for corporate stocks; and the markets for hot dogs and similar goods sold by many street vendors in a city. Like all markets, competitive markets bring together sellers, who want high prices to gain more profit, and buyers, who want low prices to gain more value for themselves.

TMP-0151.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0151.text: AP® EXAM TIP The supply and demand graph is not expected to be on the AP® Business with Personal Finance exam. However, seeing how things work helps many people learn. This visual aid might help you understand how market prices are determined. It also illustrates how price affects the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied. If it doesn’t help you, don’t worry about it. Let’s examine the market for peanuts to see how prices are established in a highly competitive market. The price of peanuts helps peanut farmers decide the amount of time and resources they will devote to peanut production. As the price of peanuts rises, the quantity of peanuts that farmers are willing to supply increases. Farmers are willing to produce more peanuts at a high price than at a low price because a high price justifies more expenditures of time and money on peanuts. For the same reason, firms selling most products are willing to supply a larger quantity at a high price than at a low price. The supply curve in Figure 1.2-1 illustrates this common relationship between the price and the quantity supplied.

TMP-0152.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0152.text: Extended description for FIGURE 1.2-1 Where Market Prices Comes From: Supply and Demand The horizontal axis of the graph is labeled Quantity. The vertical axis is labeled Price. A concave-upward curve labeled Supply increases in Quantity and Price while a concave-upward curve labeled Demand decreases in

TMP-0153.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0153.text: Quantity and Price. Where the two curves intersect corresponds to the Equilibrium quantity on the horizontal axis and the Equilibrium price on the vertical axis. Figure 1.2-1 Where Market Prices Come From: Supply and Demand To see where market prices come from, it helps to visualize market equilibrium. The demand curve reminds us that in most cases, as price increases, the quantity demanded decreases. In contrast, the supply curve shows us that higher prices generally increase the quantity supplied. In a highly competitive market, the equilibrium price at which the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded becomes the prevailing market price.

TMP-0154.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0154.text: Left: Ira Berger/Alamy Stock Photo; right: Catherine McQueen/Getty Images Extended description for Highly Competitive Markets The first photo shows a variety of shoes displayed on a wall. The second photo shows rows of bunches of bananas hanging on a wall. In some markets, competitors offer wildly different products. In other markets, competitors sell pretty much the same thing.

TMP-0155.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0155.text: The price of peanuts also influences the quantity of peanuts customers demand , meaning the quantity they would purchase at that price if possible. To examine your demand for peanuts, we would first consider the value you receive from them. Suppose that you love peanuts and currently do not have any. Think about the most you would be willing to pay for each of your first three bags of peanuts purchased today. Since you love peanuts, you would probably be willing to pay a fairly high amount for your first bag; say, $5.00. With one bag, at least some of your peanut needs and wants would be met, so you would not pay as much for a second bag. Perhaps you would be willing to pay a moderate amount to have an extra bag to share with friends or save for later; say, $3.00. You probably have little use for a third bag of peanuts, so let’s say you would be willing to pay at most $0.50 for it. We will suppose you have no interest in additional bags of peanuts. By this reasoning, you would buy three bags of peanuts for a price of $0.50 or less because the first three bags are worth at least that much to you. At a price above $0.50 you would not buy the third bag that is only worth $0.50 to you. For up to $3.00, you would still buy the first two bags because those bags are worth $3.00 or more to you. For a price above $3.00 but not above $5.00, you would only buy the one bag that is worth

TMP-0156.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0156.text: $5.00 to you. For a price above $5.00, you would buy no peanuts because even the first bag is only worth $5.00 to you. Market Prices in Competitive Markets The quantity of peanuts that most customers will purchase decreases as the price increases, just as it did for you. This behavior obeys the law of demand : a price increase generally leads to a decrease in the quantity demanded. Many people like to visualize the inverse relationship between the price of a product and the quantity demanded with a demand curve as shown in Figure 1.2-1 . That relationship is important to the pricing decisions every business must make. It is tempting to assume that revenue will increase if the price rises, but the law of demand reminds us that a higher price generally results in fewer sales. Whether revenue increases after a price increase depends on the relative size of the price increase and the quantity decrease. If customers are sensitive to the price, a higher price might actually decrease revenue. For example, consider what would happen to the revenue a peanut seller receives from you if the price increased from $4.50 to $5.50. It

TMP-0157.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0157.text: would decrease from $4.50 to zero because you would buy one bag for $4.50 and zero bags for $5.50. Now consider how the quantity of peanuts customers are willing to buy compares with the quantity farmers are willing to supply at various prices. At a low price, the quantity customers are willing to buy is high and the quantity farmers are willing to supply is low. The result is a shortage of peanuts. At a high price, the quantity customers are willing to buy is low and the quantity farmers are willing to supply is high, resulting in a surplus of peanuts. Somewhere in between the price that causes a shortage and the price that causes a surplus is a price at which the quantity demanded by consumers equals the quantity supplied by farmers. That price is the equilibrium price because it brings the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied into equilibrium. The quantity bought and sold at the equilibrium price is called the equilibrium quantity . In a highly competitive market like the peanut market, interactions between sellers seeking higher prices and buyers seeking lower prices cause the rival firms to converge on the equilibrium price. That price becomes the prevailing market price , meaning the price generally charged by firms throughout the market. Why? Because if there is a shortage of peanuts, rather than having customers lining up to pay a low price for the

TMP-0158.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0158.text: relatively small quantity of peanuts supplied, farmers will raise their price. And if there is a surplus of peanuts, rather than sitting on piles of peanuts that nobody wants, farmers will lower their price to sell more. Those responses to prices below or above the equilibrium price guide the market price to the equilibrium price. market price The price generally charged by firms throughout the market. It seems improbable that every firm would charge the same price, but recall that the many firms in a perfectly competitive market sell exactly the same thing and that customers are fully informed about how much firms are charging. If a county fair has many peanut vendors selling identical peanuts, it would be hard for one vendor to charge a higher price than the others. Customers would bypass the vendor with a higher price and visit one of the many other vendors selling the same peanuts for less. So, every firm in a perfectly competitive market takes the market price as given rather than independently choosing its own price. In contrast, a firm is said to have market power if it has influence over the price it charges. In monopolies and other markets with imperfect competition, sellers have choices to make about how high to set prices. We will examine monopolies in the next section and pricing strategies in Module 2.5.

TMP-0159.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0159.text: Perfectly competitive markets are relatively good at creating value because the equilibrium price leads to the sale of every unit of the product that is worth more to customers than the cost to firms of providing it. If the price were higher, customers would buy fewer units. If the price were lower, firms would supply fewer units. Either way, the reduction in the quantity bought and sold at a nonequilibrium price would lower the value gained from the product. Although more competition creates more value, competition lowers the profit most firms desire. Suppose producers of Spanish peanuts are earning a handsome profit. More farmers will enter the market in pursuit of that profit. With more farmers, the supply increases and the price falls. More farmers grow Spanish peanuts until their price is just high enough to entice the existing farmers to continue operating—that is, until the typical farm takes in just enough revenue to cover every sort of cost it faces, but nothing more. One way to make profit sustainable is to gain market power, the extreme case of which we discuss next.

TMP-0160.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0160.text: Monopolies A firm has plenty of market power to influence prices in a monopoly , which is a market with only one firm. The lone business selling a good or service in a monopoly market is called a monopolist . As the only provider of long-distance passenger rail service in the United States, Amtrak is an example of a monopolist. monopoly A market with only one seller. We noted that peanut buyers could switch vendors if one vendor raised its price. In contrast, Amtrak customers cannot switch to a competing rail service if Amtrak raises its price. Being the sole firm in a monopoly gives Amtrak some leeway to choose its price. However, a monopolist must be careful not to set its price too high. After all, monopolies aren’t exempt from the law of demand. A monopolist cannot charge whatever price it wants because customers: (1) have only so much money to spend; (2) may have other options, such as driving or flying instead of taking a train; and (3) can go without many products if necessary. But unlike a firm in a perfectly competitive market, a monopolist can raise its price without losing all of its customers to competitors.

TMP-0161.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0161.text: Mario Tama/Getty Images If you want to see the country by rail, you really have only one option: Amtrak, the sole provider of this service in the United States. A monopolist can earn a profit if consumer demand is sufficiently high and costs are sufficiently low. To continue earning profit in the long run, a monopolist needs a barrier

TMP-0162.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0162.text: to competitors who would otherwise enter the market seeking profit. Later in this module, we will discuss specific barriers to entry such as patents or control over scarce resources. By examining markets with lots of competition and those with none at all, we can more easily see the effects of competition and the reasons businesses avoid it. You may be wondering about the markets with some middling amount of competition that you observe daily, like the markets for fast food and blue jeans. The difficulty of nailing down what happens in those markets makes an in-depth examination better suited for later courses. However, allow us to address your curiosity by mentioning three other common types of market structure. A duopoly is a market dominated by two firms. For example, two firms—the Coca-Cola Company and PepsiCo—dominate the cola market. The oil market is described as an oligopoly because it is dominated by a small number of large firms. Other examples of oligopolies include the markets for air travel, automobiles, and telecommunications. And a monopolistically competitive market has many firms selling similar but not identical products, such as different types of fast food or clothing. Firms in monopolies, duopolies, and monopolistically competitive markets

TMP-0163.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0163.text: enjoy the market power needed to have some say about prices. To gain market power, firms pursue competitive advantage.

TMP-0164.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0164.text: Competitive Advantage LG What strategies can a business use to achieve competitive advantage in a market? We have seen that the prospects for lasting profit are slim when many firms sell an identical product and competitors can easily enter the market. A firm seeking profit should consider a strategy that helps it stand out from rival businesses , which are other businesses competing in the same market. Competitive advantage makes that possible. Competitive advantage is a firm’s position of superiority over competitors. That superiority enables the firm to create more value for customers, which leads to more sales, greater market share, and the potential for increased profit for the firm. rival businesses Other businesses that compete in the same market as a given firm. competitive advantage A firm’s position of superiority over competitors.

TMP-0165.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0165.text: Sources of Competitive Advantage The many sources of competitive advantage can be grouped into three broad categories: cost, focus, and product differentiation. In the cost category are strategies for producing goods and services at a relatively low cost and charging low prices that appeal to customers. This strategy serves especially well for firms whose product is difficult to differentiate from rival firms’ products. Corn is hard to differentiate, but one farmer may find ways to produce corn more efficiently than other farmers. Focus refers to serving a narrow portion of the market, often termed a “niche.” A niche market is a segment of a broader market where the firm’s products meet very specific needs. Makers of gluten-free bread, triathlon gear, and luxury pet furniture serve niche markets. Product differentiation means offering something that is unavailable from competitors. Companies can differentiate their offerings in many ways, such as by offering a unique feature, a convenient delivery method, or a higher level of quality or customer service. In Unit 2 , we will see how marketing strategies involving

TMP-0166.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0166.text: advertising and promotions can help differentiate a product in the eyes of consumers. product differentiation Offering something that is unavailable from competitors. These sources of competitive advantage are elements in four common business strategies which we will discuss next.

TMP-0167.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0167.text: Khim Hoe Ng/Alamy Stock Photo Lefty’s in San Francisco, founded by entrepreneur Margaret Majua, is a store filled with products made for left- handed people. It gains competitive advantage by focusing on a narrow niche market.

TMP-0168.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0168.text: Four Strategies for Competitive Advantage Competitive advantage is a key to business success. Harvard business professor Michael E. Porter described what are known as the four generic strategies for creating competitive advantage: 1. Cost leadership is a strategy of adopting efficient production processes and streamlining operations to cut costs below those of competitors. The firm can then offer lower prices that appeal to price-sensitive customers. For example, Walmart follows a cost leadership strategy with a no-frills, high-volume approach to retailing supported by a state-of-the-art supply system. The Aldi grocery store chain cuts costs by having relatively few advertisements, workers, expensive brands, and store hours. And IKEA reduces its costs by selling furniture that is assembled by the customer rather than by workers in a factory. The cost leadership strategy applies to products in a broad market such as groceries, furniture, or general merchandise.

TMP-0169.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0169.text: Allen Creative/Alamy Stock Photo Aldi uses a cost leadership strategy, offering reduced prices to compete for customers. 2. Differentiation is a strategy of providing something desirable that rival firms do not offer. Differentiation can be in design, quality, functionality, brand image, customer service, packaging, mode of delivery, sustainability, or convenience, among other

TMP-0170.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0170.text: attributes. For example, Apple differentiates its computers and devices with innovative designs, Trader Joe’s boasts of particularly high-quality grocery products, Patagonia makes clothing with organic cotton to support its commitment to the environment, and Nike differentiates its brand with athlete endorsements. Firms with a differentiation strategy aim to attract attention within a broad market, such as computers, groceries, outdoor clothing, or sportswear. 3. Cost focus is a strategy of lowering costs and beating competitors’ prices in a niche market where products meet a specific need. This strategy is similar to cost leadership but with a focus on a narrow market. For example, a motel chain could offer the lowest-priced lodging designed especially for families with kids or for business travelers or for extended stays. There are cheaper fast-food restaurants, but for Louisiana-style fried chicken and seafood, it’s hard to beat the prices at Popeyes Louisiana Kitchen. And Spirit Airlines isn’t for everyone, but the company caters to price-sensitive customers with no-frills flights in North and South America. 4. Differentiation focus is a strategy of providing unique, specialized goods or services to a niche market. By offering an improved fit for the needs of a narrow market, a firm can gain competitive advantage over firms with less suitable offerings. For

TMP-0171.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0171.text: instance, the Square Reader from Block, Inc., allows small businesses to accept credit card payments using a mobile device. Rolls Royce targets a small segment of the automobile market with its cars that cater to high-income individuals who prioritize luxury, superior engineering, and customizable features. Figure 1.2-2 illustrates the different types of strategies a firm can adopt to gain competitive advantage and define its position within an industry. For competitive advantage, a firm might compete on cost or differentiation, and for focus, a firm might compete in a narrow or broad market. These choices determine the firm’s overall competitive strategy and provide focus and direction for the organization. According to Michael Porter, firms that choose a clear strategy have a better opportunity to achieve competitive advantage. If a firm tries to compete both with cost and with differentiation, or in both broad and narrow market segments, Porter warns that it might become “stuck in the middle.”

TMP-0172.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0172.text: Competitive advantage Low cost Unique product Copyright © BFW Publishers Target Broad Stuck in the middle Cost leadership Differentiation Narrow Cost focus Differentiation focus Extended description for Figure 1.2-2 Porter's Generic Strategy ⓘ The matrix is divided into two columns and two rows. The columns are labeled Competitive advantage . The rows are labeled Target . The information reads as follows: Low Cost, Cost leadership; Broad: Cost leadership Low Cost, Cost focus; Narrow: Cost focus

TMP-0173.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0173.text: Unique product, Differentiation; Broad: Differentiation Unique product, Differentiation focus; Narrow: Differentiation focus At the center of the matrix, a circle intersecting all boxes of the table reads: Stuck in the middle. FIGURE 1.2-2 Porter’s Generic Strategies Porter’s four generic strategies outline how a business can target either a broad or a niche market and emphasize either low costs or unique offerings to achieve competitive advantage. AP ® EXAM TIP Competitive advantage is a central business concept that is likely to appear on the AP ® Exam. It is worthwhile to take careful notes on this concept and quiz yourself to ensure that you understand it well.

TMP-0174.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0174.text: Stuck in the Middle While his four generic strategies are useful to many organizations, Porter cautions against using more than one at the same time, because they are not necessarily compatible with each other. There are various risks inherent in each strategy, and trying to please everyone at once poses a large risk of getting “stuck in the middle” in a place of mediocrity. Firms that are stuck in the middle lose focus on the direction of the organization and fail to establish a core group of customers. Their goods or services are not differentiated enough to attract a large customer base and their prices are too high to compete with the cost leaders. The company that aims for mid-range prices and typical products with the goal of having everyone as a customer can find itself far from that ideal. Roast beef sandwich chain Arby’s is a good example of a company that became stuck in the middle. Around 2010, its roast beef sandwiches were not priced to compete effectively with other fast-food offerings, nor was its menu sufficiently differentiated to generate profit. Parent company Wendy’s sold Arby’s in 2011 due to its poor performance. Since then, Arby’s has made a comeback by focusing on quality meats, new products, renovated restaurants, and innovative marketing strategies. With these

TMP-0175.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0175.text: moves and its now-famous “We Have the Meats” campaign to highlight its differences, Arby’s was able to become “unstuck” enough to compete with the other major players in the fast-food industry.

TMP-0176.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas

TMP-0177.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0177.text: Extended description for Arby’s A bag reads: Arby’s MEAT CRAFT; TURKEY, CHICKEN, ROAST BEEF. A sandwich box in front of the bag reads, MEAT CRAFT. A cup beside the bag and behind the box reads, Arby’s. All three items show the Arby’s name in the brand’s signature 10- gallon hat silhouette. Arby’s changed its strategy and got unstuck. Barriers to Entry Competitive advantage provides profit only for as long as the advantage lasts. Competitive advantage can be sustained by barriers to entry , which are obstacles that make it difficult for new competitors to enter the market. Barriers can be legal rights, regulations that limit rivals, high startup costs, limited access to resources, and low prices enabled by large-scale production.

TMP-0178.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0178.text: barriers to entry Obstacles that deter new competitors from entering a market. LEGAL BARRIERS Society can often benefit from something new that requires considerable time and expense to create. Examples include cures for disease, textbooks, artwork, and computer software. But if competition can quickly drive down prices and profit, individuals and firms are less inclined to invest time and money in new creations. The government can encourage innovation with intellectual property rights , which are legal rights granted to protect creations of the mind. For example, the government can provide opportunities for profit with patents, copyrights, and trademarks. intellectual property rights Legal rights, such as patents, copyrights, and trademarks, that protect creations of the mind. • A patent grants its holder the right to be the only seller of an invention for a designated period of time. In the United States, the typical patent life is 20 years. By eliminating competition and enabling profit, patents help justify large expenditures to develop new products. For example, pharmaceutical companies typically spend over $1 billion to develop and test a successful new drug.

TMP-0179.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0179.text: • copyright gives its holder the exclusive right to sell an original work. Architecture, artwork, photographs, software, songs, and writings are all protected by copyrights. Copyrights generally last for the creator’s lifetime plus 70 years. • trademark is a word, phrase, symbol, or design that distinguishes the products of one firm from those of its competitors. The registration of a trademark with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office can provide exclusive rights for an unlimited period of time, although paperwork updates are required. The Nike swoosh and the stitching on the back pocket of Levi’s jeans are examples of trademarks. You might also recognize this registered trademark: AP ® . Regulations While some regulations are designed to encourage competition, others can have a limiting effect on rivals. For example, regulations mandate that healthcare professionals such as nurses, doctors, and dentists obtain licenses. Other occupations that require licenses include electricians, barbers, real estate agents, pharmacists, teachers, lawyers, and accountants. Licensing requirements can protect consumers against unqualified workers. It would be daunting to board an airplane whose pilot lacked a license. But

TMP-0180.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0180.text: strict licensing requirements also represent a barrier that limits the amount of competition. Other regulations that limit competition include land-use regulations and trade restrictions. For example, zoning regulations in some areas prohibit the development of farmland, which limits the entry of new shopping malls and apartment complexes. Competition from other countries is thwarted by tariffs, which are taxes on imports that raise the prices of goods produced abroad. High Startup Costs Startup costs are the expenses a new business faces as it prepares to open for the first time. For some types of businesses, the startup costs are so high that no other barrier is needed to limit competition. The cost of launching a new car manufacturer, railway, hospital, or college is prohibitive to most potential competitors. If the size of the local market does not justify the cost of starting more than one of a particular type of business, that barrier to entry is insurmountable. The first business of that type will be a monopolist. If you live in a small town, you probably only have one hospital. In other cases, there might be enough customers to support some competition,

TMP-0181.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0181.text: but the high startup costs limit the number of potential rivals who make the large, risky investment needed to become a competitor. Control of Resources The rechargeable battery in a cell phone is made of lithium, the world supply of which is largely controlled by only seven providers. One of them, a mining company called SQM, holds the rights to extract lithium from an ancient lakebed in Chile that holds over one-quarter of the world’s known lithium supply. The tight control of lithium supplies creates a barrier to entry into the lithium market. Talented people have market power because they control their valuable human resources. It takes a rare combination of knowledge, effort, and natural ability to be among the best entrepreneurs, surgeons, singers, gymnasts, or actors. A lot of people would like to earn as much as Beyoncé does for a concert, but the barriers to entry into the market for singers with concert tours are high. Beyond that, many consumers specifically want to go to a Beyoncé concert, and she has a monopoly on that market.

TMP-0182.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0182.text: Alex Slitz/Getty Images Barriers to entry make it hard for new artists to compete with superstars like Beyoncé. She controls a scarce resource because there is only one Beyoncé. She can copyright her songs, giving her a legal barrier. And thanks to the large scale of her music distribution, she enjoys economies of scale.

TMP-0183.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0183.text: Economies of Scale A firm experiences economies of scale if a sustained increase in the level of production leads to a decrease in the average cost of making each unit. Lower costs make it possible for a firm to charge lower prices, earn higher profits, or both. Consider a summer camp. To offer its services to, say, five campers each week, it would need a camp area, a counselor, some food, and facilities for eating, sleeping, and various activities. Now suppose the camp grows its enrollment and serves ten campers each week instead of five. If the same campground, staff, and facilities are adequate for the larger number of campers, expenses will only increase by the cost of some additional food. In that case, the average cost per camper would decrease. For example, suppose it costs a total of $500 per week to host five campers and, due to a $100 increase in food costs, it costs $600 per week to serve 10 campers. The average weekly cost per camper would fall from $500/5 = $100 to $600/10 = $60. Similarly, an oil refinery, a school, a cable company, or a t-shirt factory is likely to require a large expenditure for necessary buildings and equipment, but as production

TMP-0184.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0184.text: levels grow, those costs are spread across larger quantities of output. The result is a decrease in the average cost per unit. Economies of scale make it difficult for more firms to enter a market, because a small number of big firms can produce each unit at a lower cost than a large number of small firms. In some cities, one firm serves the whole local market as a consequence of economies of scale. Think about why there are not more energy companies in your area. A single firm can divide the enormous cost of operating a power plant across all of the customers in the area, whereas many energy companies would split the market, meaning none could get enough customers to cover their costs. With many sources of competitive advantage to consider, it is wise for a business to step back and evaluate its situation. As part of our module review, we will examine one nutty business case.

TMP-0185.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0185.text: Module 1.2 Review Learning Goals LG What happens in markets? • By bringing buyers and sellers together for the voluntary exchange of money for goods and services, markets help the economy create value. The market for a good or service is made up of buyers and sellers interacting either in person or virtually. • In a highly competitive market, interactions between sellers seeking higher prices and buyers seeking lower prices cause the rival firms to converge on the equilibrium price. That price becomes the prevailing market price charged by firms throughout the market. • Firms cannot sustain profits in the case of a perfectly competitive market, meaning there are many fully informed buyers and sellers of an identical product and firms

TMP-0186.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0186.text: can easily enter or exit the market. • A monopoly is a market with only one firm. The lone business selling a good or service in a monopoly market is called a monopolist. A monopolist’s ability to maintain profits in the long run depends on the existence of barriers to entry by competing firms. LG What strategies can a business use to achieve competitive advantage in a market? • A firm seeking profit should consider strategies for outperforming rival businesses , which are other businesses competing in the same market. Competitive advantage, or a firm’s position of superiority over competitors, makes that possible. • Sources of competitive advantage include relatively efficient production methods that lead to lower costs and prices, a narrow focus on one segment of the market, product differentiation to make the product unique in some way, and superior marketing.

TMP-0187.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0187.text: • Competitive advantage can be sustained by barriers to entry , which are obstacles that deter new competitors from entering the market. Barriers to entry can be legal rights, regulations that limit rivals, high startup costs, limited access to resources, and low prices enabled by large-scale production. As an example, the government can encourage innovation with intellectual property rights , which are legal rights granted to protect creations of the mind. Practice Your AP ® Skills Preparing for the AP ® Exam Multiple-Choice Questions 1. Markets are always a. competitive. b. in one place. c. made up of buyers and sellers.

TMP-0188.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0188.text: d. easy for new firms to enter. 2. In a highly competitive market, the market price is established by a. the most powerful seller. b. customers’ price preferences. c. the equilibrium of supply and demand. d. the cost of making each unit. 3. Which of the following is the most likely to provide a business with profit? a. a competitive market b. competitive advantage c. easy entrance by businesses into the market d. products that are identical to what competitors are selling 4. Which barrier to entry is the most likely to encourage innovation? a. regulations to limit rivals b. control of resources

TMP-0189.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0189.text: c. high startup costs d. intellectual property rights CASE STUDY Smucker’s Bloomberg/Getty Images In the crowded market for peanut butter, companies like Jif strategize to gain competitive advantage with lower costs or increased differentiation.

TMP-0190.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0190.text: Jerome Monroe Smucker founded the company known as Smucker’s in 1897 on his farm in Orrville, Ohio. In its early days, the company sold spreads, including jellies, jams, and apple butter, from the back of a horse-drawn wagon. Over the next century, innovations in packaging, advertising, and products created competitive advantage that made Smucker’s famous. For example, Smucker’s debuted a trademarked glass jar in 1938. It offered a popular low-sugar jam substitute in 1978. And in 1962, it introduced its memorable tagline, “With a name like Smucker’s, it has to be good!” The company’s specialty of spreads made it only natural for Smucker’s to acquire the Jif brand of peanut butter from Procter & Gamble in 2001. Jif differentiated itself early on by sweetening its peanut butter recipe with sugar and molasses. More recently, the company has courted customers with Jif to Go individual serving packages and with flavor innovations that include natural honey creamy, extra crunchy, and a new line of hazelnut spreads. To gain economies of scale and the resulting low costs, Jif operates the world’s largest peanut butter factory in Lexington, Kentucky. Although Jif is the leading brand of peanut butter in the United States, rivals Skippy and Peter Pan are a constant threat. With new market entrants offering

TMP-0191.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0191.text: similar products and established brands competing for shelf space in grocery stores, Jif needs new ways to create competitive advantage and differentiate itself. In this case study, you are in the driver’s seat to help this company maintain its profitability. Suppose Smucker’s hired you to lead the team tasked with building Jif’s competitive advantage for the future. In your first team meeting, four of Jif’s managers offered differing ideas about the best strategy for the company: Manager 1 favors a cost leadership strategy. She would like to cut costs and lower prices by investing in automation and expanded production facilities that achieve economies of scale. She argues that by lowering prices, Jif could capture a larger share of the market. With the increase in sales, the company could spread the cost of its new equipment over a large quantity of output. The result would be a lower average cost of producing each jar of peanut butter, which would allow the company to earn profit despite offering a low price. Manager 2 advocates a differentiation strategy. He would like to see Jif offer a fresh new wave of unique flavors, including hot honey peanut butter, caramel peanut butter, and coffee peanut butter. He contends that these offerings would help Jif

TMP-0192.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0192.text: stand out among competitors in the peanut butter market and allow the company to set a price that generates profit. Manager 3 would pursue a cost focus strategy. She recommends offering a new product that targets the market for older adults. Knowing that many older customers have limited incomes and can struggle with the removal of sticky lids, Jif would offer low prices on easy-pour bottles with a flip-off lid and a watered-down, cheaper-to-produce version of peanut butter that pours out like syrup. She argues that this strategy would allow Jif to beat competitors’ prices and gain customers in this niche market. Manager 4 favors a differentiation focus strategy of targeting the segment of the condiment market with peanut allergies. His idea is to open a separate facility that produces premium butter made from sunflowers, almonds, tahini, and soy. He argues that people with peanut allergies will flock to a superior substitute for peanut butter that enables them to enjoy the types of sandwiches and snacks they’ve been missing out on. With these premium butters, Jif could gain competitive advantage over companies with no (or lower-quality) peanut butter substitutes.

TMP-0193.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0193.text: As the team leader, you have the opportunity to choose among these possible sources of competitive advantage. Apply Your AP ® Skills 1. Identify the strategy you would recommend for Jif and explain why you favor that approach to creating value for customers. 2. Manager 1’s strategy will work well if what factor is a strong influence on the target customer’s buying decision? 3. Identify one possible barrier to entry into the market for peanut butter. 4. If you could collect one additional piece of information before deciding on a strategy for Jif, what would it be?

TMP-0194.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0194.navLabel: Module 1.3 PESTEL Factors and the Business Environment
TMP-0194.text: MODULE 1.3 PESTEL Factors and the Business Environment LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 1.3.A Describe the factors considered in PESTEL analysis 1.3.B Explain the effect of PESTEL factors on business viability and career opportunities 1.3.C Apply PESTEL analysis to evaluate a business’s opportunities and risks

TMP-0195.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0195.navLabel: Module 1.3 PESTEL Factors and the Business Environment
TMP-0195.text: Christopher Polk/Getty Images Extended description for Coke The words, SHARE A Coke , appear on the wall behind them.

TMP-0196.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0196.navLabel: Module 1.3 PESTEL Factors and the Business Environment
TMP-0196.text: In the Share a Coke campaign, the logos on Coke bottles were replaced with popular names from around the world.

TMP-0197.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0197.navLabel: Module 1.3 PESTEL Factors and the Business Environment
TMP-0197.text: PESTEL: Six Factors That Shape Markets LG What are the six PESTEL factors, and how do they shape markets? It’s wise for a business to be aware of its situation. The same is true for individuals. Think about your first day at a new school. You probably entered the campus wide-eyed, taking in the factors that would shape your future there. It’s likely you thought about who your friends and favorite teachers would be. Perhaps you worried a bit about rivals. You might have gone to an assembly to meet the school’s leaders and learn some of their rules. Maybe you thought about the Wi-Fi capabilities on campus and what was available for lunch. Businesses use similar assessments as they consider strategies and new locations.

TMP-0198.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0198.navLabel: Module 1.3 PESTEL Factors and the Business Environment
TMP-0198.text: PESTEL analysis is a tool for assessing the business environment based on factors that are political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal (see Figure 1.3-1 ). A close look at these factors improves a business’s awareness of the external influences, risks, costs, and challenges it faces. For each factor, it is important to look not only at the current situation, but also at how the situation is changing and what lies ahead. Let’s apply a PESTEL analysis to soft-drink giant Coca-Cola. PESTEL analysis A tool for assessing the business environment based on political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal factors.

TMP-0199.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0199.navLabel: Module 1.3 PESTEL Factors and the Business Environment
TMP-0199.text: P Political E Economic S Social T Technological E Environmental L Legal Copyright © BFW Publishers Extended description for Figure 1.3-1 PESTEL Analysis The letters in PESTEL read as follows: • P: Political, with an illustration of the U.S. Capitol Building. • E: Economic, with a dollar sign. • S: Social, with an illustration of three people. • T: Technological, with an illustration of a microchip. • E: Environmental, with an illustration of a tree. • L: Legal, with an illustration of a balance scale. FIGURE 1.3-1 PESTEL Analysis Careful consideration of these factors helps a business understand its external

TMP-0200.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0200.text: influences, risk factors, costs, and challenges. Political Factors Political factors include government policies and political stability. Some governments promote business activity with subsidies , which provide financial assistance in the form of cash payments, tax breaks, low-interest loans, or other financial benefits. In the United States, subsidy programs assist farms that grow crops such as corn. Those subsidies entice farmers to grow more corn and lower the cost of the corn syrup that sweetens Coca-Cola. While some business activities are encouraged, others are discouraged. Many governments limit unwanted activities—such as the use of toxic chemicals—with bans, international trade restrictions, taxes, or regulations. subsidy Financial assistance—such as cash payments, tax breaks, or low-interest loans—that a government provides to promote business activity. Mandates are authoritative orders to perform an action. Common government mandates require food manufacturers to provide nutrition labels that disclose information about products and their ingredients, such as the amount of sugar (in the

TMP-0201.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0201.text: form of corn syrup) in Coke. Coca-Cola must also comply with policies on taxation, international trade, and health and safety set by the governments in every country in which it operates. The company must also be prepared for changes in those policies that may impact its operations. mandate An order from a government to perform an action, such as providing nutrition labels. Economic Factors Economic conditions beyond the control of individual businesses influence both consumer demand and operating costs. Rising prices for ingredients and supplies cut into profits. Higher interest rates make it more expensive for businesses to borrow money. And an economic crisis exacts a heavy toll on businesses throughout the economy, because unemployment, inflation, lower levels of household income, and economic instability reduce consumer spending. Nonessential items like Coke can be hit especially hard. When times are tough, a company like Coca-Cola can improve its public image by working to position itself as a community partner, providing essentials like bottled water and vaccines. 1 When the economy is strong, a business can consider

TMP-0202.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0202.text: expanding to offer products that appeal to customers with growing paychecks, such as the Coca-Cola Company’s acquisition of European coffee chain Costa Coffee. Social Factors Cultural norms, lifestyle trends, and demographics—the measurable characteristics of consumers such as age and income—all affect consumer demand for goods and services. With sales in almost every country in the world, Coca-Cola must cater to a diverse set of customs, tastes, and preferences. For instance, Coca-Cola created 30 flavors of soft drinks, including green tea and yuzu, to appeal to its customers in Japan. In the United States, Coca-Cola catered to growing interests in a healthy lifestyle by putting less sugar in some drinks and offering new products such as Simply Pop, with natural flavoring and real fruit juice.

TMP-0203.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0203.text: Christine Brune ©Macmillan Learning Extended description for Simply Pop Beverage Can The text on the can reads as follows: Naturally flavored with other natural flavors; With Real Fruit Juice; Flavor That Pops, Juice squeezed then concentrated.

TMP-0204.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0204.text: As society becomes increasingly health conscious, beverage makers satisfy customers’ interests by creating products with less sweetener and more juice. Technological Factors Technological factors include the rate of technological innovation as well as access to technology, cybersecurity, automation, artificial intelligence, and research facilities. Coca-Cola uses the latest technologies available to boost production and expedite delivery. The company also uses social media technology to connect with consumers. Marketing Director Lucie Austin came up with the Share a Coke campaign. Consumers in more than 80 countries were encouraged to share photos of Coke bottles bearing their names on social media through the #ShareaCoke hashtag. The result? More than

TMP-0205.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0205.text: 500,000 people shared their photos, and Coca-Cola gained 25 million new Facebook followers in a single year. Environmental Factors Environmental factors such as geography, climate, natural disasters, waste management practices, and availability of both renewable and nonrenewable resources can affect business activities. For instance, a beverage manufacturer like Coca-Cola needs large supplies of clean water, a resource that is increasingly threatened in some areas. Coca-Cola must also ensure that its own water processing operations are environmentally responsible, especially when operating in the many countries suffering from severe water shortages. Consumer perspectives on environmental problems also influence business decisions. For example, encouraged by consumer interests in environmental sustainability, Coca-Cola is increasing the use of recycled material in its packaging and promotes recycling programs for its bottles and cans.

TMP-0206.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0206.text: Legal Factors Laws that govern employment, consumer protection, environmental protection, health and safety, intellectual property, and market power (known as antitrust laws) are among those that affect businesses directly. As a global company, Coca-Cola must learn and adhere to the laws of the many countries and states where it operates. For example, after the state of California mandated cancer warning labels on products containing significant levels of a chemical called 4-methylimidazole, both Coke and Pepsi modified the caramel coloring in their drinks to avoid the need for those labels. With PESTEL analysis, companies can study their business environment, look ahead, analyze risk factors that might impact operations, develop strategies to address problems, and discover new opportunities. Findings from PESTEL analysis can also feed into the frameworks for management decisions that we’ll discuss in Module 4.4.

TMP-0207.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0207.text: PESTEL Analysis, Business Viability, and Career Prospects LG How do PESTEL factors affect business opportunities and career opportunities in a market? Business Viability PESTEL analysis can reveal opportunities and threats that inform strategies for any business. In some cases, the analysis shows whether a specific type of business is viable , meaning that it has the ability to succeed in that situation. viable Able to succeed in a specific market or situation.

TMP-0208.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0208.text: Political Factors Political policies can either incentivize or limit business activities. Government-issued subsidies and mandates may increase business viability, while bans and high taxes on businesses generally reduce it. The relatively low 5.5% corporate tax rate in Barbados, for example, contributes to the viability of business operations there and attracts many multinational corporations. The 37.5% corporate tax rate in Puerto Rico, on the other hand, has the opposite effect. The overall political climate in a country can also be too hostile or volatile to allow a foreign company to operate. That is the case in North Korea, for example, which hosts no U.S. companies. Economic Factors Economic factors affect business viability because the flow of sales revenue from customers is the lifeblood of a successful firm. Most businesses rely on a stable economy with consistent spending by individuals, businesses, and government. Monthly expenditures on rent, staff, utilities, and insurance make it difficult for a business to withstand lengthy periods with limited sales. Soon after consumer spending fell during the Great Recession of 2007–2009, more than 170,000 small U.S. businesses

TMP-0209.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0209.text: became unviable and closed. The threat of similar spending dips in weak economies keeps many businesses out.

TMP-0210.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0210.text: Oleh_Slobodeniuk/Getty Images Sellers of luxuries, such as vacations, are more vulnerable to a weak economy than sellers of essentials, like healthcare.

TMP-0211.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0211.text: There are exceptions to the need for a strong economy. Sellers of essential goods and services, such as groceries and healthcare, are less affected by an unstable economy than sellers of optional luxuries, such as fancy clothing and vacations. Sellers of low-cost items such as fast food and used clothing often see increased sales when consumers face economic hardships. The same is true for repair services that substitute for new purchases, such as the services of car mechanics. And lenders such as banks receive more requests for loans when people are experiencing financial hardships. Social Factors Social factors affect business viability because they influence the needs and wants of consumers in a market. Cultural norms, trends, demographics, and rates of population growth all drive preferences for goods and services. For example, a PESTEL analysis of a proposed hamburger restaurant in Nepal would raise some red flags. The country’s 24 million Hindu citizens generally avoid eating beef because cows are sacred in Hinduism. Beyond the social factor, there is a legal factor: Nepal bans the slaughter of cows, which would necessitate an outside source of hamburger meat. Given that assessment, a vegetarian restaurant might be more viable.

TMP-0212.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0212.text: Technological Factors Technological factors are especially important to the viability of e-commerce businesses that rely on the internet for their sales transactions. Although internet access reaches far and wide, some areas of most countries still have relatively slow internet service. There are also areas with few technicians who can repair advanced electronic devices. Businesses whose production, distribution, or communications rely on technology may find some locations unviable. For example, Amazon Web Services found some rural areas in the United States and Europe unviable for new data centers, because they did not meet Amazon’s extraordinary needs for power supplies and broadband internet services. Environmental Factors Environmental factors such as climate and resource availability help determine the viability of many businesses. Agricultural products, such as coffee and the cacao used to make chocolate, require tropical climates unavailable in most of the United States. Frequent natural disasters make some locations less viable for certain businesses. For example, luxury hotel chains prefer Caribbean islands such as Aruba that have relatively

TMP-0213.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0213.text: few hurricanes. And given the choice, developers of high-rise buildings may prefer Houston over Los Angeles due to the lower risk of earthquakes. Consumer attitudes toward environmental issues also affect business viability. Where a significant number of consumers are focused on environmental problems, they may be willing to pay extra for organic produce, recycled paper, or fuel-efficient cars. Where there is little appetite for products or production methods that pollute less and cost more, businesses with an environmental mission may be unviable. Legal Factors Legal factors are critical to business viability because they prohibit some businesses and make others costly to operate. For example, alcohol sales are illegal in most parts of Saudi Arabia, making a liquor store unviable. And if you are thinking of opening a restaurant in the United States, your PESTEL analysis may reveal the legal requirement for an expensive ventilation system to remove cooking fumes.

TMP-0214.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0214.text: Career Opportunities The PESTEL factors that make a location viable or unviable for businesses help determine local career opportunities. In a fast-growing economy with needs for new stores, offices, and homes, the viability of construction and real estate firms creates many jobs in those industries. In locations like Seattle, Washington, where PESTEL factors are inviting to technology firms such as Microsoft and Amazon, there are many opportunities for careers in software engineering, e-commerce, and data science. And rural areas with laws, economies, environments, and communities that support agriculture are the place to find farming jobs. Where the PESTEL factors are lacking for a given industry, jobs in that industry are hard to come by. Why do people who love wilderness areas often live in cities? Because the forests, prairies, mountains, and wetlands so cherished for an excursion don’t provide the PESTEL factors to support many types of businesses. If you want to work in tourism, you might find a job near the wilderness. If a career in banking is your dream, the job prospects will be better where economic, technological, and other PESTEL factors are inviting for financial institutions.

TMP-0215.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0215.text: Alexander Spatari/Getty Images Why is New York City the largest city in the United States? In part because its tax laws, massive economy, skilled workforce, and access to technology attract many industries that create many jobs. Workers seeking careers in financial services, fashion, media, entertainment, retail, and law, for example, know that New York offers many opportunities.

TMP-0216.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0216.text: Changes in PESTEL Factors Things change. PESTEL factors are affected by changing government leadership, economic ups and downs, social trends, technological advances, environmental awareness, and new legislation. With altered PESTEL factors come changes in business viability and career opportunities. For example, Detroit, Michigan, was once the booming heart of the U.S. automobile industry. Over the last half-century, Detroit faced economic downturns and increased competition from international rivals. U.S. auto production declined, and automakers experienced significant layoffs. Detroit’s population fell by more than half, its economy weakened, and in 2013, the city filed for bankruptcy due to massive debt. These changes made the city unviable for many businesses. However, falling real estate prices, relatively low wages, advanced technology, and new tax incentives have made Detroit viable for many new companies. Technology-related companies such as Airspace Link and a branch of Google are helping to revive Detroit’s economy.

TMP-0217.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0217.text: ERIC PIERMONT/Getty Images PESTEL analysis helps companies decide where to build their factories.

TMP-0218.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0218.text: Using PESTEL Analysis LG How do businesses apply the PESTEL framework to evaluate a potential new market? Decisions about new or expanding businesses always involve risks and are seldom easy. By applying the PESTEL framework, a business can analyze its opportunities, gauge the severity of threats, and hope to avoid the pitfalls of poor planning. A business will be more inclined to enter a market where PESTEL factors are favorable and in keeping with its business model. In making this decision, the company evaluates how these external factors interact with its needed resources, production capabilities, and target customers. Let’s consider how PESTEL analysis might play out for a yogurt company named Lactual that is considering opening a new factory in a city on the opposite side of the country. The CEO conducts a PESTEL analysis and determines the following:

TMP-0219.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0219.text: The city government in the proposed location has offered to charge no property taxes for the factory’s first year of operations. The city has also promised to improve the roads leading to the proposed factory site so that delivery trucks and employees can easily get in and out. The city’s economy is recovering from a period of high unemployment caused by the recent closure of a clothing manufacturer that employed 1,300 workers. The average incomes of local workers are now lower than normal, although Lactual’s customers are spread across a much broader area that has not been affected by the city’s hard times. The CEO notes that the former clothing factory’s workers might serve well at Lactual, especially in roles that do not require yogurt expertise, such as maintenance, delivery, and sales. The CEO considers social factors related to the regional market for yogurt that the new factory would serve. This part of the country is home to many health-conscious consumers who live active lifestyles and care about nutrition. With its high calcium and probiotics, yogurt is experiencing growing popularity, with 2% annual growth in sales. Those trends have persisted for the past five years. The automation and robotics that Lactual would use in the factory can be shipped to the new location. However, there are no technical support experts in the area

TMP-0220.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0220.text: that service those types of technology. Lactual would need to hire two experts from elsewhere and employ them at the factory. The new city does have sufficient internet availability to serve Lactual’s needs. The area surrounding the city has an environment well suited for the dairy cattle needed to supply milk for yogurt production. Water needs are a possible threat, however. The yogurt factory would require a significant amount of water for production and cleaning purposes. There is currently enough water in the local river to support Lactual’s needs. However, increasing agricultural uses upstream have gradually decreased the river’s water volume. It is projected that within ten years, it may become necessary to truck in water from 100 miles away. In the state where the city is located, the laws about product labeling, health claims about the product, and patent protection are similar to those in other places where Lactual makes yogurt. Laws governing food safety and worker safety are also acceptable. Unlike other locations, however, the state being considered requires a special ultra-high-temperature milk pasteurization process that makes milk safer and longer lasting. That process would increase the cost of making yogurt by 3%.

TMP-0221.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0221.text: While a real PESTEL analysis would involve a large volume of numbers and comparisons, this simplified example illustrates how these types of key findings would help a business like Lactual make better choices. Finally, it is important to recognize that the best location for a business today may not be the best location for the business in the future. PESTEL factors may change in ways that impact production, distribution, and access to resources, as well as customers’ wants, needs, and budgets. Such changes can affect a business’s viability, even in a market where that business once flourished. McDonald’s, Nike, Oracle, Tesla, and Boeing are among the companies that have moved their corporate headquarters in pursuit of a more favorable business environment. Businesses can’t predict the future, but they can do their best, when examining PESTEL factors, to consider what changes are likely and how these changes could impact them.

TMP-0222.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0222.text: Module 1.3 Review Learning Goals LG What are the six PESTEL factors, and how do they shape markets? PESTEL analysis is a tool for assessing the business environment based on factors that are political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal. With PESTEL analysis, companies can study their business environment, consider risk factors, develop strategies to address problems, and discover new opportunities. Political factors include government policies and political stability. Some governments promote business activity with subsidies, which provide financial assistance in the form of cash payments, tax breaks, low-interest loans, or other financial benefits. Mandates are authoritative orders to perform an action, such as

TMP-0223.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0223.text: government mandates that require food manufacturers to disclose product information on nutrition labels. Economic factors include the strength of the economy, changing economy-wide price levels, interest rates, and economic crises, which can lead to unemployment, inflation, lower levels of household income, and economic instability. Social factors include societal behaviors and trends that might affect consumer demand for goods and services. Technological factors include the rate of technological innovation as well as access to technology, cybersecurity, automation, artificial intelligence, and research facilities. Environmental factors such as geography, climate, natural disasters, waste management practices, and resource availability can affect business activities. Legal factors include laws that govern employment, consumer protection, environmental protection, health and safety, intellectual property, and market power. LG How do PESTEL factors affect business opportunities and career opportunities in a market?

TMP-0224.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0224.text: PESTEL analysis can reveal opportunities and threats that inform strategies for any business. In some cases, the analysis shows whether a specific type of business is viable , meaning that it has the ability to succeed in that situation. The PESTEL factors that make a location viable or unviable for businesses help determine local career opportunities in those types of businesses. PESTEL factors are affected by changing government leadership, economic ups and downs, social trends, technological advances, environmental awareness, and new legislation. With altered PESTEL factors come changes in business viability and career opportunities. LG How do businesses apply the PESTEL framework to evaluate a potential new market? When evaluating a market, businesses assess how each of the six PESTEL factors influences the business’s prospects for success. They evaluate whether these factors

TMP-0225.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0225.text: align with their resource requirements, production processes, and target customers’ preferences. Companies are more likely to enter markets where PESTEL factors support their specific needs. The framework also helps businesses anticipate how changes in these factors might affect long-term viability by impacting customer behavior, production systems, and resource accessibility. Practice Your AP ® Skills Preparing for the AP ® Exam MULTIPLE-CHOICE QUESTIONS 1. PESTEL analysis is used to evaluate a. a firm’s internal strengths and weaknesses. b. external factors that could impact a firm’s decision making. c. a firm’s financial performance over time.

TMP-0226.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0226.text: d. a firm’s share of sales in the market. 2. The Es in PESTEL stand for a. economic and environmental. b. entry and exit. c. earnings and entrepreneur. d. equity and evaluation. 3. How does PESTEL analysis relate to the interests of workers? a. It is the way workers determine the value of their compensation package. b. It helps to determine which businesses create jobs in an area. c. It is used to analyze policies to assist workers who lose their jobs. d. It is a business tool that does not affect workers. 4. PESTEL analysis typically informs decisions about a. social trends. b. environmental policy.

TMP-0227.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0227.text: c. legal rules. d. business viability. CASE STUDY Allbirds Bloomberg/Getty Images Allbirds used new technology to produce shoes that addressed both consumer trends and environmental factors.

TMP-0228.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0228.text: Allbirds was established in 2016 after its founder, Tim Brown, looked at the footwear market and saw unmet interest in shoes made from natural fibers. As a former professional soccer player, Tim had been sponsored by major sneaker brands, so he was keenly aware of how pervasive synthetic materials were in the footwear market. As a native New Zealander, Tim was also familiar with the versatility of merino wool. Tim teamed up with Joey Zwillinger, a biotechnology engineer in the United States, and the two began working on shoes they called Wool Runners made with New Zealand merino wool. As they sourced their materials, Tim and Joey were aware of growing consumer interest in environmental sustainability. This prompted the use of renewable materials beyond wool, such as castor bean oil in their soles and recycled cardboard in their packaging. Their shoelaces were made from recycled plastic bottles. The shoes were an instant success, and Allbirds quickly became one of the fastest-growing shoe companies in the world. Just two years after launch, the company sold its millionth pair of shoes. Allbirds continues to innovate with new technologies to satisfy its environmentally minded target customers. Its shoes are made from recycled

TMP-0229.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0229.text: synthetics and a growing variety of renewable materials, including eucalyptus tree fiber and plant-based leather. The company even invented a shoe-sole material, Sweet-Foam, made from sustainably grown sugarcane. As Allbirds expanded overseas and encountered cultural differences in customer expectations and behaviors, the company made some changes. For example, in order to establish itself in China—where customers are more likely to shop on large e-commerce sites than on individual brand websites—Allbirds had to relinquish control over its distribution model and partner with an online marketplace called Alibaba Tmall. Allbirds also quickly learned that its eco-friendly design was not a major selling point in the Chinese market. When Allbirds instead advertised that the wool parts of its shoes were produced in the same factories as luxury Italian brands, sales in China increased. Though Allbirds modified its brand messaging for China, it retained an internal focus on building innovative shoes with a minimal environmental impact. In 2025, Allbirds introduced the first shoe made without adding to carbon emissions, the Mo.oNSHOT Zero. The company also released information on how to make zero-carbon shoes for anyone in the industry to use.

TMP-0230.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0230.text: Few companies can escape legal factors, and Allbirds has had its share of days in court. In 2022, the company faced a lawsuit alleging that Allbirds had made misleading claims about the environmental impact of its shoes and the welfare of the sheep that provided its wool. In the end, the court dismissed the lawsuit, saying that the company’s measures of environmental impact were acceptable. Nonetheless, this and multiple subsequent lawsuits have threatened the company’s viability. Apply Your AP ® Skills 1. Suppose that Allbirds would like to expand its production and sales into a new country. One of the countries being considered is facing economic hardships including layoffs. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of choosing that country. 2. How is a key source of Allbirds’ competitive advantage in the United States threatened by the legal issues confronting the company? 3. Explain why technological factors are important to Allbirds. 4. What type of factor required special focus as Allbirds expanded into other countries? Explain your answer.
