TMP-0232.text: M O D U L E 1 . 4 How Do Business Ideas Originate? LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 1.4.A Explain how businesses come up with ideas for new products 1.4.B Discuss the inherent risks and rewards of developing a new product 1.4.C Describe a process for generating, testing, and refining new ideas

headings.text: M O D U L E 1 . 4

TMP-0233.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0233.navLabel: Module 1.4 How Do Business Ideas Originate?
TMP-0233.text: undefined undefined/Getty Images New products come from fresh ideas. In this module, you will learn where product ideas come from and how to test them. Then, in the case study, you will weigh in on a new product idea that may or may not be garbage.

TMP-0234.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0234.text: From Ideas Come Opportunities LG Where do business ideas come from? All businesses can benefit from new ideas, but let’s start at the beginning with the launch of a business. The ingredients in the recipe for a successful new business include, among other things, an idea, an opportunity, and an entrepreneur. An entrepreneur is the one who creates a business by initiating the activities, organizing the inputs, and assuming many of the risks of running the business. Some entrepreneurs are brimming with ideas for marketable products. Media personality Oprah Winfrey and business magnates Richard Branson and Chaithanya Sama are among those described as serial entrepreneurs because they launch one new business venture after another. Other entrepreneurs land on ideas after considerable searching or inspiration. Every entrepreneur must sift through their options carefully to avoid investing in an idea that goes nowhere.

TMP-0235.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0235.text: entrepreneur Someone who creates a business by initiating the activities, organizing the inputs, and assuming many of the risks of running the business. To an entrepreneur, an opportunity is a set of circumstances favorable for the creation of value by offering a good or service that is new or different from existing offerings. Ideas are the starting point for business opportunities. An idea for a new product can lead to a business opportunity if it is something people would find desirable and be willing to pay for. An otherwise good product idea that potential customers aren’t eager to buy is likely to be a bad idea for a business. For example, McDonald’s had a good idea to keep the ingredients in the McDLT sandwich at their intended temperature until mealtime. In a Styrofoam box with two sections, a “cool” side held lettuce, tomato, cheese, and half the bun and a “hot” side held a burger and the other half of the bun. Consumer reaction to the overhyped, overpackaged McDLT ranged from cool to lukewarm, and McDonald’s scrapped the sandwich. opportunity A set of circumstances favorable for the creation of value by offering a new or modified good or service.

TMP-0236.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0236.text: You’ve probably had some pretty good and pretty bad ideas of your own. The vital importance of ideas—and the risk of bad ones—makes them a focus for successful businesses. This module explores the development, improvement, testing, and refinement of ideas. Pathways to Product Ideas In this section, we discuss four general pathways entrepreneurs and existing businesses can take to identify ideas for business opportunities. These pathways are summarized in Figure 1.4-1 .

TMP-0237.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0237.text: The Find Pathway Experience or observe an unmet need and create a solution. WWW The Search Pathway Actively seek ideas using market and technical research. The Effectuate Pathway Apply existing skills, knowledge, and resources to solve a problem. The Ideate Pathway Generate new product ideas by brainstorming and experimenting. Copyright © BFW Publishers

TMP-0238.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0238.text: Extended description for Figure 1.4-1 Four Pathways to Product Ideas The first icon on the roadway shows a woman looking through binoculars. Text reads: The Find Pathway . Experience or observe an unmet need and create a solution. The second icon on the roadway shows a magnifying glass highlighting a web search bar. Text reads: The Search Pathway . Text reads: The Ideate Pathway . Generate new product ideas by brainstorming and experimenting. FIGURE 1.4-1 Four Pathways to Product Ideas

TMP-0239.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0239.text: AP ® Exam Tip For the AP ® exam, you should be able to explain how entrepreneurs and existing businesses generate new product ideas. The methods used along each pathway should be helpful for both projects and exam questions. The pathways are named for convenience and those names are not likely to be tested. The Find Pathway The find pathway is a straightforward and common source of product ideas that result from chance encounters with unmet needs. Following this pathway, an individual observes or experiences an unmet need and creates a solution that becomes a commercial product. For example, Nick Woodman was a surfer who was frustrated by the inability to capture good images of surfing action. He figured out a way for surfers to strap a camera onto their bodies. That idea led to the development of GoPro cameras, which are now worn by adventurers of all types around the world. As another example, Kavita Shukla experienced food waste in her community due to the spoilage of fresh produce. Her grandmother had taught her a home remedy for food-borne illnesses: a tea made with spices that were natural inhibitors of bacteria and

TMP-0240.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0240.text: fungi. That lesson inspired Shukla to invent FreshPaper, an organic paper product infused with spoilage inhibitors that is stored with produce to keep it fresh longer. She patented her invention while still in high school. Today, FreshPaper is sold in over 100 countries. The Search Pathway Entrepreneurs and existing businesses take the search pathway when they are unsure about what type of product to sell and set out to look for opportunities. A deliberate search process can uncover problems or solutions that were not readily apparent. Market research is a search for unmet needs that typically involves observing, surveying, or interviewing consumers, analyzing trends, or studying competitors. For example, a market research team from Procter & Gamble visited consumers’ homes and observed people’s frustrations when cleaning kitchen floors with a traditional wet mop. That search for needs resulted in the invention of an alternative cleaning tool, the Swiffer, which cleans floors with disposable cloths wrapped around a rectangular mop head at the end of a pole. Millions of consumers adopted that more convenient way to clean.

TMP-0241.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0241.text: market research The process of observing, surveying, or interviewing consumers, analyzing trends, or studying competitors in order to identify unmet needs. To develop new ideas and capabilities, some businesses use technical research , which is the application of scientific and engineering principles to investigate new products or the improvement of existing ones. Technical research by companies including Bell Labs, IBM, Hewlett-Packard, and Corning led to the touch-screen capabilities we now have in phones and other popular smart devices. technical research The application of scientific and engineering principles to investigate new products or the improvement of existing ones. The Effectuate Pathway To effectuate is to produce a result or make something happen. Entrepreneurs take the effectuation path by applying their skills, knowledge, and resources to develop ideas and create opportunities. Scientists and inventors take this path by applying their skills to experimentation that leads to discoveries with commercial applications. Effectuation often involves partnering with people who have complementary abilities, because few

TMP-0242.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0242.text: people possess all the skills required to make a product successful. Pulling together the people who have what it takes to make the sale of a useful product possible is what the creation of business opportunities is all about. To develop your own opportunities for projects in this class or beyond, think about what you would be good at. Focus on what you know, who you know, and who you are. Your role as an entrepreneur is to take action by offering a product that is carefully chosen to match your abilities. After developing a product, pay careful attention to the way consumers respond to it. Successful entrepreneurs typically use several rounds, or iterations , of evaluation and feedback to further refine and improve their product. Jim Poss is an entrepreneur who took the effectuation path. Poss founded Bigbelly, a company that designs solar-powered trash compactors. When he was starting out, Poss considered what he already knew. His background in engineering, geology, and environmental science pointed him in the direction of machinery that could reduce waste and save energy. Next, he identified people he knew who could help him develop his idea. Two of his friends were engineering students who could help with the machinery, and another had a background in renewable energy, which gave him insights about solar energy. Once they had an early prototype of the trash compactor,

TMP-0243.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0243.text: Poss took action and sold the concept to a ski resort in Vail, Colorado, where collecting trash from remote ski lodges was both expensive and time consuming. That implementation of the product allowed another iteration of evaluation and feedback that helped the team improve their invention by adding more storage, wheels, and wireless sensors to alert the operator when the bin was full. As the product improved, so did sales. Today, Bigbelly serves more than 2,500 customers in over 60 countries.

TMP-0244.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0244.text: joel zatz/Alamy Stock Photo Bigbelly solar trash compactors came from an entrepreneur who followed the effectuation pathway by leveraging his skills in

TMP-0245.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0245.text: engineering and environmental science. The Ideate Pathway Sometimes product ideas come not from an unmet need, a search, or an application of skills, but from the minds of people hunting for an idea. Ideation is the creative process of generating new ideas. This can occur when a gap in the market is evident but the solution is elusive, or after research reveals unmet needs. Consider the high cost of traditional hotels that used to leave lower-income travelers overextended or camping. What has ideation by entrepreneurs done to address this clear gap in the hospitality market? Many Japanese cities now have capsule hotels that provide guests with an inexpensive personal space just large enough for a mattress. Lock Ridge Park in Lancaster, Kentucky, offers lodging in concrete tube “O-tels,” covered wagons, and shipping containers converted into comfortable housing. And Brian Chesky, Joe Gebbia, and Nathan Blecharczyk founded Airbnb to connect homeowners who had extra space with travelers seeking affordable accommodations, creating a new marketplace for short-term rentals.

TMP-0246.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0246.text: In some cases, ideation serves needs we were not even aware of. Consumers didn’t know they needed a smartphone until after smartphones were created. Today, it’s hard for many of us to imagine living without one. That newly discovered need has become a huge business opportunity. Before exploring the evaluation and improvement of ideas like these, we will consider the importance of moving forward with the right ideas.

TMP-0247.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0247.text: Risks and Rewards of Product Development LG What are the risks and rewards of bringing a new product to market? A successful product can provide large and varied rewards to its developers. A long stream of profits is one of those relished rewards. It is enticing to imagine the tremendous wealth created by the iPad, the Rubik’s Cube, the Toyota Corolla, and the cholesterol-lowering drug Lipitor. Of course, money is not the only valued reward. Many people have a true passion for their work and receive great satisfaction from solving problems in their field. For example, actress Sofia Vergara cofounded a talent management firm called Latin World Entertainment because she had a passion for helping Hispanic people find agents. And some entrepreneurs seek fame, an impressive resume, a positive impact on the environment, or the joy of helping others.

TMP-0248.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0248.text: AFF/Alamy Stock Photo The rewards of developing new goods and services are not just financial. Sofia Vergara cofounded a talent management company because she was passionate about helping Hispanic people find representation in the entertainment world.

TMP-0249.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0249.text: It is fortunate that many incentives for entrepreneurship exist, because without them, the risks of failure and the expense of product development might prevent a healthy supply of needed innovations. To bring a new product to market, a business must devote money, materials, and time to product design and manufacturing. In many cases, the costs of research and development (R&D) are substantial. For example, pharmaceutical companies sometimes spend over $4 billion dollars to develop and test a new drug. Businesses have spent decades and tens of billions of dollars working on self-driving cars, with more expenditures to come. The challenges of obtaining financing, setting up and staffing a manufacturing facility, sourcing materials, and complying with safety standards also take no small amount of time or money. Beyond that, the successful introduction of a new product or business generally requires an ambitious marketing campaign. Even a small business—a restaurant, a bookstore, a dog grooming salon—requires a sizable financial investment and carries the risk of loss. Many new businesses take two to three years to become profitable. There is no guarantee that the commitments of time and resources will be rewarded with enough revenue to provide profit.

TMP-0250.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0250.text: Bloomberg/Getty Images Extended description for Risky Business The windows of the store feature popular cartoon characters, party balloons, and a young boy blowing out the candles on a birthday cake.

TMP-0251.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0251.text: It is risky to open a business. After making sizable expenditures on facilities, inventory, staff, and legal requirements, almost half of all private businesses do not survive their first five years. Many new businesses run into trouble. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports that almost half of all private businesses do not survive their first five years. Failure with any of the challenges of starting a business can jeopardize the success of an otherwise good product. For example, Elio Motors developed a three-wheeled vehicle that was efficient, attractive, and desired by large numbers of consumers. However, an inability to obtain sufficient financing for the manufacturing stage led to delays of the product launch for a decade and counting. This course will address many of the critical steps of entrepreneurship to help you avoid possible pitfalls. The first step to doing things right is to carefully choose and improve your product idea.

TMP-0252.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0252.text: The Design-Thinking Process LG How are new ideas tested and refined? In the quest for business opportunities, successful approaches combine close examination of problems with ideation and the evaluation of ideas. Among the popular methods is design thinking , a problem-solving process with five stages: (1) empathize with the target audience by learning about potential customers; (2) define the problem; (3) ideate about solutions; (4) create a prototype to represent the product idea; and (5) test the product. Table 1.4-1 explains each of these stages. design thinking A problem-solving process with five stages: (1) empathize with the target audience by learning about potential customers; (2) define the problem; (3) ideate about solutions; (4) create a prototype to represent the product idea; and (5) test the product.

TMP-0253.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0253.text: Table 1.4-1 The Five Stages of Design Thinking Empathize This is an information-gathering stage of surveying, interviewing, observing, and gathering insights to gain a deep understanding of the needs and wants of the target audience. Define The design team uses information collected in the empathize stage to clearly articulate the primary problem to be addressed. It is common to frame the problem with “How might we …” questions, such as “How might we help reduce food waste in high school cafeterias?” or “How might we provide better entertainment on school buses?” Ideate Brainstorming generates a broad range of possible solutions. Then the ideas are narrowed and refined to land on a starting point for product development. Prototype A simple representation of the product idea provides opportunities for experimentation and refinement by the design team. Test At this stage, early versions of the product are shared with potential users for validation and feedback. Initial rounds of testing might be conducted with simple prototypes, while later rounds use functional versions called minimum viable products. The tests can reveal which elements of the idea are useful, popular, problematic, or in need of polishing. The design-thinking process allows a business to quickly develop prototypes and test ideas. Careful attention to consumer needs and feedback focuses the design process on products that truly create value. As shown in Figure 1.4-2 , the process is nonlinear, which means that it is not a matter of completing the five stages in order and then

TMP-0254.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0254.text: moving on. Instead, after prototyping or testing, the team may return to one of the earlier stages to better define the problem, come up with more ideas, or change the prototype. After the test stage is completed with high favorability, the design team can move on to a broader introduction to consumers. Let’s examine more closely how businesses test their products. Then we will apply this method to a real problem.

TMP-0255.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0255.text: Empathize Define Ideate Test Prototype Copyright © BFW Publishers

TMP-0256.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0256.text: Extended description for Figure 1.4-2 The Design-Thinking Process i The first icon shows two shaking hands. Accompanying text reads, Empathize. An arrow from Empathize points to an icon of a bullseye. Accompanying text reads, Define. An arrow from Define points to an icon of a head and a rotating circle. A light bulb appears inside the head with text that reads, Ideate. The arrow from the head points to an icon of a document with a design. Accompanying text reads, Prototype.

TMP-0257.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0257.text: The arrow from the document points to an icon of a magnifying glass with two gears with text that reads, Test. The arrow from the magnifying glass points back to the Ideate head with light bulb. FIGURE 1.4-2 The Design-Thinking Process Testing Ideas The advancement of a product idea implies an educated guess, or hypothesis, that the product would be deemed valuable by customers. The evaluation and refinement of an idea should involve the validation of that hypothesis by testing the response of potential customers to the product. Some food products and services can easily be tested by offering samples or demonstrations. But for a manufactured good or a software product,

TMP-0258.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0258.text: testing is a challenge, because the final product will take a lot of time and money to develop. Prototypes and minimum viable products are used to solve that problem. A prototype is a preliminary depiction or model of a product that is created to explore and validate ideas. Prototypes are used initially for internal review and eventually, in some cases, for sampling by customers. A prototype might be a sketch or diagram. digital representation. video portrayal. model made with a 3D printer or out of cardboard or clay. miniature version. working model. prototype A preliminary depiction or model of a product that is created to explore and validate ideas.

TMP-0259.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0259.text: mangpor2004/Shutterstock The prototype for a new app can be a set of drawings that show the elements of each screen. For a webpage or app, the prototype can be a drawing or digital representation called a wireframe that demonstrates the key elements of the idea. This visual framework is like the blueprint for a house—it is not functional, but it gives developers a good understanding of what the product will be like. A prototype is generally made quickly and at minimal expense. Developers can then reflect on the current iteration of their product before committing further to the idea or making changes.

TMP-0260.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0260.text: The resemblance of a prototype to the final product can be described in terms of its “fidelity.” A low-fidelity prototype is a rough, simple representation of the product, such as a sketch or wireframe. A high-fidelity prototype more closely resembles the final product, and might be a 3D printed model or an interactive version of an app. While prototypes simulate the product and help the team validate its design, it is also important for early adopters to test the product’s core functionality. A minimum viable product (MVP) is the simplest version of a product that serves its intended purpose and allows for customer feedback. An MVP includes only the core features of a product without the cosmetic extras that would take more time and expense to add in. With an MVP, a firm can get its product into the hands of customers early in the development process and learn about adjustments and additions that would help the product satisfy needs and solve problems. For example, video game developers like to use MVPs to get feedback from players on game mechanics and design choices. minimum viable product (MVP) The simplest version of a product that serves its intended purpose and allows for customer feedback.

TMP-0261.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0261.text: Applying the Design-Thinking Method Let’s apply each step of the design-thinking method to a small business: a food truck. Mobile food is nothing new. Coffee, hot dogs, ice cream, and burgers have long been sold from mobile trailers, cars, and trucks. Suppose that a group of entrepreneurs wants to launch a new food truck that satisfies the needs and wants of customers who are not well served by existing food trucks. Maybe the food is different. Maybe the locations served are different. Maybe the pricing or advertising is different. The design-thinking method can improve the odds of success as these entrepreneurs hit the road with a new food truck. Empathize In the first stage of design thinking, the team will empathize with customers by learning about their needs, wants, and problems. The entrepreneurs might go to the streets, festivals, concerts, and farmers markets where food trucks congregate and survey customers about what might be missing. Additional information could be collected with interviews, observations, and online questionnaires. Suppose the primary finding from this research is that customers are satisfied with the location and

TMP-0262.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0262.text: pricing of food trucks, but would really value a healthier alternative to the current offerings. Many people prefer quick options that are healthier than traditional fast food, and menus that cater to customers who avoid meat, dairy, gluten, sodium, nuts, or sugar. Define In the define stage, the team frames the problem with a “How might we …” sentence. Given the information collected in the empathize step, the team might ask: “How might we improve the food truck experience for people with dietary restrictions?” or “How might we create a truck with healthy food?” Suppose the team decides to define their question as, “How might we serve people who cannot eat at traditional food trucks?” Ideate In the ideate stage, the team can brainstorm a long list of potential solutions. Brainstorming is the technique of encouraging participants to think freely and propose ideas without fear of criticism. Creative thought in a judgment-free environment often results in a large pool of ideas from which great ideas emerge. Mediocre ideas can trigger better ideas, and participants can combine questionable ideas to build new

TMP-0263.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0263.text: thoughts. During the brainstorming process, every idea is captured, perhaps on sticky notes, a whiteboard, or a flip chart. Entrepreneurs may use AI tools such as ChatGPT to generate ideas based on consumer behavior, emerging trends, and gaps in the market. At this stage, all ideas are welcome and there is no criticism of ideas because not-great ideas often lead to great ideas. After a brainstorming session, the ideas are reviewed, narrowed down, and refined. Figure 1.4-3 shows possible ideas that could come out of the brainstorming session for this new food truck.

TMP-0264.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0264.text: Seasonal salads Healthy grain bowls Color-code menu for specific diets/ restrictions Vegetarian Indian food Go to health- related events BRAINSTORM Go near unhealthy restaurants Pop-ups at sporting events and races Target area dominated by fast food Target “food deserts” Full gluten free menu Copyright © BFW Publishers Extended description for FIGURE 1.4-3 Brainstorming Ideas on sticky notes surrounding the word BRAINSTORM on the board read as follows: Seasonal salads Healthy grain bowls

TMP-0265.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0265.text: Color-code menu for specific diets or restrictions Vegetarian Indian food Go to health-related events Go near unhealthy restaurants Pop-ups at sporting events and races Target area dominated by fast food Target “food deserts” Full gluten free menu FIGURE 1.4-3 Brainstorming In the ideate stage, the team can brainstorm many potential solutions and share them in a judgment-free environment to encourage creativity. brainstorming The technique of encouraging participants to think freely and propose ideas without fear of criticism. After many ideas have been advanced, the team can discuss the pros and cons of each possibility and gradually narrow down the solutions until a small number remain. Ideas can often be combined, especially when they pertain to differing aspects of the product, such as location, content, size, and appearance. If there is disagreement over the one

TMP-0266.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0266.text: best option to start with, the prototyping and testing stages can help to narrow the options further by providing additional input and opportunities for assessment. We will suppose the food truck team decides to start with the idea of serving gluten-free pasta with sauces that include dairy-free and meat-free options. They will color code the menu to indicate which menu items satisfy each interest, and they will experiment with each of the ideas for where to locate the truck. Prototype In the prototype stage, a representation of the solution is created to allow early evaluation by the team and, in the next stage, by customers. A model of several possible versions of the truck’s design could easily be constructed with cardboard to help reviewers choose between different possibilities. Samples of the food could be created and tried by the team members. If the prototypes show little potential, the team may want to go back to their list of ideas, or perhaps even brainstorm some more. Test The fifth stage of the design-thinking method is testing . After any appropriate revisions in the truck design and menu in response to internal reviews, the design and

TMP-0267.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0267.text: food samples could be rolled out to potential customers. The team could set up a booth at a festival or farmers market to test the popularity of their menu items. They could also bring two possible cardboard versions of the truck design and have the customers vote on one. Based on the sales and feedback received in these tests, the team can decide to return to any of the previous stages or go forward with the current solutions.

TMP-0268.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0268.text: JSMimages/Alamy Stock Photo The design-thinking method helps entrepreneurs develop, refine, and test ideas before going all-in. This increases the odds that the business’s offerings will match customers’ needs and wants. The design-thinking method helps entrepreneurs come up with ideas, refine them, and evaluate whether they would receive sufficient demand in the marketplace. The process of developing prototypes and MVPs can also reveal whether the team has the skills necessary to execute the ideas. If no one involved in the food truck can make a

TMP-0269.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0269.text: delicious gluten-free pasta dish, the team should think about who they can hire to make this idea successful, or whether they should go back to the ideation or brainstorming stages and seek a more feasible idea. Regardless of the method of ideation, separating out the better ideas is one of the more challenging and important tasks. Every one of us is capable of generating a broad range of ideas. The evaluation methods discussed in this module help an entrepreneur test the hypothesis that a product idea will succeed, and revise the idea if the hypothesis is rejected.

TMP-0270.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0270.text: Module 1.4 Review Learning Goals LG Where do business ideas come from? • Business ideas originate with an entrepreneur , who creates a business by initiating the activities, organizing the inputs, and assuming many of the risks of running the business. • Ideas are the starting point for business opportunities. An opportunity is a set of circumstances favorable for the creation of value by offering a new or modified good or service. • Entrepreneurs and existing businesses take four general pathways to identify ideas. On the find pathway, individuals identify product ideas by observing or experiencing unmet needs. Following the search pathway, an entrepreneur actively

TMP-0271.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0271.text: seeks ideas, using different kinds of research to identify needs. Using market research , an entrepreneur searches for unmet needs by observing, surveying, or interviewing consumers, analyzing trends, or studying competitors. Technical research is the application of scientific and engineering principles to investigate new products or the improvement of existing ones. Those following the effectuate pathway apply their existing skills and knowledge to solve a problem. Those taking the ideate pathway come up with ideas through brainstorming and experimenting. Ideation is the creative process of generating new ideas. LG What are the risks and rewards of bringing a new product to market? • Product development involves the prospect of profits, but losses are common, especially in the early years of a new business. • At risk are the large expenditures required to launch a new product or business. Entrepreneurs and existing businesses take risks with their time and money, incentivized by the possibility of profits and the satisfaction of solving problems and pursuing passions.

TMP-0272.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0272.text: LG How are new ideas tested and refined? • The design-thinking process has five steps: (1) empathize with the target audience by learning about their needs and wants; (2) define the problem; (3) ideate about solutions; (4) create a prototype to represent the product idea; and (5) test the product. • After a problem is identified, brainstorming can encourage participants to think freely about solutions and propose ideas without fear of criticism. Then comes prototyping and testing. A prototype is a preliminary depiction or model of a product that is created to explore and validate ideas. A minimum viable product (MVP) is the simplest version of a product that serves its intended purpose and allows for customer feedback. If the prototyping or testing stages reveal issues, the team returns to one of the earlier stages to better define the problem, come up with more ideas, or change the prototype.

They learned that trash cans often get in the way and never seem to be where they are needed. After discussing these problems, Garbagemania decided to tackle the question, “How might we help office workers improve the efficiency of trash can placement?” In a brainstorming session that welcomed all ideas no matter how crazy they sounded, the design team came up with ideas that ranged from hanging trash cans from the ceiling to integrating them into the office furniture. The design team eventually settled on the idea of a remote-controlled trash can. The can would have wheels on the bottom and a remote-control device for navigation. A “home” button would send the can to a corner of the room where it is out of the way. Other preprogrammed buttons would send the can to locations where the user might want to discard trash, such as next to a desk or conference

TMP-0278.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas

To provide a reasonable profit margin, the company is considering selling the trash cans to retail stores for $50 each and recommending a retail price of $85. Garbagemania can apply for a patent for the invention because it is new, useful, and nonobvious (patents are not granted for obvious modifications of existing products). The company is unsure about the marketability of its idea and would like to test the hypothesis that a remote-controlled trash can would be valued by consumers. TMP-0280.text: MODULE 1.5 Vision LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 1.5.A Explain how core values and core competencies guide business decisions and individual choices 1.5.B Evaluate vision and mission statements and discuss their purpose 1.5.C Describe the goals of businesses, nonprofit organizations, and social enterprises

TMP-0281.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0281.text: John’s Crazy Socks The mission of John’s Crazy Socks is to spread happiness. Other organizations seek to serve veterans, artists, stranded motorists, or injured animals.

TMP-0282.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0282.text: Core Values and Core Competencies LG What are core values and core competencies, and how do they shape decisions made by individuals and businesses? You can learn a lot about a company by examining its core mission and values. Consider John’s Crazy Socks, which sells socks with fun patterns and colors out of a small warehouse in Melville, New York. Cofounder John Cronin and his father, Mark, came up with the idea of John’s Crazy Socks while brainstorming ideas for a new business. They thought about creating a food truck business, but neither could cook. Then John, who has Down syndrome, suggested selling socks to commemorate World Down Syndrome Day, a day traditionally celebrated by wearing colorful, mismatched socks. The duo started designing and selling all types of crazy socks through their website.

TMP-0283.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0283.text: Their inspirational story is matched by an equally inspiring mission to spread happiness. That mission influences everything the company does. John, the company’s Chief Happiness Officer, adds to the joy of crazy socks by including a personalized thank-you note and some candy with each order. The company’s tireless focus on its mission led to strong sales from the beginning. Today, John’s Crazy Socks sells more than 2,000 styles of socks from about 20 suppliers. The company partners with charities that receive $2 per pair of “charity awareness socks,” and 5% of the company’s annual profits goes to the Special Olympics. The mission to spread happiness guides organizational culture at John’s Crazy Socks as well. The company employs people of differing abilities, including people who have been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder and Down syndrome. John and Mark believe in equal rights and advocate for employment opportunities for people with differing abilities. They even testified before the U.S. House Committee on Small Business. Like many businesses, the success of John’s Crazy Socks has a lot to do with its core values.

TMP-0284.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0284.text: Core Values Core values are underlying principles and beliefs that shape decision making for companies and individuals. The core values of individuals can include honesty, respect, and commitment to serving others. Your core values will help determine, for example, what educational choices you make and what career you find fulfilling. A company’s stance on issues ranging from empathy and transparency to employee safety and reliable service reflects its core values. Decisions driven by these values contribute to the company’s identity and help to distinguish it from competitors. core values Underlying principles and beliefs that shape decision making for companies and individuals. Companies communicate their core values internally to set expectations for employee behavior and to clarify preferred practices. Many companies also promote their core values publicly to inform customers about priorities and goals and to attract customers with similar values. Sharing admirable core values can contribute to corporate success. Consider Dutch chocolate manufacturer Tony’s Chocolonely, whose mission is to make chocolate without relying on child labor, deforestation, or the exploitation of farmers. So many customers share those values and want to support the mission that Tony’s

TMP-0285.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0285.text: Chocolonely has become the most successful chocolate brand in the Netherlands. The company’s next goal is to gain popularity in other European countries and in the United States. One core value of the American Express Company (Amex) is customer commitment: “We strive to be essential to our customers by delivering exceptional products, services and experiences every day—and promise to have their backs in everything we do.” “ 1 Amex card holders are called “members” to make them feel like they are part of a special club. Amex goes the extra mile for customers even in unusual circumstances. In one case, a hotel café manager called the Amex team to inform them that he had accidentally sold a cake to an Amex card member that was supposed to be only for display. The cake had harmful chemicals in it, and he was concerned about the health impact on the customer. The Amex team found out who used their card at the café around the time when the cake was sold and tracked down the customer before the cake was consumed. This story shows how a company can live by its values even when the specific situation is beyond anything that would be discussed in employee training.

TMP-0286.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0286.text: Oleg Moiseyenko/Alamy Stock Photo American Express values strong customer relationships—and that’s why its members value American Express. Core Competencies While core values reflect principles and beliefs, core competencies are capabilities or strengths that enable an individual or a business to stand out among rivals and deliver

TMP-0287.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0287.text: value in unique ways. For an individual, core competencies can include skills in time management, communication, teamwork, or problem solving. For a company, core competencies can stem from superior technologies, expertise, or capabilities. Business leaders are wise to ask themselves, “What are we particularly good at?” It might be fast service, quality control, research and development, or innovation. Some companies offer exceptional customer service, while others excel at innovation, communication, or ethical behavior. When evaluating new opportunities and deciding how to allocate resources, businesses take their core competencies into account. By devoting resources to core competencies, businesses can differentiate themselves from competitors and develop competitive advantage. core competencies Capabilities or strengths that enable an individual or a business to stand out among rivals and deliver value in unique ways. Think of a successful organization and you can probably identify core competencies that help it meet customer needs. Apple excels at simple, elegant product designs. Walmart offers low prices enabled by economies of scale (discussed in Module 1.2 ) and superior product distribution systems. Williams College has a steadfast focus on academic excellence. Your own skills, abilities, and strengths are core competencies—

TMP-0288.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0288.text: which include being a great student, considering that you are in this course and completing the assigned reading. AP ® EXAM TIP Don’t confuse core values and core competencies. Core values reflect the principles and beliefs a business feels are important. Core competencies are what the business is good at. It may help to think of core values as “what” the business believes in and the competencies as “how” it will outperform rivals.

TMP-0289.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0289.text: Ralf-Finn Hestoft/Getty Images Walmart’s core competencies include efficient product distribution and inventory management, both of which help to keep shelves stocked and prices low. Great missions, visions, values, and competencies are not the only essential ingredients in a successful business. Without the right culture to support everything the

TMP-0290.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0290.text: organization is trying to do, failure can follow despite the best intentions. Organizational culture shapes employee behavior and drives engagement, innovation, and productivity. AP ® SKILL TIP To develop skills in concept application, try to identify the core values and core competencies of the businesses around you. For example, what do you see as the core values and core competencies of McDonald’s? Target? Baskin-Robbins?

TMP-0291.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0291.text: Vision and Mission LG What are vision statements and mission statements and how do they differ? At the beginning of this module, we learned about John’s Crazy Socks, a company with the vision of demonstrating what people with differing abilities can do and the mission of spreading happiness. Let’s consider how other companies express their visions and pursue their missions. Vision A vision describes the values and aims of an organization—the impact it wants to make and what it wants to become. Companies typically promote their vision through a vision statement , which is a concise summary of the organization’s core values and aspirations. The audience for a vision statement is often within the company, where it can help shape decisions and unite employees around common ambitions. The vision

TMP-0292.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0292.text: may also be shared with external audiences so that prospective customers and investors understand what the company wants to achieve. vision statement A concise summary of an organization’s most important values and aspirations. An effective business leader brings the organization’s vision to life by reinforcing it to employees and making it an integral part of their work life. Consider online retailer Zappos, whose vision is to “inspire the world by showing it’s possible to simultaneously deliver happiness to customers, as well as employees, vendors, shareholders, and the community, in a long-term, sustainable way.” 2 The importance of happy customers is reinforced throughout the organization by fun rewards for strong customer service. For example, when a Zappos employee demonstrates excellent customer service, someone rings a bell and everybody congratulates that person. Other acknowledgments include a public word of thanks and a handwritten note. Celebrating efforts that contribute to the company vision is a powerful way to motivate employees to do their best.

TMP-0293.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0293.text: Mission Although the two terms are easily confused, a mission is different from a vision. While a business’s vision describes values and aspirations, a mission indicates what the business does to fulfill its purpose. Companies articulate their mission in a mission statement, which is typically a brief description of why the organization exists and how it will achieve its long-term goals. That statement reflects the company’s core beliefs, the types of products or services it provides, and the customers it serves. mission statement A brief description of why an organization exists and what it does to achieve its long-term goals. A good mission statement is simple and memorable. It should convey the company’s contribution to society, evoke emotion, and differentiate the company from competitors. As with vision statements, the audience for mission statements includes employees, customers, and investors. Clarity on the mission can help workers make day-to-day decisions that serve the business’s long-term goals. Ideally, a mission statement will also endear customers to the company and attract investors who are moved by the business’s purpose and way of doing things. The inspirational “spread happiness” mission at John’s Crazy Socks accomplishes those goals.

TMP-0294.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0294.text: By illuminating an organization’s purpose and how it meets its objectives, a mission statement can guide and focus a company. An example is U.S. children’s media and toy company GoldieBlox. Its mission is “to reach girls at a young age, and introduce them (and oftentimes, their parents) to Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math.” GoldieBlox’s mission to challenge gender stereotypes about fields of interest guides its overall strategy. The company has attracted millennial and Gen Z employees who share the goal of making a profound impact in the toy space. The many ways GoldieBlox follows its mission include demonstrating its eye-opening products at children’s events and obtaining feedback from the GoldieBlox “Kid Council.” GoldieBlox founder Debbie Sterling commented, “It’s these moments of getting to see how our work lights up a kid’s face that reminds everyone, in the most visceral way, why we show up to work every day.” 3

TMP-0295.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0295.text: ZUMA Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo Debbie Sterling, founder of GoldieBlox, started her company to teach girls engineering principles using toys. That mission still guides the company’s strategy today.

TMP-0296.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0296.text: Vision, Mission, and Organizational Culture When you’re considering working for a particular company, you’re bound to have lots of questions, such as: What do they pay? What hours am I expected to work? What kind of benefits do they offer? But an important question you should also ask about a company is: What’s the culture like? Some people link culture to the fun perks offered by some companies, like free cafés and ping-pong tables. But culture is more than just free drinks and games. Organizational culture is a pattern of shared norms, rules, values, and beliefs that guide the attitudes and behaviors within a business. In other words, it describes the personality of the organization. Every organization has a personality, and some employees fit into some cultures better than others. There is no one-size-fits-all type of culture because not every company or industry is the same. GOOD AND BAD ORGANIZATIONAL CULTURES Organizational culture has a direct impact on business. Ineffective work cultures lead to disengaged employees, poor customer service, high turnover, and falling company profits. Problematic organizational cultures have caused some of the biggest business scandals over the past decade. For example, multinational financial services company

TMP-0297.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0297.text: Wells Fargo agreed to pay $3 billion to resolve a scandal after its employees opened millions of fake bank accounts without customer authorization in response to the company’s overly aggressive sales targets. 4 The pressurized work culture had led employees to take extreme measures to keep up with daily goals. Another example is from the early days of ride-sharing company Uber, which was accused of having a toxic work culture characterized by sexual harassment, discrimination, and aggressive behavior. 5 In response, the company replaced its CEO and introduced a new set of cultural values that included, “We do the right thing. Period.” 6 The new culture has coincided with healthy growth for the company.

TMP-0298.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0298.text: halbergman/Getty Images Over the past 10 years, the culture within the ride-sharing company Uber changed from toxic to supportive, and its net income changed from negative to positive. That could be a coincidence, but culture matters. Strong, engaging work cultures underpin many of the most successful companies and, not surprisingly, the companies that people most want to work for. Table 1.4-1 lists

TMP-0299.text: the best places to work according to Fortune Magazine . The best workers can be picky about their employers and choose to work in companies with positive, welcoming corporate cultures. This creates a double bonus for companies with cultures that help workers thrive: They attract the top talent, and they help everyone be more productive. TMP-0301.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0301.text: Organizations and Their Goals LG What are the differing goals of businesses, social enterprises, and nonprofit organizations? Recall from Module 1.1 that an organization is a structured group of people formed to achieve common goals, and a business is an organization generally formed to seek profit. Any business can have goals beyond profit. Social enterprises are businesses that focus primarily on social goals while also earning profit, while nonprofit organizations earn no profit that is kept by their owners. Let’s consider all of these types of organizations in more detail. Businesses In the pursuit of profit, businesses strive to distinguish themselves from competitors and build a reputation that will provide long-term stability and growth. Higher revenues

TMP-0302.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0302.text: or lower costs will increase profits, but business missions can include a variety of other interests. Status matters for some companies, which may set their sights on being the biggest or the best in their industry. In other cases, alongside profit, goals include community development, technological innovation, ethics, security, disaster relief, or education. Microsoft is an example of a company whose primary focus is profit, but its mission is to “empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more.” That mission influences how the company conducts itself as it pursues empowerment with support of education and opportunity. 7 For example, in a recent school year, Microsoft and its partners helped to train almost 10 million educators and students worldwide in computer science skills. Those interests are important to the company, but Microsoft is a traditional business in the sense that its overarching goal is to generate profits as a software, electronics, and hardware company. As we’ll see next, some businesses have other priorities.

TMP-0303.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0303.text: Social Enterprises A social enterprise is an organization that adopts commercial strategies primarily to achieve social objectives. Social enterprises seek profit both to finance their social mission and for their owners. For instance, Ben & Jerry’s is a social enterprise with a dual mission. Its business is ice cream, and it does earn profit, but it maintains a strong focus on support for workers, communities, farmers, animals, and the environment. social enterprise An organization that adopts commercial strategies primarily to achieve social objectives. Social enterprises have much in common with traditional businesses. With innovations, strategies, and marketing, both types of organizations pursue profit by serving customers. But social enterprises differ from traditional businesses, because their social objectives are what motivate the goal of profit. Social enterprises can achieve their goals with the products they offer, the way they operate, or their financial model. For example, LifeStraw makes water purification devices with a focus on providing clean water to communities with waterborne diseases. Greyston Bakery operates with an “open hiring” policy that omits background checks

TMP-0304.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0304.text: and resumes, giving employment opportunities to people whose life history normally presents barriers. And TOMS (Tomorrow’s Shoes) donates one-third of its profits to social and environmental programs. These businesses have a central goal of solving societal problems, but they do try to earn profit. Nonprofit organizations forego the drive for profit and focus their efforts on creating positive change for society. Nonprofit Organizations A nonprofit organization exists to serve the public good and does not generate profit for its owners. By law, the organization must reinvest any surplus of revenues over costs back into its programs. Some nonprofits, such as Wikipedia, rely almost entirely on donations and grants to fund their activities. Others, such as nonprofit hospitals, do generate revenue from the sale of goods and services, but reinvest all of that revenue into the organization. Another example is Goodwill Industries, which uses sales in its thrift stores to support community programs that provide education, job training, transportation, and housing. Many nonprofits qualify for exemptions from state and federal income taxes, and in some cases, they are exempt from sales and property taxes

TMP-0305.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0305.text: as well. Most schools, churches, and humanitarian organizations such as Oxfam and UNICEF are examples of nonprofits. nonprofit organization An organization that does not generate profit for its owners; if revenues exceed costs, the excess is reinvested back into the organization.

TMP-0306.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0306.text: UCG/Getty Images Goodwill is a nonprofit organization that runs largely on donations. Like all nonprofits, Goodwill uses any surplus of revenues over costs to fund programs in support of the organization’s mission.

TMP-0307.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0307.text: Module 1.5 Review Learning Goals LG What are core values and core competencies, and how do they shape decisions made by individuals and businesses? • Core values are the underlying principles and beliefs that guide your actions and those of your business. Core competencies are the unique capabilities or strengths that give you—or your business—a competitive advantage. • Together, core values and core competencies form the basis of decisions. LG What are vision statements and mission statements and how do they differ?
