TMP-0314.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0314.text: Many high schools have a formal mission statement and vision statement. They can usually be found on the school’s website. Read those if they are available. Your school’s leaders may reference these as they consider policies on issues like cheating, bullying, dress codes, and academic rigor. Consider how the mission and vision of your school influence your experience as a student. Can you tell whether your school’s priority is academics or athletics? Is the safety of students and faculty a clear goal? Are there policies that advance a mission of student learning, such as codes of conduct? Is your school focused on college-bound students as well as career and technical education? Based on your experience and observations, analyze the culture at your school. Consider everything around you, from the posters on the walls to the recurring rituals, practices, and behaviors. Perhaps, there are traditions around sports, holidays, and special events. The school’s emails, presentations by administrators, and communications on social media may also contain messages that convey the organization’s goals and influence its culture. If your school has a mascot, consider how that symbol fits with the school, its mission, and its broader culture.

TMP-0315.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0315.text: Apply Your AP ® Skills 1. Is your school a traditional business, a social enterprise, or a nonprofit? Explain your answer. 2. Explain how your school’s core competencies differ from those of another school in your area. 3. From your observations, how would you describe the mission of your school? 4. How would you describe the culture at your school? 5. Suppose you were the principal of a high school with the vision of empowering students to become effective leaders and lifelong learners. Provide two specific examples of how you would convey this vision to the students and faculty at your school.

TMP-0316.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0316.text: MODULE 1.6 Business Ethics LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 1.6.A Describe how business leaders encourage ethical behavior in their organizations 1.6.B Discuss solutions to the ethical dilemmas that businesses face

TMP-0317.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0317.text: SEAN GLADWELL/Getty Images Customers use other customers’ reviews to make important decisions about goods and services. Where do you draw the line between right and wrong when leaving a review? Would you give a misleading review to help a friend or receive a free product?

TMP-0318.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0318.text: Why Ethics Matter in Business LG What problems result from unethical behavior and how can business leaders encourage ethical behavior in their organizations? Module 1.5 explained that businesses have their own cultures built on shared norms, views, values, and beliefs. A company’s ethics play an important role in its culture. Whether a company behaves ethically—or not—can have profound effects on the business’s owners, employees, customers, creditors, and surrounding community. Even within a business that has admirable values and a clear mission, struggles between right and wrong challenge individuals at every level. Should a salesperson recommend a product even if it doesn’t really serve the customer’s needs? Is it acceptable for a company to charge more when customers have no other choice but to buy its product? Suppliers, customers, and shareholders face ethical dilemmas as well. In this module, we will explore how businesses handle decisions about right and wrong.

TMP-0319.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0319.text: Ethics is the study of right and wrong behavior. You face decisions about ethics daily. Is it okay to copy a friend’s homework? Should you lie to protect a family member’s feelings? Will you tip your server at a restaurant? These decisions all depend on what you believe to be right and wrong. Business ethics is the application of ethical standards to all aspects of a business. Questions of right and wrong arise daily as organizations make hard calls about the hiring process, manufacturing practices, and the treatment of stakeholders including workers, suppliers, and customers. business ethics The application of ethical standards to all aspects of a business. Incentives for Unethical Behavior As people navigate tough decisions in the business world and in everyday life, there are few guardrails and many temptations to make questionable choices. The driving forces behind both good and bad behavior are known as incentives . An incentive is anything that motivates or encourages a person to do something. Unfortunately, there are often incentives to do something unethical. incentive Anything that motivates or encourages a person to do something.

TMP-0320.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0320.text: A business focused on profit has an incentive to pay low wages, regardless of whether they are fair wages. For a sales or marketing team that is rewarded for increases in sales, there are incentives to exaggerate a product’s appeal and to conceal problems and risks. And many types of manufacturers face tradeoffs between increasing the speed of production to gain profit and slowing the speed of production to improve worker safety. For example, severe injuries are common in the meatpacking industry, where workers wield sharp knives and saws to process livestock. There, the incentive for profit comes at the cost of a faster pace and more accidental amputations of fingers and hands. Incentive structures like these can motivate unethical choices at every level of a business. Employees with grievances may consider stealing company property. The accounting department might be tempted to falsify documents when a company is in poor financial health. And managers could contemplate concealing information if a product is found to cause harm to consumers. All of these temptations to do the wrong thing make it important to consider ways to encourage people to do the right thing.

TMP-0321.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0321.text: Encouraging Ethical Behavior We all need a nudge to do the right thing once in a while, or perhaps more of a push or a pull. The best way is seldom the easy way, and selfish behavior often stands in the way of ethical behavior. Lying, cheating, and stealing can lead to a fast buck today and business failure tomorrow. With so much that can go wrong with unethical behavior, businesses make intentional efforts to guide people in the right direction. This section explores those road maps to morality. AP ® Exam Tip The coverage in this course stresses ways to encourage ethical behavior more than ways to identify it. Go into the test armed with multiple ways to guide workers in the right direction so that you are more likely to have a relevant approach for an unpredictable situation. Codes of Conduct The starting point for encouraging ethical decisions within a business is to clarify expectations for worker behavior. This can be done formally with a code of conduct , which is a document that details the rules, expectations, and standards for conduct

TMP-0322.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0322.text: within an organization. Where one exists, employees typically sign a code of conduct during the onboarding process that introduces new employees to their workplace. Table 1.6-1 outlines some common elements of a code of conduct. code of conduct A document that details the rules, expectations, and standards for conduct within an organization. Table 1.6-1 Codes of Conduct Section or element What it covers Compliance with Laws and Regulations • Laws and safety regulations • Anticompetitive practices and whistleblower protections for workers who report wrongdoing within the business Confidentiality • Policies for protecting customer, employee, and company information Conflicts of Interest • Instructions for disclosing and managing situations in which personal interests could cloud judgments about workplace decisions Ethical Behavior • Guidelines for honesty and ethical decisions

TMP-0323.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0323.text: Dispute Resolution • Stipulations on how internal disputes will be resolved • May include alternative dispute resolution techniques such as mediation or arbitration Ethical use of AI • Expectations and boundaries that guide how employees use AI at work • Rules to ensure transparency, accuracy, and legal compliance Entertainment and Gifts • Rules related to giving or accepting gifts, meals, or other favors • Designed to avoid subtle (or not so subtle) forms of bribery General Employee Conduct • Expectations related to things like professionalism, work contributions, respectful behavior, integrity, and dress code Relationships • Guidelines for appropriate relationships with customers, employees, donors, and other stakeholders Workplace Health and Safety • Company rules about substance use, safety standards, and emergency procedures

TMP-0324.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0324.text: A code of conduct helps employees behave ethically by clarifying the line between acceptable and unacceptable behavior. When missteps occur, this document helps managers identify specific violations and can provide guidance on the appropriate remedies. Some businesses have a code of ethics , which helps the organization regulate behavior by outlining relatively broad ethical principles and values. Whereas a code of ethics provides a foundation for guidance, trust, and accountability, a code of conduct translates those principles into specific rules for day-to-day behavior. Training Training programs encourage ethical behavior by teaching employees what behavior is appropriate and explaining effective ways to do the right thing. Mentoring programs can pair employees with good role models within the organization to reinforce ethical practices. Many companies use workshops, videos, or readings to educate employees about acceptable decisions. Common topics for training programs include: • Bribery and Corruption

TMP-0325.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0325.text: • Boundaries for Customer and Vendor Relationships • Data Privacy and Security • Safe and ethical use of AI • Environmental and Social Responsibility • Ethics and Decision Making • Financial Conduct and Fraud • Harassment and Discrimination • Whistleblowing and Reporting Mechanisms • Workplace Relationships As you enter organizations of any type, you will likely encounter training programs on some of these topics. Popular modes of delivery include videos that employees watch on their own, with quiz questions along the way to provide incentives for watching.

TMP-0326.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0326.text: Incentives DNY59/Getty Images A positive incentive is sometimes called a “carrot” because, just as a carrot can entice a donkey to move forward, a reward can motivate a person to do something. A negative incentive is referred to as a

TMP-0327.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0327.text: “stick,” which has been used as punishment for a donkey that refuses to move forward. Businesses can encourage ethical behavior—and discourage unethical behavior—with incentives. Some incentives are positive, in the form of rewards; others are negative, in the form of punishments. Either way, the undeniable power of incentives makes them the go-to method most businesses use to elicit ethical behavior. Positive incentives play a valuable role in promoting ethical behavior because a wide range of undesirable behavior does not violate a law or code of conduct. Without breaking any rules or regulations, an employee can be unkind, impatient, or uncaring to coworkers or customers. Leaders use several approaches to promote better behavior using incentives. These include: • Reward Programs. Businesses can identify employees who have behaved ethically or provided exceptional customer service with peer reviews, customer surveys, comment boxes, or other opportunities for feedback. To reward desirable behavior, a business may provide money, time off, a special meal, or a gift card to anyone who reaches a designated level of achievement, such as receiving five positive customer

TMP-0328.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0328.text: reviews. As we will discuss further in Module 4.1 , many businesses also reward behavior that goes beyond ethics, such as hard work and activities that embody the company’s core values. • Public Recognition. Public recognition for ethical behavior can be as informal as a manager telling a flattering story about an employee’s act of kindness during a team meeting. Employee of the Month programs, “walls of fame,” and company newsletters are among other ways to spotlight employees who have behaved admirably. Businesses themselves may also win public recognition for ethical behavior. For example, some chambers of commerce grant an annual business ethics award to a business with priorities beyond profits, and the Ethisphere Institute publicly recognizes the companies it considers the most ethical in the world. • Celebrations of Milestones. Performance benchmarks and goal setting motivate employees to behave ethically. Organizations encourage good behavior with events that mark achievements. Signage can trumpet milestones such as 250 five-star customer ratings, 1,000 hours of volunteer work, or $10,000 in charitable contributions. Year-end award ceremonies are among the celebratory events used to acknowledge ethical accomplishments. When Luther College reduced its

TMP-0329.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0329.text: greenhouse gas emissions by over 70%—aided by student efforts to cut food and energy waste—the institution held a celebration to mark its progress. All such acknowledgement of ethical behavior serves to reinforce and energize commitments to do what is best for an organization and its stakeholders. Businesses use negative incentives to discourage unethical behavior. It is common for businesses to impose internal repercussions such as warnings, suspensions, or termination for ethical transgressions that include dishonesty, harassment, theft, and violations of safety rules. Many businesses also struggle with staffing problems due to chronic employee absences. Walmart adopts a point system that penalizes employees for tardiness or unexcused absences. An employee might earn half a point for arriving late, one point for an unexcused absence with advance notice, and two points for simply not showing up for work. After accumulating five points, an employee could face termination. The need for ethical behavior goes both ways. It is important for businesses to have provisions for people who are ill or experiencing an emergency. A common approach is to allow additional missed days for employees who have a doctor’s note verifying an illness.

TMP-0330.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0330.text: Marjorie Kamys Cotera/Alamy Stock Photo Extended description for Safety Record The sign in the forefront reads Service Center, N P , New Process Steel. We have worked 225 days without an accident. In the background, large

TMP-0331.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0331.text: metal tubes of various shapes and sizes are on the floor. Violations of safety rules can endanger workers. Businesses with considerable safety risks often incentivize safe behavior with signage and rewards for good safety records. Modeling Ethical Behavior You can talk the talk, but can you walk the walk? A business leader who visibly does the right thing can encourage ethical behavior by serving as a good role model. Consistent exhibits of integrity, honesty, and transparency by managers set the standard for behavior in an organization. When Starbucks’ leaders pay more for coffee beans than they need to by choosing suppliers who pay agricultural workers fair wages, employees see that their company cares about doing the right thing. When the manager of a tire store tells a customer they do not need new tires yet, that sets a tone of honesty for the entire store. And when the Mark Cuban Cost Plus Pharmacy sets its prices by simply adding a relatively low 15% to the pharmacy’s cost for the drug (plus any pharmacy labor and shipping fees), it becomes clear that transparency is a key goal at that company.

TMP-0332.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0332.navLabel: The Importance of Ethical Business Practices
TMP-0332.text: Business encounters with ethics go beyond ethical dilemmas and efforts to develop an ethical corporate culture. In Module 1.3 , we learned how PESTEL analysis considers political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal factors, all of which are inescapably linked to ethics. In later modules, we will discuss, for example, the ethics of financial management and reporting. The tools in this chapter apply to many of the ethical puzzles that lie ahead. The Importance of Ethical Business Practices Business decisions that maximize profit in the short term do not always align with long-term success. Nestlé, Macy’s, Heinz, Levi’s, and Coca-Cola, like many other companies, have survived since the nineteenth century. The prospect of lasting success gives companies reason to play the long game by forgoing risky—and often unethical— strategies for quick profits. Once-thriving companies that famously include Enron, WorldCom, Refco, Lehman Brothers, and Theranos failed after misrepresenting their financial situation or product and creating an ethical scandal. For example, Theranos falsely claimed its blood-testing technology could accurately test a few drops of blood for hundreds of medical tests quickly and inexpensively. Beyond the costly legal

headings.text: The Importance of Ethical Business Practices

TMP-0333.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0333.navLabel: The Importance of Ethical Business Practices
TMP-0333.text: ramifications of their fraudulent behavior, these companies lost the trust on which customer loyalty is built. The unethical sourcing of products is another example of business conduct that influences public perceptions. Some customers avoid companies that source products from war zones where revenues might fund violence, that grow cotton using toxic chemical pesticides, or that slaughter animals in inhumane ways before selling their meat. There are also parts of the world where goods are made using child labor or forced labor. The U.S. Department of Labor maintains a list of products made around the world using these types of labor. 1 The list includes artificial flowers made in China, green beans grown in Mexico, and carpets made in India.

TMP-0334.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0334.navLabel: The Importance of Ethical Business Practices
TMP-0334.text: Hindustan Times/Getty Images Is it ethical for a business to source products from a factory that uses child labor? Both customers and employees respond to unethical business behavior. Almost all U.S. workers say that ethics is important to their choice of an employer. 2 Over a third of

TMP-0335.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0335.navLabel: The Importance of Ethical Business Practices
TMP-0335.text: workers report having left an employer for ethical reasons. And more than half of U.S. customers have stopped buying a good or service to protest a business’s behavior. 3 In contrast, businesses that uphold high ethical standards often appeal to customers. When Warby Parker provides glasses to those in need or Greyston Bakery creates employment opportunities for marginalized communities, those companies add an ethical dimension to their appeal. Many customers, employees, and investors are drawn to companies with respectable moral boundaries. Ethical business behavior also increases customer and employee loyalty and the prices customers are willing to pay. 4 Business relationships with customers and employees are so vulnerable to ethical scandals that companies such as Uber, BP, and Toyota have spent tens of millions of dollars on image repair. After accusations of unethical behavior, approaches range from expressing regret to denying any wrongdoing. Some companies take corrective actions, and others focus on spreading the blame. Most probably wish they had done the right thing in the first place. Consider the case of Volkswagen, which installed software in diesel-powered cars that allowed them to pass emissions tests despite emitting illegal levels of pollution. The

TMP-0336.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0336.navLabel: The Importance of Ethical Business Practices
TMP-0336.text: company admitted wrongdoing and paid billions of dollars’ worth of fines and compensation to the customers it deceived. Ten years later, after paying for the legal settlements, overhauling its leadership, and launching major marketing campaigns to repair its corporate image, Volkswagen was still struggling to regain its reputation as a trustworthy automaker.

TMP-0337.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0337.navLabel: The Importance of Ethical Business Practices
TMP-0337.text: Kirsty O’Connor - PA Images/Getty Images Extended description for Volkswagen's False Emissions Data The huge banner is held aloft by two women and three men. It shows a figure wearing a gas mask with the Volkswagen logo on the mask. The text on

TMP-0338.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0338.navLabel: The Importance of Ethical Business Practices
TMP-0338.text: its right reads, VW: CLEAN AIR CHEATS. Volkswagen’s decision to falsify emissions data resulted in the loss of customer trust—and cost the company billions of dollars.

TMP-0339.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0339.navLabel: The Importance of Ethical Business Practices
TMP-0339.text: Sorting Out Ethical Dilemmas in Business LG What strategies can business leaders use to address ethical dilemmas? A question of right or wrong may have no clear answer. Because the boundaries for acceptable behavior can be fuzzy, ethical dilemmas abound. In business, an ethical dilemma arises when core values conflict with business goals or with each other. For example, a core value of honesty about product features can conflict with the goal of profit if dishonesty leads to more profit. Or a core value of offering healthy products can conflict with a core value of offering affordable products if healthy products are often more expensive to produce than unhealthy products. ethical dilemma A situation that arises when core values conflict with business goals or with each other.

TMP-0340.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0340.navLabel: The Importance of Ethical Business Practices
TMP-0340.text: AP ® Skills Tip One of the key course skills is decision making. Ethical dilemmas challenge managers to decide among imperfect options. If asked to make a decision about a case, unless the question states otherwise, clearly explain not only your decision but also the reasoning behind it and the options you considered. An ethical dilemma presents two or more options, each of which is questionable from an ethical standpoint. An electronics company might face a dilemma over whether to be honest about the short battery life of its smartphones or accept a loss of sales that causes layoffs for employees. A news organization can save time and money by posting AI-generated stories, but only at the risk of inaccurate or insensitive content that could undermine the company’s credibility. And a cake company might have to decide between using a cheap sweetener linked to serious diseases or an expensive sweetener that makes its products unaffordable to many customers. Two approaches are common for business-related ethical dilemmas. Business leaders can ask themselves either:

TMP-0341.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0341.text: 1. Which option creates the largest net benefit (or the smallest net cost) for our stakeholders? or 2. Which option is best aligned with the mission of the business and its vision for the future? Weighing Costs and Benefits The first approach is to compare the costs and benefits of each option to stakeholders. The net benefit of any option is its total benefit minus its total cost. If the total cost exceeds the total benefit, the net benefit is negative, and we can refer to the excess of cost over benefit as the net cost . The inclusion of stakeholders forces the question of which stakeholders to consider. There are two broad categories of stakeholders. Internal stakeholders are people directly involved in the activities of the organization, such as employees, managers, owners, and members of the board of directors. External stakeholders are people outside of the organization who are affected by its activities. Depending on the situation, external stakeholders could include customers, suppliers, lenders, community members, retailers that sell the product, and government agencies that regulate it. We

TMP-0342.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0342.text: will first assume that external stakeholders are considered. A second example (refer to A Deeper Dive: Finding the Option with the Largest Net Benefit ) examines the effect of disregarding external stakeholders when applying the largest-net-benefit criterion. internal stakeholders Those directly involved in the activities of an organization, such as employees, managers, owners, and members of the board of directors. external stakeholders Those outside of an organization who are affected by its activities, such as customers, suppliers, lenders, community members, retailers, and government agencies. Let’s say you manage a company that makes hot sauce. The fumes from hot sauce production are released into the air, and they can irritate the eyes, noses, and throats of people in the surrounding community. 5 With a higher smokestack on the factory, the fumes are more effectively carried up and away from the community. You must decide whether to buy a short smokestack for $20,000 or a tall smokestack for $35,000.

TMP-0343.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0343.text: Bloomberg/Getty Images Hot sauce production creates fumes that can be a nuisance to the surrounding community. If the law doesn’t protect the community from harm, the company faces an ethical dilemma about its level of care for those external stakeholders.

TMP-0344.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0344.text: Suppose a short smokestack would provide $27,000 worth of benefits to the community by sending some of the fumes into the atmosphere rather than into the surrounding neighborhoods. * The net benefit of the short smokestack is thus $27,000 – $20,000 = $7,000. The benefit of the short smokestack exceeds the cost, giving it a positive net benefit, but that does not mean it is the best option. It is important to examine the other possibility to see which option provides the largest net benefit. A tall smokestack would provide $50,000 worth of benefits by carrying even more of the fumes away from the people below. The net benefit of the tall smokestack is $50,000 – $35,000 = $15,000. So, even though the tall smokestack is more expensive and the short smokestack provides a net benefit, the tall smokestack is the better choice based on the largest-net-benefit criterion. Its net benefit of $15,000 is larger than the short smokestack’s net benefit of $7,000. A Deeper Dive: Finding the Option with the Largest Net Benefit provides another application of this criterion.

TMP-0345.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0345.text: A DEEPER DIVE Finding the Option with the Largest Net Benefit Suppose you lead a company that produces clothing irons and other small household appliances. You discover that 50,000 irons in your distribution facility have a faulty temperature gauge. About once every 100 uses, the temperature on these irons rises so high that they will burn a hole through any clothing they touch. The irons do not pose a fire safety threat when used as directed. The irons cannot be fixed. It is possible, but unlikely, that customers will determine that a gauge defect caused the damage to their clothing. After all, the overheating occurs so rarely that customers will be unable to replicate the problem in any short period of time. You must decide whether to discard the irons or sell them. If you sell the irons, $1.5 million in sales revenue will provide benefits to internal stakeholders in the form of wages and profits. The relevant external stakeholders in this case are the customers and the retail stores that carry your irons. Those stores will gain $0.75 million in profits from the sales of your product. Customers can purchase other brands of irons from other stores, so customers would not receive an added benefit from the sale of your irons. The cost to internal stakeholders of selling the irons is not straightforward. Maybe customers won’t figure out that their rare clothes-burning incidents are caused by a defective gauge. Maybe the gauge defect will be discovered, irons will be returned, negative reviews will accumulate, and the company’s brand will suffer. Analysis of these problems is aided by estimating their values in dollars. One way to think about the expected cost of these possibilities is to imagine an insurance

TMP-0346.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0346.text: policy was available to cover the associated costs if the irons were sold. The most the company would pay for that insurance represents the expected cost of those possibilities and the associated uncertainty that comes with the decision to sell the irons. After studying the possibilities and risks, you would be willing to pay $1 million to insure against the costs. So, the company places a $1 million value on the possible costs to internal stakeholders. The cost to external stakeholders of selling the irons is the clothing damage. You estimate that customers will collectively experience $5 million worth of clothing losses. Considering all stakeholders, the total benefit of selling the irons is $1.5 million for internal stakeholders plus $0.75 million for external stakeholders, which is $2.25 million. The total cost of selling the irons is an estimated $1 million in costs to internal stakeholders and $5 million in costs to external stakeholders, for a total cost of $6 million. The net benefit is $2.25 million minus $6 million, which is negative $3.75 million. In other words, selling the irons has a net cost of $3.75 million. There is no gain received from not selling the irons. Since the irons are already made, there is also no cost of not selling them. The cost of making them has already been incurred, so no cost savings is available. The net benefit (and net cost) of not selling the irons is thus 0 – 0 = 0. Since a net cost of zero is less than a net cost of $3.75 million, considering all stakeholders, it is better not to sell the irons. If you consider only internal stakeholders, the benefit of selling the irons is $1.5 million in sales, and the cost is $1 million worth of returns and tarnished reputation. The net benefit of selling the irons is then $1.5 million – $1 million = $0.5 million. The net benefit of not selling the irons is again zero. So, you would sell the irons if you cared only about internal stakeholders, but discard the irons if you cared about all stakeholders.

TMP-0347.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0347.text: A Focus on Values The second approach to business-related ethical dilemmas is to consider the mission, vision, and underlying values of the business. If a hot sauce company aims to contribute to the growth and well-being of its community, it should invest in fume dissipation. And if an appliance company like the one discussed in A Deeper Dive seeks to serve customers with superior products and be a trusted source of home appliances, revealing product defects is the appropriate decision. If profit maximization is a business’s solitary mission, however, the second criterion would point to the alternative decisions. One would hope that companies care enough about their customers to protect their safety. Several classic cases reveal that companies are not always ethical in their handling of dangerous products. Cigarette companies such as Altria Group Inc. (formerly Philip Morris) failed to warn customers about the health risks of cigarettes. The Ford Motor Company did not fix a design defect that made the gas tank on its Pinto model vulnerable to explosion upon rear impact. And the Dow Corning Corporation sold silicone breast implants that allegedly leaked and caused serious health problems for customers.

TMP-0348.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas

TMP-0349.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0349.text: Sometimes, there are tradeoffs between profit and ethics. Often, the ethical path is also the path toward business success. * You might wonder how these values could be estimated. Economists have several ways of estimating the benefits of avoiding this type of nuisance. For example, they could study the effect on housing prices in a community before and after the nuisance, or they could survey residents to see how much they would be willing to pay to avoid the nuisance.

When a printer company must decide between serving customers well with long-lasting products or maximizing profits by making products that must be replaced often, the company faces a(n) a. incentive. b. ethical dilemma.

TMP-0354.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0354.text: c. core value. d. external stakeholder. 4. Customers are considered a. internal stakeholders. b. external stakeholders. c. middling stakeholders. d. nonstakeholders.

TMP-0355.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0355.text: CASE STUDY Keurig Dr Pepper Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Businesses face ethical dilemmas, like whether to pursue profit at the possible expense of children’s health. Keurig Dr Pepper is a North American beverage company with over 125 brands, 30 manufacturing sites, and 28,000 employees. Their mission is: “Drink Well. Do Good,” which includes having a “positive impact for our people, communities, and planet.” Their vision is “a beverage for every need, anytime, anywhere.” 6 Keurig Dr

TMP-0356.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0356.text: Pepper is also a profit-seeking business. The company’s core values and goals create ethical dilemmas, because sometimes having positive impacts on people and communities conflicts with maximizing profit. One of Keurig Dr Pepper’s ethical dilemmas involves marketing to customers who may not know what is best for their health. For example, like all sellers of soda, the company must decide whether to advertise sugary drinks to children. The practice would increase profits, but children may not understand the links between excessive sugar consumption and various health problems. Suppose you calculate that the net benefits of advertising sugary drinks to children are negative if all internal and external stakeholders are considered, but positive if only internal stakeholders are considered. As another possible approach, the Children’s Food & Beverage Advertising Initiative (CFBAI) asks companies to voluntarily pledge not to advertise food or beverages to children unless those products meet specific nutritional requirements. The leaders of Keurig Dr Pepper have all of this to consider, along with their mission, as they determine their marketing strategy.

TMP-0357.text: Apply Your AP ® Skills 1. Identify four stakeholders in this business and explain how each might be affected by the decision to market sugary drinks to children. 2. What do you see as the three best options this company could use to resolve its ethical dilemma? 3. Explain what you would decide if you were the chief executive officer of this company based on one of the approaches you provided in Question 2.

TMP-0358.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0358.text: M O D U L E 1 . 7 Organization, Roles, and Responsibilities LG L E A R N I N G G O A L S In this module, you will learn to: 1.7.A Describe common types of business organization and their pros and cons 1.7.B Explain the leadership roles for sole proprietors and partners 1.7.C Discuss the leadership roles within large business organizations 1.7.D Describe the functions of specialized departments within organizations

headings.text: M O D U L E 1 . 7

TMP-0359.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0359.text: Bloomberg/Getty Images As businesses grow, they often switch from one business type to another. For example, Papa John’s started as a sole proprietorship and later became a corporation. In this module, you will learn about these and other business types and the reasons business owners love them and leave them.

TMP-0360.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0360.text: Types of Business Organization LG What are the four most common types of business organization, and what are the advantages and disadvantages of each? From your local dentist’s office to the company that made your refrigerator, every business has a legal structure based on its size, purpose, industry, and growth plans. That structure determines how decisions are made about the business, who is liable for the business’s debts, what taxes are paid, what records must be kept, and what regulations apply. Legal structure also determines how a business can raise funds. The money and other assets businesses need to cover day-to-day financial obligations and invest in growth are financial capital. Where the financial context makes the meaning clear, you may find financial capital described simply as “capital.” (We will discuss financial capital in detail in Module 3.5 .)

TMP-0361.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0361.text: In most cases, an entrepreneur can choose among several legal structures. It is important to understand the differences among them. The relevant laws vary from state to state and country to country, so anyone starting a business should study the available options for their particular situation before making a final selection. Let’s examine some of the most popular legal structures, commonly described as business types, and the advantages—and disadvantages—of each one. Sole Proprietorship A sole proprietorship is a business owned and controlled by one person. This is the simplest and most inexpensive legal structure to adopt. Although roughly 75% of all U.S. businesses are sole proprietorships, only about 5% of all business revenue is received by these businesses, so this type of firm is common but typically small. sole proprietorship A business that is owned and controlled by one person. A sole proprietorship is easy to form. In many jurisdictions and industries, no legal filing is required to establish a sole proprietorship. Where licenses or permits are necessary, the entrepreneur may simply need to pay a nominal fee to obtain the right

TMP-0362.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0362.text: license or permit. For example, to start a painting business, you might need a home improvement contractor license. To establish a business that sells goods or services that are subject to a sales tax, you will need a sales tax permit or license. While a sole proprietor enjoys simplicity and control, the legal structure has its drawbacks. The owner is exposed to all the risks, legal responsibilities, and liabilities of the business. For example, say the owner borrowed money to run the business, but then lost a major customer and was unable to repay the loan. Or perhaps the business’s delivery truck was involved in an accident that injured a pedestrian. The sole proprietor is personally responsible for dealing with the debts and legal claims resulting from the misfortunes of the business. This responsibility is called personal liability. With nothing protecting the individual’s personal assets from the business’s obligations and liabilities, this can lead to severe personal losses and bankruptcy. Some of the other business structures we will discuss help to protect against personal losses. The legal structure of a business also affects its ability to finance investments in growth. Unit 3 explains how corporations can sell stocks or bonds to raise capital. Sole proprietorships cannot sell stocks and generally do not issue bonds. Many sole proprietors bootstrap their business, meaning that their financial capital comes from

TMP-0363.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0363.text: personal savings, revenue from the business, or the sale of personal assets. For example, John Schnatter sold his Chevrolet Camaro Z28 to get the cash needed to start building his Papa John’s pizza empire. Loans from banks, credit unions, friends, and family are also a possibility. Crowdfunding is another possible source of capital for most types of business, including sole proprietorships. On crowdfunding websites, entrepreneurs post their project ideas and backers pledge money to support the projects, sometimes in exchange for rewards such as samples or discounts. For example, Pebble smartwatches and Oculus Rift virtual reality headsets began with assistance from Kickstarter crowdfunding campaigns.

TMP-0364.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas

TMP-0365.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0365.text: Several years after founding eBay as a sole proprietorship, chairperson Pierre Omidyar—shown here with CEO Meg Whitman—created a corporation. The inability of sole proprietorships to sell stocks or bonds can impede their growth. Many large organizations began as sole proprietorships and then transitioned into another legal structure for reasons that include greater access to funds for growth, protection from liability, and a desire to spread the workload across more people. An example is eBay, which Pierre Omidyar launched as a sole proprietorship in 1995. Omidyar partnered with Jeff Skoll in 1996 and created a corporation in 1998. Figure 1.7-1 outlines the benefits and drawbacks of a sole proprietorship.

TMP-0366.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0366.text: Pros • Simple business structure • Owner is entitled to all profits • Full control • Personal liability • Personal and business assets can overlap • Harder to raise capital Cons Copyright © BFW Publishers Extended description for Figure 1.7-1 A Sole Proprietorship An upward pointing arrow reads Pros. The accompanying list reads as follows: • Simple business structure • Owner is entitled to all profits • Full control An downward pointing arrow reads Cons. The accompanying list reads as follows:

TMP-0367.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0367.text: • Personal liability • Personal and business assets can overlap • Harder to raise capital Figure 1.7-1 A Sole Proprietorship Partnership A partnership involves two or more people who share the ownership, management, and profits or losses of a business. As with a sole proprietorship, setting up a general partnership is relatively low cost and straightforward. Suppose you and your business partner decide to open a café. To qualify for general partnership legal status, you and your partner must be involved in the business and contribute money, property, labor, or skill to the café. You and your partner will share the profits and losses. partnership A business involving two or more people who share ownership, management, and profits and losses.

TMP-0368.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0368.text: Although partnership arrangements can be quite flexible, it is wise to have a formal agreement drafted by a legal expert to lay out the terms of the partnership. Typically, this agreement will cover how profits and losses will be divided, each partner’s rights and contributions, and the consequences of one partner leaving the business for any reason. Partnerships face the same limitations on fundraising as sole proprietorships. They don’t raise capital by selling stocks or bonds. However, it can be easier to self-fund or “bootstrap” a business with several partners pooling their resources. When Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne started Apple Computer as a partnership, Jobs sold his Volkswagen minibus and Wozniak sold his programmable calculator to help fund the venture. Partners can also combine their borrowing power to help raise funds. Sharing the burden of funding and running a business with someone also has its drawbacks. Relationships have a way of falling apart. For instance, within four years of launching Facebook, only one of the five founders, Mark Zuckerberg, was still an executive in the company.

TMP-0369.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0369.text: Liability also complicates a partnership. Each partner in a general partnership is personally liable for the company’s financial obligations. This is called joint and several liability because partners can be held responsible together (jointly) and individually (severally) for the entire obligation. In a worst-case scenario, this means that if one partner is responsible for running the company into the ground, all the partners are liable for the losses. If some partners cannot pay anything, the other partners will be liable for the full amount. Therefore, before entering into a partnership, it is essential that the partners know each other well, establish a high degree of trust, and document the partnership agreement. Limited Liability Company Individuals and groups that want a relatively simple business structure without personal liability for business debts can organize as a limited liability company. A limited liability company (LLC) is a business structure that offers legal protection for owners by separating their personal assets from the business’s assets. Most states allow an LLC to have any number of owners, who are called “members.” An LLC is a separate legal entity, which means members are usually not responsible for the debts or liabilities of the business.

TMP-0370.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0370.text: limited liability company (LLC) A business structure offering legal protection for owners by separating personal from business assets. Like corporations, if all goes well, LLCs can have perpetual existence. Unlike corporations, LLCs cannot issue stock to fund strategies for future growth, nor do they typically issue bonds. The bootstrapping methods of sole proprietorships and partnerships are common among LLCs as well. Loans, grants, and crowdfunding can supplement the capital raised from member contributions. It is advisable for LLCs with multiple members to enter into an ownership agreement, which is part of a broader operating agreement that outlines how the business will be managed and run. Small LLCs are often managed directly by their members. Larger LLCs typically appoint a board of managers to handle operational and strategic decisions. LLCs aren’t for everyone. Some small businesses face very little liability risk and prefer to avoid the paperwork and fees involved in becoming an LLC. But by pairing the benefits of sole proprietorships and general partnerships with the limited liability of

TMP-0371.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0371.text: corporations, the LLC structure provides a popular choice second only to sole proprietorships among U.S. businesses. AP ® Exam TIP Although there are other legal structures in the business world, the four basic structures discussed in this module are most common, and they are also the ones most likely to appear on the AP ® Exam. Corporation A corporation is owned by an unlimited number of shareholders but is a legal entity apart from its owners. Each shareholder has contributed money or other assets in exchange for shares of stock that represent partial ownership of the corporation. Relative to a business structure with a small number of owners, the many owners of a corporation have considerably less control over decisions and receive a correspondingly small share of profits. A corporation is formed by filing articles of incorporation with the Secretary of State where the business is located. There are several types of

TMP-0372.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0372.text: corporations. The most common is what the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) designates as a “C corporation” or “C corp,” which we will refer to as simply a corporation. corporation A business owned by shareholders that is a legal entity apart from its owners. A corporation generally protects its owners from being personally liable for the corporation’s debts and other obligations. As a separate legal entity, the corporation’s liabilities are its own. If a corporation is sued or loses money for any reason, the value of shareholders’ stock may go down, but the shareholders’ losses are limited to the value of their stock. Another advantage to a corporation is its additional options for raising capital. Like the federal, state, and local government, a corporation can issue bonds, which is a way to borrow money without relying on a bank loan. Investors buy bonds from corporations in exchange for regular interest payments and repayment of the original purchase amount on a specified future date. Corporations can also issue shares of stock, which is a way to transfer partial ownership of the corporation to investors in exchange for capital. Investors in bonds and stocks bear the risk that the corporation will fail, in which case the bonds and stocks will have little or no value.

TMP-0373.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0373.text: If the corporation does not fail, as a separate entity, it benefits from the ability to operate long after the demise of its current owners. The prospect of perpetual existence allows the corporation to plan for long-term growth. Perpetual existence also appeals to investors, who can hope for strong returns on their investments even if current leaders leave, retire, or pass away. Disadvantages of corporations include the relative complexity of the legal requirements. A corporation generally must name a president or chief executive officer, a secretary, and a treasurer. It must also name a board of directors to oversee management of the corporation. In addition to filing articles of incorporation, most states require an annual report and annual shareholder and board of directors meetings. The principal types of legal structures we have described are summarized in Table 1.7- 1 . Table 1.7-1 Types of Legal Structures Business Entity Structure Liability Fundraising

TMP-0374.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0374.text: Sole Proprietorship One owner Unlimited Bootstrapping, bank loans, crowdfunding Partnership Two or more partners Unlimited, joint and several Bootstrapping, bank loans, crowdfunding Limited Liability Company (LLC) Members, optional board of managers Limited Bootstrapping, bank loans, crowdfunding Corporation Directors, officers, stockholders Limited Bootstrapping, bank loans, stocks, bonds, crowdfunding AP ® Skills TIP Having studied the pros and cons of these types of legal structures, think about a business you would like to open and choose an appropriate legal structure for that business. Then practice communicating the advantages and disadvantages of your chosen legal structure. By explaining them to a classmate, friend, or family member, you will build two essential skills for this course: communication skills and understanding of the concepts.

TMP-0375.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0375.text: Roles and Responsibilities in Sole Proprietorships and Partnerships LG What do business owners do in sole proprietorships and partnerships? Unlike large corporations, which we will turn to next, most businesses are relatively small and have a simple organizational structure. In a sole proprietorship, the one owner—the sole proprietor—is responsible for all of the decisions about the business. That person wears many hats, often being in charge of leadership, marketing, product development, finances, manufacturing, and customer service, among other things. The rewards that person receives for taking primary responsibility for all aspects of their business include being entitled to any profits the business earns. Like a sole proprietor, the partners in a general partnership play many roles in the business and have primary responsibility for all decisions. Partners typically divide up

TMP-0376.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0376.text: the roles based on each partner’s skills, experiences, and preferences. They also share in the profits and losses of the business.

TMP-0377.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0377.text: Left: Tony Tallec/Alamy Stock Photo; right: Graham Prentice/ Alamy Stock Photo Extended description for Consultants and Businesses In the first photo, a woman wearing headphones works on a laptop. The second photo shows a business sign for the company BRYAN CAVE LEIGHTON PAISNER. A logo on the sign shows the letters B C L P overlapping. Influencers, freelance writers, and consultants often run their businesses as sole proprietors. Many law firms are set up as partnerships named after the partners.

TMP-0378.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0378.text: Roles and Responsibilities in Larger Organizations LG How are large businesses typically organized? A small business like your local pizza shop might simply have an owner or manager who oversees a few employees. A large business has multiple departments and added layers of complexity that require more levels of leadership. An organizational structure is a framework that defines the hierarchy, roles, and relationships of people and departments within an organization. Figure 1.7-2 illustrates a conventional “top-down” organizational structure of a large corporation. There are a variety of other ways in which businesses may choose to organize roles and responsibilities, but we will focus on this typical organizational structure.

TMP-0379.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0379.text: Board of Directors Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Chief Operating Officer (COO) Operations Staff Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Accounting and Finance Staff Chief Marketing Officer (CMO) Marketing Staff Chief Information Officer (CIO) Information Technology Staff Chief Technology Officer (CTO) Software and Engineering Staff Copyright © BFW Publishers Extended description for Figure 1.7-2 An Example of Organizational Structure The flowchart reads as follows: • Board of Directors ○ Chief Executive Officer (C E O) ▪ Chief Operating Officer (C O O) ▪ Operations Staff

TMP-0380.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0380.text: ▪ Chief Financial Officer (C F O) ▪ Accounting and Finance Staff ▪ Chief Marketing Officer (C M O) ▪ Marketing Staff ▪ Chief Information Officer (C I O) ▪ Information Technology Staff ▪ Chief Technology Officer (C T O) ▪ Software and Engineering Staff Figure 1.7-2 An Example of Organizational Structure organizational structure A framework that defines the hierarchy, roles, and relationships of people and departments within an organization.

TMP-0381.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0381.text: In the case study for this module, we will examine a relatively flat organizational structure in which employees have more authority to make decisions and more flexibility to choose their own roles. However, the advantages of a top-down or hierarchical structure make it the choice of most businesses. A clear chain of command lets employees know what their role is and who to report to. Leaders at several levels guide the direction of the business. Those leaders are able to make strategic decisions more swiftly than could be expected if all employees were involved. Strong and effective leadership at the top can help an organization pull out of a slump or pull away from the competition. And specialization by departments at lower levels of the hierarchy delegates responsibilities to people who develop expertise and efficiency in their areas. Leadership At the top of a corporation is the board of directors , which is a group of individuals elected by company shareholders to oversee the leadership and strategy of the organization. Every company that sells shares of stock to the public must have a board of directors. Next in the hierarchy is the chief executive officer (CEO) , who is the highest-ranking executive in the company. The CEO reports to the board of directors.

TMP-0382.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0382.text: board of directors A group of people elected by company shareholders to oversee the organization’s leadership and strategy. chief executive officer (CEO) The highest-ranking executive in a corporation. Reporting directly to the CEO is a team of high-level executives collectively referred to as the C-suite, because their titles typically begin with the letter “C” as in “Chief.” Table 1.7-2 outlines some common C-suite roles. The C-suite may also include officers over human resources, security, ethics, and compliance (with regulations), among other areas. The staff below the C-suite typically includes directors and/or department managers who report to the executives, and employees who report to the middle management. Table 1.7-2 Who’s in the C-Suite? Title Responsibilities Chief executive officer (CEO) Makes major decisions, creates a corporate vision, oversees operations, communicates with the board of directors about company strategy, and is responsible for the company’s performance.

TMP-0383.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0383.text: Chief operating officer (COO) Oversees the sourcing of materials, the production process, and the implementation of the company’s business strategies as efficiently as possible. Chief financial officer (CFO) Responsible for the financial operations of the company. This officer develops financial strategies, budgets, and forecasts; manages cash flow; and analyzes financial risks. Chief marketing officer (CMO) Responsible for marketing strategies that communicate the value of the company’s products to customers. Chief information officer (CIO) Oversees the planning, development, and implementation of technology inside the organization. Chief technology officer (CTO) Responsible for externally facing technology creation and design, anticipating customer needs and focusing on emerging technologies. Outsourcing Some of the roles and responsibilities of a business can be handled with greater expertise, or at a lower cost, by a business that specializes in that type of work. The business can outsource those functions, meaning that another business is hired to complete the work. Outsourcing is common for tasks that require specific skills that employees at many businesses lack, such as legal services, accounting, staff recruitment, social media management, and technical support. A business may also

TMP-0384.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0384.text: outsource some of its functions when labor costs are high and another firm can get the job done for less. An insurance company that wants to provide after-hours customer support might hire a call-center business that employs hundreds of workers to answer phone calls and exchange information. And a company that sells jewelry might hire a security company to protect its assets rather than trying to hire and train a group of employees for a role very different from anything in the skill set of a jeweler. outsourcing A business’s hiring of another business to handle some of its functions.

TMP-0385.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0385.text: Specialized Departments LG What specialized departments are typical in a larger business, and what are their roles? Within most large businesses, specialized departments focus on narrow functions such as finance or human resources management. Within these departments, employees develop and apply expertise that improves the efficiency of the organization. Rather than having many specialized departments, a small business may hire other businesses with expertise in areas such as accounting and marketing to handle those types of work. In this section, we explore six key specialized departments to learn what tasks they tackle.

TMP-0386.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0386.text: Sales and Marketing Businesses often combine sales and marketing teams into a single department where they collaborate to identify, reach, and attract customers and generate revenue for the business. Sales refers to the activities that generate revenue by finding potential customers, engaging them, and converting them into buyers. Salespeople cultivate relationships with customers and work to provide product solutions that meet their needs. For instance, in a store that sells smartphones, salespeople will try to identify likely buyers, determine what products will suit their interests, and provide information about features, pricing, and product support that encourage a purchase. But what got the potential customers through the door at that smartphone store may have been the work of the marketing team. sales The activities that generate revenue by finding potential customers, engaging them, and converting them into buyers. Marketing is the process of generating awareness of a company’s brand and helping people find value in the company’s products. Without successful marketing, many companies would collapse due to a lack of customers, which would result in few sales

TMP-0387.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0387.text: and little or no profit. Marketers conduct research to analyze the needs of potential customers and launch campaigns to spark interest in a company’s brand and products. Marketers work to identify a specific group of people who are most likely to buy the company’s products and then target that group with influential messaging and promotions. For example, the marketing team at Apple views young, affluent consumers as likely buyers of their smartphones. To market to that group, the team develops advertising filled with personalities and music that appeal to young people and places the ads in digital spaces popular among the target audience. marketing The process of generating awareness of a company’s brand and helping people find value in the company’s products. While sales is about creating relationships and converting a potential customer into a paying customer, marketing is more about building and communicating a brand to a target market. Think of marketing as more strategic—bigger view—and sales as more tactical—getting the customer to actually pay for a product or service. Salespeople generally have shorter-term goals than marketers, often focusing on achieving monthly sales goals rather than long-term brand awareness. Table 1.7-3 outlines the differences between sales and marketing.

TMP-0388.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0388.text: Table 1.7-3 The Differences Between Sales and Marketing Sales Marketing Goals Reach sales quotas, build customer base, sell product Communicate product, service, brand Time frame Shorter-term view Longer-term view Focus Generate sales revenue Build interest Connection to customer Build a relationship Popularize a brand Research and Development It is much easier to succeed with marketing and sales if the products are just what customers desire, which is what research and development (R&D) teams aim to deliver. The research and development department focuses on innovation by developing and improving goods and services to meet customers’ needs. Businesses invest in research and development to stay ahead of the competition with cutting-edge products. Research and development teams conduct market research to learn what is needed. They create

TMP-0389.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0389.text: and test new products. And they collaborate with other departments to make sure new product concepts fit into the overall mission of the business. research and development department A department focusing on innovation by developing and improving goods and services to meet customers’ needs. The Boeing Company invests more than $3 billion in research and development each year to drive innovation in the aerospace and defense industries. Its recent projects include self-driving, all-electric air taxis; unmanned aircraft that can take off from aircraft carriers and refuel other planes; and new inkjet printing processes for painting airplanes. Operations Operations are a business’s activities that create and deliver products. Smooth- running, efficient operations are essential for all companies and critical for business success. The operations department oversees the production process and develops systems to deliver products to customers. Operations managers monitor the company’s

TMP-0390.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0390.text: systems and processes with the goal of reducing the costs of materials, labor, and technology. operations department A department overseeing the production process and developing systems to deliver products to customers. For a company to compete successfully within an industry, it must convert resources into goods or services as efficiently as possible. Typically, an operations manager directs the production process of transforming inputs into outputs . For example, Starbucks’ inputs include human resources (people), facilities and processes (roasting plants, warehouses), technology (data and digital technology), raw materials (coffee beans), and other materials (paper cups, ceramic cups, lids), which are converted into outputs such as goods (a cup of high-quality, fair-trade coffee and other products) and services (retail and café space) to meet customer desires and demands. Companies like Starbucks must work hard to continually improve their production processes by focusing on quality, and eliminating or reducing costs without sacrificing that quality.

TMP-0391.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0391.text: Finance The finance department is responsible for managing a business’s financial dealings. This department monitors the availability of funds for business operations, takes steps to obtain more funds when necessary, and collects data on business trends and economic activity relevant to the business. The finance department funnels this information into strategy recommendations, reports to investors, budget planning, assessments of financial risks, and filings of government documents in compliance with tax laws and financial-reporting requirements. The finance department takes care of paying suppliers and, in most cases, employees. finance department A department responsible for managing a business’s financial dealings. Funds are essential to a business the way water is essential for a human being. Without adequate funds, employees cannot be paid, supplies cannot be purchased, machines cannot be fixed, and selling space cannot be rented. The finance department uses risk assessments, reports, and budgets to foresee and avoid shortfalls. In the face of financial struggles, effective strategies by the finance department can be critical to a business’s survival and recovery. When funds are low, this department can try to raise

TMP-0392.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0392.text: funds by taking out loans, selling stock, or collecting unpaid invoices. In a dire situation, the finance department can identify root causes, implement cost-cutting measures, and negotiate an extended payment timeline with those who are owed money. SDI Productions/Getty Images Finance departments collect many different kinds of data and funnel it into the strategy, budget planning, and risk assessments that keep firms financially healthy.

TMP-0393.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0393.text: Accounting The accounting department keeps track of day-to-day transactions related to earnings, expenditures, assets (what the company owns), and liabilities (what the company owes). This department is often housed within the finance department. The accounting department is responsible for creating the financial statements that leaders use to make sound financial decisions, as we will discuss in Unit 3 . Its financial records also assist with budget planning, projections of future financial conditions, tax preparation, and compliance with financial regulations. accounting department A department that keeps track of day-to-day transactions related to a business’s earnings, expenditures, assets, and liabilities. For a retail store such as Target, the accounting department’s roles include recording daily sales, monitoring the money held in cash registers, and documenting the cost of goods and the value of inventory. For a Ford dealership, the accounting department keeps track of money that should be coming in from car buyers and helps to assure that the dealership’s bills for rent, cars, staffing, utilities, advertising, and other expenses are paid. In every case, the accounting department can improve financial transparency,

TMP-0394.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0394.text: compliance with regulations, and decisions about how the business uses its limited resources. Human Resources Human resource management (HRM) is the practice of recruiting, hiring, training, and evaluating an organization’s employees. The human resources department focuses on putting people with the right skills, knowledge, and motivation in the right places to serve the needs of the business and its various departments. Human resource policies affect every aspect of your job in a business, including your salary, training, behavioral conduct, promotions, performance reviews, compensation, and benefits. Without the HRM function, employees would be left without any support. Effective HRM leads to more satisfied employees. Businesses with more satisfied employees have lower turnover, higher productivity, increased profits, and greater employee loyalty. human resources department A department focused on putting people with the right skills, knowledge, and motivation in the right places to serve the needs of a business and its various departments.

TMP-0395.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0395.text: Managers in every type of organization know that success depends on the quality of employees. Exceptionally talented workers can give a company an enormous competitive and strategic advantage over rivals. Yet, today’s organizations struggle to fill positions because they cannot find the right people to match the skills they are seeking. Workforce shortages and failure to attract or retain talented workers are among the top risks for organizations in North America. 1 Grocery store chain Trader Joe’s runs an exemplary HRM program. Employees are given comprehensive customer service training, enjoy a great deal of autonomy in how they interact with customers, and receive above-average compensation and benefits. Because of its HRM strategy, Trader Joe’s has successfully attracted and retained talented employees and helped them be productive. With that skilled and satisfied workforce, the company built a flourishing business with happy customers.

TMP-0396.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0396.text: Bloomberg/Getty Images Thanks to Trader Joe’s successful HRM strategy, Glassdoor recently named the grocery store chain one of the best places in the United States to work.

TMP-0397.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0397.text: Module 1.7 Review Learning Goals LG What are the four most common types of business organization, and what are the advantages and disadvantages of each? • A sole proprietorship is a business owned and controlled by one person. This is the simplest and most inexpensive legal structure to adopt. • A partnership involves two or more people who share the ownership, management, and profits or losses of a business. In both a partnership and a sole proprietorship, the owners are responsible for the debts and legal claims resulting from the misfortunes of the business. • A limited liability company (LLC) is a business structure that combines the relatively simple business structure of sole proprietorships and partnerships with

TMP-0398.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0398.text: the limited liability of a corporation. LLCs generally do not issue bonds or stocks. LLCs aren’t for everyone. Some small businesses face very little liability risk and prefer to avoid the paperwork and fees involved in becoming an LLC. • A corporation is owned by shareholders but is a legal entity apart from its owners. A corporation is more complex to set up and run, but it generally protects its owners from being personally liable for the corporation’s debts and other obligations. Another advantage to a corporation is its ability to raise capital by issuing bonds or shares of stock. LG What do business owners do in sole proprietorships and partnerships? • Sole proprietorships and partnerships are relatively simple and inexpensive legal structures to adopt. • In a sole proprietorship, the one owner is responsible for all decisions about the business and may be in charge of leadership, marketing, product development, finances, manufacturing, and customer service, among other roles. The sole proprietor is entitled to any profits the business earns.

TMP-0399.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0399.text: • Like a sole proprietor, the partners in a partnership play many roles in the business and have primary responsibility for all decisions. Partners typically divide up the roles based on each partner’s skills, experiences, and preferences. They also share in the business’s profits and losses. LG How are large businesses typically organized? • An organizational structure is a framework that defines the hierarchy, roles, and relationships of people and departments within an organization. • At the top of a corporation is the board of directors , a group of individuals elected by company shareholders to oversee the leadership and strategy of the organization. • Next in the hierarchy of command is the chief executive officer (CEO) , who is the highest-ranking executive in the company. • Below the CEO is the C-suite of other leaders such as the chief operating officer, the chief financial officer, and the chief marketing officer. Below them are the staff of their respective departments.

TMP-0400.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0400.text: • Some of the roles and responsibilities of a business can be handled with greater expertise, or at a lower cost, by a business that specializes in that type of work. The business can outsource those functions, meaning that another business is hired to complete the work. LG What specialized departments are typical in a larger business, and what are their roles? • As businesses grow, so do the benefits from specialized departments. Within these departments, employees develop and apply expertise that improves the efficiency of the organization. • Sales refers to the activities that generate revenue by finding potential customers, engaging them, and converting them into buyers. Marketing is the process of generating awareness of a company’s brand and helping people find value in the company’s products. Sales and marketing are often combined into a single department.

TMP-0401.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0401.text: • The research and development department focuses on innovation by developing and improving goods and services to meet customers’ needs. • Operations are a business’s activities that create and deliver products. Smooth-running, efficient operations are essential for all companies and critical for business success. The operations department oversees the production process and develops systems to deliver products to customers. • The finance department is responsible for managing a business’s financial dealings. • The accounting department keeps track of day-to-day transactions related to earnings, expenditures, assets (what the company owns), and liabilities (what the company owes). • The human resources department focuses on putting people with the right skills, knowledge, and motivation in the right places to serve the needs of the business and its various departments.
