TMP-0405.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0405.text: CASE STUDY Zappos Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images Zappos, now a subsidiary of Amazon, sells a billion dollars’ worth of shoes annually. Its secret to success includes openness to experimentation with organizational structure. We’ll learn just how unusual the structure at Zappos is in this module’s case study.

TMP-0406.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0406.text: When you consider buying shoes online, you might go to Zappos. Founded in 1999 by entrepreneur Nick Swinmurn with $2 million, sold to Amazon in 2009 for $2 billion, and consistently recognized as a great place to work, Zappos is hailed as a company that cares about its 1,500 employees’ happiness. The company’s core values, listed below, give insight into what it feels like to work at Zappos. 2 Zappos’s 10 Core Values: 1. Deliver WOW Through Service 2. Embrace and Drive Change 3. Create Fun and A Little Weirdness 4. Be Adventurous, Creative, and Open-Minded 5. Pursue Growth and Learning 6. Build Open and Honest Relationships with Communication 7. Build a Positive Team and Family Spirit 8. Do More With Less 9. Be Passionate and Determined 10. Be Humble

TMP-0407.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0407.text: The rapid growth of Zappos from a small, “innovative and quirky” startup to a much larger corporation had the potential to threaten everything that made Zappos exceptional—the employees and culture. To address this issue, in 2013 Zappos made the controversial move to organize the company as holacracy , which is a decentralized way of structuring a company that distributes decision-making power throughout the organization. Within a holacracy , people do not have job titles and are self-managed. Zappos desired a structure that would give employees more freedom and autonomy but also encourage growth and productivity. Rather than following the more common hierarchical structure populated with top management, middle managers, supervisors, and subordinates, the organization was divided into small teams called “circles” of employees. Prior to the transition, Zappos had 150 departments that eventually evolved into 500 circles. Within these circles, the employees would come together to decide what work each person would excel in. They were given the freedom to design their own roles and guidelines. John Bunch, a lead organizational designer at Zappos, explained that the new model meant stepping

TMP-0408.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0408.text: away from traditional ideas of what “work” means, and empowering individual team members with personal accountability: It’s not leaderless. There are certainly people who hold a bigger scope of purpose for the organization than others. What it does do is distribute leadership into each role. Everyone is expected to lead and be an entrepreneur in their own roles, and Holacracy empowers them to do so. 3 The transition to holacracy was challenging. Not everyone was comfortable working in such an environment. Employees who didn’t embrace the new structure were offered severance packages; 18% of Zappos employees accepted the offer and left. Over the first decade of its experiment, Zappos moved away from pure holacracy. 4 In search of the best balance of autonomy, guidance, and incentives, the company reintroduced managers and increased incentives for customer service. Each circle became responsible for its own profits and losses while maintaining the collaborative focus and flexibility of a circular organizational structure.

TMP-0410.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0410.text: MODULE 1.8 Supply Chains LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 1.8.A Discuss the key factors in production and distribution decisions 1.8.B Describe the elements of supply chains 1.8.C Explain how supply chain management can provide a competitive advantage

TMP-0411.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0411.text: AzmanL/Getty Images Artisan-made bread is not cheap, but it appeals to customers who like high-quality, local products that are made by hand in traditional ways.

TMP-0412.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0412.text: The Production Process LG What factors shape a business’s production process? Whether they sell belts, bagels, or bird cages, businesses that sell goods must choose among production processes ranging from handcrafting by artisans to mass production in factories. A business will consider its core competencies, the priorities of its customers, and the competitive landscape, and then choose among production options of various sizes and levels of mechanization. We will explore the benefits and costs at two extremes of these possibilities: artisan processes and mass-production processes. Many businesses adopt a middle ground, hoping to enjoy some of the benefits of both ends of the range at a moderate cost.

TMP-0413.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0413.text: Artisan Processes Artisan processes involve skilled craftspeople who employ traditional, minimally mechanized production processes to make goods in limited quantities. Artisans make everything from cheese to furniture to clothing. The quality of their goods is typically high. Their prices tend to be high as well, because their labor-intensive processes require more of a worker’s time per unit of output. Those prices also reflect the need for workers with a high level of skill. It takes years of training and practice to gain expertise in the creation of jewelry, ceramics, and textiles by hand. In contrast, the machines that mass produce these products in factories can be operated by a relatively small number of workers with weeks or months of experience. artisan processes Production processes involving skilled craftspeople who employ traditional, nonmechanized methods to make goods in limited quantities. Key benefits of artisan processes include the high quality of products, the ability to make unique, customized items, and the elevated value consumers place on traditional, hand-crafted goods. In many cases, artisan-made products are made to serve a local market, and customers appreciate the opportunity to support their community. Artisans

TMP-0414.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0414.text: may use detail-oriented, authentic, or creative methods that appeal to specific customer segments. Artisan production processes also reduce the need for large investments in capital such as machinery and factories. The cons of artisan processes include higher labor costs, longer production times, and the resulting need for higher prices. The reliance on skilled workers can make staffing a challenge and limit the ability to scale up production in the event that demand for an artisan product grows. And the nonuniform nature of handmade products can lead to quality inconsistencies and customer dissatisfaction. The advisability of artisan processes depends on the product and the market. This method becomes feasible if the market is small or if a business is targeting a small portion of a larger market. The high costs of artisan production can be justified if customers value high-quality, traditional, or handmade goods. Artisan processes can also serve businesses with limited financial resources. For example, Coco Chanel started sewing as a young girl living in an orphanage. She later became a seamstress and clothing designer. After years of making clothing using artisan processes, her company became famous. She then had the need and the finances to scale up production, which could only meet demand by relying more and more on mass-production processes.

TMP-0415.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0415.text: Mass-Production Processes The processes used to make Wonder Bread, Kraft cheese, and Gap clothing are very different from artisan processes. Mass-production processes involve manufacturing large quantities of a standardized good. The use of assembly lines, machinery, robots, and various forms of technology in mass production minimizes the need for worker involvement. This automation also leads to increased uniformity and consistency in the final product and increases the speed of production. Due to high production levels, the cost of machinery is spread across many units of output and the business experiences economies of scale (discussed in Module 1.2 ). The primary benefits of mass production are thus standardization, speed, volume, and low per-unit costs. mass-production processes Production processes that involve manufacturing large quantities of a standardized good.

TMP-0416.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0416.text: OLIVER CHASSIGNOLE/Getty Images Mass-produced bread appeals to customers who appreciate its lower price and consistent quality—and it is widely available in stores because it is made in large quantities. The cons of mass production include high startup costs for the business, limited customization, and the environmental impact of production processes that require a lot

TMP-0417.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0417.text: of energy and create waste. The repetitive tasks of factory work can also lead to worker dissatisfaction. And mass-produced goods are less appealing to consumers looking for local, traditional, or handmade products. Mass production works well for businesses that target a large number of customers who value consistency and affordability. Examples of mass-produced products include packaged foods such as cereal, consumer electronics such as televisions, basic clothing items such as shoes, and automobiles. Table 1.8-1 summarizes the pros and cons of artisan and mass-production processes. Table 1.8-1 Common Pros and Cons of Production Processes Artisan Processes Mass-Production Processes Pros High quality Uniqueness Handmade items Locally made items Low startup costs Standardization Speed Volume Low per-unit costs Low prices

TMP-0419.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0419.text: Supply Chains LG What are supply chains, and how do businesses manage them? If you want to sell something, you must have something to sell. If you want to make something, you must have something to make it with. Even service providers such as banks, hospitals, and schools need skilled workers, data, technology, materials, and supplies to support their work. Most businesses rely on supply chains that get things to where they are needed. A supply chain is a network of people, processes, and organizations that provide everything necessary for the creation and delivery of a good or service. Supply chains may operate on a local, regional, or global level. supply chain A network of people, processes, and organizations that provide everything necessary for the creation and delivery of a good or service.

TMP-0420.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0420.navLabel: The Supply Chain for a Good
TMP-0420.text: The Supply Chain for a Good A good’s supply chain journey begins when the product is a glimmer in an entrepreneur’s eye and ends with the good in consumers’ hands. As shown in Figure 1.8-1 , this includes the stages of planning, sourcing, production, distribution, retail sales, and utilization: Planning: With research and planning, a business determines what inputs are needed to provide its good. These may include raw materials, such as wheat or cotton, as well as component parts , such as hinges for doors or memory chips for computers. Sourcing: Raw materials are extracted or harvested, then processed into usable materials or component parts, and transported to a manufacturing facility. Production: Raw materials and component parts are turned into a finished product. Distribution: The good is transported to distribution centers and retail stores. Retail sales: The good is delivered to consumers and payments are collected. Utilization: Manufacturers and retailers collect feedback from customers to improve their product, provide product support, and accept returns.

headings.text: The Supply Chain for a Good

TMP-0421.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0421.navLabel: The Supply Chain for a Good
TMP-0421.text: Planning › Sourcing › Production › Distribution › Retail Sales › Utilization Copyright © BFW Publishers Extended description for Figure 1.8-1 The Supply Chain for a Good ⓘ Figure 1.8-1 The Supply Chain for a Good At the heart of this process is the flow of raw materials to manufacturers, the distribution of goods to retailers, and the delivery of goods and services to consumers. Along the way, many products are handled by intermediaries who form a link along the supply chain. One example is suppliers, who buy raw materials or manufactured goods from one business and sell them to another business. For example, in Figure 1.8-2 , a supplier buys grain from a farm and sells it to a cereal manufacturer. Similar to suppliers but generally further along in the supply chain are distributors , who typically buy products from manufacturers and sell them to retail stores. In Figure 1.8-2 , a distributor buys cereal from the cereal manufacturer and sells it to grocery stores.

TMP-0423.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0423.navLabel: The Supply Chain for a Good
TMP-0423.text: Figure 1.8-2 The Supply Chain for Cereal distributor A business that typically buys products from manufacturers and sells them to retail stores. Like people when they take a journey, at various points along their paths, materials and goods need a place to stay. Many types of grains, for example, are harvested in the fall and then stored in warehouses or other storage facilities until they are needed. Warehouses can hold items for extended periods of time. Distribution centers specialize in receiving items from manufacturers, suppliers, or storage facilities that are quickly sent to retailers or customers. Some distribution centers are owned by large retailers such as Amazon and Walmart. Others are owned by independent distributors. Distribution centers are located near major highways, airports, or rail lines where delivery vehicles have easy access. A distribution center can serve as a central hub for many types of goods. From there, the mix of goods desired by a particular retailer can be combined and delivered. Without these intermediaries, each manufacturer would have to send its own truck to each retailer, which would be very inefficient.

TMP-0424.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0424.navLabel: The Supply Chain for a Good
TMP-0424.text: distribution centers Facilities that specialize in receiving items from manufacturers, suppliers, or storage facilities that are quickly sent to retailers or customers. As another example of a supply chain in action, consider what it takes to get a wool sweater to you. Before you can wear a wool sweater, a sheep farm must collect wool and store it until it is needed. A supplier then delivers the wool to a textile mill that spins it into yarn. The yarn is then sold to a sweater manufacturer to be woven into sweaters. Then the sweaters go to a distribution center where they are loaded up on trucks with other products and delivered to clothing stores, one of which finally gets a sweater to you. All of the planning, procurement of materials, production, distribution, and delivery along this journey is part of the supply chain for wool sweaters.

TMP-0425.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0425.navLabel: The Supply Chain for a Good
TMP-0425.text: David Anderson Empty shelves in grocery stores during the COVID-19 pandemic were symptomatic of supply chain disruptions that caused shortages of household essentials, such as toilet paper and baby formula.

TMP-0426.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0426.navLabel: The Supply Chain for a Service
TMP-0426.text: The Supply Chain for a Service Barbershops, auto mechanics, concert halls, and gyms are among the businesses that provide services rather than goods. The supply chain for a service provides the employees, skills, processes, supplies, information, and delivery systems needed to offer the service to customers. The supply chain for a service is less about moving materials and goods around than about providing human resources, communications, facilities, and equipment. That said, most service providers do need some physical items. Healthcare providers need medicine, childcare providers need diapers, housepainters need paint, and law firms need office supplies. Consider the companies that provide cloud computing services, such as iCloud and Google Drive. They rely on teams of employees with advanced skills in computing. They require information about consumer demand and cloud computing processes. And they use large server farms filled with computer servers that store all your files. The supply chain delivers the people, capabilities, processes, and equipment the companies need and the web-based platforms that give you access to their services.

headings.text: The Supply Chain for a Service

TMP-0427.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0427.navLabel: The Supply Chain for a Service
TMP-0427.text: Unlike for most goods, customers must be present when many types of services are provided. For instance, the supply chain for teaching, professional sports, therapy, live music, financial advising, and medical services must deliver ways to bring service providers and customers together. That leads to the provision of classrooms, stadiums, clinics, conference rooms, concert halls, and video conferencing platforms. The supply chain for a service spans the entire life of that product. Before a service can be provided, decisions must be made about what will be delivered, how, when, by whom, and for whom. Then the inputs are acquired and the delivery channels are established. Finally, the provider of any service or good is wise to seek feedback on the product and try to make it better. Figure 1.8-3 shows the stages of planning, sourcing, delivery, and follow-up for a service: Planning: Assessing customer needs, designing the service, and ensuring the availability of necessary inputs such as workers and technology. Sourcing: Obtaining the people, facilities, equipment, technology, supplies, and other inputs needed to provide the service. Delivery: Performing the service and granting customers access, which can involve scheduling appointments, selling tickets, and other support services.

TMP-0428.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0428.navLabel: The Supply Chain for a Service
TMP-0428.text: Follow-up: The process of collecting customer feedback, handling returns, and refining the service to assure quality and customer satisfaction. Planning ➤ Sourcing ➤ Delivery ➤ Follow up Copyright © BFW Publishers Extended description for Figure 1.8-3 The Supply Chain for a Service The flowchart reads as follows: Planning Sourcing Delivery Follow up Figure 1.8-3 The Supply Chain for a Service

TMP-0429.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0429.navLabel: The Supply Chain for a Service
TMP-0429.text: thianchai sitthikongsak/Getty Images An auto repair shop’s product is a service. To deliver that service well, the shop needs skilled workers, and those workers require a reliable supply of auto parts, tools, equipment, and work space. The shop also needs a system for scheduling customer appointments and accommodating walk-ins. Ideally, the business owners will take account of customers’ feedback to refine and improve their service.

TMP-0430.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0430.navLabel: The Supply Chain for a Service
TMP-0430.text: Consider the supply chain for an auto repair shop called Unbreak Your Brakes located in a mountain town in Colorado. In the planning stage, the business would consider the needs of its customers. Drivers in the mountains have particular needs for repairs of brakes and engine cooling systems. Unbreak Your Brakes will want to design a service that ensures the availability of workers with expertise in these repairs. The business should also plan for a steady availability of parts such as brake pads, radiators, water pumps, hoses, and cooling fans. In the sourcing stage, the business will obtain the needed staff, parts, installation equipment, and supplies such as engine coolant. Sources of parts can include automakers who supply OEM (original equipment manufacturer) parts, which means they are made by the same company that made the vehicle. Other sources include companies like Bosch, which provide “aftermarket” parts (parts not made by the automobile’s manufacturer) that typically cost less than OEM parts. Large distributors such as NAPA Auto Parts purchase parts from manufacturers and ship them to auto repair shops like this one.

TMP-0431.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0431.navLabel: The Supply Chain for a Service
TMP-0431.text: For the delivery stage, Unbreak Your Brakes will determine the best way to provide auto repairs to its customers. The shop’s location, hours, staffing, communication with customers, and payment process are all elements of delivery. The business may decide to schedule customer appointments or provide services on a first-come, first-served basis. Perhaps, the shop will have a tow truck that brings broken-down cars in for customers. And it should ensure a mechanic with expertise in each type of common repair is scheduled during all hours of operation. The follow-up stage for Unbreak Your Brakes is a time to work on customer satisfaction and quality control. To make sure the service was successful, a quick call or email to each car owner the day after the repair would help cement the shop’s relationship with customers. A more detailed customer survey could identify areas of strength and weakness within the service-delivery system. The shop must also decide how it will handle customers who are unhappy with their repairs. Those customers are often ready to sever ties with the business and post negative reviews on social media, but friendly treatment and follow-up to complete the repair can regain their trust and loyalty.

TMP-0432.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0432.text: For both services and goods, the complexity of the supply chains and the underlying decision making justify careful considerations and oversight from a dedicated type of management, as discussed in the next two sections. Considerations When Choosing Suppliers Decisions about sources are complicated by tradeoffs, and that’s not just for businesses. When you choose where to buy your food, phone, or backpack, you have options that are cheaper but riskier, because the quality of cheaper brands may be inferior. The most convenient food stores nearby may be smaller, with higher prices and less selection than the larger stores farther away. And the car companies with the best reputations may make you wait longer for delivery or charge premium prices. Businesses face the same types of dilemmas. When choosing suppliers, businesses assess the factors of quality, cost, convenience, risk, and efficiency. Common decisions between high-quality, high-cost suppliers and low-quality, low-cost suppliers often hinge on the business’s strategy. If superior quality for the final product is the goal, the more expensive suppliers may be the best choice. If

TMP-0433.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0433.text: the business seeks competitive advantage through low prices, the sacrifice of quality is more appropriate. Businesses that depend on flexibility and speed in their supply chain should choose suppliers that are convenient and efficient. For example, a restaurant facing unpredictable spikes in daily demand needs easy access to extra food supplied and will choose a local supplier that responds quickly to orders. In contrast, a bike manufacturer with firm plans for next year’s production levels may know it needs 1,000 bike wheels in six months. That company can choose a relatively inconvenient source on the other side of the world if it offers better prices or quality. The suppliers with the lowest prices are often relatively unknown or far away. Suppliers with questionable reputations present the risks of quality issues or production errors. Relatively distant suppliers can jeopardize the supply chain due to risks of political instability that interrupts trade or natural disasters somewhere on the path between the business and the source. These potential problems—along with risks of resource shortages and price increases that can occur anywhere—motivate careful choices to protect the competitive advantage that supply chains can convey, as we’ll examine next.

TMP-0434.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas

TMP-0435.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0435.text: Using a Supply Chain to Gain Competitive Advantage LG How do strategies for competitive advantage affect supply chain decisions? Every business needs people to oversee the flow of inputs, information, goods or services, and payments from their source to their destination. A large company is likely to have a supply chain manager and a dedicated staff to coordinate the activities within the supply chain. In a small business, the people who handle supply chain issues might be the same people who design the advertising and sweep the floor. Either way, the supply chain team can achieve more than simply getting things where they need to go. The team can also aim to boost profits by reducing costs, improving quality, and limiting competition in ways that create competitive advantage.

TMP-0436.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0436.text: Competitive Advantage from Low Prices Businesses can set themselves apart by finding ways to lower costs and then passing some of the savings on to consumers. Consider Toyota, whose supply chain is set up to bring auto parts to factories just in time for them to be put onto cars on the assembly line. That “just in time” system avoids the need for large storage facilities at Toyota car factories. It also saves time and money on moving car parts from storage facilities to assembly lines, because delivery trucks from suppliers go straight to the assembly area where the parts are quickly used. The efficiency of Toyota’s supply chain gives that company a cost advantage in the competitive auto market. Improving production efficiency like Toyota did is one of several ways a superior supply chain can provide a business with competitive advantage. Two others that also relate to cost are scaling up and finding low-cost sources. By scaling up the size of its operations, a business can benefit from the spreading of costs (described as economies of scale in Module 1.2 ). For example, suppose a company that makes baseball bats can make twice as many bats per week in the same factory by adding a second shift in the evening. The labor and materials costs will increase, but the cost of the factory and equipment can now be spread over many more bats.

TMP-0437.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0437.text: Scaling up brings additional cost savings from the ability to purchase wood and other inputs in larger volumes—and usually at a lower cost. Beyond the benefits of purchasing in bulk, some businesses obtain lower prices from suppliers by negotiating long-term contracts. By agreeing to purchase from the same wood supplier for many years, the bat manufacturer provides a valuable commitment to the supplier that can encourage leniency on prices.

TMP-0438.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0438.text: picture alliance/Getty Images By scaling up, a baseball bat company could spread the cost of its factory and equipment over many more bats. Module 1.7 explained that when something can be produced at a lower cost by another business, it’s wise to benefit from those cost advantages. Outsourcing is the practice of sourcing a good or a service from another organization. For example, many hotels are

TMP-0439.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0439.text: great at providing a comfortable lodging experience, but efficient sheet and towel washing may not be a core competency. Those hotels typically outsource their laundry service by hiring another firm to pick up the dirty items and return with them efficiently cleaned. Low-cost sources are sometimes found by looking inward at the business’s core competencies. There may be some inputs that the business can make at a relatively low cost itself. Insourcing is the practice of sourcing a good or service from within the organization that was previously outsourced. For example, GE Appliances used to outsource more of the manufacture of its refrigerators and dishwashers to other countries, but after reviewing the capabilities of its U.S. manufacturing facilities, the company found that it could save money by producing more of its own appliances. Lower costs are not the only source of supply chain–related competitive advantage. Another is faster delivery. Many of today’s customers have busy lifestyles and appreciate fast access to products and services. A pizza restaurant that finds faster ways to prepare and deliver pizzas will appeal to hungry diners. And an online retailer that gets its products in the mail a day faster than the competition will have an easier time winning shoppers over.

TMP-0440.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0440.text: AP ® EXAM TIP If an exam question asks how a supply chain can provide competitive advantage in a particular case, be specific in your answer. Don’t just say, “by saving money” or “by making products better.” Explain how a business might gain competitive advantage in the given scenario. If the case is about a coffee bean roaster, you might say that the company can scale up to allow bulk purchases of unroasted beans and spread the cost of roasting equipment across more units of output. Then you can discuss the business’s ability to offer lower prices as a result of the cost savings. Competitive Advantage from Quality Another strategy for gaining competitive advantage is to differentiate products based on quality, as we learned in Module 1.2 . A business might gain access to materials, goods, or services that are superior to what competitors have available. For example, Armani Exchange makes shirts out of pima cotton, whose longer, smoother fibers create a high-quality garment. In service industries, the differentiators can include workers with special skills. That is the case for technology company Nvidia, which prides itself on a workforce with outstanding technical skills that help the company produce exceptional computer chips and graphics cards.

TMP-0441.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0441.text: Quality drives many supply chain decisions for a company like Starbucks, which takes pride in providing high-quality coffee beverages. Starbucks has developed a highly efficient supply chain that spans countries all over the world. The company builds good relationships with coffee bean growers and roasters whose products meet its standards. This helps Starbucks satisfy the demands of its customers and ensure it has the right product, in the right quantity, at the right price. Table 1.8-2 outlines how the Starbucks supply chain works from bean to cup. Table 1.8-2 Starbucks’ Supply Chain: Bean to Cup Sourcing Starbucks sources its coffee beans from almost 30,000 coffee farms all over the world in countries such as Brazil, Colombia, and Mexico and as far-flung as Saudi Arabia, Kenya, and Tanzania. Suppliers must adhere to the Starbucks standards known as Coffee and Farmer Equity (CAFE) and Coffee Sourcing Guidelines (CSG). These standards prohibit suppliers from using forced or child labor and require farms to implement safe work conditions. Supplier relationship management Starbucks continuously works with its suppliers to ensure that operations are running smoothly and that each coffee bean is produced at the highest quality.

TMP-0442.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0442.text: Manufacturing and distribution Starbucks runs highly efficient manufacturing and distribution processes. The raw beans from suppliers are sent to one of Starbucks’ storage facilities (there are six in total), where they are roasted and packaged. The beans are then dispatched to a Starbucks distribution center, and then sent to regional warehouses where they are delivered to retail stores. Delivery and sale Starbucks makes 70,000 deliveries every week all over the world. Its ability to keep up with cutting-edge technology is a huge part of its success. For example, customers can use the Starbucks app to order, pay, and find their closest Starbucks store. Competitive Advantage from Barriers to Entry Some businesses gain competitive advantage by building barriers that inhibit competition. Module 1.2 explained a broad set of barriers to entry . Barriers related to supply chains include restrictive or exclusive agreements with suppliers or distributors. In such agreements, a business can agree to purchase from a supplier only if that supplier does not provide its product to any other business. For example, if Walmart negotiates an exclusive supply agreement with the Quaker Oats company to sell Pumpkin Spice Instant Oatmeal, shoppers must visit Walmart to buy that good. Restrictive or exclusive agreements with suppliers make it difficult or impossible for competitors to provide goods of the same quality.

TMP-0443.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0443.text: Similar agreements are sometimes made in service industries, which can limit access to individuals with special skills and abilities. Exclusivity clauses in employment contracts can prevent a worker from doing any work for a competing employer while working under that contract. Record labels usually require musical artists to sign exclusive contracts that prohibit them from recording with other labels. In other cases, an agreement limits competitors’ ability to access customers. For instance, if the Coca-Cola Company stipulates that restaurants that sell Coke cannot sell Pepsi, that eliminates those restaurants as distribution channels for PepsiCo’s products. By limiting the ways a competitor can deliver its product to customers, a business gains competitive advantage.

TMP-0444.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0444.text: Module 1.8 Review Learning Goals LG What factors shape a business’s production process? A business will consider its core competencies, the priorities of its customers, and the competitive landscape, and then choose among production options of various sizes and levels of mechanization. Artisan processes involve skilled craftspeople who employ traditional, minimally mechanized production processes to make goods in limited quantities. This method becomes feasible if the market is small or if a business is targeting a small portion of a larger market. The high costs of artisan processes can be justified if customers value high-quality, traditional, or handmade goods.

TMP-0445.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0445.text: Mass-production processes involve manufacturing large quantities of a standardized good. The primary benefits of mass production are standardization, speed, volume, and low per-unit costs. LG What are supply chains, and how do businesses manage them? A supply chain is a network of people, processes, and organizations that provide everything necessary for the creation and delivery of a good or service. A good’s supply chain includes the stages of planning, sourcing, production, distribution, retail sales, and utilization. Suppliers buy raw materials or manufactured goods from one business and sell them to another business. Distributors typically buy products from manufacturers and sell them to retail stores. Distribution centers specialize in receiving items from manufacturers, suppliers, or storage facilities that are quickly sent to retailers or customers. The supply chain for a service provides the employees, skills, processes, supplies, information, and delivery systems needed to provide the service to customers. The

TMP-0446.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0446.text: supply chain for a service includes the stages of planning, sourcing, delivery, and follow-up. LG How do strategies for competitive advantage affect supply chain decisions? A superior supply chain can provide competitive advantage by reducing costs, improving quality, or allowing faster delivery. Strategies to lower cost include improving production efficiency, scaling up, insourcing, and outsourcing. To improve quality, a business might gain access to superior materials, goods, or services, or to workers with special skills. Some businesses gain competitive advantage by building barriers that inhibit competition, including restrictive or exclusive agreements with suppliers or distributors. In such agreements, a business can agree to purchase from a supplier only if that supplier does not provide its product to any other business. Similar agreements are sometimes made in service industries, which can limit access to individuals with special skills and abilities. In other cases, an agreement limits

TMP-0447.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0447.text: competitors’ ability to access customers. For example, an agreement can stipulate that sellers of a business’s product cannot also sell competing products. TMP-0450.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0450.text: With more than 8,400 properties operating in 140 countries and territories, it may be hard to believe that Hilton Worldwide grew out of a one-hotel business. Hilton was founded in 1919 by American businessman Conrad Hilton, who purchased the Mobley Hotel in Cisco, Texas, with the goal of building a hotel chain that would provide the best customer experience for its guests. Over the years, the company acquired and built more hotels and resorts to become the lodging powerhouse it is today. Hilton now employs over 180,000 employees and has a net worth of more than $60 billion. Its newer brands include Motto, a “hostel-style micro-hotel”; Signia, targeted at business travelers; and Tempo, a “lifestyle-first luxury hotel.” How does a company grow from being a one-hotel business to having thousands of properties around the world? For Hilton, strategic operations and supply chain management have been critical components of its success. Hilton Supply Management (HSM), which manages the operations and procurement for the Hilton portfolio, is the world’s largest hospitality-focused, end-to-end supply chain provider. Below are some strategies HSM uses to help control quality and drive profitability at its Hilton-branded properties:

TMP-0451.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0451.text: Leveraging its size and massive customer base to negotiate relatively low prices for the 500,000 unique products (from toiletries and linens for guests to cleaning supplies for the housekeeping staff) that it sources from more than 1,200 unique suppliers Developing global and regional pricing agreements to offer the best value for customers Offering furniture, fixtures, and equipment (FF&E) services to help owners complete hotel renovations within their budgets Providing technology resources like its eProcurement platform and Customer Portal so hotel owners can track operations and supply chain activity in real time Building strong supplier and vendor relationships HSM is committed to more than just efficiency and quality control. As part of Hilton’s Travel with Purpose 2030 Goals, the organization has pledged to double the number of diverse suppliers, double its social impact investment, and reduce its carbon emissions, water use, and waste generation by half or more. 1

TMP-0467.text: 5. Describe one example of ethical behavior in a business context. 6. Briefly identify and explain one way your organization can promote ethical behavior for its workforce. 7. Identify two roles or positions that may exist within your firm to protect your company from unethical behavior in the workplace. 8. Explain one way in which supply chains may add or reduce costs for your business. Refer to the case study below when answering Questions 9–11. In 2011, Michael Preysman and Jesse Farmer cofounded Everlane, a clothing company focused on ethical sourcing and radical price transparency. Initially, the brand operated as direct-to-consumer with a target demographic of educated men between 25 and 45 years old. Eventually, Everlane opened retail locations in New York City and San Francisco. As the company grew, it branched out to include a women’s clothing line, while maintaining its focus on casual and office attire. Today, Everlane operates an e- commerce platform along with 11 U.S. store locations in major metropolitan areas. 2

TMP-0468.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0468.text: What makes Everlane unique among retailers is its model of radical transparency . For most companies, consumers know only the final price of the good they’re purchasing. Everlane wanted to show consumers how the company arrives at that price, with every level of sourcing spelled out on its website. 3 Everlane has also initiated a call for “Cleaner Fashion.” This is in stark contrast to today’s “fast-fashion” companies, which offer low prices but come with considerable ethical issues in sourcing, labor, and materials. Ninety-five percent of the cotton used in Everlane apparel is certified organic, regenerative (farmed using methods that restore the land), or recycled. This is especially appealing to millennials and Gen Z consumers, who are more conscious of the environmental impact of their choices than previous generations.

TMP-0469.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0469.text: Many of Everlane’s practices are appealing to its target consumers. Everlane’s leadership produces a highly detailed impact report annually covering its materials, sourcing, and sustainability practices. This allows consumers to understand the production processes of the company in much greater depth. Because Everlane is privately held, it is not required to produce annual financial reports for the public like a company with shares traded on one of the major stock exchanges. 4 In 2020, Everlane came under scrutiny. Internal investigations revealed that employees had used offensive and discriminatory language in the workplace, and that

TMP-0470.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0470.text: management had exhibited inappropriate conduct toward staff. The COVID-19 pandemic also hurt the company, resulting in the layoff of 290 employees while Everlane was fighting unionizing efforts from its workforce. Another major criticism of the company has been that, despite daily emails from potential customers requesting a broader array of clothing sizes, Everlane does not offer extended sizing in its stores or on its website. And while Everlane has marketed itself as a company committed to radical transparency, less than a decade after its establishment, it found itself under fire for failing to track greenhouse gases across its product line. 5 In 2024, Everlane hired a new CEO, Alfred Chang. In fashion, new products come out seasonally, creating tension between sustainability and market-driven industry trends. To combat this, Everlane has created a line of apparel known as the “forever wardrobe.” While the prices are higher than those of fast- fashion companies, the clothes — such as the popular ’90s Forever Jean ($148) — are made to last. In a complex and highly competitive market, it remains to be seen how Everlane will navigate its second decade, balancing sustainability with profitability.

TMP-0472.text: AP ® Skills Workshop: Concept Application Preparing for the AP ® Exam What are the five course skills for this AP® course? There are five skills you’ll need to build for this course. Two of them are Business Skills: Concept Application and Entrepreneurship. The other three are Professional and Leadership Skills: Decision Making, Collaboration, and Communication. You will find five AP® Skills Workshops in this text — one at the end of each of the five units, with each workshop addressing one of the Course Skills. In this workshop, we will focus on Concept Application. Identify Concept Application It is essential to recognize the unique terms and concepts used in the world of business, so that you can begin to think like a business owner and entrepreneur. Concept application is the process of taking what you’ve learned in these modules and thinking about how it shows up or could be used in real-life situations. Applying concepts helps to make them more meaningful and memorable. Understand Concept Application Understanding how to apply these terms and ideas in real-world scenarios will be required for success in this course and on the AP® Exam. Concept application may be tested in the multiple-

TMP-0473.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0473.text: choice section as well as the free-response section of the exam. In this AP® Skills Workshop, we will work to ensure that you understand the concept of competitive advantage. Let’s start with a self-test: Describe the concept of competitive advantage within a business context. Answer: A competitive advantage is a firm’s position of superiority over its competitors. That superiority enables the firm to create more value for its customers, which leads to greater sales, market share, and profit for the firm. Identifying a firm’s competitive advantage is key to understanding what companies have to offer in the marketplace. Buyers have many choices when it comes to the types of products and services they support with their money. A competitive advantage gives buyers a reason to select one product over its competitors. To put concept application into action, let’s consider a real-world example. Children have long enjoyed playing with water, particularly during warmer months. In 1989, NASA engineer Lonnie Johnson invented a toy he called the Power Drencher. The first model was produced and sold by Larami Corporation in 1990, which later rebranded it as the Super Soaker. Unlike previous toy squirt guns, which had low pressure and could spray only very small quantities of water a short distance, the Super Soaker featured an air pressure chamber and a water reservoir. This allowed the toy to blast water 25–50 feet away with accuracy. Kids could play different games with friends that would have been impossible with older models. The toy became so popular that Larami, the corporate owner of the product, was purchased by toy and entertainment giant Hasbro.

TMP-0474.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0474.text: Left: Thomas England/Getty Images; right: Lucy Lambriex/Getty Images Extended description for Super Soakers The first photo shows engineer Lonnie Johnson standing with his creation, the Super Soaker water toy, in his hands. The second photo shows a group of young women outdoors, some seated on grass while others stand. They all look at a woman shooting water from a Super Soaker water toy. Engineer Lonnie Johnson, shown with his invention, achieved a competitive advantage that helped

TMP-0475.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0475.text: Super Soakers capture a large share of the market. Let’s test your knowledge again: Explain the competitive advantage of Johnson’s product. Answer: Johnson’s competitive advantage was that his toy outperformed old water pistols in nearly every way. It could squirt water farther, featured a stronger spray, and could hold much more water due to the attached reservoir. Another important business concept that is key to this example is that of the target demographic . The target demographic is a set of common characteristics of a group of people that a firm seeks to reach with its marketing. They are the most likely customers for the product or service. Characteristics may include age, income level, lifestyle, geographic region, interests, or racial and ethnic identities. The target demographic for the Super Soaker was children between the ages of 7 and 14. Johnson’s own 7-year-old daughter was one of the first to try it out. If Super Soaker’s ads focused on business professionals between 25 and 40 years old who spent most of their time indoors, it’s unlikely that the Super Soaker would have become the most popular water toy ever — generating over $1 billion in sales revenue with 200+ million units sold. While a few business professionals might have been interested, they would not have generated enough sales to meet overhead expenses. Marketing and advertising efforts aimed at the target demographic were key to the Super Soaker’s success.

Business Canvas Project Application Project-Based Learning The Business Canvas Project is a course-long practice in entrepreneurship that is part of this AP® course and exam. (You can learn more about the Business Model Canvas in the Appendix to this textbook.) You may work individually on the project or in a small group of two or three students. You will have the opportunity to choose an idea of your own and execute it over four phases. 1. Develop an idea for a good or service that addresses a specific customer need, want, or problem. This may be a brand-new good or service, or an existing one that is modified with some improvement.

TMP-0477.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas
TMP-0477.text: 2. Formulate a business hypothesis that you will test later. The business hypothesis should be no more than one or two complete sentences. Example: The WholeBodySnacks Company seeks to create simple snacks from all-natural ingredients that can be enjoyed by student athletes or anyone seeking to improve their nutrition on the go. Note: You should not copy that hypothesis. Think of it as a model for applying your own business idea to a particular target demographic. The value proposition — a message summarizing how a product serves customer needs better than the alternatives — should be evident from your business hypothesis. 3. Conduct customer interviews, focus groups, or surveys to help determine if your product idea would be a good fit for the target demographic. These interviews may include your classmates or other individuals from your school community, neighborhood, or workplace. A good survey offers a range of feedback options for customers to specify the strength of their reaction to your idea. Many surveys are done anonymously but still have enough identifying characteristics to establish who the target demographic may be. 4. Use the data collected in your interviews, focus group, or survey research to evaluate the desirability, viability, and feasibility of your idea. Your teacher may ask you to present this formally in a slideshow presentation in class or using a written report format.

TMP-0478.groupTitle: Unit 1 Businesses, Competition, and New Ideas

TMP-0481.text: MODULES 2.1 Marketing to Customers 2.2 Consumer Behavior 2.3 Market Research 2.4 Product 2.5 Price 2.6 Place and Channels 2.7 Promotion and Marketing Communications Marketing Keeps Businesses Afloat As you enter whatever work life you choose, you will need to pay taxes. The process of filing taxes in the United States can be complicated. As businesses do, they have created products to make that daunting task easier. One such business, Intuit, began in the early 1980s with the intention to simplify other types of financial puzzles. Intuit’s first product was Quicken, a software application that helps users manage their budgets and pay bills. The company experienced rapid growth and currently has 18,200 employees in 16 offices across 7 countries.

TMP-0482.text: Today, Intuit’s products include a suite of financial management software geared toward individuals and small businesses. Individuals can use Intuit’s TurboTax to file their taxes and Credit Karma to manage their personal finances. Its other products, QuickBooks and Mailchimp, are marketed toward small businesses. QuickBooks is a bookkeeping software system; Mailchimp is an email marketing campaign service. According to the company website, Intuit’s marketing strategy has evolved from a “house of brands” to a “connected brand ecosystem.” This strategy aligns with the company’s mission, “powering prosperity around the world,” along with its promise to customers of “more money, no work, complete confidence.” Intuit owes its success to strong marketing campaigns, which showcase how Intuit products can improve customers’ lives by solving significant problems. Because small businesses are a target market for the company, Intuit invests in mission-driven marketing campaigns that encourage and support entrepreneurs. During the COVID-19 pandemic—when many small businesses were struggling—it partnered with baseball legend and investor Alex Rodriguez on a video marketing campaign called “Journey to Success,” which showed the ups and downs that business owners experienced on their paths to success. Intuit aired a 2022 Super Bowl commercial showing how QuickBooks

TMP-0483.text: helps small businesses manage their finances. The company is also working to meet the needs of a variety of racial and ethnic groups. To that end, it has launched a marketing campaign for TurboTax products serving Latino taxpayers, which include Spanish-language tools and access to a bilingual tax expert. 1 When a company like Intuit sets its sights on new customers, its marketing campaigns make all the difference. Intuit knows all too well that marketing missteps can threaten a company’s future. An Intuit marketing campaign for TurboTax using the tagline, “Free, free, free” led to a lawsuit and a $141 million settlement because customers were misled about the cost of tax-filing services. 2 As Intuit seeks to expand its customer base, which products should it highlight? What promotions should it run? Where should it offer its services? And what prices should it charge? These and related marketing questions are the focus of Unit 2 . TMP-0484.text: Bloomberg/Getty Images If you want your product to fly off the shelves, it’s not enough to make it well; you must also market it well.

TMP-0485.text: MODULE 2.1 Marketing to Customers LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 2.1.A Explain the purpose of marketing and how marketers obtain and use customer data 2.1.B Discuss market segmentation and the identification of target customers 2.1.C Explain why and how businesses develop relationships with customers 2.1.D Discuss risks associated with the collection and use of customer data

TMP-0486.text: Johnny Greig/Getty Images How did you discover the items in your wardrobe? Have you been influenced?

TMP-0487.text: Marketing and Customer Data LG What is marketing and what role does data play in it? How did you discover your favorite pair of shoes? Did you see an influencer wearing them in a video? Were they featured in a TV commercial or on a billboard? Do the players on your favorite sports team wear them? If any sort of sponsorship or advertising helped you find your prized possessions, you can thank a marketing team. Marketing is the process of promoting, selling, and delivering products that satisfy customers’ identified needs and wants. Marketers conduct research to analyze potential customers’ problems and launch campaigns to spark interest in a company’s brand and products. Without marketing, most companies would fail due to lack of customers, sales, and profit. To boost the numbers in those three areas, marketing teams closely examine other numbers and factual information known as data.

TMP-0488.text: marketing The process of promoting, selling, and delivering products that satisfy customers’ needs and wants. Uses for Customer Data Guesswork leads to mistakes. Businesses prefer to make informed decisions, and when those decisions are about marketing, the information they seek is about customers. Customer data is information businesses collect about their customers to better understand, serve, and engage them. That data helps businesses determine what products would best satisfy customer needs, which customers would most benefit from the products, and how to reach those customers. customer data Information that businesses collect about their customers to better understand, serve, and engage them. Businesses collect data that includes customers’ contact information, personal characteristics, shopping behavior, response to marketing communications, feedback on products, and use of devices. Demographic data is descriptive information about people’s identity, situation, and background. This data identifies measurable characteristics of customers, such as age, gender, race, occupation, income level,

TMP-0489.text: education, marital status, and location. Demographic data helps businesses understand and serve their potential customers. They can use this information to tailor their goods, services, and communications. For example, if a bakery learns that the customers in its market are mostly older adults, it can optimize its marketing efforts by using traditional advertising such as newspapers, radio, and billboards rather than social media platforms popular among teenagers for communication. demographic data Descriptive information about people’s identity, situation, and background. Psychographic data is information on people’s cognitive (mental) and behavioral characteristics. This includes customers’ interests, values, beliefs, attitudes, emotions, lifestyles, motivations, and preferences. Businesses use psychographic data to align their brand with their intended customers’ way of thinking. For instance, if a company that makes frozen dinners finds that its customers are health conscious, it will increase sales by developing dinners low in fat, sugar, and salt and by stressing the health benefits of its meals in marketing campaigns. If a sock company learns that fair labor practices motivate many of its potential customers, it can devote resources to improving worker safety in its factories, and tout that in its advertising.

TMP-0490.text: psychographic data Information on people’s cognitive and behavioral characteristics. Figure 2.1-1 provides examples of demographic data and psychographic data for a high school student. Businesses use both types of data to group customers for targeted marketing efforts.

TMP-0491.text: Demographic data Psychographic data miniseries/Getty Images Female Country music fan 17 years old Values human rights $ Household income of $105,000 per year Risk-averse Texas native Extravert High school student Vegetarian Speaks English and Spanish Aspires to travel globally

Many free online platforms such as Instagram, Google, and X collect data from customers’ registration and online behavior and sell that data to other businesses. Organizations with subscriptions often sell their subscriber lists to businesses with products that would appeal to people on that list. For instance, magazines that cater to exercise enthusiasts may sell their subscriber lists to businesses selling exercise equipment.

TMP-0494.text: SDI Productions/Getty Images If you’re receiving special offers for items you buy regularly, the marketing team has your number. Businesses also collect data for themselves. The grocery retailer Kroger uses information collected from shopping transactions to create customized mailings with coupons for the products customers prefer to buy. Other sources of customer data

TMP-0495.text: include surveys, interviews, and click-tracking of online behavior. Some businesses monitor social media posts to study customer sentiments, follow trends, learn about competitors, and address negativity about their own businesses. For example, Southwest Airlines has customer service experts monitor social media outlets closely to address complaints that may go viral and cause a public relations disaster. When filmmaker Kevin Smith was removed from a Southwest flight due to his size, his social media posts about the incident were quickly followed by an apology and explanation of seating policy from Southwest’s response team. The incident still went viral, but the company used its information to mitigate the situation.

TMP-0496.text: Market Segmentation and Targeting LG How do businesses identify their target customers? Think about the market for groceries. Everyone needs food, so that market is large and diverse. People who prioritize fresh food shop at farmers’ markets. People who prefer home delivery shop online at places like Instacart. Health-conscious people may shop at natural food stores like Whole Foods. Other people prioritize low prices and shop at discount stores like Save A Lot or warehouse clubs such as Costco. People who want a quick-and-easy shopping experience go to convenience stores like Circle K. And people who want a variety of international foods shop at specialty grocers such as El Rancho Supermercado or H-Mart. A grocer who tries to please everyone risks becoming stuck in the middle—offering nothing that stands out as particularly fresh, convenient, healthy, affordable, or special.

TMP-0497.text: Rather than risking the fate of pleasing few by trying to please too many, many businesses take a divide-and-conquer approach. AP ® Skill TIP The skills developed in this course include the ability to identify solutions to business problems. If a case involves a business that has spread itself too thin by trying to serve too many people, market segmentation may be the approach you’re looking for. Consider whether a narrower focus would allow the business to better understand and serve customers while reducing marketing costs with targeted advertising. Market segmentation is the process of dividing a market into approachable groups based on wants, needs, common interests, common behaviors, and demands. For groceries, common interests in foods of various types, at differing price levels, from varying sources define segments of the market. Segmenting the market allows a business to narrow its focus, understand its customers, and provide appropriate products and prices in the right places. Later in this unit, we will discuss strategies for each of these marketing feats. We will also explain how promotions depend on the segment of people most likely to become the business’s customers.

TMP-0498.text: market segmentation The process of dividing a market into groups based on wants, needs, common interests and behaviors, and demands.

TMP-0499.text: Top: tupungato/Getty Images; bottom left: Convery flowers/Alamy Stock Photo; bottom right: jackietraveller/Alamy Stock Photo Extended description for Gap, Incorporated Stores The first photo shows the storefront for an Old Navy store. The second photo shows a GAP storefront. A large red sign in the window reads, Sale, Up To 75 percent off. The third photo shows a two-story Banana Republic storefront. Red Sale signs appear in windows on both the first and second floors of the store.

TMP-0500.text: Gap Inc. segments the clothing market, offering trendy, affordable clothing at its Old Navy stores, slightly more expensive everyday basics at its Gap stores, and pricier contemporary classics at its Banana Republic stores. A target market is the segment of consumers a business chooses to prioritize with focused marketing efforts. Some businesses choose to target multiple segments. For example, Walmart targets shoppers seeking discount prices, families in need of food, clothing, and baby products, and people seeking the convenience of finding almost everything they need in one store. Having identified one or more target markets, a marketing team studies the characteristics of that segment and tailors products, advertisements, and customer service efforts to those particular consumers.

TMP-0501.text: Types of Segments There are four types of market segmentation used by marketers: demographic segmentation, geographic segmentation, psychographic segmentation, and behavioral segmentation (see Figure 2.1-2). Combined, these methods of segmentation help companies better understand who their customers are, what their lives are like, and how to reach them.

TMP-0502.text: Demographic Geographic Psychographic Behavioral • Age • Education • Income • Gender • Occupation • Ethnicity • Family size • Nationality • Location • Climate • Population • Language • Values • Opinions • Personality traits • Attitudes • Lifestyle • Hobbies • Beliefs • Fears • Interests • Purchasing habits • Consumption • Brand loyalty • Lifestyle • Product usage Extended description for FIGURE 2.1-2 Four Main Types of Market Segmentation The table reads as follows: • Demographic (Icon of a group of three people) ○ Age ○ Education ○ Income ○ Gender ○ Occupation ○ Ethnicity ○ Family size ○ Nationality • Geographic (Icon of location) ○ Location ○ Climate ○ Population ○ Language • Psychographic (Icon of a thought bubble) ○ Values ○ Opinions ○ Personality traits ○ Attitudes ○ Lifestyle ○ Hobbies ○ Beliefs ○ Fears ○ Interests • Behavioral (Icon of a person holding a shopping cart) ○ Purchasing habits ○ Consumption ○ Brand loyalty ○ Lifestyle ○ Product usage Copyright © BFW Publishers

TMP-0504.text: Figure 2.1-2 Four Main Types of Market Segmentation 1. DEMOGRAPHIC SEGMENTATION Demographic segmentation divides a market by demographic factors such as age, education, income, gender, occupation, ethnicity, family size, and nationality. For example, luxury pen manufacturer Montblanc worked with London-based e-commerce company Yieldify to target customers based on their income. As Montblanc customers are typically high earners, Yieldify launched a variety of promotions for Father’s Day on the Montblanc website. The Father’s Day deal offered a free gift to customers spending

TMP-0505.text: over $275, which aligned with the spending expectations of its market and boosted sales among those targeted. Although demographics are useful in identifying target customers, they provide an incomplete representation of customers and their preferences. Businesses consider geographic, psychographic, and behavioral characteristics to build a more detailed picture.

TMP-0506.text: Bloomberg/Getty Images It is evident from the design of the Montblanc store in Beverly Hills, California, that the company typically targets customers with high incomes. 2. GEOGRAPHIC SEGMENTATION Geographic segmentation divides the market based on geographical features such as location, climate, language, or population density. Knowledge of where customers are located helps companies understand the needs, preferences, and interests of customers,

TMP-0507.text: which allows them to be more specific with their ads and messaging. For example, a swimwear brand that segments its market by climate would not focus on Alaska residents in January. Geographic segmentation also allows focus on a particular service area. For example, before opening a new restaurant that serves a particular part of town, you should consider that geographic segment of the market. You would first examine research on how far people are typically willing to travel to visit a restaurant like yours.3 If that distance is 5 miles, you would then study the population within 5 miles of the intended restaurant location to learn if there are enough customers who fit the demographic profile of a likely customer at your restaurant. 3. PSYCHOGRAPHIC SEGMENTATION Psychographic segmentation considers the psychological aspects of behavior such as values, opinions, personality traits, attitudes, lifestyle, hobbies, beliefs, fears, and interests. This information is useful for finding out the likes and dislikes of different customers, how they live and work, and what their needs may be. For example, a fitness company may use psychographic segmentation to search for people who care about

TMP-0508.text: healthy living and exercise, while a dance club may not target customers who show a strong preference for quiet pursuits like reading. Although psychographic data is useful, it is difficult to find and even harder to analyze for accuracy. For instance, Facebook may be able to provide some information about customers’ likes and dislikes, but it is not easy to pinpoint in-depth details like fears without conducting expensive market research such as focus groups, observation, interviewing, and surveying. 4. BEHAVIORAL SEGMENTATION Behavioral segmentation divides markets based on customer behaviors and decision- making patterns. These behaviors include customers’ online purchasing habits, how often they use a product or service, previous products they’ve used, the actions they take on websites (such as time spent using a site), or their loyalty to a certain brand. For example, family restaurant Ladles, based in South Carolina, rewards customers for their loyalty by offering a $2 discount on their next purchase. By using behavioral segmentation, companies can understand how customers interact with their products and services and target them more effectively.

TMP-0509.text: Benefits of Segmenting a Market Imagine if the entire United States were one market: hundreds of millions of people, each with their own countless needs and demands. It would be impossible for any company to cater to such a vast market. This is why market segmentation is so vital for companies: It allows them to limit the field of customers, tailor their offerings to better meet customers’ needs, and earn revenue more efficiently. It’s too expensive to market to everyone. A company must decide who is most likely to buy its products and develop its marketing plan accordingly. There are five main benefits to customer segmentation: increased brand loyalty, improved marketing messages, differentiated brands, growth and expansion opportunities, and enhanced profits. 1. INCREASED BRAND LOYALTY By identifying specific market segments, companies are better able to serve customers’ wants and needs. This allows them to build a better relationship with their customers, leading to brand loyalty and higher customer retention. In the United States, Amazon is often cited as the company with the greatest brand loyalty in online retail. Table 2.1-1 lists customer loyalty leaders in 2024.

TMP-0510.text: Table 2.1-1 Top 10 Brands with the Most Loyal Customers in 2024 1. Apple (Smartphones) 2. Amazon (Online retail) 3. TikTok (Social networking) 4. Domino’s (Pizza) 5. Netflix (Video streaming) 6. YouTube (Social networking) 7. Samsung (Smartphones) 8. Levi Strauss (Apparel retailers) 9. Dunkin’ (Coffee) 10. Mattel (Toys) Information from Brand Keys Customer Loyalty List 2024.Retrieved from https://brandkeys.com/wp- content/uploads/2024/09/2024-Loyalty-Leaders-Top-100-List.pdf. 2. STRONGER AND CLEARER MARKETING MESSAGES When a company focuses on a specific group, it can target customers in that segment with clear, specific marketing communications. Communication happens between company and customer through social media, email, and other forms of advertising. A

TMP-0511.text: common way to send a strong, clear message is by adopting a tagline—a short, memorable phrase or motto to convey the purpose or value of a brand or product. Think Nike’s Just Do It. Even colleges and universities are targeting different segments of students. Check out some of the college taglines in Table 2.1-2. Do any of them speak to you? Table 2.1-2 College Taglines Think big. We do. (The University of Rhode Island) Education is the light of the mind. (Centre College) The wind of freedom blows. (Stanford University) Whoever seeks, finds. (La Trobe University) This is what’s wildly possible. (University of Kentucky) Where tomorrow begins. (Florida Atlantic University) Light, truth, courage. (Northeastern University) Knowledge is liberty. (James Madison University) Look behind, look here, look ahead. (City College of New York) Open space. Open minds. (University of Idaho) The place of useful learning. (University of Strathclyde)

TMP-0512.text: Truth lies open to all. (University of Lancaster) Be boundless. (University of Washington) Seek knowledge throughout life. (University of Hertfordshire) Tough enough to inspire a world of good. (Wheelock College) To develop leaders of character dedicated to serving the greater good. (Texas A&M University) 3. DIFFERENTIATED BRANDS Targeting specific customer segments enables companies to gain a deeper understanding of the customer and to market more effectively to them, building brand loyalty. This approach elevates companies above their competitors through differentiation. When the COVID-19 pandemic forced much of global communication online, the use of videoconferencing software surged, keeping the world connected and a bit more content. Zoom differentiated itself quickly, becoming a market leader despite competitors including Skype, Google Hangouts, Microsoft Teams, Webex, and many others. Zoom targeted segments such as educational institutions, which needed a reliable service for online learning, and differentiated itself with a simple interface and affordable prices.

TMP-0513.text: 4. BETTER OPPORTUNITIES FOR GROWTH AND EXPANSION Brand loyalty, clear messaging, and differentiation lead to more customers, and those customers are keen to experience new products from these same companies. For example, a primary target market for Uber is people who need transportation in urban areas. That focus gave rise to Uber’s ride-sharing app. It has also led Uber to expand in the direction of driverless cars, in partnership with autonomous car designers Waymo and Cruise. 5. ENHANCED PROFITS Targeting everyone, or thinking that everyone in the world can be your customer, rarely works. It is wise for a company to target a core market segment, focus on serving that segment well, and then expand. For example, Crocs, Inc., began as a small company that made shoes designed for boating before expanding to serve all sorts of people seeking comfortable, casual footwear.

TMP-0514.text: Creating a Customer Profile After a business chooses its target market and has a clear understanding of its segment of the market, it can further characterize its target customers—individuals whose needs, wants, and preferences make them most likely to purchase a product. A customer profile—sometimes referred to as a buyer persona—is a fictional representation of the business’s ideal customer. Data from market research and any existing sales experience can inform decisions about the appropriate interests, challenges, and motivations for the customer profile. Identifying an ideal customer allows the company to search within demographic and geographic segments and consider psychographic and behavioral data that fit the customer profile. target customers Individuals whose characteristics make them more likely to purchase a product. customer profile A fictional representation of a business’s target customer. As an example, let’s consider a company that plans a new podcast. The theme is the “gig economy,” which encompasses individuals working and earning income from a series of projects rather than a single career. When the podcast company analyzes data

TMP-0515.text: from similar shows, it realizes that many listeners are young parents whose attachment to their families makes them value flexibility as they contemplate their next career move. With this in mind, the company defines its ideal listener (customer) with the persona shown in Figure 2.1-3.

TMP-0519.text: How does the company then use this persona? Whenever it is brainstorming new podcast topics or guests, it will use “Cooper” as a sounding board. Would Cooper listen to this episode? What guest would Cooper like to hear from? What topics would appeal to him? How can we create a better relationship with Cooper? Focusing on a target is more effective and less expensive than trying to appeal to everyone. Companies can use their target customers and customer profiles to inform product design, set prices, and focus their advertising efforts.

TMP-0520.text: Customer Relationships What role do customer relationships play in marketing? Strong relationships with customer segments help a company understand its customers and be in a position to identify new needs, solve new problems, and innovate. Healthy customer relationships contribute to brand loyalty and word-of- mouth advertising, both of which help businesses increase sales and break into new markets. Consider the cookie company Crumbl, which launched its first store in Logan, Utah, in 2017. Crumbl baked up warm customer sentiment with influencer marketing, engaging social media challenges,⁴, and the use of customer feedback to inform product development for its weekly new flavor releases. Adoring customers spread the word, and Crumbl now sells over 1 million cookies every day at more than 1,000 locations worldwide.

TMP-0521.text: Strategies for Building Relationships Like Crumbl, many companies build strong relationships by treating people to great products and by treating them well in other ways, too. Costco earns customer trust and retention with fair pricing and a generous 100% satisfaction guarantee on most products. Buc-ee’s convenience centers became tourist destinations by providing famously clean restrooms, up to 120 gas pumps, and snack foods galore. And toymaker Mattel inspires excellent customer service with the reminder that every product support call is made for a child who loves their toy and really wants it to work.⁵ More generally, businesses that maintain high standards for every aspect of the user experience cultivate loyal customers who share their good experiences far and wide. Another way to build lasting relationships is with personalized service. For a local shoe store, bank, or café, that can mean the employees learn about their customers and suggest products or services that suit their particular needs. A big business such as Meta, Samsung, or Walmart can use AI to analyze customer data, allowing them to deliver personalized service despite no human being familiar with the customers. After you establish an online account with Walmart, upon logging in to shop, you can expect

TMP-0522.text: the platform to know your name, the location of your local store, and your shopping preferences.
