TMP-0524.text: Perfume and cosmetics company Lancôme has a customer loyalty program that rewards members with points for making purchases and completing tasks. As customers earn more points, they move to higher membership levels with better benefits. The internet and social media make it easier than ever to connect with consumers and strengthen relationships. Online satisfaction surveys allow customers to offer feedback, which is valuable both as a source of data and because customers appreciate the ability to have input. And businesses ranging from sandwich shops to airlines use app-based reward programs to nurture relationships. These programs boost loyalty by

TMP-0525.text: encouraging customers to accumulate points for making purchases or completing tasks such as writing reviews. The Benefits of Good Relationships Healthy customer relationships pay off in numerous ways. Satisfied customers speak highly of a business. That word-of-mouth advertising lowers the customer acquisition cost, which is the marketing cost of acquiring a new customer. To find the customer acquisition cost, a business divides the total marketing, advertising, and sales cost of acquiring customers by the total number of customers acquired. This can be done for any time period. For example, if a restaurant spent $12,000 last year to acquire 240 new customers, its customer acquisition cost for the year was $12,000/240 = $50. customer acquisition cost The marketing cost of acquiring a new customer; calculated by dividing the total marketing, advertising, and sales cost of acquiring customers by the total number of customers acquired. Good relationships add to the customer lifetime value, which is the estimated amount of money that a customer will spend on a business’s products over the course of their relationship. If your dentist expects you to spend an average of $500 per year for

TMP-0526.text: their services for the next 10 years and then switch dentists, your customer lifetime value to your dentist is 10 × $500 = $5,000. If a better relationship with your dentist would lead you to stay with that dentist for 25 years, your customer lifetime value would be 25 × $500 = $12,500. In that case, the improved customer relationship would increase your dentist’s revenue by $12,500 − $5,000 = $7,500. customer lifetime value The estimated amount of money that a customer will spend on a business’s products over the course of the customer-business relationship. High customer lifetime values justify large customer acquisition costs. You may have noticed businesses offering big discounts or free gifts to first-time buyers at online stores, new members of health clubs, and new subscribers to streaming services. Many businesses also reward customers for referrals, which are existing customers’ recommendations of a business to potential customers. For example, customers sometimes receive $25 for referring a friend to TurboTax. Other types of reward programs common at airlines, hotels, rental car companies, and restaurants promote long-term relationships by giving free goods or services to customers who have made many purchases.

TMP-0527.text: referral An existing customer’s recommendation of a business to a potential customer.

TMP-0528.text: Using Data Responsibly What risks are associated with the collection and use of customer data? Our increasingly online lives dangle data in front of businesses in ways that present ethical dilemmas for companies and consumers. Every online search, purchase, and social media post, along with our very presence in a geographical location, leaves a trail of data that can be collected, compiled, and stored in ways that arguably violate our privacy. Often customers are not aware that their data is being collected, and even when they are, it is hard to know all the ways that it is being used. Data is often shared with, or sold to, third parties such as advertisers, social media platforms, and business partners. This raises concerns about the appropriate use of data. Should businesses be able to collect customers’ data without their permission? Should there be limits on what companies can do with the data they obtain? What responsibilities do businesses have for protecting customer data from bad actors? Policymakers must grapple with what is

TMP-0529.text: acceptable. Businesses contend with the risks of data breaches and reputational damage. And consumers must decide how to navigate the many requests from businesses for their information.

TMP-0532.text: This privacy statement from technology company Oracle explains how the personal data it collects may be used. Privacy Concerns Does the amount of data you share with online retailers, banks, healthcare providers, and social media companies make you feel vulnerable? You may not like the idea of businesses tracking your shopping behavior and accessing your personal information. If you read the fine print before giving your consent for a company to use your data, you might be surprised by the breadth of data collected and the types of sharing with other companies. Although that use of data is legal, it can be problematic. Many consumers want the products they buy, the amounts they spend, the websites they visit, and the level of income they receive, among other sensitive data, to remain private. Indeed, most Americans feel that the risks associated with customer data collection exceed the benefits.6 For that reason, the collection and use of data may be a factor in some customers’ decisions about where to shop. And if sensitive information is exposed in a breach, it can harm the business’s reputation.

TMP-0533.text: A related concern is that businesses can use personal data to sort consumers into groups and treat them differently on the basis of generalizations and stereotypes. As we have learned, targeting market segments with customized messages is a popular marketing strategy. Companies receive criticism for using customer data to target more vulnerable populations such as older adults, children, and marginalized groups with ads that are misleading or promote overspending. Data-driven social media campaigns allow advertisers to target some customers and exclude others based on race, gender, and sexual orientation, which fuels debates in marketing circles. Sources of controversy include dark ads, which are shown to some market segments but not others. In one case, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development accused Facebook of unlawful discrimination by restricting housing- related ads based on race, color, national origin, religion, familial status, sex, and disability.7 In another case, the American Civil Liberties Union alleged that Facebook was excluding women from receiving a particular set of job postings.8

TMP-0534.text: Security Concerns Consumer data can fall into the wrong hands, especially if it is not well secured. Even if consumers and businesses are okay with data being collected and used for marketing purposes, the computer system holding that data might be accessed or hacked by bad actors who steal the data with criminal intent. Data breaches, in which data is stolen and sold or used for criminal purposes, are a growing problem. Stolen data can be used to commit identity theft, which is the fraudulent use of someone’s data to impersonate them and access their bank accounts, borrow money, or obtain services such as healthcare or phone services. data breach An event in which data is stolen and sold or used for criminal purposes. identity theft The fraudulent use of someone’s data to impersonate them and access their bank accounts, borrow money, or obtain services such as healthcare or phone services. Banks, healthcare companies, colleges, and retailers are among the frequent targets of hackers. Data breaches threaten the reputations of these organizations, for whom trust is essential. Recent data-breach victims include Western Alliance Bank, Change

TMP-0535.text: Healthcare, and the University of Michigan. Some breaches expose the data of millions of customers. For example, unauthorized actors gained access to data records for almost 57 million customers of clothing retailer Hot Topic in 2024. And sensitive personal health records, social security numbers, birth dates, and addresses for 5.8 million people were stolen in a data breach of pharmacy services provider PharMerica in 2023. AP® EXAM TIP If an exam question asks you to take a stand on a controversial topic like data privacy, explain yourself clearly and incorporate course concepts. Focus on the quality of your answer rather than its length. Your score may depend on the specific reasoning behind your decision and the stated pros and cons of that decision.

TMP-0536.text: Module 2.1 Review Learning Goals What is marketing and what role does data play in it? Marketing is the process of identifying and satisfying customer interests by promotion and providing goods and services. Guesswork leads to mistakes. Businesses prefer to make informed decisions, and when those decisions are about marketing, the information they seek is about customers. Customer data is information businesses collect about their customers to better understand, serve, and engage them. Demographic data is descriptive information about people’s identity, situation, and background, such as age, gender, race, and location. Psychographic data is information on people’s cognitive and behavioral characteristics, such as interests, values, motivations, and preferences.

TMP-0537.text: How do businesses identify their target customers? Businesses use market segmentation to divide a market into approachable groups based on wants, needs, common interests, common behaviors, and demands. A target market is the segment of consumers a business chooses to prioritize with focused marketing efforts. Businesses segment markets based on demographic, geographic, psychographic, and behavioral characteristics. Market segmentation makes it easier for a business to understand its customers and serve their needs. By narrowing the business’s focus, segmentation can also improve marketing efficiency and customer satisfaction. A business can further characterize the type of customer it aims to serve by identifying target customers—individuals whose characteristics make them more likely to purchase a product—and creating a customer profile, which is a fictional representation of the business’s ideal customer. Identifying an ideal customer allows the company to search within demographic and geographic segments and consider psychographic and behavioral data that fit the customer profile.

TMP-0538.text: What role do customer relationships play in marketing? Strong relationships with customers enable businesses to anticipate and meet customer needs. Strong relationships with customers can lower the customer acquisition cost, which is the marketing cost of acquiring a new customer. These relationships also add to the customer lifetime value, which is the total revenue received from a customer throughout their relationship with the business. Many businesses reward customers for referrals, which are existing customers’ recommendations of a business to potential customers. What risks are associated with the collection and use of customer data? Data collection for marketing purposes raises privacy and security issues. Customers don’t always know what data is being collected or how it is used.

TMP-0539.text: Data breaches, in which data is stolen and sold or used for criminal purposes, are not uncommon. Stolen data can be used to commit identity theft, which is the use of someone’s data to impersonate them and access their bank accounts, borrow money, or obtain services such as healthcare or phone services. Some businesses use consumer data to direct business communications to particular market segments, which creates openings for bias and discrimination. TMP-0542.text: CASE STUDY Walmart Joe Raedle/Getty Images Extended description for Walmart Additional registers are open and checking out customers. Long lines extend from each of the three registers.

TMP-0543.text: While you are checking out, Walmart is checking you out, collecting data on your spending habits and shopping preferences. Today, companies of all sizes collect and analyze volumes of data every day. Business leaders use data-driven insights to make decisions and identify problems. As the world’s largest retailer, Walmart uses cutting-edge data analysis to improve its efficiency. With nearly 12,000 stores selling thousands of unique items daily, Walmart generates unimaginably large sums of data about its products, customers, marketing efforts, stores, supply chain, and inventory. Beyond collecting raw data on these areas, it processes, consolidates, and analyzes the data to create valuable information. By revealing problems and improving predictions of consumer demand and staffing needs, that information helps the company boost customer satisfaction, sales, and profitability. Walmart uses a customer relationship management system to track customer purchasing patterns and preferences. The marketing team analyzes data on

TMP-0544.text: purchases and online search activities to make personalized offers and product recommendations. Shoppers receive targeted advertisements based on their preferences. And the company encourages customer loyalty with its Walmart+ membership program that includes Walmart Rewards, which are earned with purchases of eligible goods and can be redeemed for discounts on purchases. No one likes long lines at the grocery store, so Walmart adjusts its staffing based on data from past store activity at each location during each hour of the day. Another common example of data-driven decisions involves the selection of products and their placement within stores. In a store as large as a Walmart, the physical location of a product can heavily impact its sales. Shoppers leave a trail of data at every location. By analyzing purchase data, Walmart learns which products are commonly purchased together and can increase sales by placing those products together within stores so they are easy to find. Examples include peanut butter and jelly, camping gear and first-aid kits, and flour and yeast. Data is also used to predict what will be purchased when. We aren’t just talking about seasonal and holiday products. After analyzing purchases before hurricanes in the southern part of the United States, Walmart learned that customers prepare

TMP-0545.text: for these storms by stocking up on strawberry Pop-Tarts. With that information, the company knew to order additional Pop-Tart inventory ahead of hurricane season. Walmart’s privacy notice indicates that the data it may collect or receive includes names; contact information; government-issued identifiers such as driver’s license numbers; browsing and search activity; purchase history; demographic information such as age, ethnicity, and income; financial account numbers; physical location; and, in some cases, background checks and criminal convictions.9 Walmart also shares customer data with third parties that include advertisers, publishers, social media platforms, and data technology vendors. Walmart secures personal information with “reasonable information security measures, including physical, administrative, and technical safeguards.” Breaches of Walmart’s data reportedly include a hacking attack that led to unauthorized customer charges in 2025,10 a leak of retirement plan data in 2024,11 a breach of employee data between 2023 and 2024,12 and breaches of customer data in 2021 and 2018.13

TMP-0547.text: MODULE 2.2 Consumer Behavior LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 2.2.A Discuss key influences on consumer decisions 2.2.B Explain legal and technological factors that determine purchasing patterns 2.2.C Describe Cialdini’s principles of influence and how they affect marketing decisions

TMP-0548.text: Christian Vierig/Getty Images To serve consumers well, a business must understand what drives their purchases.

TMP-0549.text: Determinants of Consumer Behavior How and why do consumers make purchasing decisions? You buy things because you need or want them. It’s harder to explain which specific things you buy when many choices are available. Which brands satisfy your need for clothing? Do you want a bike or a scooter? Consumer behavior is the set of selection, purchase, and consumption activities consumers use to address their needs and wants. Insights into consumer behavior are valuable to businesses. Marketing teams raise questions such as: Why do customers prefer certain products or services over others? How do they view competitors’ offerings? Where do they prefer to make purchases? How much are they willing to pay? And what factors influence buying decisions? This knowledge helps businesses choose what products to offer, predict future trends, increase customer retention, enhance customer service, and plan effective marketing strategies.

TMP-0550.text: consumer behavior The set of selection, purchase, and consumption activities consumers use to address their needs and wants. Some products are purchased mostly for the functional value derived from the problems they solve. For example, you might have purchased a backpack to solve the problem of how to carry your textbooks. But not all value is functional. Consider the true story of a marketing professor who, after walking into class on a cold, snowy day, noticed that several of his students were wearing popular—and very expensive—Canada Goose–branded jackets. He asked one of those students why he purchased the jacket. “Because it keeps me warm,” the student replied. The professor then turned to a student who came in with a similar-looking jacket from a far less-expensive brand and asked why she purchased the jacket she was wearing. This student also replied, “Because it keeps me warm.” The professor asked the class: If both jackets provide the same functional value, why did some students buy a jacket that costs more than twice as much as other jackets? The answers about feeling “hip,” “successful,” and “cool” exhibited the emotional value derived from how a product makes customers feel. Similarly, you might feel excitement when you purchase a new phone. You might feel a sense of pride when you purchase a

TMP-0551.text: frame for your diploma. You might feel love and connection when you buy someone flowers. And you might feel confident and empowered when you purchase formal clothing. These are the types of emotions many companies tap into when they market their goods and services to consumers. How Consumers Make Decisions In markets with rival goods angling for your interest, effective advertising and product availability may sway your decisions. It’s wise to consider prices and features as you make your picks. But the attention these factors deserve depends on how large and consequential the purchase is. For small or routine purchases, the decision process is often simple. You may periodically buy the same types of snacks and hair products, and you probably don’t spend much time deliberating over which lip balm or bottled water to buy. That’s wise, because it takes time and perhaps money to scrutinize product options. The benefits of deep research into daily purchases seldom exceed the costs. The story is different for major purchases. When you need a new bike or phone, the use of a rational decision-making process is justified—you will want to systematically evaluate each alternative and gradually narrow things down. To identify the purchase

TMP-0552.text: that best suits your needs, a good start, if possible, is to sample the options: test ride the bikes, try out the phones at the store, try on the outfits. To narrow the possibilities, many consumers like to list the pros and cons of the main contenders. For example, if you are choosing between two bikes, you could list the best and worst features of the bikes side by side and home in on key deciding factors, such as whether it is better to have a cargo rack or a more comfortable seat. A large purchase may justify a financial investment in input from an expert, like the advice of a mechanic on a car purchase or the recommendation of an independent product-testing organization such as Consumer Reports on a home appliance. After considerable research, information gathering, reading of reviews and evaluation of alternatives, a better final decision can be made. However, the best decision is not the same from everyone, due to several other influential factors. Influential Factors Every consumer is different. We each place our own value on the products available for purchase. Some people would pay a lot to ride a roller coaster, take a knitting class, eat spicy food, or go camping, and other people would pay not to have to do those

TMP-0553.text: things. A solid understanding of how consumers differ is built on familiarity with four types of factors that influence consumer behavior. Personal Factors We are all unique in our own way. Personal factors are characteristics of consumers that help to determine what individuals need and want, as well as what they have the ability to buy. Examples include age, personality, gender, education, occupation, income level, and lifestyle. You may want acne cream because you are going through puberty, art supplies because you love to paint, and tennis shoes because you have an active lifestyle. The person who sits next to you in class may prefer moisturizing cream, a chemistry set, and cowboy boots. And a student’s decision to purchase a puffer coat from Canada Goose or from Uniqlo reflects personal factors relating to income level and lifestyle. personal factors Consumer characteristics that help to determine what individuals need and want, as well as what they have the ability to buy.

TMP-0554.text: Psychological Factors Maybe you, like the students who chose their coat because it made them feel hip or cool, have made purchases based on feelings. Psychological factors are mental and emotional processes that influence what consumers feel is important to buy. Examples include perceptions, attitudes, individual motivations, beliefs, opinions, values, and learning. Your inherited traits, upbringing, and experiences help shape your consumption patterns and determine what motivates you to make purchases. Perhaps you want to buy Halloween decorations because you are passionate about holidays and coffee from a local roaster because you feel it is important to support local businesses. What you learned from prior experiences with pets might make you PetSmart’s best customer or someone who never buys or adopts another pet. psychological factors Mental and emotional processes that influence what consumers feel is important to buy. Social and Cultural Factors When more than a few people show up for class wearing the same coat, it’s possible that their purchases were influenced by other people. Sociological factors are social

TMP-0555.text: and cultural influences that help determine what consumers find appropriate, desirable, and acceptable to buy. Friends, family, peers, various types of media, and culture provide role models, pressure, inspiration, and expectations to make certain purchases. You may want to buy a varsity jacket because your friends wear them, a spring break trip because that’s part of your high school culture, and a ticket to the county fair because that’s a popular event in your community. sociological factors Social and cultural influences that help determine what consumers find appropriate, desirable, and acceptable to buy. Cultural norms are unwritten standards or expectations for behavior among members of a culture. These norms help businesses anticipate the timing and types of purchases. For example, a large segment of the population in India does not eat beef because cows are sacred in the predominant Hindu religion. McDonald’s operates hundreds of restaurants in India, but it doesn’t sell burgers made from beef. Instead, it sells things like the Pizza McPuff and the McAloo Tikki Burger—a fried potato patty with spices. Cultural traditions, rituals, and holidays also drive predictable consumer behavior. This explains the fireworks stands that appear before the Fourth of July in the United States and the abundance of flowers for sale around Valentine’s Day.

TMP-0556.text: Fast-Food Tourist/Alamy Stock Photo Businesses that understand purchasing patterns can anticipate sales and cater to repeat customers. Purchasing patterns are influenced by cultural norms, which prompted McDonald’s to sell products like the McAloo Tikki (shown here) rather than beef-based burgers in India, where most customers do not eat beef. Situational Factors Perhaps you bought your coat because the weather suddenly turned cold, or you were in a rush, or a persuasive salesperson convinced you it was a good purchase. Situational

TMP-0557.text: AP® factors are temporary influences specific to the consumer’s circumstances or conditions that affect purchasing decisions. These can include physical states such as hunger or fatigue, task-dependent factors such as buying for a friend or for personal use, issues of time pressure, relationships with people who are present, and elements of the location—such as music, lighting, and product displays. situational factors Temporary influences specific to the consumer’s circumstances or conditions that affect purchasing decisions. Situational factors are generally short lived. But personal, psychological, sociological, and cultural factors can encourage patterns of consumer behavior that inform marketing decisions. Patterns also stem from legal and technological factors, which we’ll explore next. EXAM TIP As you prepare for the exam, it is wise to consider different angles that questions on key content areas could take. Regarding consumer behavior, an exam question might ask about the possible influences on a particular type of purchase. Alternatively, a question could ask what type of factor (personal, psychological, social and cultural, situational) a particular influence is. With these

TMP-0558.text: possibilities in mind, you should know the meaning of each type of factor as well as examples of each type of influence.

TMP-0559.text: Influences on Purchasing Patterns LG How do legal and technological factors influence consumer behavior? Humans are creatures of habit. Your use of apps, consumption of foods, travel, and sources of entertainment may reflect routines of consumption behavior. Businesses pay close attention to ways in which consumer behavior is predictable. That is, they study purchasing patterns, which are habits or trends in consumer behavior over time. Marketing teams can observe these patterns in the timing of purchases, preferences for brands, selections of products, and locations of purchases. purchasing patterns Habits or trends in consumer behavior over time. Along with the personal, psychological, social, and cultural factors discussed earlier, legal and technical factors are key determinants of purchasing patterns. In this section,

TMP-0560.text: we’ll examine how businesses can incorporate these factors into their marketing strategies because they are observable, substantial influences. Laws and Policies Laws and policies help determine consumer behavior by steering people away from fraudulent or unsafe products. Laws against deceptive marketing prevent businesses from making unsubstantiated claims that, for example, their products cure disease or cause weight loss. Some legal factors give rise to substitute products. A ban on Red 3, a petroleum-based food dye, led to the development of natural red dyes made from insects, fruits, vegetables, and algae. And taxes on cigarettes lower demand and promote substitutes like nicotine gum. Other policies are designed to steer consumers toward products with potential benefits. Subsidies for solar panels and electric cars have been shown to increase the demand for those goods. Requirements that football players, triathlon competitors, construction workers, and many bikers, skiers, and climbers wear safety helmets help to prevent head injuries while driving a billion-dollar industry for protective headgear. And

TMP-0561.text: stricter U.S. import restrictions on cars from China would increase the demand for cars made in the United States. Technology and Innovation A few decades ago, almost all shopping was done in person at stores or by mail order. The arrival of the internet and online retailers in the 1990s began to transform consumer behavior. Smartphones, which became available in the 2010s, now provide product information, reviews, and buying opportunities on devices many consumers always have with them. This means there is no time of day and almost no location that constrains purchasing patterns. The ability to purchase groceries, concert tickets, travel reservations, or almost anything else—anywhere, at any time, with just a few clicks—has also transformed some marketing strategies. Prior to ever-present shopping opportunities, unplanned purchasing known as impulse buying largely occurred during shopping trips. As they still do, stores would place lip balm, candy bars, gift cards, and other small, inexpensive items near the cash register to tempt customers as they prepared to pay. Purchasing patterns were tied to access to stores rather than to mere interest in goods or services. With customers

TMP-0562.text: shopping online, marketing strategies can offer instant gratification. If it’s nighttime and you have an impulse to buy a gift card for a family member’s birthday, very little is stopping you. Businesses also use technology to “gamify” shopping by making the experience resemble game playing. Online stores offer digital rewards, loyalty points, online auctions, and digital versions of actual games such as the McDonald’s Monopoly Double Peel game. Among other examples, Sling streaming service has spin-to-win games, Sephora cosmetics has tiered levels of shopping status, and Chipotle Mexican Grill offers badges for loyal customers.

TMP-0563.text: Extended description for Starbucks Rewards Text on the page reads, FREE COFFEE IS A TAP AWAY. Join now to start earning Rewards. Button: Join Now. Or join in the app (hyperlink) for the best experience. Technology affects purchasing patterns by offering customer engagement anytime, anywhere, and by making

TMP-0564.text: shopping resemble a game with point systems and rewards.

TMP-0565.text: LG Consumer Psychology: Cialdini’s Seven Principles of Influence What are Cialdini’s seven principles of influence and how do they affect marketing decisions? We’ve discussed some key influences on buying behavior. The best marketing strategies also consider how potential customers think. For some insight on that, we will explore a bit of consumer psychology, which is the study of how and why consumers make purchasing decisions. If you’ve ever felt obligated to buy something after receiving a free sample, or compelled to buy a product that is trending in your friend group, consumer psychology was at play. consumer psychology The study of how and why consumers make purchasing decisions.

TMP-0566.text: Psychologist and marketing professor Robert Cialdini outlined seven principles of influence, summarized in Figure 2.2-1. Cialdini’s principles help marketing teams understand how to motivate consumers based on the way they think.1 Let’s consider each principle in detail.

TMP-0567.text: Extended description for Figure 2.2-1 Cialdini's Seven Principles of Influence The illustration shows a circle. At the center of the circle is a smaller circle that reads, Persuasion. Wedges around the small circle, Persuasion form the larger circle. The wedges read as follows: • Unity (Icon of a group of four people with joined hands): People are motivated by their feelings or belonging. • Scarcity (Icon of a diamond): People want what is rare. • Authority (Icon of a hammer): Expertise and credibility promote trust. • Consensus (Icon of a group of three people): People want to align with their social group. • Liking (Icon of a thumbs-up): People are more persuaded by others they like or relate to. • Reciprocity (Icon of shaking hands): Give and you are more likely to receive. • Consistency (Icon of a calendar): People like to stay true to their values and commitments.

TMP-0568.text: Figure 2.2-1 Cialdini’s Seven Principles of Influence

TMP-0569.text: The Scarcity Principle What do fine art, trading cards, and limited-edition Air Jordans have in common? They are valuable because they are not widely available. The scarcity principle holds that consumers want things more when they are perceived as being rare. Classic examples of products whose prices rise with rarity are baseball cards, stamps, and coins. You may also place special value on limited-edition products such as comic books, games, video game skins, or fragrances. To get some mileage out of the scarcity principle, fast food restaurants sometimes offer items for a limited time only, like the McDonald’s McRib and the Starbucks Pumpkin Spice Latte. And some clothing brands offer limited releases to create artificial scarcity that drives up interest. the scarcity principle The idea that consumers want things more when they are perceived as being rare.

TMP-0570.text: Mike Kemp/Getty Images Clothing brands such as Supreme create limited-release products to drive up interest. Here, fans of the brand line up to secure a scarce clothing item.

TMP-0571.text: The Authority Principle Because there are so many exaggerated claims about products being “great” if not “the best,” the credibility of an authority makes an important difference. The authority principle states that consumers are more likely to buy something if it is endorsed by an authority figure. When advertisements feature people with titles such as Dr., Ph.D., or CEO, or people wearing clothing such as scrubs, police uniforms, or suits, the intent may be to signal authority. Olympians are often featured in ads for items like swimwear, skis, and sports drinks for the same reason. And when accomplished athletes like Angel Reese, Caitlyn Clark, Shohei Ohtani, and Juan Soto endorse products from Reebok, Nike, New Balance, and Under Armour, they lend their authority to these brands. the authority principle The idea that consumers are more likely to buy something if it is endorsed by an authority figure. The Consensus Principle When you are deciding what type of clothing to wear to school, what to do on the weekend, or what type of transportation to use, you may look to the people around you

TMP-0572.text: for input on what is acceptable or fashionable. The consensus principle holds that consumers are motivated to buy when their social group is in general agreement about the desirability of a product. Sometimes we receive this influence by direct observation. The fashion trends visible among members of your friend group may spread rapidly. In other cases, the consensus principle is conveyed in the form of reviews or social media testimonials. When a cosmetics item such as Milk Makeup Cooling Water Jelly Tints goes viral on TikTok, that’s the consensus principle in action. the consensus principle The idea that consumers are motivated to buy when their social group is in general agreement about the desirability of a product. The Liking Principle When your favorite megastore promotes back-to-school products, it probably features likeable young people who reflect its target audience. The liking principle states that consumers are more inclined to make purchases from people they like or can relate to. This principle applies to the salespeople in stores you visit and the people in advertisements who are pitching (trying to sell) a product to you. When a star athlete

TMP-0573.text: appears in an advertisement for a local car dealership, they are probably not there because they are an authority on cars. Instead, it is because the athlete is liked by members of the community. Consumers’ connection with people carries over to the products those people are selling. the liking principle The idea that consumers are more inclined to make purchases from people they like or can relate to. The Reciprocity Principle Supermarkets, cookie stores, and cheese shops are among the eateries that provide free samples. News websites and various apps provide free trials. Part of the reason is so that consumers get a taste of the product or service, but there’s more to it. Even if the consumer already knows what the product is like, after receiving something for free, the consumer is more likely to become a paying customer. That’s the essence of the reciprocity principle: Consumers feel more obligated to buy something when the seller gives them something of value.

TMP-0574.text: the reciprocity principle The idea that consumers feel more obligated to buy something when the seller gives them something of value. The Consistency Principle The consistency principle states that consumers are attracted to products that are consistent with their self-image, values, and commitments. Once they have made a decision or taken a stand, they tend to behave in alignment with that position. Organizations can benefit from this principle by gaining a minor commitment. A charity might ask for a very small donation, knowing that future behavior is likely to follow that lead. Gyms often invite people to commit to a fitness goal, which is a win-win for the people and the gym if the new fitness devotees end up starting or extending a membership. Similar efforts to start customers down a path of desirable consistency include handing out “support local business” buttons, inviting people to sign up for organization newsletters, and encouraging membership in loyalty programs. the consistency principle The idea that consumers are attracted to products that are consistent with their self-image, values, and commitments.

TMP-0575.text: Andrew Aitchison/Getty Images Extended description for Consumers Additional barrels of vegetables are clustered around the carrot bin in a colorful display. A sign above the produce reads, "We work closely with local growers to reduce food miles and support the local community!".

TMP-0576.text: Consumers are attracted to products that are consistent with their self-image, values, and commitments, such as supporting local businesses. The Unity Principle Group identity can also influence customers. The unity principle states that consumers are motivated to purchase a product by feelings of belonging to a group that purchases that product. The unity principle differs from the liking principle in that the influencers don’t simply have similarities to the influenced person; the influenced person shares an identity with the influencers. For example, Disney enthusiasts share an identity as members of that fan base, and they are influenced to wear pins and clothing with Disney logos when other fans do the same. the unity principle The idea that consumers are motivated to purchase a product by feelings of belonging to a group that purchases that product.

TMP-0577.text: Membership in online communities also boosts a sense of unity. Owners of Trek bicycles, Ford Mustang cars, Nike shoes, and GoPro cameras are among the groups with their own online spaces. Businesses also promote unity by inviting customers to cocreate products. If you have ideas for new IKEA furniture, Dewalt tools, LEGO toys, or Starbucks drinks, they will welcome your thoughts. Do Cialdini’s principles explain many of your purchases? Perhaps the situational factor of cold weather has influenced you to buy a sweater, or the psychological factor of fearing spiders has led you to buy bug spray. These seven drivers of consumer behavior are key considerations for businesses small and large. In the Case Study, you will see how pharmaceutical giant Merck navigates consumer behavior driven by healthcare needs and distrust of pharmaceutical makers.

TMP-0578.text: LG Module 2.2 Review Learning Goals How and why do consumers make purchasing decisions? • Consumer behavior is the set of selection, purchase, and consumption activities consumers use to address their needs and wants. Routine and inexpensive purchasing decisions are often made quickly, but many consumers apply a rational decision-making process of systematically evaluating product options when making more consequential decisions. • Values that consumers place on products include the functional value of their problem-solving ability and the emotional value of how they make consumers feel. What consumers want and need differs on the basis of many types of factors.

TMP-0579.text: LG • Personal factors are characteristics of consumers that help to determine what individuals need and want as well as what they have the ability to buy. • Psychological factors are mental and emotional processes that influence what consumers feel is important to buy. • Sociological factors are social and cultural influences that help determine what consumers find appropriate, desirable, and acceptable to buy. • Situational factors are temporary influences specific to the consumer's circumstances or conditions that affect purchasing decisions. How do legal and technological factors influence consumer behavior? • Businesses study purchasing patterns, which are habits or trends in consumer behavior over time. • Key determinants of purchasing patterns include laws, policies, and technology. Many laws and policies are designed to steer consumers away from fraudulent and unsafe products and toward products with potential benefits. Technology allows

TMP-0580.text: consumers to shop almost anywhere at any time, thanks to online stores and smartphones. LG What are Cialdini’s seven principles of influence and how do they affect marketing decisions? • Consumer psychology is the study of how and why consumers make purchasing decisions. Psychologist Robert Cialdini offers seven principles of influence that businesses consider when making marketing decisions. • According to the scarcity principle, consumers want things more when they are perceived as being rare. • The authority principle says that consumers are more likely to buy something if it is endorsed by an authority figure. • The consensus principle says that consumers are motivated to buy when their social group is in general agreement about the desirability of the product. • The liking principle says that consumers are more inclined to make purchases from people they like or can relate to.

TMP-0581.text: • The reciprocity principle says that consumers feel more obligated to buy something when the seller gives them something of value. • The consistency principle says that consumers are attracted to products that are consistent with their self-image and values. • The unity principle says that consumers are motivated to purchase a product by feelings of belonging to a group that purchases that product. Practice Your AP® Skills Preparing for the AP® Exam MULTIPLE-CHOICE QUESTIONS 1. John went to the bookstore to buy a book for his class. While he was there, he also bought a candy bar that reminded him of his grandmother. Which statement best describes the value each item provided? a. Both the book and the candy bar provided John with functional value only.

TMP-0582.text: b. The candy bar provided functional value while the book provided emotional value. c. Both the book and the candy bar provided emotional value. d. The book provided functional value and the candy bar provided emotional value. 2. Your friend could have saved $1,000 by buying her car from a dealer 50 miles away. Instead, she chose to buy from a local dealer because it felt good to support the local economy. Which factors most influenced her behavior? a. personal factors b. psychological factors c. social and cultural factors d. situational factors 3. Gary wants to dedicate his life to studying poetry. He goes to his local bookstore and buys several collections of poems and books about how to analyze poems. Which factors most influenced his purchasing decision?

TMP-0583.text: a. personal factors b. psychological factors c. social and cultural factors d. situational factors 4. Swimwear manufacturer Aqua Sphere sponsored 23-time Olympic swimming champion Michael Phelps, who is more respected for his swimming expertise than for his charisma. Which principle of influence on buying behavior is Aqua Sphere most likely relying on to justify this investment? a. scarcity principle b. authority principle c. consensus principle d. liking principle 5. Each behavior described below is paired with one of Cialdini’s Seven Principles of Influence. Which behavior is paired with the wrong principle?

TMP-0584.text: a. Consensus principle: People check for favorable reviews before trying a new restaurant. b. Reciprocity principle: Supermarkets offer free samples to encourage customers to buy the product. c. Consistency principle: Consumers repeatedly buy the same brand of jeans out of habit. d. Unity principle: Sports fans purchase team merchandise to feel a sense of belonging.

TMP-0585.text: CASE STUDY Merck’s Pharmaceutical Marketing Timon Schneider/Alamy Stock Photo Extended description for Merck The phone screen displays a screenshot from a web page for Merck, which reads, Our areas of focus. We focus on scientific innovation to deliver medicines and vaccines that may help millions of people around the world. A photo from an electron microscope shows a cluster of three cells. Oncology. We work to deliver innovations that extend and improve the lives of people with cancer. Learn about oncology (hyperlink). Behind the phone, a signboard reads, MERCK with its logo.

TMP-0586.text: Businesses like Merck try to develop products that consumers need or want. Whether those products are popular depends on consumer behavior. We’ve discussed factors that influence consumer behavior. For the multinational pharmaceutical giant Merck, the factors revolve around health issues. With more than 50 pharmaceutical products in its product portfolio, the company specializes in addressing a range of illnesses, including type 2 diabetes, cancer, nervous-system

TMP-0587.text: disorders, and cardiovascular, respiratory, and infectious diseases. Customers with these challenges represent market segments for which different drugs may help. Merck rose from humble beginnings in 1668 as a drugstore owned by the Merck family in Darmstadt, Germany. In 1891, 23-year-old George Merck founded the U.S. arm of Merck in New York City, which grew into the pharmaceutical giant that Merck is today. Its annual sales of over $60 billion place it among the 100 largest U.S. companies. Merck has innovated in the healthcare industry throughout its history. In 1898, it sold the first commercially available smallpox vaccine in the United States. It manufactured the first measles vaccine in 1963 and the first mumps vaccine in 1967. Recently, it released a COVID-19 treatment pill called Molnupiravir, which is used to treat patients for whom other COVID-19 treatments will not work. Another new drug from Merck, Keytruda, was found to reduce the risk of early lung cancer returning in patients who had already undergone lung surgery by 24%. The pharmaceutical market is complex. Patients, families, healthcare providers, and insurance companies are involved in choosing, prescribing, using, and paying for drugs. Healthcare providers can recommend or oppose certain pharmaceutical treatments. Insurance coverage can dictate what drugs are affordable to patients.

TMP-0588.text: And before any of those decisions are made, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requires that three phases of clinical trials show that new drugs are safe, effective, and high quality. There has been much debate over the positive and negative effects of direct-to- consumer (DTC) advertising for pharmaceuticals. The United States and New Zealand are the only countries that allow drug companies to advertise prescription drugs directly to consumers. In the 1980s, the FDA ruled in favor of DTC advertisements, hoping they would help consumers understand the benefits and risks of various drugs. In 1981, Merck debuted the first DTC print advertisement, promoting its pneumonia vaccine. Pharmaceutical companies must follow rigid rules for disclosing side effects and related issues in their advertisements. When viewers in the United Kingdom watched Oprah Winfrey’s famous interview of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, they were shocked by the long lists of side effects that were part of the U.S. drug ads aired during the broadcast. “American adverts make me feel like I’m in some post- apocalyptic world,” one tweet read.2

TMP-0589.text: Pharma ads are still controversial in the United States. Some people believe that ads are needed to place more responsibility for healthcare management in consumers’ hands. Ads may motivate people to seek treatment for various illnesses and to ask their doctor about therapy options, potential outcomes, and costs. In contrast, the American Medical Association (AMA) unsuccessfully called for a ban on drug advertising in 2015. AMA members were concerned that DTC ads inflate consumer demand for unnecessarily expensive drugs.3 Both sides generally agree that pharmaceutical advertising affects consumer behavior. When it comes to decisions about healthcare, customers want information they can trust. Although the internet provides more information than ever before about diseases and cures, many of the sources are unchecked and unreliable. Research shows that consumers also lack trust in pharmaceutical manufacturers.4 To bolster consumer perceptions of Merck’s credibility, the company tries to be transparent, sharing information about clinical trials, political contributions, grants to other organizations, and payments to health professionals.5 Merck also has a compliance program designed to avoid violations of laws and company policies, and a code of conduct that clarifies its commitment to high ethical standards. 6

TMP-0590.text: APPLY YOUR AP® SKILLS 1. Identify the four different types of decision makers that Merck might want to target with marketing efforts due to their influence on drug-buying decisions. 2. What is an example of a personal factor other than illness that you believe could influence a consumer’s decision to purchase Merck’s products? Explain your answer. 3. Explain one possible reason for laws in most countries that prohibit DTC advertising. 4. Suppose you are on Merck’s marketing team. Identify a spokesperson you would choose to promote Merck’s products and justify your selection on the basis of one of Cialdini’s seven principles of influence.

TMP-0591.text: MODULE 2.3 Market Research LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 2.3.A Explain the purpose and methods of market research 2.3.B Differentiate between primary-source and secondary-source research 2.3.C Describe the process of hypothesis testing 2.3.D Interpret charts and graphs used for data visualization

TMP-0592.text: Connect Images/Henglein and Steets/Getty Images Is there a business opportunity here? Market research informs business decisions by revealing consumer needs and wants.

TMP-0593.text: The Data and the Task LG What is market research and why is it useful? Imagine your company is eager to meet the needs of consumers, but you’re unsure what product is up to the task. It’s time for some market research, which is the process of collecting and interpreting information about consumer demand, competitors, and market trends. The best offering for your company depends on consumer needs, wants, and purchasing behavior. Whether you can fill a market need depends on the products, pricing, and availability of competitors’ products. And the wisdom of entering a market depends on market conditions such as the number of potential customers and any trends in the popularity of that product. To sort all of that out, your company needs data. market research The process of collecting and interpreting information about consumer demand, competitors, and market trends.

TMP-0594.text: Quantitative and Qualitative Data All data falls into one of two categories. Quantitative data is expressed using numbers. Any count or measurement with a numerical value is quantitative data. Suppose you live in an area with plenty of snow and are considering opening a shop that rents sleds near a popular sledding hill. If you want to know how many visitors to the area like to go sledding, how often they would rent a sled, or how much they would pay for a sled rental, you are seeking quantitative data. quantitative data Information expressed using numbers. Qualitative data is expressed through words or images rather than numbers. Questions of what, why, and how are answered with qualitative data. If your business wants descriptions of the types of sleds customers would prefer, explanations for why more people do not currently go sledding, or examples of how promotional materials for the business would look, you need qualitative data. If potential customers tell you that they don’t sled because it is too cold, you can use that qualitative data to inform decisions about whether to also rent out snowsuits. Customer descriptions or drawings of their ideal sleds would be useful as you choose your sled design.

TMP-0595.text: qualitative data Information expressed through words or images. Is It the Right Product? As you consider a specific product offering, there are many relevant questions you could address with market research. Three questions are particularly important because an answer of “no” to any one of them should steer you away from that product choice: 1. Is the product desirable to consumers? Data on the needs and wants of consumers will answer this question. Does the product achieve a problem-solution fit (as we discussed in Module 1.1)? You certainly don’t want to sink a lot of time and money into an undesirable product offering. A sled-rental shop would be a bad idea if the popular trend is snowboarding. 2. Is the product feasible to provide? A product is feasible if the company is able to offer it given existing legal and regulatory requirements and the available resources, time, and technology. If your plan is to provide horse-drawn sleigh rides, you should research the possibilities for boarding horses in that area and taking sleighs through the available roads or paths. If you’re planning a new app, consider

TMP-0596.navLabel: Taking It to the Next Level
TMP-0596.text: the software programming skills of your staff or the cost of hiring an outside team to develop the app. 3. Is the product viable? A viable product offers enough value to customers in the intended market to command a price that will support the business’s financial needs. If people are unwilling to pay enough for a sled rental to cover your costs and provide worthwhile profit, you’ll want to explore other opportunities. feasibility Whether a company can offer a product given the limits of existing legal and regulatory requirements, available resources, time, and technology. viability Whether a product can offer intended customers enough value to be profitable. Market research helps businesses either check the boxes of desirability, feasibility, and viability, or learn that the contemplated product is not a promising choice. Taking It to the Next Level Market research is not just for new products. As the needs and wants of customers change, businesses must refine their offerings and strategies just to keep up with the

headings.text: Taking It to the Next Level

TMP-0597.navLabel: Taking It to the Next Level
TMP-0597.text: times and the competition. Business growth often requires innovations that improve existing goods and services. For example, Amazon relies heavily on market research to identify new trends and emerging market segments. That company is exploring new delivery models and broadening its offerings by including more third-party sellers—those independent merchants who sell their products through the Amazon website. And market research helped the drinkware company Stanley capture a large share of its market by modifying its existing products to appeal to a younger target market. It is common for businesses to pursue larger profits with product updates and improvements. Informing those efforts with market research can limit the time and money wasted on products that go in an unpopular direction. Next, we explore two paths toward answers to the important questions addressed by market research.

TMP-0598.navLabel: Taking It to the Next Level
TMP-0598.text: David Bokuchava/Alamy Stock Photo Stanley was founded in 1913 as a drinkware maker that served workers, soldiers, and outdoorspeople. More than 100 years later, market research helped Stanley turn its “Quencher” cup into a viral sensation among young consumers.

TMP-0599.text: Assessing Market Opportunities LG What is the difference between primary-source and secondary-source research? Pinning down the best product to bring to market requires substantial market research. The best opportunities depend on the characteristics of customers, competitors, and the overall market, and on the PESTEL factors discussed in Module 1.3. Businesses can use primary or secondary sources to obtain the data they need. A primary source is an original source of information collected directly by the researcher. Sales reports, financial records, and journal articles that present original research or firsthand findings are primary sources. If you went door-to-door asking potential customers if they would rent sleds from your shop, those interviews would be primary sources. You would be conducting primary-source research and collecting primary data. Other examples of primary sources include direct observations of customer behavior,

TMP-0600.text: surveys or experiments conducted by the researcher, and photos or videos taken by the researcher. primary source An original source of information collected directly by the researcher. A secondary source provides information that was not collected directly by the researcher. Secondary sources summarize, analyze, or interpret information from primary sources. Textbooks are generally secondary sources because the authors did not personally experience the events or collect the data they explain. If you performed market research using industry reports that summarize market trends or news articles about business research, you would be conducting secondary-source research and collecting secondary data. Other secondary sources include government publications such as the Statistical Abstracts of the United States and online platforms such as Google Trends and Statista. Many of these secondary sources are available at no cost. secondary source Information that was not collected directly by the researcher.

TMP-0601.text: Secondary-source research can help a business assess the viability of a product. The information obtained might include the current sales volume in a market, the number of customers in the market, information on market segments, and measures of the personal, psychological, social, legal, and technological factors that influence product choices, as discussed in Module 2.2 . Primary and secondary data can be either qualitative or quantitative. For example, suppose you are researching the sled and surfboard maker Agit Global North America. If you Google “number of employees Agit Global,” you might immediately find a number on a website that collects data from business reports. This is secondary data because the source is indirect. It is also quantitative data because it is numerical. If you find a sales report on Agit Global’s website, that will provide primary data because those are the original, raw numbers from the company. Again, the data is quantitative because the sales figures are numerical. If you perused the internet and found an article describing Agit Global’s collaboration with Mattel to make Barbie-themed surfboards, that would be a secondary source because it is summarizing information from other sources, and it would be qualitative because it describes the situation with words. If the article also provided numbers on

TMP-0602.text: projected sales, that would be secondary, quantitative data. And if you interviewed employees at Agit Global to get their perspective on the company’s culture, the resulting data would be primary and qualitative because you collected the words. Figure 2.3-1 summarizes the four types of data a business can use for market research. The left column is for quantitative data—counts and measurements that can be analyzed using statistics such as averages. The right column is for qualitative data, such as words used to categorize or describe something. The top and bottom rows distinguish between primary and secondary sources, which can exist for both quantitative and qualitative data.

TMP-0603.text: Quantitative Numeric, measurable Qualitative Descriptive, subjective Copyright © BFW Publishers Primary Data collected in real time for a specific purpose. Data did not exist previously. Surveys Experiments Collections of original data Counts and measures Any type of collected data Interviews Observations Focus groups Secondary Data that has already been collected and used by others. Public financial statements Market research reports Databases Company websites Annual reports Published news articles Videos Extended description for Figure 2.3-1 Types of Research Data The table shows two columns: Quantitative and Qualitative , and two rows: Primary and Secondary . The table reads as follows:

TMP-0604.text: • Column 1, Quantitative: Numeric, measurable. Row 1, Primary: Data collected in real time for a specific purpose. Data did not exist previously. ○ Surveys ○ Experiments ○ Collections of original data ○ Counts and measures ○ Any Type of Collected Data • Column 1, Quantitative: Numeric, measurable. Row 2, Secondary: Data that has already been collected and used by others. ○ Public financial statements ○ Market research reports ○ Databases • Column 2, Qualitative: Descriptive, subjective. Row 1, Primary: Data collected in real time for a specific purpose. Data did not exist previously. ○ Interviews ○ Observations ○ Focus groups

TMP-0605.text: • Column 2, Qualitative: Descriptive, subjective. Row 2, Secondary: Data that has already been collected and used by others. ○ Company websites ○ Annual reports ○ Published news articles ○ Videos Figure 2.3-1 Types of Research Data Which of these types of data a business should seek depends on the intent of the market research. Primary-source research can address specific questions about target customers because it is customizable and can be collected directly from those customers. For example, if you wanted to know what sled colors would be popular, you could ask 100 consumers in your target market their color preference. Primary-source research is also suitable to address questions about competitors if the desired information is available from the competitors’ financial statements or sales reports.

TMP-0606.text: Secondary-source research is appropriate when the goal is to learn general characteristics of customers, communities, competitors, and markets. Summaries of information about the size and age of local populations, household income levels, community events, and industry characteristics appear in government publications, newspapers, journals, and databases available to businesses. Governmental agencies such as the U.S. Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics are among the free sources of data that make secondary-source research more cost-effective than most primary-source research.

TMP-0607.text: Jim West/Alamy Stock Photo The U.S. Census Bureau conducts primary-source research, collecting survey data directly from residents on demographics such as where people live, their education, and their income. Businesses use that data to assess, for example, the viability of products, store locations, and market expansion.

TMP-0608.text: Hypothesis Testing LG How do businesses test hypotheses? Close to half of new businesses fail within five years. 1 With much that can go wrong, business decisions should not rest on hunches, intuition, or guesswork. Business leaders begin with assumptions about products, customers, or markets known as business hypotheses , but they are wise to test those hypotheses before acting on them. Let’s consider hypotheses you might make when planning a sled rental shop. When contemplating your product, you might hypothesize that consumers prefer lightweight plastic sleds over traditional wood-and-metal sleds. You might assume that sledding is most popular among families with children between 5 and 15 years old. And you might predict that consumers are willing to pay up to $10 a day to rent a good plastic sled. Before you invest in a lot of plastic sleds and market $10 rentals to the assumed target customers, however, it would be wise to do some market research.

TMP-0609.text: business hypotheses A set of assumptions about products, customers, or markets. Hypothesis testing is the process of using data to evaluate the validity of an assumption or prediction. To test your hypothesis about what consumers would pay to rent a sled, you would collect data on what consumers say they would pay, or what they actually pay elsewhere, and assess your hypothesis based on your findings. In a statistics class, you might learn formal procedures for hypothesis testing. Without diving into the rigorous mathematics of these tests, we will discuss strategies for collecting data that can be analyzed with your chosen level of rigor. hypothesis testing The process of using data to evaluate the validity of an assumption or prediction. Research Strategies for Hypothesis Testing How a business collects data for hypothesis testing depends on the best available data for the hypothesis to be tested. When no data currently exists to address a hypothesis, businesses choose among several common methods for gathering data. Depending on the type and amount of data they need, the best approach may include primary-source

TMP-0610.text: research such as surveys, focus groups, interviews, experiments, observations, or A/B testing. SURVEYS If a business wants to find out how a large number of people feel about, say, a new product, location, or promotion, a survey can do the trick. A survey is a mechanism for collecting information from a group by simply asking them questions. Surveys are a good source of qualitative data on consumer preferences, opinions, demographics, and behaviors. They can be administered directly to the target audience for a product either in person, online, by phone, or using paper questionnaires. Surveys are also useful for collecting quantitative data. A survey about consumers’ willingness to pay for sled rentals could ask respondents, “What is the most you would be willing to pay for a one-hour sled rental?” The flexibility of surveys makes them valuable to many businesses that lack data about the best way forward. survey A mechanism for collecting information from a group by asking questions.

TMP-0611.text: Focus Groups and Interviews A business that needs in-depth, qualitative answers to detailed questions will want to talk directly with its target audience. A small business could conduct one-on-one interviews with prospective customers to gather their thoughts about goods or services. Bigger businesses might conduct focus groups. A focus group is a small group of people assembled to provide qualitative data about a good, service, or idea. Participants are typically offered a small payment or reward in exchange for their time and input. A trained facilitator leads a discussion and collects information about participants’ perceptions, attitudes, opinions, and behaviors. For example, Disney uses focus groups of preschoolers to gain insights about what types of new cartoon characters would appeal to children of that age. focus group A small group of people assembled to provide qualitative data about a good, service, or idea. Unlike broad surveys, interviews and focus groups allow for follow-up questions based on initial responses, which can help the business understand the basis for unexpected answers. The nature of these discussion-based strategies, however, makes

TMP-0612.text: them time-consuming and expensive, and so it’s best to use them on only a small number of potential customers, and to choose those customers strategically. alvaro gonzalez/Getty Images Businesses assemble focus groups to obtain detailed, qualitative data from a small number of potential customers.

TMP-0613.text: Experiments and Observations Businesses use some of the same tools as scientists to test their hypotheses. One of the simplest is observation, a form of primary-source research that simply entails observing customer behavior. This typically occurs in a natural setting where customers normally purchase or use products. For example, IKEA improved its store layout by observing how customers navigate its stores, and Ford observed driver behavior to inform the design of its dashboard controls. A business can also run an experiment —a procedure carried out under controlled conditions that is used to test the validity of a hypothesis. Imagine that your business represents spinach farmers and you have a hypothesis that children would eat more spinach if they saw cartoon characters eating spinach. You could run an experiment by having half of a large group of children watch a cartoon featuring a spinach-eater and the other half watch a similar cartoon with no spinach-eater. At a post-cartoon meal featuring spinach, researchers could observe the number of children from each group that ate spinach and make a comparison. In fact, spinach-eating cartoon character

TMP-0614.text: Popeye helped save the U.S. spinach industry in the 1930s by motivating millions of children to eat that iron-rich superfood in hopes of gaining bulging muscles. 2 experiment A procedure carried out under controlled conditions that is used to test the validity of a hypothesis. A/B Testing Businesses face many dilemmas, such as whether to rent flexible sleds or rigid sleds, advertise with email or social media ads, or charge $14.00 or $17.00 for movie tickets. When a business must decide between two options like these, a popular approach is to make both available to consumers and see which one they choose. A/B testing is a type of experiment in which researchers compare responses to two or more versions of a product, promotion, or pricing strategy. Netflix uses A/B testing to determine which images known as thumbnails will appear next to recommended movies. 3 Its experiments involve showing groups of customers varying thumbnails and seeing which ones receive the most clicks.

TMP-0615.navLabel: Basic Guidelines for Data Collection and Hypothesis Testing
TMP-0615.text: A/B testing A type of experiment in which researchers compare responses to two or more versions of a product, promotion, or pricing strategy. Basic Guidelines for Data Collection and Hypothesis Testing For all types of data collection and hypothesis testing, researchers should take steps to avoid misleading results. Many books have been written about careful statistical analysis. Four guidelines will help you avoid some of the most common pitfalls. 1. A good hypothesis is specific and testable. It would be difficult to test the hypothesis that consumers love jelly beans because love is hard to define and means different things to different people. A hypothesis that consumers in your town prefer jelly beans to lollipops would be better, because its meaning is clear and its validity can be tested using any of the techniques discussed in this section. 2. Avoid making conclusions based on small amounts of data. It is tempting to survey a few potential customers about the price they would pay or study sales for a brief period after changing the store hours and make decisions based on that small

headings.text: Basic Guidelines for Data Collection and Hypothesis Testing

TMP-0616.navLabel: Basic Guidelines for Data Collection and Hypothesis Testing
TMP-0616.text: sample of consumer behavior. Of course, it is often impossible to survey every potential customer or study sales for every period. The goal is to collect enough data to prevent an unusual customer or short-term situation from skewing your results. If you survey only three customers and one of them happens to be a huge fan of your product, your data on what consumers would pay may be misleading. And if you track sales for two weeks after expanding your hours and sales are low, you might decide against the change before most customers even realize it occurred. 3. Draw data from a representative sample of target customers. Preferences vary across demographics such as ages, genders, locations, and income levels. If you plan to serve teenagers, collect data from teenagers. If the only data available is collected from senior citizens, use it with great caution if at all. The techniques of primary-source research allow businesses to customize their data collection and to research subjects who resemble their intended customers. 4. Word research questions carefully. It is important to use neutral phrasing that does not influence responses. Asking, “Do you like to go out in the cold and go sledding?” would lead to biased results because the question stresses the discomfort of winter weather. Asking, “Isn’t sledding great?” would bias respondents in favor by

TMP-0617.navLabel: Basic Guidelines for Data Collection and Hypothesis Testing
TMP-0617.text: suggesting that the activity is desirable. Asking, “In the last year, did you go sledding or wish you could go sledding?” avoids framing the question in a positive or negative way and grounds answers in the reality of respondents’ behavior and thinking. Even the best approaches to data collection and hypothesis testing are imperfect. Businesses should acknowledge the limitations of data from surveys, interviews, focus groups, and other samplings of the larger population, which can be flawed and contradictory. Predictions based on market research might not hold true for broad groups of consumers, whose influences, experiences, and preferences may not be well represented in the data. After launching a new product or business strategy, it is appropriate to reassess the underlying decisions, troubleshoot problems, consider new opportunities, and make adjustments as needed in an ongoing process of improvement.

TMP-0618.text: Data Visualization LG How can businesses use data visualization to communicate their market research findings? We have learned about the importance of data. We must also appreciate its potential complexity. When market research reveals a story about many products, sales over many periods, or multiple consumer segments, images can often narrate better than words. Data visualization is the representation of data using charts, graphs, maps, or diagrams. These visual aids communicate trends, patterns, and insights that help participants make informed decisions. Business meetings are often a flurry of bar charts, line graphs, and pie charts like the ones we’re about to discuss. data visualization The representation of data using charts, graphs, maps, or diagrams.

TMP-0619.text: It’s important to understand how each type of visual aid works, so you can choose the visualization that best captures the data or trend that you want to highlight. Bar Charts If you are thinking of selling swimwear to tourists in a beach town, you will want to consider the weather, because consumer demand will depend on warm temperatures. Your market research should include an examination of the periods during which it is warm enough for people to want to take a dip in the water. You and any possible investors in your business might look at a bar chart showing the average temperature levels in the location of your consumers over the course of a year. A bar chart displays data for multiple categories using rectangular bars whose heights or lengths indicate values for a single measure. For example, a bar chart could highlight changes in weather conditions over time, sales of products to consumers of different ages, sales data for one business over several years, or sales revenue at different store locations in the same year. In the temperature example, each bar in the chart could indicate the average temperature in a month. Figure 2.3-2 shows the bar chart for a warm spot where swimsuit sales could continue for most of the year.

For example, suppose you own toy stores in four locations. You want a chart to indicate the annual sales revenue from consumers in each age group at each store along with the total sales revenue at each store. You should also be prepared to explain what kind of graph or chart would work well to represent a specified type of data. Line Graphs A line graph is a chart with straight lines connecting data points that represent the value of some measure over time. Line graphs are useful for illustrating trends or patterns. For example, a line graph could illustrate the number of stores a company has
