TMP-0633.text: Module 2.3 Review Learning Goals LG What is market research and why is it useful? • Market research is the process of collecting and interpreting information about consumer demand, competitors, and market trends. • Quantitative data is expressed using numbers. Any count or measurement with a numerical value is quantitative data. Qualitative data is expressed through words or images rather than numbers. • Market research can indicate whether a contemplated product would be desirable to consumers, feasible, and viable. A product is feasible if the company is able to offer it given existing legal and regulatory requirements and the available resources, time, and technology. A viable product offers enough value to customers

TMP-0634.text: in the intended market to command a price that will support the business’s financial needs. LG What is the difference between primary-source and secondary-source research? • A primary source is an original source of information collected directly by the researcher. Primary-source research can address specific questions about the target customers because it is customizable and can be collected directly from those customers. • A secondary source provides information that was not collected directly by the researcher. Secondary-source research is appropriate when the goal is to learn general characteristics of customers, communities, and markets. • Primary and secondary data can be either qualitative or quantitative. LG How do businesses test hypotheses?

TMP-0635.text: • Business leaders begin with assumptions about products, customers, or markets known as business hypotheses . Hypothesis testing is the process of using data to evaluate the validity of an assumption or prediction. • A survey is a mechanism for collecting information from a group by simply asking them questions. A focus group is a small group of people gathered to provide qualitative data about a good, service, or idea. Researchers may also conduct one-on-one interviews . They may use observations of consumer behavior and conduct experiments —procedures carried out under controlled conditions that are used to test the validity of a hypothesis. A/B testing is a type of experiment in which researchers compare responses to two or more versions of a product, promotion, or pricing strategy. • When collecting data and testing hypotheses, researchers should ensure that their hypothesis is specific and testable, their conclusions are based on adequate data, their sample is representative of target customers, and their question wording is neutral. They should also acknowledge and accommodate the limitations of data collection.

TMP-0636.text: LG How can businesses use data visualization to communicate their market research findings? • Data visualization is the representation of data using charts, graphs, maps, or diagrams. Businesses choose the type of data visualization that best suits their data. • A bar chart displays data for multiple categories using rectangular bars whose heights or lengths indicate values for a single measure. In a stacked bar chart , each bar is divided into segments whose heights or lengths represent the contributions of subcategories to the whole category. A line graph is a chart with straight lines connecting data points that represent the value of some measure over time or across categories. A pie chart is a circular diagram divided into slices, the sizes of which show how various categories contributed to the total of what is being measured.

TMP-0637.text: Practice Your AP® Skills Preparing for the AP® Exam MULTIPLE-CHOICE QUESTIONS 1. You are the Vice President of Marketing for an electric car startup company. Which of the following falls outside the responsibilities of the marketing department? a. interpreting information about consumer demand for your cars b. determining the costs per unit of production c. researching the pricing and offerings of competitors d. analyzing market conditions and trends in the popularity of e-cars 2. The California Economic Forecast is a consulting firm that performs research and analysis for business and public sector clients. If the California grape growing industry hired this consulting firm to analyze and interpret data

TMP-0638.text: collected previously by the grape producers on their output and total revenue, the research and the data they used would be considered a. primary-source research and qualitative data. b. primary-source research and quantitative data. c. secondary-source research and qualitative data. d. secondary-source research and quantitative data. 3. Jacques Jeans wants to understand why sales dropped in one of its stores despite steady foot traffic. They are seeking your advice about good ways to collect information about their situation. Which of the following is accurate information you could provide to this business? a. Surveys are a good source of qualitative data, but another approach is needed to obtain quantitative data. b. Focus groups provide an opportunity for a business to obtain in-depth, qualitative answers to detailed questions by talking directly with its target audience.

TMP-0639.text: c. When a business wants to collect data from well-educated people, a popular approach is to conduct A/B testing, which focuses on people who received high grades in school. d. Because businesses use some of the same tools as scientists to test their hypotheses, data from surveys, interviews, focus groups, and A/B testing can be relied upon for accuracy and consistency. 4. Which conclusion is supported by the data depicted in the stacked bar chart shown in Figure 2.3-3 ? a. Store 1 gains more revenue from each of the age groups than any other store. b. The largest source of revenue in each store is the 21 to 40 age group. c. Store 3 gains more revenue from the 0 to 20 age group than any of the other stores. d. Store 3 gains more revenue from the 0 to 20 age group and receives more total revenue than any other store. 5. Taylor is contemplating a new product for Taylor’s Toys. She has access to a lot of old plumbing pipes that she could melt down and make into toy cars shaped

TMP-0640.text: like animals, such as mustangs, jaguars, barracudas, stingrays, colts, and broncos. Her surveys show strong consumer interest in animal-shaped cars across many demographics. The price she could charge would provide a sustainable profit based on projected production costs. However, she learned that the pipes contain lead, which is banned in the manufacturing of children’s toys. Based on criteria for evaluating product ideas, how should this opportunity be classified? a. desirable and feasible, but not viable b. desirable and viable, but not feasible c. feasible and viable, but not desirable d. desirable, but not feasible or viable

TMP-0641.text: CASE STUDY Little Cocoa Bean Photo by Carlie Febo. Reproduced with permission of Little Cocoa Bean Company. Market research helped a business called Little Cocoa Bean develop and succeed. Perhaps a future business of yours will benefit from market research in the same ways. Market research by Tracy Skelly, entrepreneur and mother of Sophia, revealed a significant problem in a large and growing market. The needs and wants of some cultures are not well served in the U.S. baby food market. Walk down the baby food

TMP-0642.text: aisle of a U.S. grocery store and you’ll see a lot of processed fruits and vegetables commonly grown on U.S. farms. Skelly’s market research revealed that the healthy, nutrient-dense foods that she grew up eating as an Afro-Latina were largely absent. “Where was the papaya, collards, chayote, and tamarind?” she thought. 4 And even if, for example, jarred plantains could be found in the baby food aisle, the manufacturing process turned a nutrient-dense food into a less healthy version of its whole-food self. As a new mother who had been making baby food from scratch for Sophia, Skelly started to do more research. She quickly learned that the brain grows more during the first 1,000 days of life than in any other period of life, and up to two-thirds of the calories babies consume are used for brain growth and development. Skelly pointed out, “What you eat in the early years of life impacts what you eat throughout life, and whole foods matter.... In communities of color, Black and Latinx die from health-related disease at a higher rate than their white counterparts. Research supports that this is connected to early food consumption and access to healthy options.”

TMP-0643.text: Inspired by the market gap and social need, Skelly founded Little Cocoa Bean in late 2019 with a mission “to show parents how to increase their child’s consumption of healthy and diverse foods by highlighting and celebrating the food that our ancestors have eaten for centuries around the globe.” Skelly’s original plan was to produce and sell nutritious, ready-made baby foods aligned with African American culture and heritage. When the COVID-19 pandemic stifled the U.S. economy, like many entrepreneurs, she quickly pivoted to a new plan. Skelly offered Instagram and Facebook Live sessions to share her recipes. Rather than selling ready-made food, she began selling the supplies her viewers needed to make their own baby food, such as storage jars, bamboo plates, microwavable sanitizing bags, and reusable food pouches. As the pandemic subsided, Skelly went back to her original concept. She found a producer and copacker for her tested recipes. She opened a physical storefront in Boston that sells her ready-made foods for infants and toddlers as well as fresh food that can be consumed on site by young children and their families. She continues to sell directly online and hopes to scale the brand and sell through grocery stores in the future.

TMP-0644.text: APPLY YOUR AP® SKILLS 1. Describe the target customer of Little Cocoa Bean. 2. What is this company’s competitive advantage? 3. When Tracy Skelly visited grocery stores, she noted what types of baby foods they were selling. Her data included descriptions such as “processed,” “sweetened,” and “culturally relevant.” Describe this data using the vocabulary in this module. 4. Suppose you wanted to determine the demand for this product in the Boston area. Explain how you would go about collecting data for your market research, and provide examples of the specific information you would obtain.

TMP-0645.text: M O D U L E 2 . 4 Product LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 2.4.A Describe common phases of product development 2.4.B Explain the importance of brand identity 2.4.C Discuss the life cycle of a product

headings.text: M O D U L E 2 . 4

TMP-0646.text: John Nordell/Getty Images To serve consumers well, a business must understand what drives their purchases.

TMP-0647.text: Product Development LG What are the phases of the product development process? Think about the last item you purchased. Maybe it was a videogame reviewed by your favorite streamer, a skin cream displayed prominently at your local pharmacy, or a new flavor of corn chips your friends were talking about. How did this good or service come about and eventually find its way to you? Businesses rely on four main areas of influence as they craft their marketing strategies. The elements of that marketing mix are the product sold, the price charged, the way the product is promoted, and the place where it is made available to customers. This mix is often described as the 4 Ps : product, price, promotion, and place. A marketing team will consider each of these elements and pursue the best combination of the 4 Ps to bring success within the target market. This module focuses on the first

TMP-0648.text: element by exploring the choice and development of a product. Upcoming modules discuss the remaining elements of the marketing mix. A product is a good or service that a business offers to meet consumer needs and wants. There is more to a product than meets the eye. Businesses make decisions about their products’ target customer, purpose, design, quality, features, packaging, branding, name, and attributes that distinguish it from rival products. With so many important details to get right, businesses should take painstaking care in the product development process of creating a new product and bringing it to market. The typical phases of product development are ideation, validation, design, messaging, production, and launch. product A good or service that a business offers to meet consumer needs and wants. product development The process of creating a new product and bringing it to market. You may have heard the old advice to “try, try again” when things don’t go well at first. Likewise, product development is an iterative process , meaning that it is common to cycle

TMP-0649.text: through several of the phases again and again, making improvements each time. The business tries to make incremental improvements each time it revisits a phase until the product tests well and is ready for market. Figure 2.4-1 illustrates iterations of ideation, validation, design, and messaging, followed by production and launch. However, a business can benefit from repeating any phase that does not go well. We’ll explore each phase next.

TMP-0652.text: Ideation The starting point for product development is an idea on which to build. As discussed in Module 1.4 , ideation is the creative process of generating new ideas. Common sources for ideas include personal experiences with unmet needs, market research, technical research and development (R&D), applications of skills or knowledge, and brainstorming. ideation The creative process of generating new ideas. Consider Hungarian newspaper editor László Bíró (1899–1985), who recognized the need for pens with smudge-free ink as he wasted time cleaning up messes left by leaky fountain pens. He combined his knowledge of fast-drying newspaper ink with the findings of previous research on ballpoint-pen technology. To advance his idea, Bíró tapped his brother György’s chemistry skills. After some brainstorming and experimentation, the two developed pen ink that was not too thin and not too thick. Thanks to this confluence of common sources for ideas, no-smudge ballpoint pens are now in offices everywhere.

TMP-0653.text: Andy445/Getty Images Some product ideas come from personal experiences with unmet needs. The inventor of the first commercially successful ballpoint pen had a strong need for a mess-free writing instrument. Other ideas come from market research, technical research and development, applications of skills, and brainstorming. AP® SKILLS TIP One of the key skills for entrepreneurs is the ability to test product ideas. Failure to test hypotheses and validate ideas can doom a project in class or in the real world. As you practice or explain entrepreneurship for this class, note the importance of validation to improve projections of whether demand for a product will be sufficient to provide worthwhile profit.

TMP-0654.text: Validation We’ve all had bad ideas that seemed like good ideas at the time. The ocean of flawed notions makes it essential to filter ideas carefully. Validation is the process of verifying that an idea solves a problem for consumers, is realistic to provide, and has the potential to generate profit. In other words, the goal is to confirm that the product idea is desirable, feasible, and viable. validation The process of verifying that an idea solves a problem for consumers, is realistic to provide, and has the potential to generate profit. Many ideas are new and interesting and yet not what consumers want to spend much money on. Pen maker Bic decided to launch a line of perfumes that consumers wrote off as unappealing. Other examples included Google Glass smart glasses, Cheetos lip balm, Crystal Pepsi, the Microsoft Zune music player, and the Segway scooter. As cool as an idea may be, it also needs product-market fit , meaning that it satisfies strong-enough market demand to be commercially viable.

TMP-0655.text: product-market fit A state achieved when a product satisfies strong-enough market demand to be commercially viable. Validation begins with internal discussions among people trusted for their insight and foresight. Depending on the product, that might include teams of managers, developers, marketers, editors, programmers, salespeople, or data analysts. As discussed in Module 2.3 , surveys, focus groups, interviews, experiments, observations, and A/B testing are used to test hypotheses about product ideas among prospective consumers. And as explained in Module 1.4 , new product ideas can be tested using a minimum viable product (MVP) that allows customers to interact with the product idea and provide feedback.

TMP-0656.text: Extended description for Cheetos Text on the beauty set packaging reads, 2 LIP GLOSS WANDS NET 0.08. FL. OZ. (2.2 ml), 1 LIP GLOSS POT NET WT 0.04 OZ. (1.1 g), 1 GLOSS COMPACT NET WEIGHT 0.11 OZ. (3.2 g), 1 LIP BALM NET WEIGHT 0.12 OZ. (3.4 g).

TMP-0657.text: Some ideas are new and interesting, but not popular. The validation stage is crucial to help a business foresee the reception a new product would receive upon launch. Design What will the product look like? How will the materials be sourced? What will make the user experience memorable? What features will set it apart from the competition? How much will production and delivery cost? These are questions about product design. As in the validation phase, input from many sources is essential to good decisions. Prototypes help developers explore possibilities. For example, during the design phase, Apple cofounder Steve Jobs would place prototypes of the company’s products in a

TMP-0658.text: central location where employees could pick them up, feel their smooth contours, and imagine themselves using the product. Apple could then gather their feedback on product design, features, and functionality —how well the product works. As developers choose features, colors, sizes, and materials, several factors influence their decisions of what is “best.” It is tempting to prioritize low-cost materials, but saving money on inputs may not add to profit if customers prioritize quality over affordability. For instance, the cost savings from making sweaters out of acrylic must be weighed against the higher prices consumers will pay for sweaters made of wool. And features must be considered with attention to what competitors are already offering. Suppose most consumers prefer large pickup trucks to small ones. If all the competing trucks are large, a truck manufacturer might maximize profit by being the only maker of compact pickup trucks and capturing the market segment with that preference. Messaging The distinguishing features implemented during the design phase are trumpeted during the messaging phase. At this point, the business develops the core communication strategy that will guide advertisements, website content, social media

TMP-0659.text: presence, email campaigns, and internal communication. The activities of the messaging phase can be summarized in five steps: 1. Identify the target audience. This allows the business to choose messages based on its understanding of who the message is for. Narrow messaging also saves money relative to a broader campaign meant to reach more people. 2. Clarify the value proposition. Potential customers need clear messages about why they should buy your product. A value proposition summarizes how a product serves customer needs better than the alternatives. When ads compare the results of washing shirts with two different laundry detergents, or of wiping up spills with two different brands of paper towels, the value proposition of the superior product is on display. Value propositions are also conveyed in advertising slogans. With Grammarly’s slogan, “Great Writing, Simplified,” the company asserts that its product will make it easier to write well.

TMP-0660.text: AirTag Buy AirTag Lose your knack for losing things. Extended description for Air Tag Text reads: Lose your knack for losing things.

TMP-0661.text: Commercial messages often highlight the product’s value proposition. This ad focuses on the AirTag’s value to people who tend to lose their valuables. 3. Develop a product-positioning strategy. The business should plan how it wants its target customers to perceive its product relative to rival products. The messaging for this strategy can reinforce perceptions of the product’s value proposition and differentiating characteristics. Some businesses build this messaging around a consistent theme that aligns with the company’s brand identity and is repeated across communication channels. For example, Disneyland positions itself as the place where families can find happiness, wonder, and joy. Its strategy includes the tagline, “the happiest place on earth,” and consistent messaging with the happiness theme appears throughout its advertising and its park. 4. Close with a call to action. Successful messaging is clear about the next step recipients should take. An email from a college might suggest that you get started on your application today. A mailing about skin cream might nudge you to ask your doctor about using the product. An ad for an online bank might urge you to visit its website today. These calls to action aim to change passive viewers into active participants.

TMP-0662.text: 5. Test messages before transmitting them. As we learned in Module 2.3 , surveys, focus groups, and A/B testing are effective ways to collect data and assess which messages resonate with potential customers. Businesses analyze data from the testing step to refine and optimize their messaging before sending the messages to their intended audience. value proposition A message summarizing how a product serves customer needs better than the alternatives. AP® EXAM TIP Don’t confuse a value proposition with competitive advantage. A value proposition is specific to a product, saying how it satisfies a need for consumers. Competitive advantage belongs to a business and refers to factors such as quick delivery or excellent customer service that help the business outperform its rivals. By placing the messaging phase before the production phase, responses to initial messages can inform the next steps. Estimates of consumer demand can guide final decisions about product design and production volume. For example, websites that allow shoppers to build virtual versions of new car models provide manufacturers with

TMP-0663.text: data on what colors, styles, and features are popular. And clicks for more information on online book announcements can inform decisions about how many copies to print in the first edition. Production In the production phase, a business collects the lessons from its ideation, validation, design prototyping, and messaging feedback and starts making the final product. Tasks in this phase begin with the decision of how much to produce. The goal is to meet consumer demand without creating a costly surplus or losing sales due to a shortage. Historical sales data for similar products may offer a starting point. In some cases, there are other clues to the level of demand, such as prerelease orders of books and electronics, early decision applications for colleges, or the results of consumer surveys. Production limits may also be imposed by the availability of materials and the capacity of the staff and facility. Unexpected challenges often confront managers in the production phase. Equipment failures, staffing problems, and delays due to licensing and permit requirements can hinder progress. It can be difficult to find enough workers in some industries, including

TMP-0664.text: healthcare, transportation, manufacturing, and agriculture, and in skilled trades like plumbing and electrical work. The business may also contend with quality-control issues such as poor-quality inputs, inconsistent quality across batches of output, and defective products. Several external factors influence the production phase as well. Module 1.8 explained supply chains, and the importance of getting the right materials to the right place at the right time for manufacturing needs. The state of the economy is relevant to all businesses, as fluctuations in income and unemployment levels add to the uncertainties of market demand. Increases in the overall price level known as inflation can affect input prices. And natural disasters such as earthquakes, fires, and storms can disrupt the manufacturing process. Resilience is the key to success in the production phase. For example, in the early days of Amazon, the company did well selling books, music, and movies. When it launched its online toy business, it began with almost twice as many toys as it ended up selling. Although that sales forecast missed the mark, the business rolled with the punches. Amazon gave a lot of toys to charities, adjusted its expectations, and went on to become the world’s largest online retailer.

TMP-0665.text: Launch At the launch phase, the product becomes available to consumers and the business focuses on building excitement around the new offering. Marketing efforts go into full swing. The business distributes its products to stores or directly to consumers, and the sales team springs into action. Some businesses generate buzz about their new products with social media posts and major launch events. Upon launching a new game console, Nintendo has been known to create first-look video trailers and bring the console on a world tour so that gamers can give it a try and follow up with word-of-mouth advertising. Although it is selling its final product, the business must be ever focused on opportunities for improvement. Every sale is a learning experience from which responses and feedback can lead to better service and new product ideas. Later in this module, we will discuss why businesses must search for opportunities to innovate even if they have a hot-selling product. Next, we will consider how a business with a new product can craft a brand identity that shapes perceptions and bolsters loyalty among consumers.

TMP-0667.text: Branding LG Why is brand identity important, and how is it developed? Hundreds of shoe companies compete to put their product on your feet. They don’t have equal opportunities to attract you as a customer due to the influence of branding. A brand is the identity of a product or business that distinguishes it from its competitors. Brands are unique to a company thanks to legal protections under trademark law, which means marketing teams can justify high expenditures to associate their brand with the characteristics most appealing to their target market. If they are successful, you would pay extra for certain brands of shoes— for example Nike, Adidas, or Asics—rather than buying shoes from a brand you have never heard of. brand The identity of a product or business that distinguishes it from its competitors.

TMP-0668.text: Businesses align their brand image with their value proposition. A company like Adidas wants buyers to choose its product because it makes them feel like champions. To that end, Adidas sponsors outstanding athletes and teams to make sure its brand logos are worn by champions. By associating the brand with the achievements and qualities customers seek, a company can build its following and nurture loyalty. The Adidas three-stripe logo represents the brand’s core values of performance, design, and craftsmanship. Beyond logos and other symbols, brands can be conveyed by names like Sketchers, color schemes like the trademarked burnt orange of the University of Texas, fonts like in the title of The New York Times , and packaging such as the Coca-Cola bottle. Maybe you can even think of an advertising jingle that makes you think immediately of a brand. A brand is intangible, having significance in consumers’ minds rather than in a physical presence. Consumers value branding because of the information it provides. Familiar, trusted brands can assure quality and consistency. Brands like Cotopaxi and Disney can represent shared values or experiences with an emotional connection. Rolex and BMW are among the brands that may convey social status.

TMP-0669.text: Many customers prioritize cost savings over the reliability and status a brand can convey. To target those customers, businesses may offer generic goods with no associated brand. Generic goods offer the same basic functionality as branded goods, but no money is spent on advertising or fancy packaging to build a brand identity. By selling generics at a relatively low price, businesses pass on some of the cost savings and appeal to cost-sensitive customers. For example, acetaminophen is the generic equivalent of Tylenol-brand pain reliever and generally has a lower price. A variation on generic goods is goods with the brand of a store, known as a private label, house brand, or store brand. Walmart’s Great Value brand, Amazon’s Amazon Basics brand, and Kroger’s Private Selection brand are popular examples. In a market with customers who prioritize quality and many competitors all claiming to sell splendid products, a reputable brand carries tremendous value. It is easy for a business to say “We sell great products!” By associating a product with a brand that represents a long history of high standards, a business says the same thing in a way consumers trust. Next, we will examine how a product with a long history may begin to fade despite its brand.

TMP-0670.text: Bloomberg/Getty Images Would you pay more for a pair of shoes from some brands than from others? If so, marketing teams have succeeded in their goal of associating their brands with the qualities you seek.

TMP-0671.text: The Product Life Cycle LG How do marketing strategies evolve over a product’s life cycle? Production and launch begin the story of a product’s life in the public eye. Like most stories, this one also has a middle and an end, but few products live happily ever after. Consider the radios, newspapers, and bean bag chairs that were popular 50 years ago. Those products were appealing and useful when introduced, but their sales declined as needs changed, new alternatives became available, and fashions evolved. If you don’t own those products now, it is because they are near or at the end of their product life cycle. The product life cycle (PLC) is the succession of stages a product goes through, from its introduction to its eventual decline and withdrawal from the market. product life cycle (PLC) The succession of stages a product goes through, from its introduction to its eventual decline and withdrawal from the market.

TMP-0672.text: A product’s life cycle resembles our own, with introduction followed by growth, maturity, and decline. Figure 2.4-2 shows a likely path for sales and profit during each of these stages of the product’s life. In this section, we will examine how consumer demand drives these stages, and how businesses use marketing strategies to address the challenges along the way.

TMP-0673.text: Introduction Growth Maturity Decline Sales and Profit ($) Sales Profit Time Copyright © BFW Publishers Extended description for Figure 2.4-2 Product Life Cycle The horizontal axis of the graph shows Time. The vertical axis shows Sales and Profit in dollars. Two lines appear on the graph: one for Sales and the other for Profit. The graph is divided into four regions across Time: Introduction, Growth, Maturity, and Decline. The approximate data appear as follows:

TMP-0674.text: • The line for Profit begins in the negative space during the introduction phase. It rises slightly into the positive during the Growth phase. It hits its highest point when Growth meets Maturity and stays high throughout the Maturity phase. The line then declines to zero during the Decline phase. • The line for Sales begins at zero during the Introduction phase but rises throughout the phase. It continues to rise during the Growth phase, reaching much higher highs than the Profit line. It continues to rise, peaking in the Maturity Phase. The line declines during the Decline phase but never drops as low as the Profit line. Figure 2.4-2 Product Life Cycle Introduction The introduction stage of the product life cycle is the period when a product is first launched into the market. Whether in a new market or one already crowded with rivals, most products start their lives as relative unknowns. A business faces losses when launching a product, both because the prior product-development process involved

TMP-0675.text: costs but no sales, and because the undiscovered product experiences weak demand. Profit remains low or negative throughout the introduction stage, as the focus is on aggressive marketing to build consumer awareness. The marketing strategy during the introduction stage is to educate consumers about the product and the brand and to create interest in making a purchase. Even with strong marketing efforts, it may take several years for sales revenue to exceed costs and produce a profit. introduction stage The stage of the product life cycle when a product is first launched into the market. Self-driving cars are in the introductory stage, as are virtual reality headsets, foldable smartphones, and lab-grown beef alternatives. With successful marketing, the demand for these products will pick up and the businesses will experience a period of growth. Businesses entice early adopters with promotions such as grand openings, free samples, and discount pricing. Apps such as Spotify, Zoom, Dropbox, and Duolingo boosted their early popularity with the freemium model of giving access to a limited version of the app for free. Many of the customers drawn in by these costless services liked them enough to pay for a full-featured “premium” version, which allowed the companies to earn profit.

TMP-0676.text: Growth The growth stage of a product’s life is when sales volume and revenue increase rapidly. Production generally rises and profit is increasingly likely in this stage due to several ongoing changes. Rising demand not only increases sales but also allows the business to charge higher prices. Higher production levels may result in lower costs due to economies of scale. Spending on marketing may decline in this stage as the product becomes known, although marketing efforts continue to expand the pool of customers and build brand loyalty. growth stage The stage of the product life cycle when sales volume and revenue increase rapidly. The profit at this stage attracts competitors who pursue their own profit by offering similar products. As rivals emerge, the marketing strategy pivots from an emphasis on product awareness to an effort to differentiate the product from alternatives. Marketing messages highlight the brand’s quality and the product’s value proposition in hopes of maintaining the momentum of growth.

TMP-0677.text: Consider KFC, whose founder, Colonel Harland Sanders, started selling chicken in 1930. Colonel Sanders’s first restaurant fit in the back of a gas station in North Corbin, Kentucky. Colonel Sanders was an ambitious self-promoter who used prominent signage, innovative cooking techniques, and an insistence on quality to help his business stand out. Before long, the demand for his “finger lickin’ good” chicken grew, as marketing efforts paid off, word spread, and the business built its reputation. By 1939, Sanders needed a 142-seat restaurant to keep up with demand. By 1952, he was selling Kentucky Fried Chicken franchises in other states. In the early 1990s, KFC expanded into Europe and South America. Today, the company has more than 30,000 locations worldwide. Maturity The maturity stage is when a product’s sales reach their peak and level off. The business would like to maintain the popularity of its product, but market conditions are changing. Any continuing increases in consumer demand are balanced by increases in competition. Rival firms now have strong footing in the market and prevent the business from charging higher prices. Knowing the next stage is decline, the business takes steps to maintain its existing market share. Common marketing strategies in the

TMP-0678.text: maturity stage include further product differentiation, lower prices to retain consumer interest, and investment in innovation to add product features or capabilities. However, these tactics cause the already stagnating profit to decline, as shown in Figure 2.4-2 . maturity stage The stage of the product life cycle when a product’s sales reach their peak and level off. Some products linger at the maturity stage for a long period. Coca-Cola has been a staple in the soft drink industry since 1892 and has gone head-to-head with rival Pepsi since 1898. Fearing decline, the company introduced a reformulated New Coke in 1985, but the original formula won out against the new one and all contenders. Even so, the Coca-Cola Company has succeeded in sustaining the maturity stage with aggressive marketing campaigns and innovative offerings, such as Coca-Cola Orange Cream, Sprite Chill Strawberry Kiwi, and Reign Tropical Storm Total Body Fuel. In other cases, however, maturity is short lived. Market saturation, declining demand, and improving alternatives have ended the maturity stage for most old products. You may have heard of compact discs, Blackberry smartphones, iPod music players, film cameras, landline telephones, and Sierra Mist soda. Those products each had their days

TMP-0679.text: of robust growth and maturity, but they could not fend off the nearly inevitable final stage. Decline Trends, preferences, and technologies change. New alternatives make many old products obsolete. And markets filled with competitors send the demand for each product downward. The decline stage is when a product experiences falling sales and revenue. Profit declines and will turn negative if revenue falls below the cost of continued operations. The most loyal customers hold on, but the product’s loss of relevance forces tough decisions about whether to discontinue sales. decline stage The stage of the product life cycle when a product experiences falling sales and revenue. In the decline stage, a business may decide to pull back on marketing efforts to cut costs and allocate resources to other products at earlier stages of the product life cycle. In other cases, the marketing strategy is to revitalize the product—perhaps with new features or designs—and prevent its demise. For example, Marvel Comics almost came to an end in the late 1990s despite efforts to innovate with new products and animation

TMP-0680.text: techniques. Since then, changes in ownership and successful promotions involving movies and digital programming have given the company new relevance and a new life. Some products experience declines that are not fatal. For instance, desktop computers and cameras maintain adequate sales to warrant continuation. By lowering expenditures on marketing and production, companies like Lenovo and Canon continue to offer these products and earn profit. The decline of other products does not justify continuation in the absence of major innovations that serve new needs. IBM typewriters were in millions of offices and homes in the twentieth century, but the company no longer makes them. Table 2.4-1 summarizes the marketing strategies you’ve just learned about. Next, we’ll examine how innovation can give products and companies new life, as it did for IBM.

TMP-0681.text: Paul Brady/Alamy Stock Photo Typewriters, once a staple in every office, are now obsolete because innovations led to new alternatives. Table 2.4-1 Summary of Marketing Strategies Stage Marketing Strategy Introduction Raise awareness, educate consumers, and generate demand Growth Differentiate the product by emphasizing the brand’s quality and the product’s value proposition Maturity Further product differentiation, attractive prices, innovation

TMP-0682.navLabel: The Role of Innovation in the Product Life Cycle
TMP-0682.text: Decline Cut marketing expenditures and focus on other products, or reinvent the product to keep it viable The Role of Innovation in the Product Life Cycle Management consultant Peter Drucker famously said that businesses must “innovate or die.” 1 The truth behind this saying is that the decline at the end of the product life cycle can be averted by innovation that creates a new product or refreshes an old one. Consider Cheerios cereal, which General Mills introduced in 1941. By the 1970s, Cheerios were losing market share to newer cereals such as Fruity Pebbles, Pink Panther Flakes, and Freakies. To renew interest in Cheerios, General Mills introduced Cinnamon Nut Cheerios in 1976 and Honey Nut Cheerios in 1979. Those flavors gave Cheerios customers something new to wake up to and sold by the millions of boxes. Flavor innovations have so effectively revived interest in Cheerios that General Mills has now created more than 30 varieties of that product. Meanwhile, Freakies cereal, which failed to innovate successfully, is no longer with us. Three general reasons motivate innovations that modify or replace products.

headings.text: The Role of Innovation in the Product Life Cycle

TMP-0683.navLabel: The Role of Innovation in the Product Life Cycle
TMP-0683.text: Adapting to Changing Needs and Wants Businesses must be nimble and adapt as markets evolve. Changing weather, wars, and natural disasters alter a population’s needs. Economic conditions change incomes and consumers’ ability to pay for goods and services. Societal trends are influenced by leaders, celebrities, movie stars, and marketing campaigns. And new products change the need for old products. Just as the automobile industry crushed the demand for horse-drawn buggies, the electric car industry may leave gasoline engines behind. Changing fashions, trends, and fads also influence the items on consumers’ shopping lists. Tie widths, skirt lengths, and pant leg shapes go in and out of style. Even sneaker soles go from minimalist to super thick. A business must be on the ball with innovation to keep up with evolving consumer needs and wants. Product Differentiation In a competitive market, profit goes to those who come up with something different. Consider the restaurant industry, which shows little mercy for redundancy. White Castle distinguished itself in 1921 by opening the first fast-food restaurant, which saved its customers valuable time. That same year, Kirby’s Pig Stand introduced the drive-in restaurant, in which waitstaff known as carhops brought food to customers in their cars.

TMP-0684.navLabel: The Role of Innovation in the Product Life Cycle
TMP-0684.text: In 1931, California Pig Stand stood out by offering drive-thru service that allowed customers to receive food in their cars without summoning carhops. In 1958, the Mawaru Genroku Sushi restaurant opened with a conveyor belt that brought food directly to customers’ tables. Fast forward to today, and restaurants continue to innovate with mobile apps that take orders, self-service kiosks, and services like DoorDash that whisk food from your choice of restaurants to your door. The story is the same in any crowded marketplace: Businesses that find a way to be a little better than the rest tend to earn a lot more profit than the rest. Increasing Competition Finally, innovation may be necessary to contend with rivals’ growing competitive advantages. Consider Samsung, which competes with Google, Vivo, Apple, and other giants in the smartphone market. As Apple creates an ecosystem of devices that work well together and Google refines the art of building sleek phones with intuitive interfaces, Samsung must do what failed former rival BlackBerry did not. Samsung invests heavily in advancements such as foldable smartphones, state-of-the-art cameras, wireless charging, and iris-scan security systems. Samsung must innovate to remain

TMP-0685.navLabel: The Role of Innovation in the Product Life Cycle
TMP-0685.text: competitive. The same is true throughout the technology industries, but also in industries ranging from air transportation to waste management.

TMP-0686.text: Module 2.4 Review Learning Goals LG What are the phases of the product development process? • A product is a good or service that a business offers to meet consumer needs and wants. • Product development is the process of designing a new product and bringing it to market. The typical phases of product development are ideation , validation, design, messaging, production, and launch. Validation is the process of verifying that an idea solves a problem for consumers, is realistic to provide, and has the potential to generate profit. • A good idea also needs product-market fit , meaning that it satisfies strong-enough market demand to be commercially viable. A value proposition summarizes how a

TMP-0687.text: product serves customers’ needs better than the alternatives. LG Why is brand identity important, and how is it developed? • A brand is the identity of a product or business that distinguishes it from its competitors. A brand is intangible, having significance in consumers’ minds rather than in a physical presence. • Consumers value branding because of the information it provides. Familiar, trusted brands can assure quality and consistency. LG How do marketing strategies evolve over a product’s life cycle? • The stages of a product’s life—the product life cycle —are introduction, growth, maturity, and decline. The introduction stage is the period when a product is first launched into the market. This stage is characterized by losses and slow sales growth. The growth stage of a product’s life is when sales volume and revenue

TMP-0688.text: increase rapidly and profit is increasingly likely. The maturity stage is when a product’s sales reach their peak and level off. The decline stage is when a product experiences falling sales and revenue. • Innovation can modify or replace a product with declining sales. Innovation is needed due to changing consumer needs and wants, business interests in product differentiation, and stiffening competition. Practice Your AP® Skills Preparing for the AP® Exam Multiple-Choice Questions 1. The correct order of the stages of product development, from beginning to end, is a. launch, ideation, validation, design, messaging, production. b. ideation, validation, design, messaging, production, launch.

TMP-0689.text: c. design, validation, ideation, messaging, production, launch. d. ideation, design, validation, messaging, launch, production. 2. Decline at the end of a product life cycle can best be averted by a. innovation. b. increased production. c. validation. d. product launch. 3. At which stage of a product’s life cycle are profits most likely to peak? a. introduction b. growth c. maturity d. decline 4. What is the best definition for a product’s value proposition? a. The manufacturer’s suggested retail price, also known as MSRP.

TMP-0690.text: b. The sum of the costs of producing the product. c. The highest price that consumers would be willing and able to pay for the product. d. A summary of how a product serves customer needs better than the alternatives. 5. What is the primary advantage of buying a generic good? a. lower prices b. better quality c. its advertising is a good reminder to buy what you need d. greater reliability

TMP-0691.text: CASE STUDY Ralph Lauren Susan Wood/Getty Images There are successful brands, and then there is Ralph Lauren, whose life is a masterclass about how branding is done. Ralph Lifshitz knew a thing or two about brand identity from a young age. At 16, he rebranded himself as Ralph Lauren. At 28, he founded the Ralph Lauren Corporation and sold neckties under the Polo brand name. Four years later, he became the first American designer to open a freestanding store, which happened

TMP-0692.text: to be on posh Rodeo Drive in Beverly Hills, California. The company’s signature Polo shirt made its debut one year later, in 1972. In the decades since, Ralph Lauren’s magical touch with ties and shirts expanded to women’s and children’s clothing, furniture, fragrances, footwear, and even restaurants. The Ralph Lauren Corporation’s reach extended around the world, and Ralph Lauren himself became a multi-billionaire. In 2025, at the age of 85, Ralph Lauren was still the executive chairman and chief creative officer for his company. Competing companies dream of a brand image like Ralph Lauren’s. The brand’s familiar logo, featuring a polo horse and rider, conveys the power to charge prices two or three times those of similar items from lesser brands. Lauren’s formula for success has not been replicated, but many of its elements are on clear display. From the beginning, the brand has been synonymous with quality. Its aesthetic encompasses a blend of neutral colors, rugged strength, subtle patterns, and classic style. Ralph Lauren clothing looks natural in a variety of settings, ranging from camping trips to weddings.

TMP-0693.text: The Ralph Lauren style has defined trends and transcended fads for more than half a century. In the 1970s and 80s, the brand became synonymous with the prep school vibe it conveyed; by the 1990s, hip-hop artists had embraced it. Today, stars like Taylor Swift and Jacob Elordi continue to inspire a younger generation of consumers to move past fast fashion and invest in the brand’s timeless clothing and accessories. While many once-great brands have resorted to sales at discount stores to expand their volume, Ralph Lauren has remained true to its roots, with uncompromising standards for materials, design, marketing, and distribution. Despite many clues to the magic of Ralph Lauren’s appeal, it remains a brand that defies both replication and decline. Apply Your AP® Skills 1. Search your social media for mentions of the Ralph Lauren brand. Based on what appears, what type of person do you think is a typical Ralph Lauren consumer?

TMP-0694.text: 2. Identify a competitive advantage of the Ralph Lauren Corporation and explain how that advantage limits direct competition with Ralph Lauren. 3. If you’re unfamiliar with Ralph Lauren’s advertising, do an online search for “Ralph Lauren ad.” How would you characterize this company’s advertising? 4. If you wanted to build a brand like Ralph Lauren, what is one strategy from that company that you would copy? Explain your answer. 5. Where do you think the Ralph Lauren polo shirt is in the product life cycle? Explain your answer.

TMP-0695.text: MODULE 2.5 Price LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 2.5.A Explain common pricing strategies 2.5.B Describe how price sensitivity and competition affect pricing decisions 2.5.C Discuss legal restrictions on pricing

TMP-0696.text: STEFANI REYNOLDS/Getty Images The temptation to raise prices must be considered carefully. If customers keep buying a similar quantity of the product at the higher price, revenue will increase. But if customers respond to a price increase by switching to a competitor’s product, sales and profit can plummet.

TMP-0697.text: Finding the Right Price LG What are some common pricing strategies? Imagine you visit the local deli and find that the price of your favorite sandwich has increased by $2. What could explain the price hike? The deli has a new pricing strategy , which is a systematic approach to determining what price to charge for a product. Would you still buy the sandwich? By raising its price, the deli is betting that enough people will pay the higher price to make its strategy pay off. In this module, we’ll explore common pricing strategies, factors that influence prices, and customers’ responses to price changes. Price is one of the 4 Ps of a product’s marketing mix, and arriving at this important number is no easy feat. pricing strategy A systematic approach to determining what price to charge for a product.

TMP-0698.text: Price Determinants There are several price determinants for a business to consider. The upper bound on prices is the most customers are willing to pay. That limit is governed by consumers’ financial situation, their options, and the perceived value of the product, which is the amount customers believe the product is worth to them. Businesses also factor in their per-unit cost , which is the average cost of producing and distributing the product, found by dividing the total cost of production and distribution by the quantity produced. perceived value The amount customers believe a product is worth to them. per-unit cost The average cost of producing and distributing the product, found by dividing the total cost of production and distribution by the quantity produced. Another consideration is the profit a price would provide from each sale. Businesses look at their per-unit profit margin , which is the price minus the per-unit cost, sometimes expressed as a percentage of the price. For example, if the per-unit cost of a pair of socks is $7 and its price is $10, the per-unit profit margin is $10 − $7 = $3 or

TMP-0699.text: $3/$10 = 30 %. Figure 2.5-1 illustrates the breakdown of this sock price into the per-unit cost and profit margin.

TMP-0700.text: $10 $7 } } Price Per-unit profit margin Per-unit cost 1 pair of socks Copyright © BFW Publishers Extended description for Figure 2.5-1 Price, Per-Unit Cost, and Per-Unit Profit Margin i The chart shows 1 pair of socks on the horizontal axis and two prices on the vertical axis, 7 dollars and 10 dollars. The area from 0 to 7 dollars is labeled Per-unit cost. The area from 7 to 10 dollars is labeled

TMP-0701.text: Per-unit profit margin. The point at 10 dollars is labeled Price. Figure 2.5-1 Price, Per-Unit Cost, and Per- Unit Profit Margin per-unit profit margin The price minus the per-unit cost, sometimes expressed as a percentage of the price. A business could attract customers and gain market share by lowering its price, but of course there are tradeoffs: A price equal to the per-unit cost would have a per-unit profit margin of zero, and a price below the per-unit cost would result in losses. Other price determinants include market demand and the prices of competitors, as discussed later in this module. Darn Tough Vermont sells its Micro Crew Midweight Hiking Sock for $26. How did the company settle on this price? It’s likely they used one of the pricing strategies discussed below.

TMP-0702.text: Common Pricing Strategies Five common pricing strategies businesses use are cost-based pricing, competitive pricing, value-based pricing, price skimming, and penetration pricing. The best strategy depends on the situation. 1. Many businesses prefer a simple pricing strategy that employees can apply quickly and easily. To implement cost-based pricing , a business takes the cost of making or obtaining the product and adds a predetermined per-unit profit margin to find the selling price. Again, the per-unit profit margin can be an amount, such as $3, or a percentage, such as 30%. Cost-based pricing is especially popular among small retail stores, which have many products to price and no analysts to track down data on the market. This strategy is also useful for service providers who want to ensure a certain profit while giving their customers options for related products. Businesses with clearly defined per-unit costs, such as a grocery delivery service, a carpet installer, or a wedding photographer, can stipulate their profit margin and add that to the cost of the chosen items. Online clothing company Everlane uses cost-based pricing as part of a strategy of “radical transparency.” By revealing its costs, including those of organic fabrics and wages that seem fair, the company

TMP-0703.text: gains a competitive advantage among consumers who like to know where their money goes. 2. With competitive pricing , a business bases its prices on competitors’ prices. In markets with significant competition, cost-based pricing could inadvertently set prices too high relative to rivals’ prices. Instead, a business may adopt a price matching strategy of charging the same price as competitors to avoid losing customers based on price. If the business feels its product lacks features that differentiate it from rival products, it might choose to forego per-unit profit and undercut the competition to attract price-sensitive customers and gain market share. If the product does have an edge over rivals, the business might charge a bit more to benefit from its differentiated features or reputation. For example, Fitbit can charge a higher price for its activity tracking watches than competitors such as Delvfire, because Fitbit is an established brand with a loyal customer base. In some cases, businesses choose to charge more than the competition to signal superiority, which is known as premium pricing . 3. Value-based pricing entails choosing prices based on customers’ perceived value of a business’s product or service. For example, Starbucks applies a value-based pricing strategy by conducting research on the value consumers place on its famous

TMP-0704.text: coffee and keeping prices at or below that level. Value-based pricing is popular among companies with highly differentiated products and for luxury brands whose prestige gives their products added value. The approach works best for companies that have access to market research on the perceived value consumers receive from their products. 4. Price skimming is a strategy of giving a product a high price when it launches and gradually lowering the price over time. This strategy helps sellers of innovative products charge the highest price that several different segments of consumers are willing to pay. The business receives a high price from eager early adopters who have a high willingness to pay. Later, they appeal to increasingly price-sensitive customers by offering a lower and lower price. For example, Hewlett-Packard introduced a handheld calculator in 1974 for $795 (more than $5,000 in today’s dollars, after adjusting for inflation). Today, you can buy a handheld calculator from the same company for less than $10. 5. The strategy of penetration pricing involves setting a low initial price to draw customers away from the competition. The price might even be set below the per-unit cost, because when introducing a product in a competitive market, the first priority is not to make profit, but to attract attention. For example, it is common for

TMP-0705.text: new internet and streaming service providers to offer introductory prices as low as zero for a limited time. After that period of enticing consumers away from their previous service providers, the price increases and profits can follow. cost-based pricing A strategy in which a business takes the cost of making or obtaining the product and adds a predetermined per-unit profit margin to find the selling price. competitive pricing A strategy in which a business bases its prices on competitors’ prices. value-based pricing A strategy in which a business chooses its prices based on customers’ perceived value of its products or services. penetration pricing A strategy in which a business sets a low initial price to draw customers away from the competition, and then increases the price.

The shows, from left to right, are Black Snow; Mayfair Witches; Fallen; Scrublands; Interview with the Vampire; A Discovery of Witches; and Sanctuary: A Witch's Tale. Penetration pricing is common among streaming services. Companies set a low initial price to attract customers and then raise the price in pursuit of profit. These and other pricing strategies provide options to consider based on the business’s product, market, target audience, competitive advantage, objectives, and available information. As we’ll discuss next, pricing strategies are also influenced by the level of competition and the legal and regulatory environment. AP ® EXAM TIP Be prepared to explain both how prices are set under each pricing strategy and what type of business would benefit from each strategy. You may be asked which strategy is appropriate for a particular business, so just knowing how the strategies work is not enough.

TMP-0709.text: Market Constraints on Pricing LG How do price sensitivity and competition affect pricing decisions? As we discussed in Module 1.2 , firms in perfectly competitive markets cannot independently raise their price and expect customers to continue buying their product. If hundreds of coffee farmers sell identical coffee beans, no one farmer can command a higher price than the others. With many firms selling the same product at the current market price, there would be no reason for a customer to pay more to one firm. The ability to raise prices without losing customers is known as pricing power . In a perfectly competitive market, individual firms have no power to influence the market or its price, but they aspire to change that in ways we will discuss next. pricing power The ability to raise prices without losing customers.

TMP-0710.text: Pricing Power The ability to raise prices and still keep customers comes from product differentiation. If your product has features or qualities that rival firms can’t match, you can charge at least a bit more than your competitors and still get sales. For example, coffee from the Kona region of Hawai’i is said to taste better than other coffees. On that basis, sellers of Kona coffee can charge substantially higher prices. Closer to home for most of us, consider the fast-food market, which contains hundreds of restaurants with differentiated products. Some restaurants successfully charge more for a hamburger than others. Those companies have developed a product with distinctive qualities, and their marketing teams have made sure we know that those burgers are flame grilled, or never frozen, or juicier, or thicker, or special in some other way. If a business is the only seller of a product in a market, that market is a monopoly, and that seller is a monopolist. The business will enjoy pricing power because no one else sells its product. That doesn’t mean the business can charge whatever it wants, because consumers are only willing to pay so much, but the business may be able to raise its price a moderate amount and not lose all its customers. In a duopoly with two firms, or an oligopoly with a small number of firms, the lack of competition similarly allows

TMP-0711.navLabel: Measuring Customers’ Responses to Price Changes
TMP-0711.text: some pricing power. Module 1.2 explained how barriers to entry such as patents, control of resources, and economies of scale can limit competition and allow monopolies, duopolies, and oligopolies to persist and maintain their pricing power. For example, the patents on many pharmaceutical drugs prevent rivals from offering the same product and grant the sellers considerable pricing power. Measuring Customers’ Responses to Price Changes It’s tempting to think that a business can increase its profit by increasing its price, but that approach may backfire. The advisability of a higher price depends on how consumers would respond to the price change. If consumers would keep buying the same quantity of bananas regardless of the price, grocers would get rich charging a fortune per pound. But banana prices remain reasonable because grocers know that consumers would respond to an astronomical price with a resounding “no.” There are some goods and services—like heart surgeries and life-saving drugs—that people will buy the same quantity of for any price they can possibly afford. And the prices for many of those goods and services are, indeed, raised to barely affordable levels.

headings.text: Measuring Customers’ Responses to Price Changes

TMP-0712.navLabel: Measuring Customers’ Responses to Price Changes
TMP-0712.text: For many products that are not essential or have good substitutes, the quantity demanded will decrease considerably as the price rises. If the price of air travel increases significantly, many consumers will change their travel plans, perhaps opting to drive, take the bus, or stay home. Like the grocer who charged a fortune for bananas, the airline that charged a lot more for flights might end up with very few customers. The important lesson is that price increases don’t necessarily add to revenue or profit, and they could subtract from both.

TMP-0713.navLabel: Measuring Customers’ Responses to Price Changes
TMP-0713.text: Cavan Images/Getty Images Airlines know that if they raise ticket prices too high, travelers can choose to hit the road instead. A business must carefully consider the likely decrease in the quantity demanded before deciding to raise its price. A common gauge for this is the price elasticity of demand , which is a measure of consumers’ responsiveness to price changes. The price

TMP-0714.navLabel: Measuring Customers’ Responses to Price Changes
TMP-0714.text: elasticity is found by dividing the percentage change in the quantity demanded by the percentage change in the price, dropping the inevitable negative sign. While we won’t do those calculations in this course, we will interpret elasticity values and learn why they are important. price elasticity of demand A measure of consumers’ responsiveness to price changes. Figure 2.5-2 summarizes the interpretation of price elasticity values. If the price elasticity of demand is greater than one, the demand is considered elastic , meaning consumers’ responsiveness to price changes is high. Demand is typically elastic if a product is not needed (leisure travel), many substitutes are available (Coca-Cola), or the product’s price represents a large share of consumers’ income (expensive furniture). Since a price increase will cause a relatively large decrease in the quantity demanded, higher prices lead to lower revenue. When contemplating a price increase, the business can compare the resulting revenue decrease with the corresponding cost decrease (because fewer items are sold) to determine whether the price increase would provide a net gain.

TMP-0716.navLabel: Measuring Customers’ Responses to Price Changes
TMP-0716.text: When demand is elastic, a price cut might add to a business’s profit. Because customers are highly responsive to price changes, a price cut will cause a relatively large increase in the quantity demanded, so lower prices increase revenue. The key question is whether the increase in revenue would exceed the increase in cost for the additional items sold. If the increase in revenue would be larger than the increase in cost, a price cut would increase profits (or decrease losses). If the price elasticity of demand is equal to one, the demand is unit elastic , meaning that the quantity demanded changes in proportion to the price change, but in the opposite direction. If price increases by 10%, the quantity demanded decreases by 10%. The result is that total revenue is unaffected by a price change. A price increase does increase profit, because production costs decrease as a result of the lower quantity demanded. However, demand is typically unit elastic only for a narrow range of prices, because prices that keep rising tend to trigger more than proportional decreases in quantity before long. If the price elasticity of demand is less than one, the demand is inelastic , meaning consumers’ sensitivity to price changes is low. The percentage change in the quantity demanded is smaller than the percentage change in price, so total revenue will increase

TMP-0717.navLabel: Measuring Customers’ Responses to Price Changes
TMP-0717.text: if the price rises and decrease if the price falls. A business with inelastic demand should increase its price to benefit from the higher revenue and the lower cost of making fewer units. Demand is typically inelastic if a product is essential (insulin for people with diabetes), has few substitutes (electricity), or takes a small share of consumers’ income (table salt). That inverse relationship between price and the quantity demanded is shown by the downward-sloping shape of the demand curve introduced in Module 1.2 . Each point along the curve corresponds with a price on the vertical axis and the quantity consumers would buy at that price on the horizontal axis. For example, point A indicates that for $10, consumers would buy 100 pairs of socks. Point B shows that for $12, consumers would buy 75 pairs of socks.

Figure 2.5-3 Market Demand If consumers would buy the same quantity at any price, the sock company could raise its price and be certain that its revenue would increase. By raising its price from $10 to $12 and still selling 100 pairs, the sock company’s total revenue would increase from $10 × 100 = $1,000 to $12 × 100 = $1,200. Production costs would stay the same because the number of socks would not change, so the additional $200 in revenue would simply contribute to profit. The downward slope of the demand curve makes the effects of a price change on revenue and profit uncertain. Depending on consumers’ sensitivity to price increases, the quantity demanded might decrease a lot or a little in response to a price increase. With the quantity demanded going down to 75 pairs of socks at a price of $12, the revenue falls to $12 × 75 = $900 at the higher price— a decrease of $1,000 − $900 = $100. If each pair of socks costs $7 to make, the decrease in quantity from 100 to 75 lowers production costs by $7 × 25 = $175. Comparing the $100 decrease in revenue with the $175 decrease in costs, there is still a net gain of $175 − $100 = $75 from increasing the

With price increases having an indeterminate effect on revenue and profit, a business should carefully consider the price elasticity of demand before making price changes that might work against financial goals.

TMP-0722.text: Legal Constraints on Pricing LG How do legal barriers affect prices? How much would you be willing to pay for medicine that would save your life? You would probably pay whatever you could get your hands on for something that important. When a company with the pricing power of a monopolist sells a product such as medicine with tremendous perceived value to consumers, the result can be a price in the millions of dollars per dose. 1 Many governments take action to protect consumers from excessive pricing power created by market power, consumer desperation, and discrimination. Laws That Promote Competition Given the price-moderating effects of rivals, some businesses try to reduce the level of competition in their market. Because that leaves consumers with fewer options and

TMP-0723.text: higher prices, it is common for governments to establish laws that restrict market power. Antitrust laws aim to promote competition and prevent unfair business practices. For example, if you are one of only two florists in town, you cannot sit down with your competitor and agree that you’ll both raise your prices. In the United States and many other countries, antitrust laws prohibit collusion , which is secretive cooperation between businesses to hinder competition. This makes it illegal for businesses to thwart the effects of competition by agreeing to all raise prices, limit supply, or divide markets into segments, each to be served by one or more designated firms. collusion Secretive cooperation between businesses to hinder competition. Antitrust laws aim to prevent monopolies and give consumers access to many products from different sellers at prices moderated by the forces of competition. However, there are exceptions to the prohibition of monopolies. As we discussed in Module 1.2 , government patents, copyrights, and trademarks create monopolies for a limited period. Without protection from immediate duplication by competitors, the commitment of time, effort, and resources to create valuable drugs, books, songs, logos, and various creative works would not be rewarded. Another exception is made for

TMP-0724.text: natural monopolies , which exist when a market could not support many competing firms. For example, the cost of setting up a power plant or a sewer system is so high that it would be impossible for many competing providers to earn enough revenue to cover their costs. Instead, the government allows these monopolies to exist, but avoids excessive profits by limiting the prices they can charge. Laws That Protect Vulnerable Consumers Disasters such as hurricanes, fires, wars, earthquakes, and epidemics can make consumers desperate for shelter, food, medicine, and other essential goods. Dire conditions make consumers insensitive to price changes—meaning demand is inelastic—and can tempt businesses to charge exorbitant prices for essentials. Price gouging is the practice of raising prices on needed goods or services during a period of crisis. Price gouging is illegal in many countries and most U.S. states. For example, when rent prices spiked after wildfires displaced hundreds of Los Angeles-area residents, hundreds of landlords and hotels received warnings that price gouging is a crime in California. price gouging The practice of raising prices on needed goods or services during a period of crisis.

TMP-0727.text: When a crisis makes consumers vulnerable to excessive prices, governments sometimes step in and limit price increases. Laws Protect Consumers from Discrimination Price discrimination is the practice of charging different customers different prices for the same product. This pricing strategy is used to increase profit by charging customers who are not price sensitive a higher price than price-sensitive customers must pay. Like monopolies, price discrimination is legal in some situations and not in others. You may have benefited from price discrimination in the form of student discounts for movie tickets or public transportation; perhaps you have grandparents who enjoy similar discounts as seniors. Car salespeople negotiate different prices with different people based on how much they appear willing and able to pay. And wholesale clubs like Sam’s Club charge less per unit when people buy in volume. Such strategies

TMP-0728.text: are legal and often used by businesses to capture different customer segments based on their willingness to pay. price discrimination The practice of charging different customers different prices for the same product. Price discrimination is prohibited in some circumstances. In the United States, it is illegal to charge different prices based on a customer’s gender, race, national origin, religion, or other characteristics protected under civil rights laws. Price discrimination is also illegal when it is intended to harm competitors. Like the pricing constraints imposed by the limits of demand, legal constraints limit businesses’ ability to pick any price they choose. In most cases, however, a business that is able to differentiate its product has choices to make about the optimal pricing strategy. In the case study for this module, we will learn how puzzle maker Ordinary Habit approached pricing decisions.

TMP-0729.text: Module 2.5 Review Learning Goals LG What are some common pricing strategies? • A pricing strategy is a systematic approach to determining what price to charge for a product. Price is one of the 4 Ps of a product’s marketing mix. • The highest price consumers are willing to pay is governed by their financial situation, their options, and the perceived value of the product, which is the amount customers believe the product is worth to them. Businesses factor in their per-unit cost , which is the average cost of producing and distributing the product, found by dividing the total cost of production and distribution by the quantity produced. The per-unit profit margin is the profit from each sale, calculated as the price minus the per-unit cost and sometimes expressed as a percentage of the price.

TMP-0730.text: • To implement cost-based pricing , a business takes the cost of making the product and adds a predetermined per-unit profit margin to find the selling price. With competitive pricing , a business bases its prices on competitors’ prices. Value-based pricing entails choosing prices based on customers’ perceived value of a business’s product or service. Price skimming is a strategy of giving a product a high price when it launches and gradually lowering the price over time. The strategy of penetration pricing involves setting a low initial price to draw customers away from the competition. LG How do price sensitivity and competition affect pricing decisions? • Market forces constrain pricing decisions. The ability to raise prices without losing customers is known as pricing power . In a perfectly competitive market, individual firms have no power to influence the market or its prices. Product differentiation can give businesses pricing power, as can barriers to entry such as patents, control of resources, and economies of scale.

TMP-0731.text: • The price elasticity of demand is a measure of consumers’ responsiveness to price changes. If the price elasticity of demand is greater than one, the demand is considered very responsive or elastic , and a price increase will decrease the quantity demanded enough to lower total revenue. If the price elasticity of demand is equal to one, the demand is unit elastic , meaning that the quantity demanded changes in proportion to the price change, but in the opposite direction, and the total revenue does not change when price changes. If the price elasticity of demand is less than one, the demand is relatively unresponsive or inelastic , and total revenue will increase if the price rises. LG How do legal barriers affect prices? • Laws and regulations also constrain pricing decisions. Monopolies are not allowed in most markets in the United States. Antitrust laws also regulate collusion , which is secretive cooperation between businesses to hinder competition. • Price gouging is the practice of raising prices on needed goods or services during a period of crisis. Price gouging is illegal in many countries and most U.S. states.

TMP-0732.text: • Price discrimination is the practice of charging different customers different prices for the same product. In the United States, it is illegal to charge different prices based on gender, race, national origin, religion, or other characteristics protected under civil rights laws.
