TMP-0865.text: MODULES 3.1 Saving for Future Purchases 3.2 Borrowing, Credit, and Debt Personal Finance: Minding Your Own Business You might not be running a company — yet — but you’re already making decisions that mirror what business leaders do every day. Like any business, you have income, expenses, goals, and choices about how to manage your finances. Whether your money comes from a part-time job, an allowance, or summer gigs, you’re learning to balance what you need now with what you’re planning for the future. Maybe you’re saving to buy your first car, to continue your education after high school, or start a small business of your own. The cost of dreams often exceeds the reality of budgets. That’s where financial planning comes in. How much should you save? When should you borrow? What’s the smartest way to make it all happen?

TMP-0866.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0866.navLabel: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0866.text: Some individuals and businesses hire financial advisers to help answer these exact questions. People with a knack for answering these questions well can turn their abilities into a career, helping others make decisions about saving, borrowing, and investing. By learning the basics of personal finance, you’re building skills that will not only help you manage your own future, but may one day allow you to help others (including other entrepreneurs) do the same. In this unit, you’ll learn how individuals plan for big purchases, manage debt, build savings, and prepare for emergencies. You’ll also explore how factors like interest rates, inflation, and financial institutions affect your money. Whether you’re saving up for a house, leading a company, or just trying to make your paycheck cover the bills, these are tools you can use for life. This unit is just the beginning. In the next unit, we’ll shift from personal finance to business finance and accounting. You’ll dive into the financial side of running a business — tracking expenses, managing financial capital, creating income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow reports. You’ll also explore ethical responsibilities in financial reporting and decision-making.

TMP-0870.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0870.text: MODULE 3.1 Saving for Future Purchases LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 3.1.A Explain why and how consumers save money 3.1.B Describe the influence of PESTEL factors on savings 3.1.C Discuss how consumers develop a savings plan

TMP-0871.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0871.text: Edwin Tan/Getty Images When you earn money, it’s best to make informed decisions about how much of it to spend and how much of it to save.

TMP-0872.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0872.text: Why Consumers Save LG What is saving, and why can it be difficult to save? We often talk about saving money when we buy something on sale or avoid a purchase. But in personal finance, saving has a narrower meaning: To save money is to set money aside for future use instead of spending it now. Saving is one of the most important habits a person can develop when managing their money. saving Setting money aside for future use instead of spending it now. Of course, knowing that you should save money is one thing — actually doing it is the real challenge. In this module, we’ll explore why saving is important, why it can be hard, and how individuals can make better decisions about spending and saving.

TMP-0873.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0873.text: Income and Saving Before thinking about saving or spending, we need to understand the nature of income. Income is any money earned from a job, investments, or other sources. As a high school student, you might not receive any income of your own. But almost 90% of adults in the United States do earn income. The primary source of income is wages earned from working for an organization such as a business, a nonprofit, or a government agency. Some people receive income from self-employment, small business earnings, or rental properties. Other sources of income include investments, government programs, pensions, and retirement accounts. income Money earned from a job, investments, or other sources. It is essential to recognize the difference between income and wealth. While income refers to the money a person earns, wealth describes the total value of their personal assets (any property they own and savings they have accumulated, including any money they inherited) minus the value of any debts. No matter how much income you earn, you are not building wealth if you don’t put some of your income into savings or other assets.

TMP-0874.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0874.text: There are plenty of reasons to save, most of which fall into three main categories: 1. Short-term savings to be prepared for emergencies. Life is full of surprises. People lose jobs, get sick, or face unexpected expenses. Having some savings set aside for emergencies helps people avoid serious financial problems. Common advice is to build an emergency fund with enough money to cover three to six months of living expenses. But even having just a few thousand dollars in savings can be a considerable asset when faced with an unexpected bill. 2. Medium-term savings to finance significant future purchases. Many desirable purchases cost more money than one paycheck can provide. A high school student might save money from a summer job to pay for a class trip, prom, or a used car; an adult working full time will typically put some money into savings to pay for significant expenses like a new car, a wedding, or new shingles on their roof. 3. Long-term savings to finance future life goals. The biggest purchases require a longer timeline. It may take 10 years to save enough for the initial payment (called a down payment ) on a house, and 20 years to build a college savings fund for a child. And it can take many decades of saving to build a retirement fund. For all of these

TMP-0875.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0875.text: goals, achievement later requires planning now. (We will revisit long-term savings in Module 5.3 .)

TMP-0876.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0876.text: Left: Photos by R A Kearton/Getty Images; right: matsou/Getty Images Extended description for Minor Emergencies The first photo shows a medium-sized dog wearing a cone around its neck. The second photo shows the Check Engine light on a car's dashboard. The light is lit up. Two additional lights for oil and battery are also lit up.

TMP-0877.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0877.text: Even minor emergencies can mean major bills. Having some money saved is the best way to prepare for these common but unexpected situations. Interest Payments When you deposit money into your account at a bank (or other financial institution, such as a credit union), they can use your money for loans to other customers. In return, for most types of accounts, the bank provides compensation in the form of interest. Interest is the money paid for the use of someone else’s money. Borrowers pay interest to banks, and banks pay interest to depositors, which makes interest a source of income. interest The cost of borrowing money, paid by the borrower to the lender. The amount of money initially deposited into a bank account, or borrowed from a bank, is called the principal . The interest paid is a percentage of the principal called the interest rate . The more savings you have, the more interest you will receive for any given interest rate. For example, if you deposit $100 and the annual interest rate is 4%,

TMP-0878.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0878.text: you will receive in interest for that year. If, instead, you deposit $200, you will receive in interest for that year. interest rate The percentage of the principal that is paid as interest on a loan over time. Flavia Morlachetti/Getty Images It’s good to put money in the bank, but make sure it’s in an interest-bearing account.

TMP-0879.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0879.text: Later in this module, we will discuss several options for where to place savings, such as in checking accounts, savings accounts, or certificates of deposit, known collectively as savings vehicles . Interest rates are higher for some savings vehicles than for others. If interest rates are higher, the bank will pay you more interest for letting it use your savings. For example, if the annual interest rate is 6% rather than 4%, you will receive $12 rather than $8 in interest that year for a $200 deposit. Higher interest rates also mean the bank will charge borrowers more interest for any given loan amount (we’ll talk more about this in Module 3.2 ). Interest rates rise and fall due to economic policies and changes in economic conditions that affect the supply and demand for money. Your own bank deposits and borrowing form part of that supply and demand. If a strong economy makes a lot of consumers like you optimistic about the ability to repay loans in the future, they may increase their demand for money, which drives interest rates up. If the supply of money available for loans increases relative to the demand for money, interest rates fall.

TMP-0880.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0880.text: Other Incentives to Save The opportunity to earn interest is just one reason to save. Many employers have adopted policies to encourage people to save for the future. Automated savings plans transfer part of each paycheck directly to a savings account. This makes it effortless to save. Some employers offer matching programs to encourage participation in retirement savings plans. They will match every dollar an employee saves for retirement up to a certain amount. That’s essentially free money for the future. automated savings plan A system that transfers a portion of your income directly into a savings account on a regular schedule.

TMP-0881.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0881.text: Cecilie_Arcurs/Getty Images If you automate your savings early and make the most of government incentives, your nest egg can grow quietly in the background while you focus on life. The U.S. government provides tax incentives for saving as well. With health savings accounts , employees can set aside money for medical expenses with pre-tax dollars , meaning the government does not require employees to pay income taxes on those

TMP-0882.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0882.text: dollars. And retirement savings plans allow people to place savings into various types of investments to prepare for retirement, and put off income taxes on those savings (including the earnings on the investments) until they are withdrawn. By making saving easier and more rewarding, all of these employer and government policies help workers prepare for the financial needs of their future. Barriers to Saving No matter what a person’s income is — or where their money comes from — everyone must decide how much to spend now and how much to save for later. For people with low incomes, saving for the future can be difficult, as almost every dollar is needed for food, housing, and other necessities today. Even people with big incomes can have difficulty saving. In 2025, fewer than half of U.S. adults had sufficient savings to pay for an unexpected $1,000 expense, such as an emergency room visit or car repair; most would rely on credit cards, borrowing from friends and family, or reducing spending elsewhere to cover the cost. 1 And more than half of U.S. adults worry that they will not have enough money saved to retire. 2

TMP-0883.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0883.text: There are many reasons people don’t save as much as they should. Let’s consider a few obstacles to adequate saving. Financial Barriers Many people struggle to save money due to financial barriers that may be hard to control. These can include limited access to banking services and credit (borrowing opportunities). As we’ve discussed, another barrier is low income, most or all of which is used to cover basic needs like food, rent, and transportation, leaving little or nothing to save. Another challenge is that both income and expenses can change unexpectedly. Income fluctuations — as may result from a reduction in work hours or the loss of a job — make it hard to stick to a savings plan. At the same time, expense fluctuations, with causes such as medical emergencies, car repairs, or rising prices, can force people to spend money they planned to save. These financial ups and downs make it hard to save for the future, even when someone is trying their best.

TMP-0884.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0884.text: Psychological Barriers Some people who make a lot of money fail to save. Once a person has enough money to meet their basic needs and access to savings vehicles, saving is a possibility. Whether it becomes a reality depends on psychological barriers , meaning internal obstacles that prevent someone from making the best choices. For example, we can be distracted from our intention to save by the urge for instant gratification — getting what we want right away instead of waiting. The desire for instant gratification can lead people to spend unnecessarily on things like eating out, new clothing, sports betting, or electronics, leaving less money to save. instant gratification The strong desire to get what you want immediately instead of waiting. A second psychological barrier is impulse buying , which is making unplanned purchases on a whim or due to a sudden impulse. The small items near the checkout counter in many stores are there to encourage impulse buying. Even someone with a substantial income can struggle to save if their spending habits involve instant gratification or impulse buying.

TMP-0885.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0885.text: impulse buying Spending money without planning, often driven by emotion or sudden desire. Overspending can happen at any level of income. This can result from lifestyle inflation , also called lifestyle creep , which is when your spending increases as your income increases. Suppose a worker named Stephen has been unable to save while earning $8 per hour. Stephen just got promoted to manager and started earning $16 an hour. He can now afford to eat out more often, upgrade his car and apartment, and travel more. But if his spending doubles like his income, he will again have no money left to save. To save, or to save more, Stephen must increase his spending by less than the increase in his income. lifestyle inflation A pattern where spending increases as income increases. (Also called lifestyle creep.)

TMP-0886.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0886.text: Marvin Tolentino/Alamy Stock Photo Instant checkout, free shipping, and fast delivery all encourage impulse buying — even if you don’t leave the house.

TMP-0887.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0887.text: The Impact of PESTEL Factors LG What external factors shape individual saving decisions? In Module 1.3 , we learned how businesses use PESTEL analysis to understand the influence of political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal factors on their decisions. Some of these same forces also shape personal saving habits. Economic Factors As much control as you may have over your own income, spending, and saving decisions, the state of the economy can influence your options in all of these areas. An economy is an overall system for the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services in a country. In the previous section, we explained that interest rates tend to rise and fall depending on economic conditions. When rates are high, that motivates consumers to put more money into savings, because interest payments will

TMP-0888.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0888.text: be relatively large. When interest rates are low, loans for cars, homes, education, and other purchases are less expensive, which leads consumers to spend more. economy A country’s overall system of money, jobs, goods, and services. In a strong economy, it is relatively easy for workers to find jobs and earn income, which can make more money available for saving. A mitigating factor that is common in a strong economy is inflation , meaning a general increase in the prices of goods and services across the entire economy. In the United States, annual inflation rates are often in the range of 2% to 4%, but most economies experience occasional bouts with much higher inflation rates. This affects the cost of living , which is the amount of money needed for basic expenses like housing, food, transportation, and healthcare for people living in a particular area. inflation A general rise in prices across the economy, which reduces the value of money over time. cost of living The amount of money needed for basic expenses like housing, food, transportation, and healthcare for people living in a particular area.

TMP-0889.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0889.text: Robert Gauthier/Getty Images When the price of essentials like gas or groceries increases, after buying what you need you may have less money left over for other things — including savings. While inflation can raise the cost of living, these two measures of price levels differ. Unlike the economy’s inflation rate, the cost of living is specific to each location within

TMP-0890.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0890.text: an economy. If you live in an area with a particularly high cost of living, saving money will be more challenging. For instance, the cost of living in Hawaii is about twice the cost of living in Ohio, so with any given amount of income, it would be harder to spend less and save more in Hawaii. Price levels also affect purchasing power , which refers to the quantity of goods and services you can buy with your money. Inflation can erode the purchasing power of savings. If prices throughout the economy are rising faster than interest payments are making your savings grow, what you can buy with your savings is decreasing. Suppose you have $100 in the bank, you like to use your money to buy carrots for $1 per pound, and your annual interest rate is 4.5%. If there were no change in the price of carrots, after one year, you could buy 104.5 pounds of carrots with your $100 in principal and your $4.50 in interest. If inflation raises the price of carrots by 10% to $1.10 per pound by the end of one year, you would then be able to buy only $104.50/$1.10 = 95 pounds of carrots. If inflation is going to erode the purchasing power of your savings, you have an incentive to spend your money now while you can buy more with it. purchasing power The ability to buy goods and services with a given amount of money.

TMP-0891.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0891.text: During an economic downturn, inflation is less likely to be a problem, but the weak economy will have other influences on savings. Earnings from investments may go down and workers might lose their jobs or face pay cuts, making it harder to save. As a mitigating factor, low levels of demand may keep prices down, assisting efforts to save. More conservative spending during a downturn and economic policies that cut interest rates or taxes may also help people save despite the struggling economy. Political Factors The government plays a significant role in shaping how and why people save. One way is through tax policies . We’ve seen that health savings accounts and retirement savings plans offer tax benefits, meaning you can save money and pay less in taxes, or pay taxes later. These incentives encourage people to save more for the future. Other policies affect consumer spending, which in turn affects the ability to save. If the government helps citizens cover childcare costs or pays for postsecondary education, like college or trade school tuition, many households will have more money available to save. Government programs like Social Security can reduce the need for

TMP-0892.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0892.text: retirement savings by serving as a partial substitute for private saving. This is valuable given the barriers to saving adequately for retirement on your own. AP ® Skills Tip As businesses and individuals pursue their financial goals, political and economic factors often influence decisions. When using information about such factors, choose sources wisely. Reliance on false or misleading information can lead to unfortunate actions. Consider the credibility of the source. Are they well-respected experts? What are their credentials? Are they unbiased? Do they fact check? Are their sources cited? Don’t let bad information lead to bad choices. Laws and Regulations Banks, credit unions, and other financial institutions must follow laws and regulations established by government agencies to protect your money. These rules are designed to protect consumers by making sure savings are handled responsibly and fairly. For example, regulations require banks to disclose key information about savings accounts, such as interest rates and fees, clearly to consumers. And government agencies oversee financial institutions to promote safety and stability, in part by

TMP-0893.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0893.text: prohibiting overly risky loans or investments and dangerously low levels of liquidity (availability of cash).

TMP-0894.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0894.text: Developing a Savings Plan LG How much should people save, and where should they put their savings? Saving is a pretty simple concept — take some of what you earn and set it aside for the future. But in order to save some of your money and make the most of your savings, it helps to have a plan. Whether you are a financial planner helping a client to prepare for the future, or a high school student trying to figure out your own future, the steps are generally the same. Assessing Income and Expenses Saving isn’t just about socking money away — it’s about understanding where your money comes from, where it goes, and what you want to achieve in the future. For this course, and conceivably for a future career, you may be asked to evaluate a savings plan for a client. Before you can help a client decide how much to save, you must closely

TMP-0895.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0895.text: examine their unique financial situation. All of this advice is also true if you are your own client! uchar/Getty Images The first step in creating a financial plan is taking a hard look at how much you earn and how much you spend.

TMP-0896.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0896.text: Start by determining your client’s current income and expenses. Their income might come from a job, an allowance, child support, gifts, or investments, among other sources. Their expenses will include everything they spend money on — rent, groceries, transportation, payments on any debt (including credit cards, car payments, or a home loan), and anything else they pay money for. If their expenses exceed their income, you can help them look for ways to cut back on expenses or increase income to make saving possible. For example, a client who lives in a city might sell their car and use public transit to cut their expenses. A parent who stays home with a young child might increase their income by offering to babysit for another family’s child. Clarifying Goals and Identifying Barriers Once you understand your client’s cash flow, it’s time to learn what they are saving for. Do they want to pay for schooling? Buy a home? Travel? Retire? Goals give savings purpose. People who set clear, realistic goals are more likely to stay motivated to save and are less likely to get tripped up by psychological barriers. Your client’s goals might be short term (like buying a new phone) or long term (like paying for a child’s future college education). Your job as a financial adviser is to help your client prioritize their

TMP-0897.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0897.text: needs and wants, grapple with what they must give up, and come up with a plan to align their income with their spending goals. JGI/Jamie Grill/Getty Images Setting goals is an important step in creating a saving plan.

TMP-0898.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0898.text: Savings Vehicles When it comes to saving money, there are many options, known collectively as savings vehicles . Banks and other financial institutions offer several types of accounts where you can deposit your money with very little risk, usually while earning interest. Each type of account has pros and cons, depending on how much money you want to save, how often you will need to access it, and how long you’re willing to keep it there. Before we dive into specific accounts, let’s consider a few types of institutions that offer them. The destination for most people’s savings is one of two types of financial institutions: commercial banks or credit unions. Commercial banks are for-profit institutions that accept deposits, make loans, and provide other financial services to businesses and the general public. Commercial banks are generally owned by shareholders. Their profit comes primarily from charging a higher interest rate for loans than they pay to depositors, as well as from fees and investments. Other types of banks include central banks like the Federal Reserve, which manage a whole country’s money supply in efforts to stabilize the economy, and investment banks, which help businesses with financial transactions such as merging with other businesses or issuing stocks and bonds.

TMP-0899.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0899.text: commercial bank A for-profit financial institution that offers services like checking and savings accounts, loans, and credit cards. Credit unions are nonprofit financial institutions that provide many of the same services as banks, including accepting deposits and making loans. Credit unions are owned by their customers, who are referred to as members . In most cases, membership in a credit union requires a common bond, such as working for a particular employer, living in a specific area, or being affiliated with a labor union, university, church, or other group. Credit unions may offer better interest rates and lower fees than traditional banks. As a disadvantage, they typically have fewer locations than major banks. credit union A nonprofit financial institution owned by its members that offers similar services to a bank, often with lower fees and better rates. Both banks and credit unions provide several choices for account types. Checking accounts (and share draft accounts at credit unions) are accounts that provide easy access to deposits for everyday financial transactions such as purchases and cash withdrawals. Money can be taken out in person at a branch of the institution, or using ATM machines, online transfers, checks, or debit cards that work like credit cards but

TMP-0900.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0900.text: draw money directly from a checking account. These accounts are convenient for shopping and paying bills, but they’re not a great place to hold savings because they usually earn little interest — or none at all. These accounts are designed to give you easy access to your money, not to make it grow. checking account A deposit account used for everyday transactions like paying bills, making purchases, or withdrawing cash. Savings accounts are designed to help deposits grow slowly over time by paying interest. These accounts are better than checking accounts for storing money you don’t need right away. However, savings accounts do have limitations. Some banks limit the number of transactions, such as withdrawals and transfers, customers can make per month. Many require a minimum deposit to open the account, or charge fees if your balance gets too low. And while savings accounts do earn interest, it’s usually a modest amount compared to other savings options. When choosing a savings account, be sure to shop around for good interest rates, easy transfers, and low (or no!) banking fees. savings account A bank account designed to store money securely and earn interest over time.

TMP-0901.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0901.text: Money market accounts (MMAs) are accounts whose funds are invested (by the bank or credit union, not the customer) in short-term, low-risk investments in the money market. MMAs provide a mix of the pros and cons of checking and savings accounts. They typically offer higher interest rates than savings accounts, so your money can grow faster. Money market accounts often come with checks and debit cards, but may limit how many times you can withdraw money each month. The minimum deposit to open an MMA or avoid fees on the account is generally higher than for savings and checking accounts. These characteristics make money market accounts a good choice for someone with enough money to cover the minimum balance and a desire for occasional access to the money. For those with a sizable amount of money and no need to access the money for a while, the next option is worth considering. money market account (MMA) A type of deposit account that combines features of checking and savings accounts, usually with a higher interest rate. Certificates of deposit (CDs) are a type of account that pays a fixed amount of interest for a predetermined period of time. CDs offer higher interest rates than savings accounts, which means your money can grow faster — but there’s a catch: You have to agree to keep your money in the account for a specific period of time, like six months,

TMP-0902.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0902.text: one year, or even five years. If you take the money out early, you’ll have to pay a penalty, so it’s not a good place for emergency savings or money you might need soon. CDs are a good choice when you have money you don’t need right away and want to earn more interest than the other account types offer. certificate of deposit (CD) An account that offers a higher interest rate in exchange for keeping money deposited for a fixed period. Deposits at commercial banks and credit unions are typically safe, especially if the deposits are not enormous. Most U.S. banks are insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), which protects deposits in accounts including checking accounts, savings accounts, money market accounts, and CDs. At FDIC-insured banks, within limits, your deposits are protected against loss in the event that your bank goes out of business. Credit unions are similarly insured by the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA). In both cases, as of 2025, the insurance coverage goes up to $250,000 per depositor, per financial institution, and per account ownership category (individual or joint, say, with a family member). So at each financial institution, you could have individual checking and savings accounts insured up to a combined total of

TMP-0903.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0903.text: $250,000, and you and someone else could have joint accounts insured up to a combined total of $500,000.

TMP-0904.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0904.text: CD SPECIAL 4.95% APY* 7-Month CD Speak to a banker to learn more. *Open a new CD with a $25,000 minimum balance to enjoy this special APY and term. Offer is subject to change without notice. FIRST REPUBLIC BANK PATRICK T. FALLON/Getty Images Extended description for C D Special Additional text reads: Seven-month C D. Speak to a banker to learn more.

TMP-0905.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0905.text: An asterisk next to the acronym A P Y corresponds to smaller text that reads. Open a new C D with a 25,000 dollar minimum balance to enjoy this special A P Y and term. Offer is subject to change without notice. A bald eagle icon appears next to the bank name, First Republic Bank. CDs earn higher interest rates than savings accounts, but only if you’re willing to lock in your money for a set period of time. Alternative Vehicles for Storing Savings If you don’t like carrying cash, you may be a frequent user of apps to send and receive money. Mobile payment accounts allow users to manage money, make payments, and send money to others using mobile devices. Examples include PayPal, Samsung Pay, Cash App, Apple Pay, and Venmo. These are not banks and may not hold funds in FDIC-insured accounts, although some app providers partner with FDIC-insured banks. Money stored in these accounts often earns little or no interest, so while they may be convenient, these accounts are not good vehicles for savings.

TMP-0906.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0906.text: mobile payment account A digital account (such as Apple Cash or Cash App) that works similarly to a checking account for spending and receiving money. Another option for savings is to invest in stocks, real estate, or a business. The value of these investments might grow more quickly than money in an interest-bearing account, but the possibility of high returns comes with the risk of losing money if these investments lose their value. For example, the stock market can go up or down a lot in a short period. That makes it a dangerous place to put money that will be needed soon, because it might be necessary to sell the stock while its price is low. For long-term savings that won’t be needed until a distant retirement, investments like stocks can make sense. The stock market tends to grow in the long run, and even if stock prices dip in the short run, a long-time horizon provides plenty of time for stock prices to recover. Even more risky are cryptocurrencies , digital currencies not connected to any central bank or government. Cryptocurrencies do not earn interest, although investors hope they will increase in value as an asset. The value of cryptocurrencies is typically volatile: It can change a lot in a very short time. The lack of interest payments and the volatility in their value make cryptocurrencies a poor vehicle for savings.

TMP-0907.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0907.text: cryptocurrency A type of digital currency that is not backed by a government or central bank. Table 3.1-1 provides an overview of common options for where you or your client can place savings. Table 3.1-1 Account Types and Their Advisability as Savings Vehicles Type of account Best for Advantages Limitations Checking or share draft account Easy access for day-to-day spending • Typically FDIC insured • Easy access with ATMs, checks, debit cards • Convenient for paying bills and receiving paychecks • Earns little or no interest • May have fees • Not a good vehicle for savings Savings account Short-term savings, emergency funds • Typically FDIC insured • Easy access with ATMs • Interest rates are usually low • May require a minimum balance • May charge fees if below a certain balance • May have limits on the number of transactions

TMP-0908.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0908.text: Money market account Short- to medium-term savings • Typically FDIC insured • Easy access with ATMs, checks, debit cards • Usually offers a higher interest rate than savings accounts • May require a minimum balance to avoid fees • May have limits on the number of transactions CDs Medium-term savings • Typically FDIC insured • Higher interest rates are locked in for set time period • Growth with little risk • Limited access to your money • Fixed interest rate means you won’t benefit if interest rates increase Mobile payment accounts Small transactions • Convenient for quickly sending money to friends, family, and businesses via smartphone • Reduces need to carry cash • Risk of fraud • Uncertain support from institution when errors or fraud occur • May charge fees • Earns little or no interest • Not a good vehicle for savings

TMP-0909.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0909.text: Filippo Bacci/Getty Images Banking apps can make creating a savings plan — and sticking to it — easier. Formalize the Plan After collecting income and expense information, exploring ways to increase income and lower expenses, identifying goals and barriers, and choosing a savings vehicle, it’s

TMP-0910.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0910.text: time to make your client’s situation concrete. A document or spreadsheet outlining the current financial situation — cash holdings, sources of income, expenditures, debts — will allow informed decisions about the best path forward. Include a list of goals with target dates. If they may not all be achievable, rank them or place stars next to the highest priority goals. Once all of the information is well thought out and organized, take steps to initiate the needed savings, monitor progress, and adapt to changes: • Automate savings. Determine the monthly savings needed to achieve the primary goals. Suppose your client needs $12,000 to buy a used car in four years (48 months). The required monthly savings depends on the interest rate and the frequency of compounding , which is when the interest you’ve earned is added to your account and you start earning interest on the interest. With an interest rate of zero, they would need to save $12,000/48 = $250 per month. The higher the interest rate and the more frequent the compounding, the less your client would need to save each month, but those calculations are beyond the scope of this course. Saving is easier when people don’t have to think about it, so consider creating an automated savings plan. This could mean having your client’s paycheck automatically deposited into a

TMP-0911.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0911.text: checking account, with $250 automatically transferred to an interest-bearing savings account each month. • Monitor progress. If the goal is to save $12,000 in four years, is your client halfway there after two years? Tracking progress can help keep a saver motivated. It’s also important to keep an eye on interest rates to make sure the money is earning the highest possible rate. If the current bank isn’t paying a good rate, shop around for another bank that pays more. If the money isn’t needed soon, consider trading easy access to funds for higher interest rates with a CD. • Adjust the plan if things change. When the situation changes, the savings plan should change, too. You can limit lifestyle inflation and build savings by increasing the automated deduction for savings as income increases. 3 So, when your client starts their first job, they might only be able to commit $200 per month to savings, but could plan to increase the contribution to $300 per month when they get their first raise. If they increase the contribution as income rises, added spending won’t prevent added saving. Saving money helps make dreams come true. It also offers resilience against life’s uncertainties. People lose jobs, go back to school, have babies, get sick, and quit jobs to

TMP-0912.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0912.text: start new businesses. Someone with a habit of saving can draw on their accumulated funds to get through tough times. Even if your client is lucky enough not to need their emergency fund, being prepared for almost anything means there is less need to worry about worst-case scenarios, and an unneeded nest egg can always be put to good use.

TMP-0913.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0913.text: Module 3.1 Review Learning Goals LG What is saving, and why can it be difficult to save? • Income is the money you earn from work, investments, or other sources. Saving means putting money aside for the future instead of spending it right away. People save for different reasons. No matter your income level, saving is key to financial stability and reaching future goals. • When you deposit money into a bank or financial institution, you’re actually loaning them your money. Interest is what borrowers pay to use someone else’s money, and the amount paid is based on the principal and the interest rate , which is the percentage charged. Incentives like automated savings plans and tax benefits can make saving easier and more rewarding.

TMP-0914.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0914.text: • Despite these incentives, saving money can be difficult. People who have lower incomes may spend all of their money on essentials, with little left over to save. Psychological barriers can also get in the way. Instant gratification is the strong desire to get what we want right away instead of waiting. This can lead to impulse buying , which is spending money without planning. As people earn more, they may fall into lifestyle inflation , which happens when spending increases along with their income, making it harder to save or build wealth. LG What external factors shape individual saving decisions? • As with business decisions, savings decisions are affected by many of the factors included in PESTEL analysis ( Module 1.3 ). Economic factors include the overall state of the economy , including the availability of jobs, the cost of living, and interest rates. Inflation is a major factor that affects the cost of living and has an impact on people’s purchasing power and ability to save. • Political factors also play a role, as the government sets tax policies and provides subsidies that can incentivize saving.

TMP-0915.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0915.text: • Laws and regulations provide incentives and protections that can encourage people to save. One such protection is the FDIC, which is a government agency that protects bank depositors. LG How much should people save, and where should they put their savings? • There are several options for storing savings, each offered by different financial institutions like commercial banks and credit unions . These institutions provide a range of account types, including checking accounts for daily use, savings accounts for short-term savings, money market accounts for short- to medium-term savings with higher interest, and certificates of deposit (CDs) for medium-term savings with locked-in rates. • While checking accounts and mobile payment accounts are convenient for everyday spending, they are not good for saving due to low or no interest. • A savings account , which earns interest, is best for storing money that’s not immediately needed. A money market account (MMA) typically offers a higher interest rate than a regular savings account. A certificate of deposit, or CD, offers a

TMP-0916.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0916.text: higher interest rate than a regular savings account, but consumers must keep their money in the CD for a specific period of time or pay a penalty. • When you invest in the stock market or in assets like cryptocurrencies , you are buying assets that might increase in value, but also might lose value. This is fundamentally different from saving. Practice Your AP ® Skills Preparing for the AP ® Exam MULTIPLE-CHOICE QUESTIONS 1. Owen just moved from Albany to New York City for a new job. His salary increased by more than 50%, but his rent doubled — even though his apartment is smaller and farther from the city center. What explains why both his salary and his rent changed? a. rising inflation

TMP-0917.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0917.text: b. differences in the cost of living c. lifestyle inflation d. a new job title with a higher pay scale 2. Kezron got a promotion and a 15% salary increase. He now spends more on eating out, gaming gear, and a new phone upgrade. What does this change in behavior represent? a. saving b. investing c. lifestyle inflation d. cost of living differences 3. Lucia wants to save $10,000 to buy a used car. She has $2,000 saved already and plans to add $150 from every paycheck. She wants an account that gives her the highest interest rate possible while still providing access to her money at all times. What type of account best fits her needs? a. a money market account

TMP-0918.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0918.text: b. a savings account c. a checking account d. stocks 4. Tommy had to drop out of community college because an unexpected $500 healthcare expense prevented him from paying his tuition bill. Which of the following would definitely help Tommy avoid this problem in the future? a. A strategy of instant gratification b. Establishment of an emergency fund c. Avoiding automated savings plans d. An impulse buying approach

TMP-0919.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0919.navLabel: CASE STUDY Starting a Job, Starting to Save
TMP-0919.text: CASE STUDY Starting a Job, Starting to Save TrixiePhoto/Getty Images When you start earning money, you need to start saving money. After graduating from college with a degree in marketing, Tonya landed her first full-time job at a small creative agency that helped businesses build their brand, promote their products, and solve communication problems. It wasn’t her dream job, but it came with a steady salary, solid benefits, and the promise of growth. On

headings.text: CASE STUDY Starting a Job, Starting to Save

TMP-0920.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0920.navLabel: CASE STUDY Starting a Job, Starting to Save
TMP-0920.text: Tonya’s first day, the HR representative led her through the options for her paycheck. The company would deposit her payment directly into her bank account. Tonya could split her direct deposit between her checking and savings accounts. The company offered to match contributions to her retirement plan up to $500 per month if she started contributing to that now. It was a lot to take in, but it made her feel like she was finally stepping into adulthood. When Tonya received her first paycheck, it was exciting to see real money in her account — but now came the decisions. After rent, groceries, student loan payments, and a few bills, she still had some money left over. She wanted to enjoy her new life — grab dinner with friends, see the occasional concert, maybe take a weekend trip. But she also knew her car wouldn’t last forever, and her phone had started glitching. She didn’t want to be caught off guard by an unexpected expense. Tonya was also thinking about the future. She knew she would have to spend $1500 on repairs and regular maintenance to keep her car running. She also had a wish list of big-ticket expenses: a new couch for her apartment, a trip to Jazz Fest in New Orleans, and perhaps getting Lasik surgery so she wouldn’t have to wear

TMP-0921.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0921.navLabel: CASE STUDY Starting a Job, Starting to Save
TMP-0921.text: glasses anymore. And, of course, she knew she should start saving for retirement — but that was decades away. Tonya took stock of her finances and started thinking about her savings goals. APPLY YOUR AP ® SKILLS 1. Tonya has asked for advice on how to prioritize her allocation of money to meet her goals. What uses for money would you suggest as her top three priorities after covering her rent, groceries, student loan payments, and bills? 2. Tonya was given the option to split her direct deposit between multiple accounts. How might she use this feature to help reach her savings goals more effectively? 3. Tonya knows she should save, and she wants to make it a priority. But she also wants to have fun now. What advice would you give her to help her balance her current wants and her future wants? 4. Tonya is unsure whether a predictable car repair counts as an emergency. In your opinion, what types of expenses should an emergency fund be used for?
