TMP-0923.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0923.text: MODULE 3.2 Borrowing, Credit, and Debt LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 3.2.A Explain why, and how, consumers borrow money 3.2.B Describe how lenders evaluate borrowers’ creditworthiness 3.2.C Explain strategies that consumers use to manage debt

TMP-0924.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0924.text: Ground Picture/Shutterstock Extended description for Borrowing The man shakes hands with the woman in the business suit. The woman beside him holds a document.

TMP-0925.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0925.text: Borrowing money can help people reach some of their biggest life goals, like going to college, buying a house, or starting a business. It’s important to understand how loans work and how to manage debt wisely.

TMP-0926.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0926.text: Borrowing and Repaying Money LG Why do consumers borrow money, and what kinds of loans might they get? Income is notorious for arriving after it is needed. Education, healthcare, vacations, weddings, and refrigerators all have upfront costs that are ill timed with the gradual arrival of paychecks from employers. Consumers borrow money so that their lifestyle can exceed their current income and accumulated savings, hopefully with confidence that their income will catch up and allow them to repay the loans. Many loans are for large and lasting investments, like a home, a car, or vocational training. People sometimes must borrow to address emergencies, such as a leaky roof, a sudden illness, or a family member in need. Borrowing can be a matter of convenience, providing quick access to funds without touching any existing savings. For all such uses, consumers appreciate how loans help them balance their income, expenses, and savings over time.

TMP-0927.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0927.text: Loans and Interest When consumers borrow money, they take on a personal liability or debt . The lending agreement between the borrower and the lender is called a loan . Consumers repay the amount they have borrowed (the principal), plus interest. As we learned in Module 3.1 , interest is the cost of borrowing money; it compensates the lender for delaying the use of their money and assuming the risk that the loan will not be repaid. The interest rate for a loan may be fixed (it remains the same over the life of the loan) or variable (it may change over time). A loan’s interest rate and repayment terms — the frequency of payments and the amount of each payment — depend on the amount of money borrowed and several factors we will discuss in this module: the lender, the loan type, and the consumer’s credit history. loan A lending agreement between a borrower and a lender. When an individual takes out a loan for a car, they don’t fully “own” the car until the loan is paid off. If the borrower fails to repay the loan, the lender can repossess the car and sell it to recover their funds. In other words, the car serves as collateral , meaning something of value that the borrower will forfeit to the lender if the loan is not repaid.

TMP-0928.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0928.text: An auto loan is an example of a secured loan , which is a loan that is backed by collateral. A mortgage loan for the purchase of a home is another example of a secured loan — if the borrower fails to repay the mortgage loan, the lender can foreclose on (take possession of) the home. Collateral makes these loans less risky for the lender, so secured loans generally have lower interest rates than unsecured loans , which are not backed by collateral. Personal loans and student loans are common types of unsecured loans. secured loan A loan that is backed by collateral. collateral Something of value that the borrower will forfeit to the lender if the loan is not repaid. unsecured loan A loan that is not backed by collateral.

TMP-0929.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0929.text: Left: KLH49/Getty Images; right: Alberto Menendez Cervero/Getty Images Extended description for Loans The first photo shows a close-up of a sign in front of a residential house. The sign reads: Bank Owned. Foreclosure. The second photo shows a person wearing a graduation cap and gown holding up their newly acquired degree. Student loans typically carry higher interest rates than mortgage loans for homes because student loans are not secured by collateral — the bank can’t take possession of someone’s education if they fail to repay their student loan.

TMP-0930.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0930.text: Types of Lenders Where do financial institutions get the money to make loans to consumers, businesses, nonprofits, and government entities? Commercial banks and credit unions (discussed in Module 3.1 ) rely on deposits from their customers to fund loans. The money that individuals, businesses, and other entities deposit into their checking or savings accounts provides the funds for financial institutions to lend to borrowers. Both commercial banks and credit unions offer loans that include personal loans, auto loans, and mortgage loans. Businesses can borrow from these institutions as well — for example, to buy equipment, expand operations, or purchase property. Even governments and nonprofits can apply for loans from these financial institutions when they need more money than they currently have. Commercial banks and credit unions are also among the businesses that offer credit cards, which effectively provide loans by allowing consumers to buy now and pay later. This kind of arrangement — where you can borrow money up to a set limit, pay it back, and then borrow it again, over and over — is called revolving credit . Another example of revolving credit is the personal lines of credit offered by commercial banks and credit

TMP-0931.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0931.text: unions, which allow customers to repeatedly draw money up to a limit and pay it off, often with lower interest rates than credit cards. Some retail stores offer loans with their in-store financing and “buy now, pay later” plans for bigger purchases, like furniture or mobile phones. Some of these plans are interest free, while others include interest and fees, so it is important to understand the terms of the loans to avoid unexpected expenses.

TMP-0932.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0932.text: Anna Barclay/Getty Images Credit cards offer unsecured loans, which typically carry higher interest rates than secured loans. While commercial banks and credit unions provide mortgage loans, mortgage lenders such as Fairway and Rocket Mortgage specialize in providing loans to help consumers purchase, build, or renovate residential properties such as homes and condominiums.

TMP-0933.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0933.text: Like other lenders, specialized mortgage companies evaluate the borrower’s finances, offer a loan for a specific term (length of time) and at a particular interest rate, and collect payments of the principal plus the interest, typically each month. And as with mortgage loans from other financial institutions, if a borrower stops making payments, the mortgage lender can foreclose on the property. Alternative financial services are nontraditional financial service providers such as payday lenders, check-cashing services, and companies offering instant tax refunds. These services can be a last resort for customers with limited access to traditional financial institutions, either due to their location, their income level, or their history with repaying debt. A payday lender offers consumers a short-term loan meant to be repaid by the borrower’s next payday. Check-cashing services cash consumers’ checks on the spot, without requiring a traditional bank account, but typically charge a significant fee. Instant tax refund services provide a loan based on the consumer’s estimated tax refund; when the actual refund arrives from the IRS, this is used to repay the loan. These services may not check their customers’ credit or banking history for signs of unpaid loans or overdrawn accounts, but they often charge high fees and interest rates.

TMP-0934.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0934.text: And if the borrower is unable to repay what they owe on time, they may need to take out another loan at additional high cost. This can quickly lead to a cycle of debt. alternative financial services Services such as payday loans, check-cashing services, and instant tax refunds, which can be accessed without a credit check or banking history and may provide quick access to cash (at a high fee). Consumer Protection Borrowers are protected by federal, state, and local laws designed to ensure that lenders are not unclear or deceptive. Federal laws require lenders to clearly communicate credit terms so that borrowers understand the conditions of their loan — the interest rate, fees, and repayment schedule. In addition, many states and local governments have their own rules that further protect consumers. For example, more than a dozen states limit or even prohibit payday lending out of concern that it targets low-income consumers and demands excessive interest rates.

TMP-0935.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0935.text: Houston Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images Extended description for Payday Lenders Several advertisements in the window appear in both English and Spanish. A sign on the sidewalk advertises Personal Loans Up to 2,500 dollars.

TMP-0936.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0936.text: Payday lenders often charge very high interest rates or fees, leading governments to regulate them in order to protect consumers. Consumer protection laws also prevent unethical collection tactics for debt collectors seeking repayment. These laws specify which methods are permitted, and generally prohibit harassment, unreasonable threats, and deceptive statements (such as falsely telling consumers they are subject to legal consequences). Lenders must also adhere to laws designed to prohibit discriminatory lending practices. These laws aim to ensure equal access to credit opportunities for all individuals. For example, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act requires that lending decisions are based only on the applicant’s income and credit history, not on personal characteristics such as race, religion, national origin, gender, marital status, or age, or on whether they receive public assistance. The act also requires lenders who deny credit to an individual to provide a written explanation. To prevent housing discrimination and ensure fair mortgage lending, the Fair Housing Act prohibits lenders from denying mortgage loans or offering inferior terms based on a long list of personal

TMP-0937.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0937.text: characteristics. Lenders who defy these laws may face fines, penalties, or even a revocation of their license to issue loans. For example, in 2017, JP Morgan Chase reached a $53 million settlement with the U.S. Department of Justice for having charged Black and Hispanic borrowers higher fees for home loans than white applicants with similar income and credit profiles. 1

TMP-0938.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0938.navLabel: Creditworthiness, Credit Reports, and Credit Scores
TMP-0938.text: Creditworthiness, Credit Reports, and Credit Scores LG How do lenders evaluate borrowers’ creditworthiness? Before lenders extend you credit, they need to assess your creditworthiness — the likelihood that if you borrow money, you will repay it on time. Anyone who lends money faces the risk that the borrower will default , meaning that they will fail to repay the loan. Someone with little or no debt, a higher income, more savings, and a history of prompt repayment of loans presents a lower risk. Commercial banks are often unwilling to lend to people who pose a high risk of default. This helps to explain why some high-risk borrowers seek loans from alternative financial services despite their typically high interest rates and fees. And if a commercial bank is willing to provide loans to high-risk borrowers, the bank, too, will typically charge them higher interest rates to compensate for the greater risk of losses.

headings.text: Creditworthiness, Credit Reports, and Credit Scores

TMP-0939.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0939.text: creditworthiness The likelihood that a borrower will repay their debt on time. default To not repay a loan. Evaluating Borrowers The risk of default motivates lenders to carefully evaluate potential borrowers. Lenders want to know, first of all, whether the loan applicant has reliable and sufficient income to repay them; so, they may want to see paychecks, tax returns, or evidence of other income sources. Lenders also consider any savings a borrower may have, taking into account whether the borrower has enough to cover not only their loan payments, but their living expenses and any unforeseen emergencies. To assess potential borrowers’ current debt, lenders consider obligations such as existing loans and credit card balances to ensure that all of the payments are manageable. Lenders may calculate a debt-to-income ratio for a loan applicant, which is the borrower’s total monthly debt payments divided by their total pre-tax monthly income. A higher ratio indicates more debt relative to income, and thus a greater risk of

TMP-0940.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0940.text: default. Lenders also consider potential borrowers’ credit history, which is collected in the form of credit reports. Credit Reports A credit report is a detailed record of an individual’s credit history. Lenders obtain credit reports from credit bureaus , also called credit reporting agencies , which collect information whenever an individual interacts with a financial institution, for example, by opening an account, receiving a loan, applying for a credit card, or making a monthly payment to repay debt. In the United States, the major credit bureaus include Experian, TransUnion, and Equifax. credit report A detailed record of one’s credit history. credit bureaus Companies that collect credit information and use it to generate credit reports; also called credit reporting agencies. After you have opened a credit card or loan, your credit reports will contain your personal information such as current and past addresses, your open and closed

TMP-0941.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0941.text: accounts at financial institutions, any businesses that have made inquiries about your credit, and any relevant financial information such as bankruptcies or foreclosures. The data in credit reports remains available for many years. Negative information, such as a late payment on a credit card, stays on your credit report for seven years; paying off or closing an account won’t “erase” it. Positive information, however, such as a steady pattern of on-time payments, stays on your credit report for ten years. Banks, apartment landlords, insurance companies, employers, and governments are among the entities that may request your credit report to assess your creditworthiness. Lenders will use it when deciding whether to approve your loan application, how much to lend, and what interest rate to charge. Landlords will use it to decide whether to rent you an apartment. Some insurance companies consider credit reports when establishing the price and other terms of a policy. Employers may factor credit report information into hiring decisions, especially for roles that involve financial management. And government agencies might access your credit report if, for example, they need to determine your eligibility for government financial assistance, collect government-related debts (such as unpaid taxes), or conduct a background check for government employment.

TMP-0942.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0942.text: Andrew Angelov/Shutterstock Monitoring your credit report at regular intervals is a simple way to stay on top of your debt and manage your creditworthiness. Credit Scores A key indicator of your creditworthiness is your credit score , which is a single number credit bureaus use to represent your level of financial responsibility. Scores generally range from 300 to 850, with higher scores reflecting better creditworthiness.

TMP-0943.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0943.text: The factors in the credit score formula include your history of paying bills on time (or not), the amount you owe, the length of your credit history, how many new credit accounts you have applied for recently (too many applications is considered a sign of risk), and the mix of different credit types (such as credit cards, loans, and mortgages) you have managed responsibly. credit score A number, based on several differently weighted factors, that represents an individual’s level of financial responsibility. A person with a low credit score has poor credit and is seen as a greater risk for a lender. Lenders may deny loans to people with poor credit, or they may charge higher interest rates to compensate for the greater risks. Your credit score can also affect what cellphone plans you are eligible for, how much you pay as a security deposit on an apartment, and whether a landlord is willing to rent you an apartment at all. So it is important to manage your debt wisely.

TMP-0944.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0944.text: Managing Debt LG What strategies do consumers use to manage their debt? Large amounts of debt carry serious consequences for a consumer. The correspondingly large monthly payments cut into the income borrowers have available to save, invest, put toward living expenses (rent, utilities, groceries), or spend on some fun leisure activities. And a large debt obligation makes it more likely that unforeseen circumstances or poor planning will prevent debt repayment. The loss of a job, a family crisis, or a medical emergency can disrupt income, while monthly loan payments remain the same. Even for borrowers who maintain a steady income, poor planning can lead to unmanageable levels of debt. Too many loans, too-large loans, or loans with high interest rates can result in unsustainably high monthly payments that get borrowers into financial trouble.

TMP-0945.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0945.text: Strategies for Smart Borrowing While debt can be a problem, it can also bring opportunity for those who manage it well. When used effectively, debt can be a powerful tool, enabling investments in education, home ownership, and entrepreneurship. In this section, we explain several strategies borrowers can adopt for managing debt and using credit wisely. Building and Maintaining a High Credit Score As discussed in the previous section, your credit score is a representation of your creditworthiness. Building and maintaining a high credit score (ideally 700 or above) demonstrates financial responsibility, leading lenders to see a borrower as a lower risk. With a credit score that signals reliability, customers gain opportunities to save money on loans, insurance, apartments, and cellphone plans, which can make monthly payments more manageable and saving more realistic. Optimizing Loan Terms Borrowers can also shop around for better loan terms, rather than settling for what’s offered or continuing to pay off loans with out-of-date interest rates. If interest rates

TMP-0946.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0946.text: have dropped since the loan was received, borrowers may refinance their existing loans by taking out a new loan to replace the old loan. This strategy allows them to take advantage of lower interest rates, or to improve loan terms, for example by paying lower monthly payments over a longer period. Paying Off High-Interest Loans Another key strategy for managing debt is to pay off high-interest loans as quickly as possible. For example, credit cards tend to charge relatively high interest rates. They generally require a minimum monthly payment (often 2% to 4% of your outstanding balance), but as long as you make this payment on time, you are able to carry over the remaining balance from month to month. Many consumers are tempted to carry credit card debt. The problem is that the interest rate is high and the interest is compounded , meaning that customers pay interest on past interest charges they have not yet paid off. This adds up quickly, getting many consumers into financial trouble. Most credit card companies compound interest daily, meaning that tomorrow you will pay interest on the interest charged today. For a simplified example, see the deeper dive box.

TMP-0947.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0947.text: Paying your credit card bill in full every month allows you to enjoy the convenience of credit card use without paying the relatively high interest rates. To adopt this strategy, avoid charging anything that you won’t be able to pay for in a month’s time. And if you absolutely must buy something that you can’t pay off soon, and lower-interest loans are not an option, prioritize paying it off as soon as you can — before the accumulation of interest charges becomes unmanageable. A DEEPER DIVE The Cost of Credit Let’s consider a simplified situation with an annual percentage rate (APR) of 15% compounded monthly (not daily, as is the norm) and a minimum monthly payment of $50. In the first month, you purchase a $1,000 sofa, and you pay only the $50 minimum. Assuming you purchase nothing else with this credit card and you make the minimum payment each month, Table 3.2-1 shows the interest charges and balances over the course of a year. Table 3.2-1 Paying Off a Purchase with Minimum Payments Month Starting balance Interest charged (15% annually, or 1.25% per month) New balance after interest is added Final balance after $50 minimum payment Month 1 $1000 $12.50 $1012.50 $962.50

TMP-0948.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing

TMP-0949.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0949.text: $1,000 − $517.74 = $482.26. Your interest payments over the course of the year would thus be . If we extended this table for another 12 months of data, we would see that after 23 monthly payments of $50 and a final payment of the remaining $7.94 owed, you would have paid a total of $1,157.94 — the $1,000 price of the sofa, plus an additional $157.94 of interest. And if you made any late payments, the late fees would be added to these costs. Improving Credit Scores One way to improve your financial opportunities is to increase your credit score. Anyone on a mission to raise their score and keep it high should understand how credit scores are calculated. There are two main scoring models with their own formulas: Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) Score and VantageScore. We will consider the commonly used FICO Score as our example. This model considers five factors and gives each factor a different weight in calculating your score, which will range from 300 to 850 points. The factors and their weights are shown in Table 3.2-2 . Table 3.2-2 Calculating Your FICO Score Factor Weight in determining score Explanation

TMP-0950.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0950.text: Payment history 35% Have you made your past loan and bill payments on time? Late or missed payments can decrease your score sharply. Credit utilization 30% Are you maxing out your credit cards? Using less of your available credit limit improves your score. Length of credit history 15% Are you new to borrowing money? A long history of using the same credit accounts improves your score. Mix of credit types 10% Do you have experience with a mix of credit types (such as loans and credit cards)? A proven record with a variety of credit sources improves your score. Applications for new credit 10% Have you applied for several credit accounts within a short period? Having fewer recent applications improves your score.

TMP-0951.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0951.text: blackCAT/Getty Images Credit cards can be helpful or harmful, depending on how they are used. If you get one, try not to charge anything that you can’t pay off in full when the bill arrives. Notice in Table 3.2-2 that the factor with the greatest weight is a history of making payments on time. Even one late payment could drop a score by as many as 50 to 100

TMP-0952.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0952.text: points. Paying off existing debt — especially credit card debt — will increase your credit score, as will keeping your spending well below your credit limit. Someone with a $20,000 credit limit and $18,000 in balances is using 90% of their available credit, and is seen as a riskier loan candidate than someone with that same credit limit and $4,000 in balances — only 20% of their available credit. Experts recommend using no more than 30% of your available credit, and ideally using 10% or less for the best possible credit score. Getting the Right Loan It is worthwhile to shop around for loans. Different lenders might offer different interest rates, fees, and repayment terms, and their requirements for approval may differ. For a large purchase that’s paid off over a long period of time, even a minor rate difference will add up over the life of a loan. Another strategy for lowering loan payments is to make a larger-than-necessary down payment , which is an upfront payment for part of the purchase price. For example, a mortgage lender typically requires a down payment of some percentage of the home price before granting a loan for the remainder. If the requirement is 10% but you have

TMP-0953.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0953.text: enough income or savings to pay 15% as a down payment, you will have less to borrow, which means lower monthly payments and less interest paid over the life of the loan. And a larger down payment lowers the lender’s risk of not being able to recoup the amount they have lent upon foreclosure, so lenders sometimes offer lower interest rates to reward higher down payments. down payment An initial payment for part of the cost of a purchase, using some of the borrower’s income or savings. When Debt Becomes Unmanageable As we’ve noted, unforeseen circumstances or poor financial planning can make a person’s debt unmanageable. When that happens, the consequences can include damage to credit scores, actions from collection agencies hired to recover unpaid debts, foreclosure on a home, and repossession of cars and other personal property by lenders. When those outcomes loom, borrowers have options that range from credit counseling that helps people manage their debt, to bankruptcy, which can eliminate some debt but has a more drastic impact on a person’s credit history.

TMP-0954.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0954.text: Debt Management Assistance Everybody needs a helping hand once in a while. For people struggling with debt, there are several available types of debt management assistance , which refers to services designed to help individuals or businesses reduce and manage their debt. Many nonprofit credit counseling organizations and individual financial professionals offer debt management services. This section sheds some light on the options of credit counseling, debt management plans, debt settlement programs, and debt consolidation. debt management assistance Services available for people who are struggling with debt, including credit counseling, debt management plans, debt settlement programs, and debt consolidation. Credit counseling. Nonprofit credit counselors can help people understand their finances, give budgeting and debt management advice, and provide free workshops and educational materials. A credit counseling agency can also set up a debt management plan (DMP) to establish a single monthly payment that the client makes to the agency, which in turn pays the client’s creditors. A credit counselor works with the client and the client’s creditors to develop a payment schedule. Creditors may be willing to waive

TMP-0955.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0955.text: fees or lower interest rates for people enrolled in a debt management plan. A DMP can thus provide convenience, accountability, and perhaps even savings for the client. Debt settlement. People with significant credit card debt sometimes turn to debt settlement programs , which differ from debt management plans and are typically provided by for-profit companies. In a debt settlement program, the client usually stops making their monthly payments to creditors and instead sets aside money every month in a special account. Meanwhile, the debt settlement company negotiates with the client’s creditors, in hopes that they will agree to settle the client’s debt for a lump sum (single) payment of less than what they owe. If a settlement is reached, the client pays the agreed-upon amount from their special account and the debt settlement company takes its fee. This can be a risky process. Stopping payments can severely damage the client’s credit, and if some or all of the creditors don’t agree to settle, they can take legal action to demand repayment of the loan plus additional fees and interest. The fees charged by debt settlement companies can also be substantial, and fraudulent debt settlement programs are a significant concern. Debt consolidation. Banks, credit unions, and online lenders may offer debt consolidation loans, which allow borrowers to take out a new loan to pay off multiple

TMP-0956.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0956.text: debts. This new loan usually has a lower interest rate, and people may find it more manageable to make a single monthly payment. But most debt consolidation loans have fees in addition to interest charges, so this can be a more expensive option. And if the loan is secured with collateral — say, the borrower’s home — the borrower risks losing a valuable asset if their payments are late or they cannot pay off the loan.

TMP-0957.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0957.text: Capuski/Getty Images Some people with unmanageable debt benefit from nonprofit credit counseling services, which provide advice and education, and can set up a debt management plan.

TMP-0958.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0958.text: BANKRUPTCY As discussed further in Module 3.7 , bankruptcy is a legal process available when an individual or organization is unable to repay outstanding debts. Bankruptcy eliminates some unsecured debts and helps borrowers establish plans to repay other debts, such as for taxes, fines, child support, alimony, and student loans. Bankruptcy may be a fresh start, but it is not a “clean slate.” Bankruptcy information remains on a person’s credit report for seven to ten years, depending on the type of bankruptcy. Because lenders perceive someone with a bankruptcy as a high-risk borrower, they may reject their loan applications or charge a relatively high interest rate. Those with a bankruptcy on their record may also have trouble renting a home or securing some types of jobs. Due to its negative, long-lasting impact on a person’s credit history, bankruptcy is generally considered a strategy of last resort.

TMP-0959.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0959.text: Module 3.2 Review Learning Goals LG Why do consumers borrow money, and what kinds of loans might they get? • Consumers borrow money because the large upfront cost of major purchases is poorly timed with the gradual flow of paychecks and other income. They also borrow to address emergencies, or for the convenience of quick access to cash without dipping into savings. • When consumers borrow money, they take on a personal liability or debt, and they must repay the money according to the repayment terms. Consumers repay what they have borrowed, plus interest, based on an interest rate that may be fixed or variable. A loan’s interest rate and repayment terms differ by lender, loan type, credit history, and the amount of money.

TMP-0960.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0960.text: • Secured loans are backed by collateral — something that the borrower will forfeit to the lender if the loan is not repaid. Because secured loans are less risky for the lender, they generally have lower interest rates than unsecured loans , which are not backed by collateral. • Commercial banks and credit unions depend on deposits from their customers to fund loans. • Credit card companies, retail stores, and mortgage lenders also lend money to consumers. Alternative financial services such as payday loans, check-cashing services, and instant tax refunds also provide loans. These services should be used with caution because they typically involve high fees and interest rates, and can lead to a cycle of debt, with loans taken out to cover other loans. • Consumer protection laws aim to prevent unclear loan terms, deceptive lenders, unethical debt collection tactics, and discriminatory lending practices. LG How do lenders evaluate borrowers’ creditworthiness?

TMP-0961.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0961.text: • Lenders assess potential borrowers’ credit worthiness — the likelihood that if someone borrows money, they will repay it on time. Lenders face the risk of default , meaning the borrower fails to repay the loan. Someone with little or no existing debt, higher income, more savings, and a history or prompt repayment of loans presents a lower risk of default. • Lenders who are willing to lend to high-risk borrowers, including alternative financial services, typically charge higher interest rates and fees. • A credit report is a detailed record of an individual’s credit history. This information is compiled by credit bureaus , also called credit reporting agencies , which collect information every time an individual interacts with a financial institution. The data in your credit report remains available for many years. Businesses or other entities may request your credit report to assess your creditworthiness. • A key indicator of your creditworthiness is your credit score , which is a single number that represents your level of financial responsibility. The two most common scoring models are FICO Score and VantageScore. These scores are used by lenders, insurance companies, potential landlords, potential employers, and other entities, such as government agencies.

TMP-0962.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0962.text: LG What strategies do consumers use to manage their debt? • Bigger debts, and higher interest rates on loans, necessitate higher monthly loan payments. These payments reduce the amount of income a consumer has left to spend or save. • Unforeseen circumstances or poor planning can hinder a borrower’s ability to repay their debt. Strategies for borrowing wisely include building and maintaining a high credit score, shopping for better loan terms, and paying off high-interest loans as quickly as possible. • When trying to raise your credit score, keep in mind that credit scoring models such as the FICO Score take into account factors such as payment history, credit utilization, length of credit history, mix of credit types, and applications for new credit. • By comparing what lenders are offering, borrowers can pursue the most favorable loan terms. Making a larger-than-necessary down payment — the initial payment for part of the cost of the purchase — can also translate to lower monthly payments and better terms from lenders.

TMP-0963.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing
TMP-0963.text: • When debt becomes unmanageable, the consequences can be serious and may include damage to credit scores, actions from collection agencies, and even property seizures. There are several types of debt management assistance available, meaning services designed to help individuals or businesses reduce and manage their debt. Examples include credit counseling, debt management plans, debt settlement programs, and debt consolidation. Bankruptcy is a legal process that eliminates certain debts and helps borrowers establish a plan to repay other debts. Because of its negative, long-lasting impact on a person’s credit, bankruptcy is generally considered a last resort. Practice Your AP ® Skills Preparing for the AP ® Exam Multiple-Choice Questions 1. TMP-0966.text: CASE STUDY Current Debt, Future Goals Hiraman/Getty Images Car trouble can mean money trouble. Jalen is 25 years old and works full-time as an administrative assistant. For the last couple of years, he’s been earning just enough to cover his rent, groceries,

TMP-0967.text: student loan payments, and the usual bills, with little left over for nonnecessities. It hasn’t been easy — his budget was tight, and he often felt like one unexpected expense could throw everything off. That expense came last year when his car, an older model with over 100,000 miles on it, broke down in the middle of winter. The repair bill was nearly $1,200. Without any emergency savings, Jalen had no choice but to charge the entire amount to his credit card, which charges a 16% interest rate. Since then, other unexpected costs — like a doctor’s visit and a big utility bill — added to the balance. At one point, he owed more than $2,000, and the high interest charges made it hard to make real progress in paying it off. Jalen has been paying only the minimum payment every month, and he missed several payments when money was especially tight. Jalen’s circumstances recently started to change. He got a raise at work, his first significant bump in pay since starting the job. His student loan has a 6% interest rate and his minimum payment for that stayed the same. His rent didn’t go up this year either, so now, finally, he has more money at the end of each month than he needs to make his minimum required payments.

TMP-0968.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 1 Personal Saving and Borrowing

TMP-0968.text: With this new financial cushion, Jalen is beginning to have options for what to do with his money. TMP-0973.text: MODULES 3.3 Accounting and Financial Management 3.4 Business Expenses 3.5 Financial Capital 3.6 The Income Statement 3.7 The Balance Sheet and Net Worth 3.8 The Cash Flow Statement 3.9 Ethics and Financial Reporting It Takes Money to Make Money The mother-daughter team of Cassandra and India Ayala started a restaurant business called The Bumbling Bee. Their concept was plant-based “vegan junk food” that would satisfy people’s cravings for items like shakes and burgers in a healthy way. They tested their concept on a small scale with a food truck in 2019. That was a big hit, so they followed up with a brick-and-mortar restaurant the same year, and a second food truck and restaurant in 2020.

TMP-0974.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0974.navLabel: UNIT 3 PART 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0974.text: Despite sales of $324,000 in 2020, the company needed more money to pay for its operating expenses and growth. Cassandra and India appeared on the television show Shark Tank , on which a panel of successful entrepreneurs hears sales pitches from fledgling entrepreneurs who are seeking financial support. The panel decided that The Bumbling Bee had not differentiated itself enough from competing eateries to warrant their investments, and denied the company any funding. The Bumbling Bee received new customers thanks to the television appearance, but the short-lived increase in business was not enough to carry it through the doldrums of the COVID-19 pandemic. With many customers feeling safer eating at home, restaurant revenues were down sharply nationwide, and The Bumbling Bee was reduced to just one food truck and no restaurants. In 2023, the Ayalas invested another $10,000 to bring the food truck to the College of William and Mary, but the revenue was insufficient to maintain that operation. They decided to pivot to a new business concept they felt might have greater appeal. In 2024, they turned The Bumbling Bee food truck into a business called Solana Street Food, with a new menu featuring Puerto Rican flavors with carnivore, vegetarian, vegan, and

TMP-0975.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0975.navLabel: UNIT 3 PART 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0975.text: gluten-free options. That business is still serving tacos, nachos, and empanadas as of this writing. In their entrepreneurial adventures, the Ayalas found that financial shortfalls drove key decisions about their food-truck business. Money fuels business opportunities and growth, but it doesn’t come easily. Individuals face related challenges, even if they never go into business. Money creates opportunities for education, homes, cars, and healthcare, among other critical needs and wants. And, as for businesses like this one, the need for money often comes long before the availability of money. In the modules ahead, we’ll learn how businesses and individuals can navigate financial challenges by planning well, limiting spending, saving when possible, borrowing when necessary, keeping good records, and managing finances responsibly. TMP-0979.text: Igor Suka/Getty Images By capturing data from every transaction, businesses can track everything from sales revenue and inventory to each customer’s purchasing patterns.

TMP-0980.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0980.text: Tracking Financial Data LG Why do consumers and businesses collect and evaluate financial data? The hustle and bustle at the checkout counters of your local grocery store is a flurry of financial transactions. The store is selling cartloads of food items to customers and receiving payments in various forms. Behind the scenes, many more transactions are happening. The business is paying employees for their work, suppliers for their goods and services, utility companies for water, gas, and electricity, banks for loans, landlords for property, and tax collectors for government services. A successful business also has profits to distribute among owners. That’s a lot to keep track of, so many stakeholders rely on careful recordkeeping and summaries of those transactions. In this module, we will examine why and how businesses track financial data and how consumers can monitor their own transactions.

TMP-0981.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0981.text: Why Accounting Matters Accounting is the process of recording, organizing, and reporting financial data. Billionaire CEO Warren Buffett described accounting as the “language of business.” Buffett told a young intern that accounting should be studied like a foreign language because it is important to business success but takes time to grasp. 1 In later modules, we will study financial statements , which are formal summaries of a business’s financial data for a specific time period or date. Those statements convey information about the business’s financial transactions as well as its assets (what it owns), liabilities (what it owes), and owners’ equity (its net worth to the owners, meaning the value of assets minus liabilities). accounting The process of recording, organizing, and reporting financial data. financial statements Formal summaries of a business’s financial data for a specific time period or date. You may or may not have interest in becoming an accountant, but every future businessperson should learn the language of accounting well enough to understand what financial data reveals about an organization. Suppose you start a T-shirt printing

TMP-0982.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0982.text: business and invest $10,000 of your own money to buy equipment and supplies. You run the business for a month and want to know your profit or loss and whether any of your original investment is available to spend. You can use accounting practices to find the answers.

TMP-0983.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0983.text: heshphoto/Getty Images You may be making T-shirts, but is your business making money? Accounting will determine the answer. If you have carefully recorded your business transactions over the month, you might learn the following:

TMP-0984.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0984.text: • You have spent $3,500 out of the $10,000 investment on printing equipment and expenses, which means $10,000 − $3,500 = $6,500 of that investment remains. • You have made $5,000 in sales to customers. Your gross (before taxes) profit is $5,000 − $3,500 = $1,500. • You owe $300 in taxes on that profit, leaving you with $6,500 + $5,000 − $300 = $11,200 in cash available for other purposes. With this information, you are better prepared to make decisions about whether to expand, seek loans, change staffing levels, spend more on advertising, or pivot to a new product.

TMP-0985.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0985.text: courtneyk/Getty Images Accounting is a process of recording, sorting, retrieving, and reporting financial data. Understanding the language of accounting is a critical business skill.

TMP-0986.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0986.text: These transactions affect your personal assets, liabilities, and net worth. Your money and the things you own are assets, your loans are liabilities, and your net worth is the difference between the value of your assets and the value of your liabilities. Even though individuals are not required to record or report all of their financial transactions, it’s always a good idea to keep track of your personal finances. Perhaps you have dabbled in accounting practices by tracking deposits and withdrawals for a Venmo, Cash App, or checking account. Individuals, like businesses and governments, benefit from financial plans or budgets that guide their spending. Having an organized system for tracking your personal financial transactions can help you stay within your budget and make it easier to save. And good accounting practices can help you build good credit, which, as we discussed in Module 3.2 , is essential if you ever want to borrow money to buy a car or a home, or to start a new business. Who Uses Accounting Information? In the business world, accounting information serves a wide array of internal users within the firm and external users outside the firm. Internal users include business owners, managers, and employees. External users include investors, suppliers,

TMP-0987.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0987.text: creditors, customers, and the government. Financial statements address three fundamental questions for stakeholders: 1. Is the business profitable? 2. Is the business financially healthy? 3. Does the business have enough cash to operate and meet financial obligations? Beyond its importance for decision-making purposes, some reporting of financial information is required by law. The Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) . are a set of rules and standards for financial reporting by publicly traded companies in the United States. GAAP cover the definitions of terms, accounting methods, and reporting requirements for accounting information. For example, GAAP requires all U.S. companies that sell shares of stock to the public to file quarterly and annual reports that disclose all positive and negative financial information with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The SEC makes those reports available to the public so that any interested stakeholder can study them. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) A set of rules and standards for financial reporting by publicly traded companies in the United States.

TMP-0988.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0988.text: The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) is responsible for issuing and updating GAAP to ensure consistency, transparency, and comparability in financial reporting across different companies and time periods. Although the FASB is a private organization that operates independently from the government, the SEC recognizes this board as the authority over accounting standards for public companies. Figure 3.3-1 provides an overview of the sources, purposes, and users of accounting information. Business operations such as selling goods, hiring employees, and manufacturing goods generate financial transactions. Accountants collect data on the resulting revenue and expenses, along with the investments and loans used to finance the expenses. That data is summarized in financial reports to inform the internal and external stakeholders about the company’s financial position.

TMP-0992.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0992.text: Among the internal users of accounting information are owners, who use it to assess overall profitability and guide strategic decision making. Managers need financial data to evaluate progress toward goals and the availability of cash. And employees use this information to ensure that the company is profitable enough to provide the promised compensation and offer opportunities for career development. Dire financial data can lead employees to seek work elsewhere, while strong financial data is a draw for prospective employees seeking job security and competitive salaries. Among the external users are investors , who provide financial support for business ventures with the expectation of receiving a favorable return on their investment. Potential investors should examine financial statements as part of their due diligence process of carefully evaluating risks and rewards prior to their decision to invest. Current investors rely on financial information to assess their prospects for profit and the advisability of making any changes in their investment portfolio. Lenders such as banks and other financial institutions need financial information to establish the company’s ability to pay back their debts. Suppliers may consider a company’s finances to gauge whether the company can pay its bills when due. And the government is interested in a company’s financial information for taxation and regulatory purposes.

TMP-0993.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting

TMP-0994.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0994.text: Accounting and Finance Departments LG What is the purpose of accounting and finance departments? The many important uses of financial information have given rise to specialized areas of accounting to serve particular needs. Large companies also have dedicated departments to tackle assorted financial tasks. In this section, we will examine the functions of accounting departments and finance departments. Accounting Departments Many large corporations have a dedicated accounting department that records all financial transactions, summarizes those transactions in reports and statements, and ensures compliance with tax laws and regulations. The accounting department may also manage payments to suppliers and employees, help to identify money-saving

TMP-0995.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0995.text: opportunities for the company, and conduct internal audits to monitor financial practices. accounting department The department that records all financial transactions, summarizes those transactions in reports and statements, and ensures compliance with tax laws and regulations. We’ve learned that business leaders can have roles that are primarily inward-facing or outward-facing. For example, human resource managers serve stakeholders within a corporation by taking care of staffing needs, while public relations managers connect with outside stakeholders to improve the company’s image. Managerial accountants and financial accountants have similarly inward and outward focuses, respectively. • Managerial accountants serve managers and other internal stakeholders by providing financial information used to plan and make decisions. Their work is often forward looking, providing forecasts and informing budget plans. The resulting financial reports are customized to fit the needs of managers rather than adhering to strict external guidelines such as GAAP. • Financial accountants serve primarily external stakeholders, such as investors, lenders, and shareholders by recording financial transactions and providing

TMP-0996.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0996.text: financial statements. Their work focuses on past transactions rather than trying to predict future trends. Financial accountants at public companies are required to follow the GAAP standards. managerial accountants Accountants who serve managers and other internal stakeholders by providing financial information used to plan and make decisions. financial accountants Accountants who serve external stakeholders such as investors, lenders, and shareholders by recording financial transactions and providing financial statements.

TMP-0997.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0997.text: Spencer Platt/Getty Images Extended description for New York Stock Exchange Additional employees and scores of monitors appear in the background.

TMP-0998.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0998.text: The stock markets allow millions of investors to own shares of companies. Wise investors examine businesses’ financial statements, which are created by financial accountants, before deciding where to invest their money. A small business might assign both managerial and financial accounting tasks to a single person. Both types of accounting make use of the same basic financial data. Some businesses outsource accounting tasks to a company like Accenture or Deloitte. And some small business owners handle their own accounting, sometimes with the help of specialized software such as QuickBooks. As a business scales up, it makes more sense to hire specialized staff and divide the managerial and financial accounting tasks. It is common for a medium-to-large sized company to hire a controller to analyze the financial data for forecasting and budgeting purposes and an accounting manager to oversee the financial accounting side of the department. AP® EXAM TIP An exam question could ask what advice you would give to business leaders about which experts or departments should handle a particular financial task. A solid understanding of the difference between the key types of accountants (managerial and financial) and departments (accounting and finance) will help you pinpoint the best people and places to handle a burning issue.

TMP-0999.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-0999.text: Finance Departments One of the internal users of data collected by the accounting department is the finance department , which analyzes financial data and guides strategy decisions to optimize the company’s financial performance. This department is likely to weigh in on decisions about budgets, goals, investments, funding, cost control, and risk management. The finance department may also make recommendations about major expenditures on equipment or expansion, long-term financial plans, and potential mergers with other companies. While the accounting department records each transaction and keeps track of where all the money is going, the finance department focuses on managing that money and growing the company in responsible ways. finance department The department that analyzes financial data collected by the accounting department and guides strategy decisions to optimize a company’s financial performance.

TMP-1000.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1000.text: Darren McCollester/Getty Images Guidance from the PepsiCo finance department, under the direction of Indra Nooyi, led the company to merge with Quaker Oats, which owned Gatorade. Product diversification provided more financial stability and profit to a company that had been heavily dependent on soft drinks. Although finance departments are out of customers’ view, the outcomes of their work are quite visible to customers — and vital to many businesses. Consider the finance

TMP-1001.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1001.text: department at PepsiCo, which was led by chief financial officer Indra Nooyi during a period of critical growth and change in the early 2000s. Her department oversaw a diversification of PepsiCo that made the company less vulnerable to changes in the popularity of its soft drinks. Nooyi advised the company to acquire juice-maker Tropicana and merge with Quaker Oats, which owned sports drink Gatorade. She also directed a restructuring of the company that included separating PepsiCo from Tricon, a company now called Yum! Brands that owns Pizza Hut, KFC, and Taco Bell. After six years leading the finance department, Nooyi’s work providing financial stability to PepsiCo earned her the position of chief executive officer. Consumers Hire Financial Professionals, Too The accounting process of recording, organizing, and reporting financial data that is so central to business operations is also part of many consumers’ lives. The options available for the preparation of an individual’s income taxes are similar to those for business owners. Individuals can comply with the reporting requirements personally, often using software programs such as TaxSlayer and TurboTax to assist with the process. The U.S. Internal Revenue Service (IRS), which is the agency that administers tax laws, makes free tax software available to qualified taxpayers through the IRS Free

TMP-1002.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1002.text: File program. And many individuals choose to hire a certified public accountant (CPA) — an accounting professional licensed by a state board of accountancy to provide tax advice and assist individuals and businesses with tax law compliance, including the completion of tax forms. The advisability of seeking outside assistance with taxes depends on: the complexity of the individual’s financial situation, the time they have available for preparing taxes, their willingness to pay for outside help, and their level of comfort with completing their own tax return. In most cases, it is not necessary to hire a CPA, but they are helpful in complicated situations.

TMP-1003.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1003.text: FangXiaNuo/Getty Images When tax season approaches, individuals and small businesses like this one may seek the assistance of a certified public accountant. If you are seeking a loan, a loan officer at a bank or credit union will generally talk with you about options at no cost. Individuals with a significant amount of money to

TMP-1004.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1004.text: invest can benefit from consultation with paid financial professionals. A financial adviser is someone who can offer advice on investment strategies that align with a client’s financial situation and attitudes toward risk. Financial advisers may also provide guidance on insurance and savings plans for college or retirement. Some financial advisers will manage an investment portfolio for customers, meaning that they handle the investments and assist with decisions about what to buy and sell. financial adviser A professional who offers advice on investment strategies that align with a client’s financial situation and attitudes toward risk. Accountants and financial advisers charge for their services. They may charge an hourly rate, a flat fee, or a percentage of the investment portfolio being managed. Always be clear on the cost of services before agreeing to purchase them. It is also important to consider licensing, certification, education, and experience when choosing a financial professional to manage investments or provide advice. For example, a CPA has licensing from the American Institution of Public Accountants and can handle situations with the IRS that other tax preparers cannot. However, for straightforward tax returns with a low risk of being audited by the IRS, a non-CPA tax preparer may serve well and offer lower fees.

TMP-1005.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1005.text: Beyond clarity on fees, it is appropriate to ask for references. A financial professional should be willing to give you the names of other customers who can vouch for their ethical behavior. When hiring a financial adviser, it is also relevant to ask whether the adviser is a fiduciary financial adviser , meaning that they are bound by legal and ethical standards to act in your best interest. Nonfiduciary advisers can act in their own best interest rather than in yours, which can create a dangerous conflict of interest. A credential of certified financial planner (CFP) or registered investment adviser (RIA) generally indicates that the professional is held to a fiduciary standard.

TMP-1006.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1006.text: Module 3.3 Review Learning Goals Accounting is the process of recording, organizing, and reporting financial data. A key product of accounting is financial statements , which are formal summaries of a business’s financial data for a specific time period or date. Accounting statements address the fundamental questions of whether the business is profitable, whether it is financially healthy, and whether its cash holdings are sufficient to meet financial obligations. Like businesses, individuals carry out many financial transactions, including purchases, sales, investments, and loans. For both individuals and businesses, these transactions affect the value of assets, liabilities, and net worth.

TMP-1007.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1007.text: The Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) are a set of rules and standards for financial reporting in the United States that apply to publicly traded companies. LG What is the purpose of accounting and finance departments? Many large corporations have an accounting department that records all financial transactions, summarizes those transactions in reports and statements, and ensures compliance with tax laws and regulations. Managerial accountants serve managers and other internal stakeholders by providing financial information used to plan and make decisions. Financial accountants serve primarily external stakeholders such as investors, lenders, and shareholders by recording financial transactions and providing financial statements. A finance department analyzes financial data and guides strategy decisions to optimize the company’s financial performance. This department informs decisions about budgets, goals, investments, funding, cost control, and risk management. The

TMP-1008.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1008.text: finance department may also make recommendations about major expenditures on equipment or expansion, long-term financial plans, and potential mergers with other companies. The accounting process of recording, organizing, and reporting financial data practiced in businesses is also part of many consumers’ lives. When it comes to preparing income taxes or making key financial decisions about investments, insurance, and loans, consumers have several options. Some consumers hire a certified public accountant to assist with tax forms and compliance with tax laws. Depending on the complexity of their situation, the time and money available to them, and their level of comfort with the tasks at hand, consumers can choose to act independently or hire a financial adviser , who can offer advice on investment strategies that align with the client’s financial situation and attitudes toward risk.

TMP-1012.text: CASE STUDY Accenture picture alliance/Getty Images Quantum computers are among the newer technological tools that make innovations possible in fields like accounting and finance. When you think of innovative companies, which ones come to mind? Perhaps Google’s parent company Alphabet, chip maker NVIDIA, or drug maker Novartis. You may not immediately think of a company like Accenture, a management consulting and technology firm headquartered in Dublin, Ireland, that has its

TMP-1013.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1013.text: origins in accounting. Accenture began as the business and technology consulting division of the highly successful accounting firm Arthur Andersen, founded in the early 1950s. It eventually split off from the accounting firm as Andersen Consulting, and the name changed to Accenture in 2001. Today, the company has a strong focus on innovation; even its name stresses innovation, as it is derived from “accent on the future.” 2 Ranked in the top half of the Fortune Global 500 list, Accenture is a multinational company with $64 billion in annual revenue. It has diversified into many business services, including finance and accounting, strategy and consulting, technology solutions, and customer service innovations. The company has more than 800,000 employees serving clients in over 120 countries. 3 With a whopping 7,400 patents and patents pending, the company fulfills its purpose: “To deliver on the promise of technology and human ingenuity. We help our clients become the next and best versions of themselves.” 4 Accenture provides expertise in financial and accounting processes. For example, it ran finance and accounting functions for global energy giant British Petroleum (BP), applying is intelligent automation and analytics capabilities to improve

TMP-1014.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1014.text: efficiency and productivity. 5 Accenture is also an innovator when it comes to helping clients transfer more of their information, including accounting-related data, to the cloud networks of remote servers. Accenture explains that this will help banks improve scalability, efficiency, agility, and security. 6 Accenture is proposing innovations that use artificial intelligence (AI) in the world of accounting and finance. AI can improve the accuracy and efficiency of routine processes and administrative tasks, allowing workers to spend more time on tasks that are complicated and require judgment and imagination. Banks also can use AI to engage with, advise, assist, and sell to customers in a much more personalized way. Accenture also has its eye on quantum computing technologies, which could be the next big disruptor in the realm of business. Quantum computers solve complex problems and analyze large data sets far faster than traditional computers. The financial services industry is among several with broad applications for quantum computing. With the ability to quickly and thoroughly analyze large or unstructured data sets, financial institutions can use the technology to make more timely and appropriate investment decisions.

TMP-1015.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1015.text: While quantum computing can speed things up for the AI and financial services industries, it can also help cybercriminals cause trouble. By vastly increasing processing power, quantum computers pose a threat to encryption methods used to secure electronic transfers of information. To counter the dark side of quantum technology, Accenture partnered with post-quantum cybersecurity provider QuSecure. Together, these companies hope to offer the benefits of cutting-edge computing while guarding clients against the vulnerabilities of incredible computing power in the wrong hands. 7 Industries are increasingly using partnerships to jumpstart the integration of quantum computing. Accenture is positioning itself to be just such a partner. The company has already announced it is partnering with IonQ, which is designing the hardware for quantum computing. Accenture proposes that its “experience and skills in quantum, coupled with its ability to design and create customized industry solutions tailored to IonQ’s quantum computing technology, will help more companies innovate and become quantum ready.” 8

TMP-1017.text: MODULE 3.4 Business Expenses LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 3.4.A Identify the costs of starting a new business 3.4.B Categorize the expenses of operating a business

TMP-1018.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1018.text: DAVID GRAY/Getty Images There are many costs to opening a McDonald’s restaurant. On top of the costs of food, staffing, and rent, the entrepreneur must pay for everything from the speaker system at the drive-thru to the golden arches out front. The McDonald’s Corporation also receives a franchise fee and royalties based on a percentage of sales.

TMP-1019.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1019.navLabel: The Cost of Starting a New Business
TMP-1019.text: The Cost of Starting a New Business LG What costs are associated with launching a new product or business? It’s not hard to imagine that a power plant or an aerospace company like Northrop Grumman would be wildly expensive to launch, but let’s consider a business that is more down to earth. Suppose you wanted to open a McDonald’s restaurant. You would need to buy a McDonald’s franchise , meaning that you would pay a fee to the McDonald’s Corporation in exchange for the right to use its name and business model. McDonald’s requires that franchisees have a minimum of $750,000 in nonborrowed, available personal funds to invest in the business. 1 A $45,000 franchise fee is paid directly to the company. The rest of that money, or more, would be needed for expenses that include cooking equipment such as fryers, signage including the golden arches, a drive-thru speaker system, digital menu boards, and inventory like lots and lots of hamburger

headings.text: The Cost of Starting a New Business

TMP-1020.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1020.navLabel: The Cost of Starting a New Business
TMP-1020.text: patties and French fries. In this section, we examine the types of costs you might encounter when starting a business. Startup costs are the expenses a new business faces as it prepares to open for the first time. Startup costs include one-time expenditures that are made only once as the business gets its start, such as licensing fees, equipment costs, and legal fees for having a lawyer review contracts and ensure compliance with regulations. They also include initial expenses that are ongoing, meaning they are paid when the business launches and continue to be paid while the business operates. A business with a physical location will have occupancy expenses such as rent, utilities, and property taxes. Other examples of initial expenses include research and development, marketing, employees, insurance, and the production or purchase of inventory. startup costs The expenses a new business faces as it prepares to open for the first time. one-time expenses Startup costs that are paid only once as the business gets its start.

TMP-1021.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1021.navLabel: The Cost of Starting a New Business
TMP-1021.text: initial expenses Startup costs that are ongoing, meaning they are paid when the business launches and continue to be paid while the business operates. Consider a bakery like Mile Hi Foods in Colorado, which makes buns for McDonald’s. 2 The startup costs for a bakery like this would include one-time expenditures on mixers and ovens, which might last as long as the business. The bakery would also have initial expenses such as the first payments for rent and utilities (water, gas, and electricity), starting inventories of flour, oil, and yeast, and the initial payments to the bakers. Next, we will describe more of the characteristics of these recurring expenses.

TMP-1022.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1022.navLabel: The Cost of Running a Business
TMP-1022.text: The Cost of Running a Business LG What expenses are associated with running an established business? Once a business is up and running, it is done paying one-time startup costs, but it has plenty more costs to contend with. Some costs are infrequent, such as replacing a roof, paying a legal settlement, fixing a delivery truck, or implementing a new software program. Recurring costs are expenses that arise on a regular basis. In this section, we’ll learn how businesses categorize these expenses. recurring costs Expenses that arise on a regular basis. AP ® Exam TIP Make sure you understand the distinctions between one-time expenditures, initial expenses, and recurring costs. One-time expenditures and initial expenses are both startup costs, but one-time

headings.text: The Cost of Running a Business

TMP-1023.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1023.navLabel: The Cost of Running a Business
TMP-1023.text: expenditures are only made once, whereas initial expenses are ongoing. And the difference between initial expenses and recurring costs is in the timing: Initial expenses necessarily begin as the business gets going, which isn’t necessarily true for recurring costs. And recurring costs generally arise on a regular basis, whereas initial expenses can be ongoing but irregular.
