TMP-1024.text: Monty Rakusen/Getty Images Extended description for Commercial Kitchen The wall of the kitchen is lined with dozens of ovens. A second employee appears in the background pushing a wheeled cart. Several carts appear in the

TMP-1025.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1025.text: background, lined with baked goods. The startup costs for a commercial kitchen include a large, one-time expenditure on ovens. Direct and Indirect Costs A direct cost is associated with the production or delivery of a particular good or service. The raw materials that go into a product, the cost of workers’ time while they make that product, the equipment devoted to that product, and any energy used specifically for that product are examples of direct costs. Bread production involves the direct costs of ingredients, the bakers’ wages, and the packaging for each loaf. In Module 3.6 , we’ll learn that some direct costs are not recurring, such as the cost of ovens for baking bread. direct cost A cost associated with the production or delivery of a particular good or service. Other costs are crucial to the business, but not exclusively for one product. An indirect cost is a cost of running the business that is not tied to the production or

TMP-1026.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1026.text: delivery of a particular good or service. Indirect costs are expenses for things that serve the business as a whole, like the cost of the sales staff, insurance, and administrative salaries. Marketing and accounting departments incur indirect costs because they are not associated with one particular good. For a bakery, indirect costs include rent, heating and air conditioning, advertising, and management. indirect cost A cost of running a business that is not tied to the production or delivery of a particular good or service. More generally, an operating expense is any cost of running a business on a day-to-day basis. Operating expenses are commonly indirect and recurring. The indirect costs mentioned above, such as sales staff, insurance, administrative salaries, rent, and advertising, are among the operating expenses required to keep the business functioning normally. Operating expenses typically do not change with the amount of output produced. Next, we’ll learn that such costs are considered fixed . operating expense Any cost of running a business on a day-to-day basis.

TMP-1027.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1027.text: fcafotodigital/Getty Images The ingredients for bread are needed when the bakery launches and on an ongoing basis afterward, so they are both startup costs and recurring costs. Because the ingredients are associated with the production of a particular product, they are also direct costs.

TMP-1028.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1028.text: Fixed and Variable Costs A recurring cost can be a fixed cost or a variable cost. A fixed cost remains the same as the quantity of output (which can be goods or services) changes. For example, the cost of having a company host the bakery’s website doesn’t change when the bakery makes more or less bread. The indirect costs and operating expenses described in the previous section, such as rent, insurance, administrative salaries, and marketing, are typically also fixed costs. That is, those costs generally stay the same whether the bakery makes 10 loaves of bread or 100 loaves of bread each day. There are also some direct costs that are fixed costs. For example, a bread oven is directly associated with bread production, making it a direct cost. But its cost will stay the same as more or less bread is made (unless the bakery makes so much bread that it needs more ovens). fixed cost A cost that remains the same as the quantity of output changes. On the other hand, the cost of ingredients and bakers’ wages does depend on how much bread is made. A variable cost increases when the level of output increases. If the bakery wants to make more bread, it must buy more flour, so flour is a variable cost. Most direct costs are variable costs. The amounts of raw materials, workers, packaging

TMP-1029.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1029.navLabel: The Cost of Goods Sold and the Cost of Sales
TMP-1029.text: supplies, and energy directly related to making a good or providing a service generally increase when output increases, making their costs variable. variable cost A cost that increases when the level of output increases. The Cost of Goods Sold and the Cost of Sales We know what you’re thinking: There aren’t enough overlapping cost-related terms. Don’t worry, there are a couple more that you will want to learn to participate in conversations about business and accounting. The cost of goods sold (COGS) is the total cost of producing the goods sold over some period. Accountants use COGS to help determine a business’s profit or loss over past months, quarters, or years. COGS includes all of the direct costs, such as the costs of raw materials and production-related supplies, wages, electricity, and equipment. COGS can also include expenses such as the cost of renting a factory, which may be necessary for the production of one or more goods. cost of goods sold (COGS) The total cost of producing goods sold over some period.

headings.text: The Cost of Goods Sold and the Cost of Sales

TMP-1030.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1030.navLabel: The Cost of Goods Sold and the Cost of Sales
TMP-1030.text: COGS excludes operating expenses that are not directly tied to production, such as rent for office spaces, marketing expenses, and insurance. The key determinant for inclusion in COGS is whether the costs are incurred for the production of goods. Table 3.4-1 summarizes the cost categories for several common cost items. Table 3.4-1 Categorizing Business Costs Cost Item Direct or Indirect? Variable or Fixed? One-Time or Recurring? COGS or Not COGS? Hourly wages of production workers Direct Variable Recurring COGS Raw materials Direct Variable Recurring COGS Rental of equipment to produce a particular good Direct Fixed Recurring COGS Rental of manufacturing facility Indirect (if it supports overall production, not a specific good) Fixed Recurring COGS Salaried sales force Indirect Fixed Recurring Not COGS Administration (office staff, accounting, HR) Indirect Fixed Recurring Not COGS Marketing Indirect Fixed Recurring Not COGS

TMP-1031.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1031.navLabel: The Cost of Goods Sold and the Cost of Sales
TMP-1031.text: Of course, not all businesses produce goods. For a business that sells goods but does not produce them, the cost of goods sold is the cost of acquiring the goods from elsewhere. For a business that provides services, there is an alternative to COGS. Service providers look at the cost of sales , which is the total cost of providing a service to customers. The cost of sales includes every cost directly related to service delivery, such as labor costs for the service providers, any materials or supplies used for service delivery, and the cost of any associated equipment, software, and travel. Operating expenses, such as marketing and administrative salaries, are not part of the cost of sales. cost of sales The total cost of providing a service to customers. For a dental office, the cost of sales would include the salaries of the dentists and hygienists; the cost of equipment like dental chairs and X-ray machines; lab fees; and the cost of supplies and materials, such as anesthetics, fillings, braces, gloves, and retainers. The cost of sales would not include operating expenses such as accounting fees, advertising, and liability insurance. Next, we’ll consider why so many businesses purchase insurance.

TMP-1032.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1032.navLabel: The Cost of Goods Sold and the Cost of Sales
TMP-1032.text: Kobus Louw/Getty Images Dentists and other service providers don’t have a cost of goods sold, but instead measure the cost of sales, which includes every cost directly related to the delivery of their service. For a dental office, that includes the salaries of service providers and the cost of equipment, supplies, and — when the dental work gets serious — anesthesia. AP ® EXAM TIP Rather than trying to memorize how each cost item is categorized, it is easier to learn the rules for belonging to each category. For example: Direct costs are tied to a particular product, and indirect

TMP-1033.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1033.text: costs are not; variable costs change when more units are made, and fixed costs do not; and only production-related costs are part of COGS. Insurance Each individual and business faces at least a small risk of a large loss. If you drive a car or your business operates a delivery truck, there is always a chance that the vehicle will damage another person’s property or injure someone. For businesses, common sources of loss include: burglary and theft damage from water or freezing temperatures wind or hail damage fire customer injuries property damage injuries caused by commercial vehicles product liability (damage caused by a product)

TMP-1034.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1034.text: workplace accidents reputational harm Clearly, a lot can go wrong. Businesses (and individuals) can purchase insurance coverage that helps to protect them from large losses. The payments for insurance are called premiums , which are typically paid to the insurance company monthly, quarterly, semi-annually (twice a year), or annually. When a covered incident such as a theft or fire occurs, the customer files a formal request or claim with the insurance company asking for compensation for the loss. After the claim is verified, the customer will receive a payment from the insurance company, subject to the details of their particular insurance policy. We’ll talk more about policy details and the insurable risks individuals face in the last unit. A troubling aspect of the business risks mentioned above is that they will inevitably occur, but no one knows who the victims will be. Insurance can spread the risk of being victimized across a large number of potential victims. If millions of businesses purchase insurance, insurance companies can collect the money paid for insurance premiums and distribute large portions of it to those suffering losses. Insurance companies also keep a portion of the premiums to support their own operations.

TMP-1035.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1035.text: The same is true for individuals. Suppose there are 1,000 homes in your community and two of them are the unfortunate victims of fire in a typical year. If each homeowner pays a $1,000 premium for fire insurance each year, an insurance company receives 1,000 × $1,000 = $1 million in premiums. That company could distribute $350,000 to each of the two unlucky victims of house fires and have $300,000 left over for expenses and profit. It is common for small businesses to start with a business owner’s insurance policy, which bundles popular types of insurance. For example, commercial property insurance covers buildings, equipment, and other property from damage or theft. General liability insurance protects against personal injuries to customers, damage to other people’s property, and lawsuits claiming the business damaged someone’s reputation, among other things. And business interruption insurance helps with losses incurred when an event such as a flood or fire prevents normal business operations. As we’ll discuss next, some types of insurance are required.

TMP-1036.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1036.text: Bloomberg/Getty Images To prepare for the possibility of a fire, a business can purchase commercial property insurance to cover building repairs, and business interruption insurance to assist with the loss of income while the business is unable to operate.

TMP-1037.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1037.text: Required Insurance Imagine being hit by a car whose driver has little money and no insurance. There might be no way to cover the damages to your health and vehicle. For such reasons, some types of insurance are mandated by law. There are also requirements for insurance imposed by lending organizations such as banks. Before you receive a loan for a car, the lender will want proof that you have insured that vehicle. This is because the car serves as collateral for the loan, meaning that if you do not repay your loan, the lender receives the car. It is therefore important for the lender to know that the car will be repaired or replaced in the event of an accident. In most states, businesses must provide workers’ compensation insurance , which covers employees who are injured or become ill while working. Likewise, businesses in all states contribute to the cost of unemployment insurance , which provides temporary financial assistance to qualified workers who become unemployed for reasons that are not their own fault. Among other examples, most states require commercial auto insurance for businesses with vehicles and liquor liability insurance for businesses that sell alcohol. There are fewer types of legally required insurance for individuals, but auto insurance is required in most states.

TMP-1038.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1038.text: workers’ compensation insurance Insurance that covers employees who are injured or become ill while working. Attitudes Toward Risk What about the many types of insurance that are optional — how much is optimal? As we will explore further in Module 5.2 , the appropriate amount of insurance for an individual or business depends on their willingness and ability to accept risk. The appeal of insurance is not that customers expect to receive more from claims than they pay in premiums. As in the house fire example discussed previously, premiums generally exceed the expected cost of claims. It is that difference between what customers pay and what they receive on average that allows insurance companies to cover their costs and seek profit. The value proposition for insurance is the avoidance of an unbearable loss. The importance of paying for insurance to spread the risk of a large loss is diminished for those who can easily afford the loss. If it wouldn’t be a big deal for a high-income individual to replace her car in the event of an accident, she might not purchase insurance with collision coverage that would pay for car repairs. She will still want

TMP-1039.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1039.text: liability coverage for her car, which covers the injuries and property damage caused to others, because there is no limit to those potential costs. Decisions to purchase optional insurance also hinge on attitudes toward risk unrelated to affordability. There are risk-loving gamblers who go out of their way to take risks and don’t always mind the uncertainty of uninsured outcomes. There are risk-neutral people who neither fear nor seek risks, and care only about the average cost of taking a risk. And there are risk-averse people who would pay to avoid the uncertainty of a risk, even if the average cost of taking the risk is zero. Suppose we play a game in which we flip a coin to determine who pays who $20. If it lands on heads, I pay you $20. If it lands on tails, you pay me $20. Would you want to play this game? A risk lover would pay some amount just for the possibility of winning, even though there is an equal chance of losing. A risk-neutral player would be indifferent between playing the game or not. This is because there is a 50% chance of winning $20 and a 50% chance of losing $20, and the expected (average) outcome is zero. A risk-averse player would pay not to have to face the uncertainty of these outcomes. This type of willingness to pay to avoid uncertainty is what leads individuals and businesses to buy insurance when they don’t have to.

TMP-1040.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1040.text: Businesses with abundant financial resources are like high-income individuals — they may be able to afford the downside risk of some insurable events. In terms of attitudes toward risk, it can be argued that a business should aim to be risk neutral. For the sake of investors and other stakeholders, it makes sense to focus on the average outcome unless a loss would cause the company financial distress. In practice, managers tend to show signs of risk aversion — and loss aversion in particular — meaning they care even more about avoiding a significant loss than about achieving a significant gain. 3 Among the results of this is an inclination to purchase an ample amount of insurance.

TMP-1041.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1041.text: Module 3.4 Review Learning Goals LG What costs are associated with launching a new product or business? Startup costs are the expenses a new business faces as it prepares to open for the first time. Startup costs include one-time expenditures that are made only once as the business gets its start, such as on licensing fees and equipment costs. They also include initial expenses that are recurring, meaning they are paid when the business launches and continue to be paid while the business operates. LG What expenses are associated with running an established business?

TMP-1042.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1042.text: Recurring costs — those that arise on an ongoing basis — are of two types. A direct cost is associated with the production or delivery of a particular good or service. An indirect cost is a cost of running the business that is not tied to the production or delivery of a particular good or service. More generally, an operating expense is any cost of running a business on a day-to-day basis. A fixed cost remains the same as the quantity of output changes. A variable cost increases when the level of output increases. The cost of goods sold (COGS) is the total cost of producing the goods sold over some period. For a business that provides services, there is an alternative to COGS. Service businesses look at the cost of sales , which is the total cost of providing a service to customers. Insurance spreads the burden of common risks across many businesses or individuals. By paying premiums to an insurance company, customers can receive insurance coverage that helps to protect them from large losses. When a covered incident such as a theft or fire occurs, the customer files a claim with the insurance company. After the claim is verified, the customer will receive a payment from the insurance company, subject to the details of their particular insurance policy.

TMP-1043.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1043.text: Some insurance is required. In most states, businesses must provide workers’ compensation insurance , which covers employees who are injured or become ill while working. When insurance is optional, the decision to buy insurance depends on the potential insurance customer’s attitude toward risk and their ability to afford the loss that might be incurred if they are not insured. TMP-1047.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1047.text: CASE STUDY Fore the Trail simonkr/Getty Images It’s no fun showing up at your favorite path without a hat, sunglasses, or water bottle. A small business could fill that need — but first, entrepreneurs must navigate the many costs of starting a business. Suppose that Anna and Danielle wanted to open a business to serve their small community in Idaho. After surveying 100 residents and tourists, they discovered a

TMP-1048.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1048.text: strong need for a shop near a popular rails-to-trails pathway. People would show up at the trailhead for a long walk, run, or bike ride and wish they had more to eat or drink, sunscreen, a hat, sunglasses, Bluetooth earbuds, a rain poncho, and a fanny pack to put their stuff in. Since their shop came before the trail and sold things for the trail, Anna and Danielle called it Fore the Trail. Anna and Danielle rented an 800-square-foot retail space for their shop. They incurred the following costs in the first month as they launched their business: Business registration and license fees: $500 Food and retail permits: $250 Insurance: $200 Lease deposit: $1,600 Monthly rent: $800 Fixtures, shelving, and interior setup: $2,000 Signage: $600 Security system installation: $400 Point of sale (checkout) system: $900

TMP-1049.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1049.text: Refrigerator for drinks: $1,100 Inventory: $4,200 Website setup: $500 Initial marketing (flyers, online ads): $700 Utilities (power, water, internet): $350 Staff wages: $17,000 Miscellaneous supplies: $250 Total for the first month: $31,350 Anna and Danielle bootstrapped the business, relying primarily on personal savings to cover the $31,350 in startup costs and all of the recurring and nonrecurring costs to follow. To make the costs more manageable, they implemented low-cost strategies such as starting small, investing a lot of their own time, and reinvesting any profits back into the business. They opened in late May to benefit from the heavy traffic during the summer tourist season. The winter months were slower, but when cold weather arrived, Anna and Danielle catered to the needs of winter walkers and cross-country skiers. Starting in late September,

TMP-1052.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1052.text: MODULE 3.5 Financial Capital LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 3.5.A Explain why businesses seek financial capital from outside sources 3.5.B Discuss potential sources for financial capital 3.5.C Describe the benefits and risks for providers of financial capital 3.5.D Evaluate a business’s pitch to potential lenders or investors

TMP-1053.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1053.text: On the show Shark Tank , contestants pitch products like Cup-a-Bug! in hopes that their business will receive financial capital from one of the investors on the celebrity panel. This module explains why businesses need a lot of money and how they get it (if they’re not a winner on Shark Tank , that is!).

TMP-1054.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1054.text: The Need for Financial Capital LG Why do businesses seek financial capital? When Justin Huang pitched his bug catcher to investors on a show called Shark Tank , he had one particular need. He already had a product called Cup-a-Bug! with the value proposition that users could easily catch a bug without killing it. He also had a business called Solid Factory that was in operation and selling his product. What he needed was money. He was working on his business’s financing , which is the process of acquiring money to start, operate, or expand a business. In the business world, the money or other assets used to pay for investments, operations, and growth is called financial capital. In this section, we dive deeper into the uses of financial capital and consider some of its sources. financing The process of acquiring money to start, operate, or expand a business.

TMP-1055.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1055.text: financial capital Money or other assets used to pay for investments, operations, and growth. Uses for Financial Capital Why does a business like Solid Factory need financial capital? We’ve learned that product development involves research, prototyping, testing, and manufacturing. The costs of those processes can be substantial. Operating a business also requires payments for utilities, materials, supplies, software, and staff. And the costs of rent, insurance, and taxes can be sizable. Financial capital is also needed for the replacement of fixed assets , which are assets such as vehicles, buildings, land, and equipment that are purchased for long-term use. Solid Factory’s fixed assets include 3D printers used to make prototypes, including an early version of the Cup-a-Bug! Fixed assets are replaced when they become worn or out of date, and those replacements are purchased with financial capital. fixed assets Assets such as vehicles, buildings, land, and equipment that are purchased for long-term use.

TMP-1056.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1056.navLabel: Bootstrapping: A Common Way to Start
TMP-1056.text: Most businesses seek growth, but increases in sales seldom happen on their own. To catch the attention of more potential customers and compel them to buy the product, large expenditures on marketing are typically needed. U.S. businesses spend over $300 billion annually on media advertising. Clearly, businesses find that devoting financial capital to marketing is a sensible, if not essential, way to increase sales volume. Businesses also face a challenge with the flow of cash in and out of their possession due to a timing problem: Many of the costs of running a business are monthly, like rent and wages, or unpredictable, like equipment replacement or repair. Numerous major costs come early in the life of the business, to create workspaces, develop products, hire employees, and attract customers. In contrast, the flow of sales revenue is gradual, uneven, and can be especially low for a new business. The availability of financial capital allows a business to bridge the gap between when money is needed and when sales revenue arrives. Next, we’ll consider the first of several sources of financial capital. Bootstrapping: A Common Way to Start When entrepreneurs start out, they often must rely on their own funds to finance their business endeavors. They are, as the saying goes, “pulling themselves up by their

headings.text: Bootstrapping: A Common Way to Start

TMP-1057.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1057.navLabel: Bootstrapping: A Common Way to Start
TMP-1057.text: bootstraps,” so this type of self-funding of a business by drawing on the founders’ own resources is called bootstrapping . Bootstrappers look to sources such as personal savings, personal bank loans, and personal credit cards to obtain financial capital for their business. bootstrapping Self-funding of a business by drawing on the founders’ own resources. Bootstrappers may turn to friends and family to supplement their personal funds. They may also turn to the crowd. Module 1.7 discussed crowdfunding, which is a source of financial capital that helps business projects get off the ground without turning to the traditional forms of external funding discussed later in this module. Entrepreneurs can post product ideas on crowdfunding websites such as GoFundMe and Kickstarter. Backers pledge financial capital in support, sometimes in exchange for rewards such as samples or discounts. Justin Huang raised $28,883 from 573 backers in a Kickstarter campaign for Cup-a-Bug! 1 That got his product going, but as Huang learned, the financial needs of successful businesses often outgrow the resources available from personal, family, and community sources.

TMP-1058.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1058.navLabel: Bootstrapping: A Common Way to Start
TMP-1058.text: Shutterstock AI/Shutterstock If you want to bring a better mousetrap to market, you will need both a good design and a source of financial capital. Many entrepreneurs use personal funds to get started.

TMP-1059.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1059.text: The Need for External Funding If all goes well, within a few years’ time, a business can hope for enough sales revenue to cover its needs for financial capital. In the meantime, the business must evaluate its situation and determine whether it is appropriate to seek external funding in the form of business loans or the sale of stocks or bonds. To do so, the entrepreneur should consider all of the potential costs of running the business. Suppose that, with inspiration from Cup-a-Bug!, you decide to launch a new product for humanely catching mice in a bowl that is called Bowl-a-Mouse. Table 3.5-1 provides an example of the costs that you might face. You then consider the

TMP-1061.text: sources of financial capital you can devote to this business project. Table 3.5-2 shows the funds you expect to have available. The price per unit is $50. Multiplying the price by the units sold, you expect to receive $50 × 200 = $10,000 in sales revenue per month in the first year, $50 × 400 = $20,000 per month in the second year, and $50 × 600 = $30,000 per month in the third year. In

TMP-1062.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1062.text: this simplified example, we will assume that there are no other expenses or revenues and that everything remains the same except the sales volume. Personal sources will fund the startup cost of $20,500, which leaves $219,000 − $20,500 = $198,500 to put toward monthly operating costs. In the first year, monthly revenues are $10,000 and monthly operating costs are $26,000, so $16,000 per month must come from elsewhere. For the first year, the 12 × $16,000 = $192,000 shortfall can come from the $198,500 in personal sources, leaving $6,500. In the second year, monthly revenues are $20,000 and monthly operating costs are $26,000, so the remaining personal funds will cover the $6,000 difference for only the first month, with $500 to spare. After that, the business will need external funding. In other words, the business has one year and one month to secure external funding from the types of sources discussed later in this module before it will run out of personal funds. In the third year, monthly revenues of $30,000 exceed monthly expenses of $26,000, so the company takes in $4,000 more in revenue than it needs for monthly expenses. At that point, the business can start recouping its prior investments, repaying any loans,

TMP-1063.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1063.text: and, after all costs are covered, earning profit. The transitional point is when the business is able to break even , which means its total revenue equals its total cost. This marks a celebrated occasion in the life of a business because, after losses are eliminated, profits can begin. break even When a business’s total revenue equals its total cost. The break-even point for any period is the number of units the company must sell to equate its total revenue and its total cost. The calculation of the break-even point takes into account the product’s price, fixed costs (those that don’t change when the level of production changes), and variable costs (those that do change when the level of production changes). Let’s calculate the break-even point for one month. Suppose the variable cost per unit is $18, which includes the costs of raw materials and hourly production workers. The fixed costs each month for things like rent, administrative salaries, insurance, and marketing add up to $16,640. Each Bowl-a-Mouse sells for a price of $50. The break-even point for a month is found as: Break-even point = Fixed costs / (Price − Variable cost per unit) = $16,640 / ($50 − $18) = 520.

TMP-1064.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1064.text: That means that the total cost equals the total revenue for that month after 520 units are sold. Starting with the 521st unit, the total revenue exceeds the total cost and the company earns profit. We’ve learned that a business needs financial capital from external sources if it does not have enough funds from personal sources to pay for startup costs and operating costs until the break-even point. Next, we’ll explore common external sources of financial capital.

TMP-1065.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1065.text: Sources of Financial Capital LG What are potential sources of financial capital? A business that needs external funding has two main options: obtain some form of loan, or exchange partial ownership of the business for money. In the business world, these methods are known as debt financing and equity financing. Most companies use a combination of both types of financing because each has unique advantages and disadvantages, as we’ll discuss in this section. Debt Financing Debt financing is the practice of borrowing funds with the intent to pay them back with interest to the lender. Banks are reluctant to lend to new businesses, whose ability to earn revenue and repay loans is unproven. For that reason, friends and family are common sources of loans for businesses in their early stages. After about two years, a

TMP-1066.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1066.text: business with a strong record of sales may seek a business bank loan. These loans are similar to personal loans, with scheduled repayments of a portion of the principal and interest on a regular basis, typically each month. And as with a personal loan, a larger loan or a higher interest rate increases the business’s cost of borrowing. debt financing The practice of borrowing funds with the intent to pay them back with interest to the lender.

TMP-1067.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1067.text: Photo: Rawpixel.com/Shutterstock Extended description for Capital Bank Text overlaid over the photo of the woman reads, Chart Your Course. We'll help you get there. A banner at the bottom of the screen reads: CAPITAL BANK: capital bank dot com. Member F D I C. Icons for Facebook and LinkedIn also appear. If a business owner’s personal funds are inadequate to fund operations until the business breaks even, external funds from debt or equity financing will be needed.

TMP-1068.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1068.text: Unlike equity financing, which we will turn to later in this module, debt financing entails no obligation to sell a portion of the company to secure capital. This means the owners have full control of the business. Another benefit to debt financing is that the relationship with the lender ends once the loan is paid back. Finally, the interest on the funds is considered a business expense, so it is tax deductible for the company — that is, the amount a company pays in interest on loans is subtracted from the profit on which taxes are paid. In contrast, dividends a company pays to its shareholders are not tax deductible. There are downsides to debt financing, too. As anyone who has been in debt knows, this method of financing depends on your ability to pay back the loan in the future — and when you’re running a business, things can go wrong. The economy or the market for your product could take a downturn, or your company could run into unforeseen difficulties, which limits its capacity to grow. This warrants careful consideration when choosing the right type of financing for your company.

TMP-1069.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1069.text: Bonds Many corporations, governments, and organizations such as colleges and churches sell bonds as a way to borrow money. A bond is a loan from an investor; the investor buys the bond from a borrower who issues (sells) the bond. When you buy a bond, you give the issuer money, and the bond is essentially an IOU to repay the money borrowed with interest. Bonds typically pay interest every six months. bond A loan from an investor; the investor buys the bond from a borrower who issues (sells) the bond. Each bond has a face value , which is the amount the borrower will pay the bondholder at the end of the loan, known as the maturity date . That is, unless the borrower runs into financial trouble and defaults , meaning that they cannot repay the loan. To give investors added inducement to make the purchase, bonds often sell for less than face value. It is also possible for a bond price to exceed face value because the interest rate paid on the bond is higher than the interest rate paid on competing investments, making it a particularly attractive option. The net return for an investor who holds a bond to maturity is the sum of the interest payments received and the gain or loss on the

TMP-1070.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1070.navLabel: Other Common Types of Business Loans
TMP-1070.text: difference between the purchase price and the face value of the bond (less any taxes and fees related to the investment). Once issued, bond prices tend to move in the opposite direction of interest rates on other investments. If interest rates rise, bonds become less appealing because money in, for example, interest-bearing CDs and savings accounts is earning more than before. This causes bond prices to fall until the gains from buying a bond are competitive with the gains from alternative investments. Bond price fluctuations pose risks for people who wish to sell their bonds before maturity, because the price might be relatively low when they want to make the sale. For bonds held until maturity, the risk is that the borrower defaults. Other Common Types of Business Loans Many other loan types are available to suit the varying needs of businesses. The interest rates of business loans depend on the length of the loan, the qualifications of the borrower, the type of loan, the lender, and the conditions in the market for loans. As with prices in other markets, more competition among lenders generally lowers the interest rate. Loans with higher risks tend to have higher interest rates. The most

headings.text: Other Common Types of Business Loans

TMP-1071.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1071.navLabel: Other Common Types of Business Loans
TMP-1071.text: common types of business loans are business term loans, lines of credit, business credit cards, and SBA loans. Business Term Loan A business term loan is a traditional bank loan to support the needs of a business. The business receives the loan amount up front. The business then repays that amount plus interest at a fixed interest rate, usually either monthly or quarterly. A short-term loan might only be for three months. Some long-term loans can extend to 25 years. Line of Credit A line of credit works similarly to a credit card: You can borrow a certain amount of money and only pay interest on the amount you have used, as long as you stay within your credit limit. Unlike a term loan, you don’t receive the money up front unless you choose to. You only use your line of credit when you need it, and if you don’t use it, you don’t have anything to pay back. A line of credit for a business is usually larger than what a credit card will allow, and the interest rate is typically more favorable. This is a popular choice for businesses, although it can be difficult for a new business to qualify.

TMP-1072.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1072.navLabel: Other Common Types of Business Loans
TMP-1072.text: Banks generally require a steady flow of income and a healthy credit history before they will approve the line of credit. Business Credit Cards Business credit cards are credit cards for business use rather than personal use. Younger businesses often use business credit cards as a short-term funding solution to acquire the capital needed to start and grow their business. It is often easier to qualify for a business credit card than for a business term loan or line of credit from a bank. SBA Loans The United States Small Business Administration (SBA) is a government agency established to assist small businesses with loans, counseling, and disaster relief. This agency offers SBA loans to small businesses that typically have lower interest rates than bank term loans. The SBA also provides financial capital to small business owners during difficult times. For example, during the COVID-19 pandemic, the SBA’s American Rescue Plan offered over $415 billion in emergency relief aid that impacted over 6 million small businesses.

TMP-1073.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1073.navLabel: Other Common Types of Business Loans
TMP-1073.text: Business loan payments must be made on time. Not doing so can lead to financial penalties and harm the credit reputation of the business, leading to decreased chances for loans in the future. This makes it especially important for business owners to understand their financial needs and when they can expect to break even. A business owner must also investigate the particular challenges in their industry, including the time it takes to obtain products, market them, and collect revenue from customers. Potential lenders will likewise study the situation carefully to assess the business’s ability to meet loan payment obligations. Later in this module, we’ll dive deeper into the risks and rewards of providing financial capital. Equity Financing Equity is the value of ownership. Equity financing is the method of acquiring financial capital through the sale of shares of ownership in a company in exchange for cash. Suppose you start a lawn care business, but you need money to purchase and repair your lawnmowing equipment. Instead of borrowing money from the bank, you decide to sell shares in your business, meaning that each person who buys a share becomes a part-owner in your lawn care business. If you were a corporation, that share of your business would be a share of stock , which represents partial ownership in a

TMP-1074.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1074.navLabel: Other Common Types of Business Loans
TMP-1074.text: company. Shares of stock can be sold in a stock exchange that is open to the public, such as the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), or privately, in a direct transaction between the buyer and the seller. By selling shares, you give up some of any future profit to investors. You also give up some control over business decisions, because the other owners will have some say. equity financing The method of acquiring financial capital through the sale of shares of ownership in a company in exchange for cash. stock A share of a business that represents partial ownership in a company. If your business earns profit, you and the other owners may decide to reinvest that profit in the business. An alternative is to divide that profit up among the owners as dividends , which are a company’s distributions of profits to its shareholders. It is common for dividends to be paid quarterly, meaning every three months. dividends A company’s distributions of profits to its shareholders.

TMP-1075.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1075.navLabel: Other Common Types of Business Loans
TMP-1075.text: Equity financing is a popular choice for startup companies that need financial capital to produce and sell their products and services and run the business. Equity financing comes from many different sources. If you sold shares of your lawn care business, you would probably start by appealing to friends and family as investors. Larger companies also make their shares available to the general public. For example, Scotts Miracle-Gro, which started out selling grass seed for lawns, is now a multinational corporation that has benefited from the public sale of shares currently worth over $3 billion. When you sell equity in your business, you are dividing control and profit in a way that can be compared with splitting a pie. When you are the only owner of the company, you own 100% of a small pie. When other people invest in the company to help start it or enhance growth, you give away some slices of the pie to those investors — but if all goes well, your pie becomes bigger. Although the company is no longer fully yours because you have given away equity in exchange for financial capital, your smaller slice of the bigger pie may be much larger than the original smaller pie you had without external financing. Kevin Plank started the sportswear company Under Armour with personal savings and credit card debt. Seeing the potential for growth beyond what he could finance with

TMP-1076.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1076.navLabel: Other Common Types of Business Loans
TMP-1076.text: bootstrapping, he sought other investors and eventually “went public” by selling shares of stock to the general public. Although his portion of the profit decreased when he shared the company’s ownership with thousands of investors, he became a billionaire because external funding allowed the company — and his share of the profit — to grow far larger than it would have been with bootstrapping alone.

TMP-1077.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1077.navLabel: Other Common Types of Business Loans
TMP-1077.text: Mike Kemp/Getty Images By selling stock to the public, Under Armour founder Kevin Plank shared the ownership of his company with many investors. The financial capital he raised that way allowed so much growth in the company that his remaining slice of ownership became more valuable than if he had owned all of the smaller company he could have financed himself. Table 3.5-3 lists some of the differences between debt and equity financing.

TMP-1078.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1078.navLabel: Other Common Types of Business Loans
TMP-1078.text: Table 3.5-3 Debt Versus Equity Financing Debt Financing Equity Financing How It Works The company borrows funds from lenders. A portion of ownership in the company is given to investors. Repayment Obligation The debt must be paid back to the lender. There is no obligation to repay the investor. Ownership and Control Lenders have no ownership in the business or say in how the business is run. Investors have voting rights and must be consulted on major business decisions. Ongoing Payments There is an obligation for the borrower to pay interest to the lender. Dividends are optional. Returns to Lenders/Investors Lenders are rewarded with interest payments for a designated period. If the business performs well, investors are rewarded with an increase in the value of their shares and possibly with dividends. Taxation Interest payments are tax deductible for the business. Dividend payments are not tax deductible for the business.

TMP-1079.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1079.navLabel: Other Common Types of Business Loans
TMP-1079.text: Benefits and Risks to Providers of Financial Capital LG What are the benefits and risks for providers of financial capital? The providers of financial capital make sacrifices in pursuit of rewards. They part with their money for some period of time, and they accept the risk of not getting it back. Even without the risk involved, it is a hardship to give up money until a later date. That money could otherwise be used to buy things today or earn interest in the bank. Beyond that, there’s no telling what could happen between now and when the money is eventually repaid. The provider’s health could deteriorate, limiting their ability to make use of the funds. Or, global events — wars, pandemics, natural disasters — could unfold, reducing the money’s value or usefulness. For these reasons, there is a time value of money , meaning that people prefer to have money now rather than in the future. Add to

TMP-1080.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1080.navLabel: Other Common Types of Business Loans
TMP-1080.text: that the possibility of the money not being returned due to business failure, and you have a whole lot of risks and sacrifices that justify compensation. Bloomberg/Getty Images Shareholders face the risk that their stocks will drop in value. For example, over a four-year period, the value of Big Lots! stock dropped from over $70 a share to less than 7 cents a share.

TMP-1081.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1081.text: What’s in It for Me? Immediately after providing equity financing, investors receive shares of stock, which are assets that can be resold. When an investor buys a share of a business’s stock, they become a shareholder in the business. Shareholders do not receive interest, but they may receive dividends if the business earns profit and decides to distribute it to shareholders rather than reinvesting it. Lenders also receive an asset immediately, because loans are assets. Many loans, including bonds, can be resold. Interest rates are generally higher for loans with higher risks. For example, junk bonds are bonds issued by companies with inferior credit ratings, meaning an inferior history of paying back loans. Junk bonds typically pay high interest rates due to the relatively high risk of default. In contrast, bonds sold by the U.S. Treasury to fund government activities pay some of the lowest interest rates, because the U.S. government almost never defaults on its payments. 2 The initial purchase of a bond or stock directly from the issuer occurs in a primary market . For example, the primary market for a stock is the initial public offering (IPO) , where investors buy shares of the stock directly from the issuing company. Secondary

TMP-1082.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1082.text: markets are where investors resell stocks, bonds, and other loans that have already been issued. For example, shares of stock can be resold in a stock market such as the New York Stock Exchange. A buyer of stock in the secondary market gains the partial ownership of the company that those shares represent. And the buyer of a corporate bond in the secondary market becomes the new lender to the business that issued the bond. secondary markets Markets in which investors resell stocks, bonds, and other loans that have already been issued. If the price of an investor’s stock goes up, the investor makes a capital gain , which is the profit earned from an asset that is sold for more than the purchase price. That gain is simply the difference between the purchase price and the sale price, so if you buy a share of stock for $100 and sell it for $110, your capital gain is $10. It’s also possible that the stock’s price will go down, in which case the investor experiences a loss. capital gain The profit earned from an asset that is sold for more than the purchase price.

TMP-1083.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1083.text: The prices of stocks and bonds go up and down depending on investor demand, business performance, and the PESTEL forces discussed in Module 1.3 . For instance, recent deregulation that lowered standards for carbon emissions raised stock prices for oil companies like Chevron and lowered stock prices for solar energy companies like SolarEdge. While both shareholders and lenders may make gains with sales in secondary markets, interest payments are the most reliable source of income for lenders, including bondholders. To assess and compare the gains from alternative investments, it is useful to calculate the annual rate of return , which is the total dollars gained (the income received plus any capital gain) divided by the price paid for the asset. Suppose you buy a share of stock at the beginning of the year for $100, receive $3 in dividends over the year, and sell the stock at the end of the year for $110. Your total dollars gained is ($110 − $100) + $3 = $13. Your annual rate of return is $13/$100 = 0.13. To express that as a percentage, we multiply by 100 to get 13 percent. rate of return The total dollars gained (the income received plus any capital gain) divided by the price paid for an asset.

TMP-1084.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1084.text: Risky Business The rate of return is not the only factor that most investors consider; another is the level of risk. Suppose two investments cost $100 today, but one has a certain value of $113 in one year and the other has a 50 percent chance of being worth $0 in one year and a 50 percent chance of being worth $226. The expected (average) outcome of each investment is $113, but the wide variety of possible outcomes creates risk for the second investment that doesn’t exist for the first. If you would prefer the first investment to the second, you care about risk. Lenders and investors take a risk when they provide financial capital to businesses. Lenders expect to be repaid with interest, which may not happen if a business struggles or shuts down. And when investors purchase shares of a company, the value of those shares — and any dividends shareholders might receive — depends on the company’s performance. If the company does poorly, the value of shares will go down. If the company goes out of business, the shares may become worthless. Module 3.4 explained that individuals and businesses have a variety of attitudes toward risk. Risk matters to most investors; what differs are the tradeoffs people are

TMP-1085.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1085.text: willing to make between the rate of return and the level of risk. The average rate of return on a bank account is typically lower than that for the stock market, but lots of people keep their money in the bank because they favor the very low risk of loss. Meanwhile, many investors put their money into stocks, because for them, the greater average rate of return is more important than the higher level of risk. These contrasting behaviors exhibit differing levels of risk tolerance (also discussed in Module 5.2 ), which is the amount of risk someone is willing or able to accept. Those with a higher risk tolerance are willing to accept a wider range of possible outcomes. risk tolerance The amount of risk someone is willing or able to accept. Investors have a low risk tolerance if they are uncomfortable with the prospect of losses. Perhaps those investors lack the financial resources to withstand bad outcomes, or they may want to use the returns soon, which leaves no time for underperforming investments to recover. Individual investors and institutional lenders (such as commercial banks) with a high risk tolerance may be willing to finance risky projects and unproven product ideas. In return, these investors and lenders generally expect a higher rate of return to compensate for the higher level of risk.

TMP-1086.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1086.text: Hiraman/Getty Images Even if you’re not on Shark Tank, it is often necessary for an entrepreneur or existing business owner to make a pitch to convince prospective lenders or investors that the business is worth funding.

TMP-1087.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1087.text: Pitching to Prospective Lenders or Investors LG What are the qualities of an effective business pitch? When it comes time for a business to seek lenders for debt financing or investors for equity funding, there is no simple spigot that turns on the flow of financial capital. Lenders and investors will want to examine a business plan , which outlines a business’s goals, value proposition, market research, marketing strategies, and financial projections. To help secure funding, that document should make a compelling case to support the specific funding request. The business plan must justify the anticipated rate of return and assure potential lenders and investors that the level of risk does not exceed expectations.

TMP-1088.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1088.text: business plan An outline of a business’s goals, value proposition, market research, marketing strategies, and financial projections. It is often necessary for the business owner to make a pitch to convince people with money that the business is a good place to put it. A pitch is a short, persuasive presentation that explains the elements of the business plan and clearly states the funding request the business is making. When considering requests for financial capital from established businesses, potential lenders and investors also study financial reports, industry data, and projections of future performance to estimate the value of the business. Such an economic valuation helps potential investors assess what a share of ownership is worth. Prospective lenders use that information to evaluate whether the business is in a good position to repay loans. pitch A short, persuasive presentation that explains the elements of the business plan and clearly states the funding request the business is making. Investors and lenders are drawn to products that convincingly offer relatively high financial returns and relatively low risks. Prospects for high returns and low risks improve when the business’s good or service fits the needs of the market well. For that

TMP-1089.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1089.text: reason, a good business pitch will emphasize the product-market fit discussed in Module 2.4 . Essentially, you’ll want to explain why your product is the solution consumers have been looking for to solve their problems or satisfy their interests. Claims of high returns and low risks are more credible when financial projections are based on solid evidence and reliable estimates. A business should rely on the best data available and make predictions using information and methods that are commonly used in that industry. For a lawn care business that is projecting future sales, estimates can be based on recent sales by similar lawn care businesses in similar cities, trends in the lawn care market, the size and demographics of the local market, the existing competition, and market research that includes surveys of potential customers. Empty assertions based on limited analysis are uncompelling — talk is cheap. It is important to craft a pitch with attention to the goals of potential lenders and investors. Consider the business’s mission and value proposition through the eyes of the funders. If key funders are all about helping older adults, emphasize how your lawn care company helps older adults. If key funders are concerned about environmental harm, emphasize the environmental benefits of your service.

TMP-1090.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1090.text: It is also wise to tout the qualifications of the leadership team and workers. Have the leaders led businesses successfully before? Do they bring enriching insights from experiences in related industries? Do the workers have special skills or remarkable performance records? An impressive team raises expectations of returns and lowers perceptions of risk. In the case study for this module, we’ll learn how a company found the funding needed to grow its business and help farmers grow their crops.

TMP-1091.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1091.text: Module 3.5 Review Learning Goals LG Why do businesses seek financial capital? • Financing is the process of acquiring money to start, operate, or expand a business. • Financial capital is money or other assets used to pay for investments, operations, and growth. Financial capital is needed for product development, operating costs, and the replacement of fixed assets , which are assets such as vehicles, buildings, land, and equipment that are purchased for long-term use. • Entrepreneurs are bootstrapping when they self-fund their business by drawing on their own resources. • A business reaches a break-even point when their total revenue equals their total cost. A business needs financial capital from external sources if it does not have

TMP-1092.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1092.text: enough funds from personal sources to pay for startup costs and operating costs until the break-even point. LG What are potential sources of financial capital? • Debt financing is the practice of borrowing funds with the intent to pay them back with interest to the lender. • A bond is a loan from an investor who buys the bond to a borrower who issues (sells) the bond. • Other common types of business loans include business term loans (traditional bank loans), lines of credit, business credit cards, and SBA loans. • Equity financing is the method of acquiring financial capital through the sale of shares of ownership in a company in exchange for cash. • Stock represents partial ownership in a company. By selling shares of stock, an entrepreneur gives up some of any future profit to investors. They also give up some control over business decisions, because the other owners will have some say.

TMP-1093.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1093.text: • If a business with shared ownership earns profit, the owners may decide to reinvest that profit in the business or divide it up among the owners as dividends , which are a company’s distributions of profits to its shareholders. LG What are the benefits and risks for providers of financial capital? • The providers of financial capital must be rewarded for parting with their money for some period of time and accepting the risk of not getting it back. Immediately after providing equity financing, investors receive shares of stock which are assets that can be resold. While gains may be made in secondary markets,

TMP-1094.text: interest payments are the most reliable compensation for lenders including bondholders and providers of business term loans. • To assess and compare the gains from alternative investments, it is useful to calculate the annual rate of return , which is the total dollars gained (the income received plus any capital gain) divided by the price paid for the asset. • Lenders and investors also consider the level of risk. Risk tolerance is the amount of financial risk someone is willing or able to accept. It takes individual investors and institutional lenders with a high risk tolerance to finance risky projects and unproven product ideas. In return, these investors and lenders generally expect a higher rate of return to compensate for the higher level of risk. LG What are the qualities of an effective business pitch? • When a business seeks lenders for debt financing or investors for equity funding, potential funders will want to examine a business plan , which outlines a business’s goals, value proposition, market research, marketing strategies, and financial projections.

TMP-1095.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1095.text: • It is often necessary for a business owner to make a pitch to convince funders to provide financial capital to the business. A pitch is a short, persuasive presentation that explains the elements of the business plan and clearly states the funding request the business is making. • When considering requests for financial capital from established businesses, potential lenders and investors also study financial reports and data about the industry to estimate the value of the business. TMP-1096.text: month. If there are no other costs, after how many lessons in a month does Sal’s break even? a. 200 b. 300 c. 600 d. 3,000 2. Good advice for a business pitch includes a. don’t include elements that overlap with the business plan. b. the longer the pitch lasts, the better. c. omit references to funders’ investment goals. d. emphasize solid evidence of high returns and low risks.

TMP-1098.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1098.text: CASE STUDY AgBiome ROMEO GACAD/Getty Images Fungicides can protect crops from disease. The benefits are large, but so are the costs: There can be substantial health and environmental effects, and it takes a lot of financial capital to develop such products. Agriculture is a $5 trillion global industry forecasted to substantially increase as the world’s population expands. By 2050, the agriculture industry must increase

TMP-1099.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1099.text: production enough to feed a projected 9.7 billion people. Growth and innovation are essential for the agriculture sector to meet this demand. Investors are taking notice of opportunities to improve agricultural productivity and are pumping billions of dollars into new agricultural technology companies. These startups focus on solutions that improve crop yields, increase efficiency, drive profitability, and, as a result, contribute to food security throughout the world. However, between 20% and 40% of crops around the world are lost to pests every year. The United Nations estimates that plant diseases account for $220 billion in economic costs annually, and invasive insects cost around $70 billion. AgBiome, a private agricultural biotechnology company based in North Carolina, develops products to address the threat of insects and disease to the global food supply. The company creates products aimed at increasing the size of crops. AgBiome’s team of scientists identifies microbiomes — the community of fungi, bacteria, and viruses living in or on a plant — that help keep the plant healthy and resistant to disease. AgBiome aims to create a suite of biological treatments that replace synthetic chemicals, leave no toxic residue on food, and reduce the number of crops lost to disease each year. For example, its Howler and Theia fungicide

TMP-1100.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1100.text: products target diseases like powdery mildew that devastate high-value fruit and vegetable crops. The company was founded in 2012, but it did not launch its first commercial fungicide product until 2020. Support from outside investors contributed to the success AgBiome achieved with its first commercial products. In its early days, AgBiome secured $17.5 million in financing from funders that included venture capitalists , meaning professional investors who pool money from their partners and help to fund young companies in exchange for a share of ownership. Two years later, the company secured its second round of financing — $34.5 million — that included grants (essentially gifts of money that need not be repaid) from organizations like the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and venture capital from a variety of organizations. When the company secured another $65 million in financing in 2018, and an additional $116 million in 2021 from new and existing investors, the chair of the AgBiome board announced, “[T]his significant fundraising will allow AgBiome to rapidly accelerate its mission to feed the world responsibly by both discovering and developing its own products as well as by identifying strategic acquisition growth opportunities.” As an example of new

TMP-1101.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1101.text: product development, following the popularity of AgBiome's Howler fungicide product, the company expanded into insecticides and herbicides in 2025. AgBiome also used its financial capital to hire more employees and continue building partnerships throughout the world. For instance, AgBiome's grant from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation enabled the company to help farmers in sub- Saharan Africa. AgBiome identified microorganisms that protect corn, sorghum, banana, and yam crops there from disease and insects. That partnership and others helped AgBiome create pest control solutions to increase crops in Africa and around the world. AgBiome was not a company with publicly traded stock. With the funding it had, the company ran into financial difficulties during the COVID-19 pandemic, when investors' appetite for funding and IPOs was weak. In 2024, AgBiome sold its Howler and Theia products to Certis Biologicals. In the same year, many of AgBiome's other assets were acquired by Ginkgo Bioworks, a publicly traded company that seeks biological solutions to problems in agriculture and other areas. The future of AgBiome as part of a larger company is unclear. As one industry expert put it, "The biological inputs pioneer has been sold for parts after failing to

TMP-1102.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1102.text: raise further capital."a Seeing how a lack of funds can rip a company apart highlights the importance of the fundraising strategies discussed in this module. APPLY YOUR AP@ SKILLS 1. AgBiome's funders also include grant providers. How do you suppose those people are rewarded for their contributions? 5. As AgBiome became financially unstable, would you have advised them to offer shares of stock to the general public if they were able to? Explain a pro and a con of that decision.
