TMP-1105.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1105.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1105.text: The Anatomy of an Income Statement LG What are the elements of a business income statement? You can't judge a business by its storefront. When it's time for a company's leaders, investors, creditors, or competitors to assess the financial health of a business, they study key financial statements. These include the balance sheet and the cash flow statement, as discussed in the next two modules, as well as the income statement. An income statement, or statement of profit and loss, summarizes a business's revenues and costs and the resulting net profit or loss over some period — typically a month, quarter, or year. To provide a breakdown of several types of profit, income statements organize information on revenue, cost of goods sold, and operating expenses, and account for interest, taxes, and nonrecurring expenses as well. Many income statements provide data for several previous periods to allow comparisons and reveal trends. In this section, we'll examine each of the typical components of an income statement.

headings.text: The Anatomy of an Income Statement

TMP-1106.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1106.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1106.text: income statement A financial statement that summarizes a business's revenues and costs and the resulting net profit or loss over a period of time. (Also known as a statement of profit and loss.) Gross Profit Measuring a business's profit is an exercise of comparing revenues and costs. An income statement breaks down these numbers as shown in Table 3.6-1. (In this table, a negative sign in parentheses indicates that the value is a cost that is subtracted from other values in the calculation of profit.) The starting point is revenue, which is the income from the business's core activities — typically sales of goods or services. Module 3.4 explained that a firm's cost of goods sold (COGS) is the total cost of producing its goods, including the cost of production-related wages, materials, supplies, and facilities. Gross profit is the profit earned after subtracting COGS from total revenue: Gross profit = Total revenue − Cost of goods sold gross profit The profit earned after subtracting COGS from total revenue (Gross profit = Total revenue − Cost of goods sold).

TMP-1107.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1107.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1107.text: In the example in Table 3.6-1, the $6,000 gross profit is found by subtracting the $4,000 cost of goods sold from the $10,000 revenue. Gross profit is just one of several types of profit. Since it does not account for several types of expenses incurred by a business, it is not what people are generally referring to when they say "profit." Table 3.6-1 Income Statement Revenue $ 10,000 (−) Cost of Goods Sold 4,000 Gross Profit 6,000 Operating Expenses (−) General and Administrative 2,000 (−) Selling 1,250 (−) Research and Development 500 Operating Profit 2,250 (−) Interest Expense 100 Pre-Tax Income 2,150 (−) Taxes 450

TMP-1108.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1108.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1108.text: Net profit $ 1,700 Operating Profit Recall that operating expenses are the costs of running a business apart from the cost of goods sold. These expenses include general and administrative expenses, selling expenses, and research and development. General and administrative expenses are the costs of maintaining daily operations, such as salaries for office workers, rent on office space, and insurance. Selling expenses are the costs of marketing, sales, and delivery of goods or services. Examples include the costs of salespeople's salaries, advertising, and shipping costs. Operating expenses are generally considered indirect costs because they are not tied to the production of a particular good or service. general and administrative expenses The costs of maintaining daily operations, such as salaries for office workers, rent on office space, and insurance. selling expenses The costs of marketing, sales, and delivery of goods or services.

TMP-1109.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1109.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1109.text: Operating profit is the business's net income before accounting for interest and tax payments. Operating profit is found by subtracting operating expenses from gross profit: Operating profit = Gross profit − Operating expenses operating profit The business's net income before accounting for interest and tax payments (Operating profit = Gross profit − Operating expenses). In Table 3.6-1, the operating profit of $2,250 is found by subtracting the $3,750 in operating expenses from the $6,000 gross profit. Pre-Tax Income It is common for businesses to obtain financial capital by borrowing money. As discussed in Module 3.5, this can include loans from commercial banks and the sale of bonds. All of these loans come with an interest expense, which is the cost of borrowing money and which must be paid to lenders. The interest expense is subtracted from

TMP-1110.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1110.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1110.text: operating profit to determine whether the business must pay income taxes, which depends on the level of pre-tax income. interest expense The cost of borrowing money. Pre-tax income is a business's income after subtracting COGS, operating expenses, and the interest expense. In the income statement, the starting point for calculating pre- tax income is operating profit (which already has COGS and operating expenses subtracted), so the formula is: Pre-tax income = Operating profit − Interest expense pre-tax income A business's income after subtracting COGS, operating expenses, and the interest expense (Pre-tax income = Operating profit − Interest expense). If pre-tax income is positive, the business must pay income tax. If the pre-tax income is zero or negative, the business has no income tax obligation. In Table 3.6-1, the pre-tax

TMP-1111.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1111.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1111.text: income is $2,250 − $100 = $2,150, which is greater than zero, so this business has some taxes to pay. Net Profit The "bottom line" in an income statement — literally, the final dollar amount at the bottom — is the net profit or income after taxes, which is the profit (or income) the business earned over the given period after deducting all costs. To calculate net profit in the income statement, the starting point is pre-tax income, so the only expense left to subtract is taxes. The formula is: Net profit = Pre-tax income − Taxes net profit The profit (or income) a business earned over a given period after deducting all costs (Net profit = Pre-tax income − Taxes). (Also known as income after taxes.) In Table 3.6-1, the net profit is $2,150 − $450 = $1,700. This is the actual earnings available for distribution to the business's owners. Next we'll learn how information in the income statement is useful to internal and external stakeholders.

TMP-1112.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1112.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement

TMP-1113.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1113.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1113.text: Financial Performance and the Income Statement LG How is an income statement used to assess a business's financial performance? The information in an income statement aids internal stakeholders in making management decisions and external stakeholders in making decisions about investments, loans, tax assessments, and supplier relationships. By comparing revenues, costs, and profits over time, stakeholders can spot trends and improve strategies for future profitability. Beyond using numbers directly from the income statement, observers are informed by several ratios or margins that compare profit to revenue and that can be calculated using data from the income statement. In this section, we examine the gross profit margin, the operating profit margin, and the net profit margin.

TMP-1114.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1114.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1114.text: Gross Profit Margin Stakeholders appreciate a number that indicates the business's success in setting pricing and managing direct costs. The gross profit margin is the ratio of gross profit to total revenue. The ratio is multiplied by 100 to express it as a percentage, so the formula is: Gross profit margin gross profit margin Gross profit x 100 Total revenue The ratio of gross profit to total revenue. The ratio is multiplied by 100 to express it as a percentage (Gross profit margin Gross profit x 100). Total revenue For the firm discussed above, this is ($6,000/$10,000) x 100 .60 x 100 60%. This means that 60% of the business's revenue remains after paying for COGS. Put another way, for each dollar of revenue, the gross profit is 60 cents.

TMP-1115.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1115.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1115.text: Higher values for the gross profit margin are better than lower ones. Let's think through what a high value for this margin tells us. Gross profit is total revenue minus the cost of goods sold, so a high value for gross profit indicates that the business is successfully charging a price (the source of revenue) well above its cost per unit of making the good. That price-cost gap can be achieved with strategies that command high prices, effective cost management, or both. The gross profit margin is the ratio of gross profit to total revenue, so a high value for this margin means that the excess of price over the cost per unit is a large percentage of the price. That excess provides more money to cover indirect costs, interest expenses, and tax expenses, and for profit. The gross profit margin can be used to compare one company's performance at several points in time, or to compare several companies within an industry. The value of a good gross profit margin depends on the industry. For example, the average gross profit margins range from slightly less than 20% in engineering and construction to over 85% in banking. Businesses that prioritize sales volume over high prices or operate in competitive markets tend to have a relatively low gross profit margin. A sizable gross profit margin shows that the company has sufficient funds for sales, marketing, product development, and other operating expenses.

TMP-1116.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1116.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1116.text: Operating Profit Margin The second margin that stakeholders find useful is the operating_profit margin, which is the ratio of operating profit to total revenue (again, multiplied by 100 to express it as a percentage). The formula is: Operating profit margin operating profit margin Operating profit x 100 Total revenue The ratio of operating profit to total revenue. The ratio is multiplied by 100 to express it as a percentage (Operating profit margin Operating profit x 100). Total revenue For the firm discussed above, this is ($2,250/$10,000) x 100 .225 x 100 22.5%. This means that 22.5% of the business's revenue remains after paying for COGS and operating expenses. In other words, the operating profit per dollar of revenue is 22.5 cents.

TMP-1117.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1117.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1117.text: The operating profit margin is used to assess how well a business is marketing and selling its product and keeping operating expenses in check. The operating profit rises when the business administers activities successfully by commanding higher prices, incurring lower COGS and operating expenses, or both. A relatively high value for the operating profit margin shows that a business's excess of revenue over COGS and operating expenses is a relatively large percentage of revenue. That excess of revenue over these costs provides funds for interest expenses, taxes, and profit. Operating profit margins vary by industry, but are often in the range of 10% to 20%. Net Profit Margin The third margin item is the net profit margin, which is the ratio of net profit to total revenue (multiplied by 100 to obtain a percentage). The formula is: Net profit margin Net profit x 100 Total revenue

TMP-1118.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1118.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1118.text: net profit margin The ratio of net profit to total revenue. The ratio is multiplied by 100 to express it as a percentage Net profit (Net profit margin x 100). Total revenue For the firm discussed above, this is ($1,700/$10,000) x 100 .17 x 100 17%. so 17% of the business's revenue — 17 cents per dollar of revenue received — is net profit. This margin indicates the percentage of revenue that is left after all expenses have been subtracted, including interest and taxes. This is used to evaluate a business's overall profitability. If this number is relatively large, the business retains a healthy portion of revenue that can be distributed to owners as income. The value of a good net profit margin depends on the industry, but a general guideline is to aim for between 5% and 20%. As with the other margins, the net profit margin can be compared to benchmarks such as the company's previous margins, the margins of other companies in the industry, or projections of these margins made in planning stages. Stakeholders are interested in whether the company's financial performance has matched that of rivals and met expectations.

TMP-1119.navLabel: The Anatomy of an Income Statement
TMP-1119.text: Figure 3.6-1 shows the gross profit margin, operating profit margin, and net profit margin for Apple Inc. over time. When these numbers change, it is useful to examine the rate of change. We’ll learn how to do that next.

TMP-1123.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1123.text: Calculating Rates of Change Whether you're wondering about the change in your monthly sales, your net profit margin, or your softball batting average, the percentage change equation will determine any data point's rate of change from one period to another. The formula for the percentage change is: Current value — Initial value Percentage change x 100 Initial value percentage change equation A formula to determine any data point's rate of change from one period to another Current value — Initial value (Percentage change x 100). Initial value Business stakeholders use this formula to study trends in numbers found in the income statement and in the margins derived from those numbers. For example, by studying the rate of change between net profit margins over time, business leaders can analyze trends in profitability and financial health. Suppose a business had a net profit

TMP-1124.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1124.text: margin of 12% in Year 1 that increased to 15% in the current year, Year 2. It could plug these numbers into the percentage change equation to find: — 12% Percentage change x 100 12% 3% x 100 12% 25% This business's net profit margin increased by 25% between Year 1 and Year 2. This is a desirable change, suggesting improved profitability due to better pricing strategies, increased sales, or lower costs. Likewise, the rates of change in revenue, costs, net income, or other margins are useful for the analysis of a business's financial performance over time. EXAM TIP The percentage change equation is applicable to any number that changes over time. A good way to remember the formula is to think, "new minus old over old," with "new" meaning the current value and "old" meaning the initial value.

TMP-1125.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1125.text: Future Income and Expenses LG Why do consumers and businesses project future revenues and costs? Careful planning, and a dash of luck, are indispensable ingredients in the recipe for future success. A thoughtful projection of what lies ahead also informs key decisions about actions now that affect outcomes later. Businesses, like individuals, make investments and determine budgets now that set the stage for future prosperity or failure. In this section, we examine the uncertainties that cloud the future and the projected income statements and budgets that shed light on the way forward.

TMP-1126.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1126.text: Changing lifestyles and social trends are sources of uncertainty as businesses try to anticipate the future demand for their products.

TMP-1127.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1127.text: Sources of Uncertainty A lot can go right, or wrong, in this ever-changing world. The political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal factors considered in PESTEL analysis (introduced in Module 1.3) can present unexpected complications. Overnight, a new trade agreement can lower the cost of importing goods and materials from other countries, or a new tariff can tax those imports. The ups and downs of the economy create uncertainties about incomes, consumption patterns, and the availability of workers. Social trends driven by aging populations, influential media stars, or changing lifestyles can alter the needs and wants of consumers. Supply chains improve with modern technology and falter due to wars, natural disasters, strikes, and other disruptions in transportation systems. Weather events such as freezes, floods, and heat waves affect the cost of agricultural goods, while environmental regulations affect the cost of production. And changes in policies on immigration, worker safety, wages and benefits, and patents are among the legal factors that can alter the business landscape. Consider an automaker planning product offerings for the next decade. The company must decide whether to invest in new electric vehicle (EV) models. It can study EV sales over recent years to understand the latest trends, yet many uncertainties remain. Changes in laws governing the average level of emissions from an automaker's cars

TMP-1128.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1128.text: could make EVs much needed, or not needed at all, to replace cars that do have emissions. New tariffs could make it more expensive to import parts from overseas. Decreases in the availability of lithium for batteries could raise the cost of producing an electric car. Improvements in manufacturing robotics could lower the production costs of EVs. And rival companies may or may not introduce new EVs that compete with the automaker's offerings. Consumers face similar uncertainties. Changes in income, health, relationships, prices, and tax policies are among the factors that help or hinder an individual's pursuit of financial goals. Given the many uncertainties, it is wise for businesses and individuals to contemplate the possibilities and plan ahead. Reasons for Projected Income Statements Despite the many unknowns, a business can use trends, announced changes, and estimates to project its revenues, costs, and income for future periods. It may be hard to predict a storm or a recession far in advance, but changes such as the rising number of high school graduates and the growing number of older consumers are no surprise. Changes in tax laws, environmental regulations, and trade agreements are often

TMP-1129.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1129.text: announced well in advance. And many numbers can be estimated based on past values and trends. Left: wera Rodsawang/Getty Images; right: Viktor Cvetkovic/Getty Images Extended description for Population Trends In the first photo, three very young girls walk down the hallway of a preschool. In the second photo, several men and women cheer for a seated man holding a cake. A sign in the background reads, Happy Retirement. Every year, a new group of toddlers begins preschool, and a cohort of older workers retires. Following population trends can help businesses estimate future needs and plan ahead.

TMP-1130.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1130.text: After putting together all available information, a business can create a projected income statement that forecasts revenues, expenses, and profits for some future period. Creating a projected income statement forces a business to think ahead and try to anticipate needs for staffing, funding, and products to meet upcoming demands. With an understanding of future needs, the business can also make better decisions about current spending. It can set aside enough cash to cover current obligations and then use the projections to determine whether extra cash is available for discretionary spending, or every remaining dollar should be saved to fill upcoming gaps between revenue and expenses. projected income statement A financial statement that forecasts revenues, expenses, and profits for some future period. Budgets for Consumer Spending Like businesses, consumers benefit from planning for future income and expenses. A budget is a plan for how to allocate available income across expenses and savings over some period, typically a month or year. The starting point is expected net pay, which is the consumer's expected income minus taxes. (In some cases, an individual will also

TMP-1131.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1131.text: have money available from other sources, such as a parent, savings, or investments, but we will assume the money comes from a paycheck.) budget A plan for how to allocate available income across expenses and savings over a period of time. Suppose the manager of a fast-food restaurant earns $3,000 per month after deducting income taxes from her pay. The manager's compensation package also includes health insurance. Table 3.6-2 provides an example of a possible budget for this manager. The payments for rent, internet, insurance, and debt payments are fixed expenses that must be paid each month. Expenditures on groceries, local transportation, utilities, travel, entertainment, and personal and miscellaneous are variable, depending on events that arise and decisions that are made each month. The remainder of this manager's budget goes for retirement savings, investments, and an emergency fund to cover unexpected expenses. Table 3.6-2 Monthly Budget for a Fast-Food Manager Category Budgeted Amount ($) Net Income (after taxes) 3,000

TMP-1133.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1133.text: Emergency Fund (repairs, health) 100 Writing out a budget like this helps consumers study their financial situation and ensure that obligations are met and needs are satisfied before money is spent on lower priorities. Before preparing a budget, a consumer might think that a splurge on extra clothing, travel, or restaurant meals is affordable. A carefully prepared budget reveals what can and cannot be spent on luxuries without dipping into money needed for necessities and higher priorities, such as paying off debt, saving for the future, and donating to charities that do important work. By noting actual expenditures on budget items at the end of each period, a consumer can track spending patterns and identify areas of expenditure that do not align with the consumer's goals. We'll dig deeper into budgeting and personal finance in Unit 5.

TMP-1134.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1134.text: Developing an Income Statement or a Projected Income Statement How are income statements and projected income statements developed? Businesses develop income statements using data collected on each financial transaction. To create a projected income statement, the business must predict future revenues and expenses and estimate future taxes. In this section, we will consider where the information for an income statement comes from and walk through how such a statement might be projected for a fictional company called Macky's Cheese Company. Tracking Current Financial Data Information for an income statement like the one in Table 3.6-1 is assembled by tracking data on a business's revenues, expenses, and taxes over the period being

TMP-1135.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1135.text: studied. Accounting software like QuickBooks and Xero, and enterprise resource planning (ERP) software such as NetSuite and Dynamics 365, assist many businesses in tracking every financial transaction and categorizing it into the appropriate account for use on the income statement. Revenue tracking involves collecting data from sales invoices, point-of-sale (checkout) systems in stores, online sales platforms such as Stripe, and recurring billing systems that charge customers for ongoing services or subscriptions. Expenses are tracked by capturing data from vendor bills and receipts, credit card and bank payments, and payroll systems for salary and wage data. Each type of spending is sorted into its expense category, such as general and administrative or selling, for use in the income statement. Income tax liabilities are tracked so that the business can deduct that tax expense from pre-tax income to determine net income. Sales taxes are tracked as a liability to the government, but rather than being considered a part of revenue or expenses on the income statement, they are simply passed on to the government. Other types of taxes, such as payroll taxes and taxes on purchases, are typically included in the expense category for that item. For example, the employer's portion of payroll taxes for sales

TMP-1136.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1136.text: staff is a selling expense. At the end of each accounting period (such as a month or quarter), the business will estimate its income tax liability on the basis of its income and the relevant tax laws. Adjustments are made after the business's tax return is filed to reconcile any differences between the estimates and the actual tax liability. With these methods of tracking current financial data, the business completes its income statement and gleans the information it provides. Next, we will examine how a business can look into the future and try to predict the financial outcomes of the coming year. Projecting Future Revenues and Expenses Suppose Macky's Cheese Company (MCC) wants to gain foresight into the revenues, costs, and profit it may have ahead by developing a projected income statement. While acknowledging that the future holds many unknowns, the company can use its past data, known trends, estimates, and any available information on upcoming changes to predict next year's values as accurately as possible.

TMP-1137.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1137.text: To estimate future revenues, MCC can consider its current revenues, planned pricing strategies, and market research on industry trends in costs and customer demand. Next year, the company plans to charge a wholesale price of $10 per pound of its premium gouda cheese. Factoring in its sales of 473,992 pounds last year and market research indicating that consumers plan to buy about 5% more cheese next year than last year, MCC predicts sales of 500,000 pounds of cheese next year. The company's projected revenue is therefore $10 x 500,000 — $5,000,000. MCC's production processes and costs of supply chain components are not expected to change between this year and next year, so MCC will base its estimate of the cost of goods sold on past experience. MCC's most recent gross profit margin was 60%, which indicates that 60% of revenue remained after paying for the cost of goods sold. This margin also tells us that 40% of revenue was used to cover COGS. With the expectation that its gross profit margin will remain the same next year, MCC can estimate its future cost of goods sold by multiplying its projected revenue by 40% (which is equivalent to 0.40): x 0.40 = Subtracting the in estimated COGS from the $5,000,000 in projected revenue leaves a gross profit of $3,000,000.

For example, the $900,000 in general and administrative expenses includes planned salaries for office workers and estimated occupancy expenses (rent, property taxes, utilities, insurance). The $300,000 in selling expenses includes projected salaries for sales staff and budgets for marketing. And MCC plans to spend $200,000 on research and development in the coming year. From its projected income statement, Macky's Cheese Company can anticipate profit in the coming year. The profit margin of 60%, the operating profit margin of 32%, and the net profit margin of 22.5% all show strong financial health. TMP-1141.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1141.text: Module 3.6 Review Learning Goals What are the elements of a business income statement? • An income statement, or statement of profit and loss, summarizes a business's revenues and costs and the resulting net profit or loss over some period, typically a month, quarter, or year. • Gross profit is the profit earned after subtracting COGS (cost of goods sold) from total revenue. Operating profit is the business's net income before accounting for interest and tax payments. Operating profit is found by subtracting operating expenses from gross profit. Operating expenses include research and development, general and administrative expenses (the costs of maintaining daily operations), and selling expenses (the costs of marketing, sales, and delivery of goods and

TMP-1142.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1142.text: services). Pre-tax income is a business's income after subtracting COGS, operating expenses, and the interest expense (the cost of borrowing money) from gross profit. The "bottom line" in an income statement is the net profit or income after taxes, which is the profit (or income) the business earned over the given period after deducting all costs. How is an income statement used to assess a business's financial performance? • The gross profit margin is the ratio of gross profit to total revenue. The ratio is multiplied by 100 to express it as a percentage. The gross profit margin indicates the portion of each dollar of revenue that remains after covering the cost of goods sold. This margin can be used to compare one company's performance in different periods, or to compare several companies within an industry. • The operating profit margin is the ratio of operating profit to total revenue (again, multiplied by 100 to express it as a percentage). A relatively high value for the operating profit margin indicates that a business's excess of revenue over COGS and operating expenses is a relatively large percentage of revenue.

TMP-1143.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1143.text: • The net profit margin is the ratio of net profit to total revenue (multiplied by 100). This margin indicates the portion of each dollar of revenue that is net profit that can be distributed to owners as income. • The percentage change equation will determine any data point's rate of change from one period to another. Why do consumers and businesses project future revenues and costs? • Sources of uncertainty for a business include the possibility of changes in any of the factors considered in PESTEL analysis. A projected income statement forecasts a business's revenues, expenses, and profits for some future period. • A budget is a plan for how to allocate available income across expenses and savings over some period, typically a month or year. Writing out a budget helps consumers study their financial situation and ensure that obligations are met and needs are satisfied before money is spent on lower priorities.

TMP-1144.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1144.text: How are income statements and projected income statements developed? • Businesses develop income statements using data collected on each financial transaction. To create a projected income statement, the business must predict future revenues and expenses and estimate future taxes. • Information for an income statement is assembled by tracking data on a business's revenues, expenses, and taxes over the period being studied. Each type of spending is sorted into its expense category for use in the income statement. • Income tax liabilities are tracked so that the business can deduct that tax expense from pre-tax income to determine net income. At the end of each accounting period, the business will estimate its income tax liability based on its income and the relevant tax laws. Adjustments are made after the business's tax return is filed to reconcile any differences between the estimates and the actual tax liability. • For projected income statements, companies use past data, known trends, estimates, and any available information on upcoming changes to predict values as accurately as possible. To estimate future revenues, a company can consider its

TMP-1157.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1157.navLabel: The Anatomy of a Balance Sheet
TMP-1157.text: The Anatomy of a Balance Sheet LG What are the components of a business's balance sheet? An income statement provides a good summary of revenue, expenditures, and profit over some period, but that does not tell the whole story. A careful assessment of a business's financial situation requires information, for example, about whether the company has enough cash to pay its bills and whether it is deep in debt. A balance sheet is a financial statement that shows a business's assets, liabilities, and owners' equity at a particular point in time. Stakeholders study the balance sheet for a snapshot of what the business owns (its assets), what is owes (its liabilities), and its net worth — its assets minus its liabilities. This section explains the components of a business's balance sheet. balance sheet A financial statement that shows a business's assets, liabilities, and owners' equity at a particular point in time.

headings.text: The Anatomy of a Balance Sheet

TMP-1158.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1158.text: net worth The difference between assets and liabilities (for any organization or individual). The net worth of a business is also called owners' equity. The Balance Sheet Equation Balance may be good for diets and investment portfolios, but when it comes to a business's assets and liabilities, imbalance can be much better than balance — or much worse. As we've just learned, the imbalance between what is owned and what is owed is net worth, which is something all individuals and organizations have. The net worth of a business — the difference between its assets and its liabilities — has its own special name: owners' equity. This represents the net value of the business that belongs to the owners. A business with balanced assets and liabilities has an owners' equity of zero, because the value of what it owns is just enough to cover what it owes. An imbalance of assets over liabilities — meaning a positive owners' equity — is desirable, because it means the business can cover its liabilities and still have value left over. And an imbalance caused by liabilities that exceed assets, which makes owners' equity negative, is a red flag for potential creditors and investors because it means the business is unable to cover its debts.

TMP-1159.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1159.text: owners' equity The difference between a business's assets and its liabilities, also known as its net worth. The "balance" in the balance sheet's title refers to the balance between a business's assets and the sum of its liabilities and owners' equity. We can examine this relationship with the balance sheet equation (also known as the fundamental accounting equation): balance sheet equation An equation showing the relationship between a business's assets and the combined total of its liabilities and owners' equity (Assets Liabilities + Owners' equity). (Also known as the fundamental accounting equation.) Assets Liabilities + Owners' equity The assets on the left side of this equation represent everything the business owns that can be used to cover liabilities. Anything that remains after covering liabilities is owners' equity. Next, we'll dive into the details on each of these categories and learn how they appear on the balance sheet.

TMP-1160.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1160.text: Components of the Balance Sheet Figure 3.7-1 illustrates common components of a balance sheet, although components and their names can vary from company to company.

TMP-1163.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1163.text: Figure 3.7-1 The Balance Sheet ASSETS The balance sheet starts with assets, which are grouped according to liquidity_, meaning the ease with which they can be converted to cash. The most liquid asset is

TMP-1164.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1164.text: cash itself, because it requires no conversion and can be spent immediately. Inventory is another example of a highly liquid asset, because the materials and goods at various stages of production that make up a business's inventory can be sold quickly and easily in exchange for cash. Property, such as land and buildings, exemplifies an asset with low liquidity, because its sale requires considerable time, negotiations over price, legal paperwork, and expenses. liquidity The ease with which an asset can be converted to cash. Current Assets. The most liquid, and thus first, asset category is current assets, which are highly liquid assets used to pay for the daily operations of the business. Current assets are generally sold or, in the case of raw materials, used up within a year. Examples include cash, short-term investments, accounts receivable, and inventory. current assets Highly liquid assets used to pay for the daily operations of a business. Cash is currency (bills and coins) and immediately accessible bank deposits, such as money held in checking accounts. Following cash on many balance sheets are short-

TMP-1165.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1165.text: term investments, which are investments that can easily be sold for cash and are expected to be sold within a year. Examples of short-term investments include treasury bills (short-term loans to the government) and commercial paper (short-term loans to corporations). It is common for companies to list their investments with the shortest term (typically less than 90 days) and least risk as cash equivalents in the same category as cash. cash Currency and immediately accessible bank deposits, such as money held in checking accounts. short-term investments Investments that can easily be sold for cash and are expected to be sold within a year. Accounts receivable refers to money owed to the business for goods or services already provided to customers. When the company delivers a product on credit and sends a bill, the company has yet to collect the money for that sale, but its expectation of receiving the owed payment makes it an account receivable. accounts receivable Money owed to a business for goods or services already provided to customers.

TMP-1166.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1166.text: Inventory_ is what the business has available to sell, as well as materials used to make goods. There are three basic types of inventory: raw materials, which include any goods or components used in the manufacturing process; work-in-process, meaning partially assembled items awaiting completion; and finished goods, which are ready to be sold. inventory What a business has available to sell, as well as materials used to make goods. Long-Term Assets. Second on the balance sheet is a group of assets that are less liquid than current assets because they cannot easily be converted to cash. These noncurrent or long-term assets help the business generate revenue over time and have a useful life that exceeds one year. Among the long-term assets are fixed assets, which are tangible (physical, able to be seen or touched) assets such as production plants, land, vehicles, machinery, and equipment. These productive assets are not intended for sale, and are used for business operations including the production, storage, or distribution of goods. long-term assets Assets that help a business generate revenue over time and have a useful life that exceeds one year.

TMP-1167.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1167.text: fixed assets Long-term assets that are tangible, such as production plants, land, vehicles, machinery, and equipment. Long-term assets include long-term investments, which are investments expected to be held for more than one year. Examples of long-term investments include stocks, bonds, real estate, and mutual funds, which we'll discuss further in Module 5=3. The goal is for these investments to provide financial returns over time, either by increasing in value or by providing interest payments or dividends. long-term investments Investments expected to be held for more than one year, such as stocks, bonds, real estate, and mutual funds. Long-term assets also include intangible assets, which are nonphysical items (unable to be seen or touched) with the potential to provide future financial benefits. Examples include patents, trademarks, copyrights, brand names, and the "goodwill" embodied in a company's reputation, customer loyalty, and relationships. intangible assets Nonphysical items with the potential to provide future financial benefits, such as patents, trademarks, copyrights, brand names, and the "goodwill" embodied in a company's reputation.

TMP-1168.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1168.text: Inventory is a category of current assets that includes raw materials, work-in-process like these incomplete ice cream treats, and finished goods.

TMP-1169.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1169.text: LIABILITIES Now we turn our attention to the items on the other side of the balance sheet equation: liabilities and owners' equity. Liabilities are financial obligations of the business, such as money it owes to lenders, suppliers, employees, or the government. On the balance sheet, liabilities are arranged on the basis of when payment for the obligation is due. liabilities Financial obligations of a business, such as money it owes to lenders, suppliers, employees, or the government. Current Liabilities. Current liabilities are obligations due within one year of the date of the balance sheet. Current liabilities include accounts payable, accrued expenses, short-term debt, and current payments on long-term debt. It is important to track these liabilities to determine whether the business has enough cash available to cover the upcoming payments. current liabilities Obligations due within one year of the date of the balance sheet.

TMP-1170.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1170.text: Accounts payable is money a business owes to its suppliers for goods and services received, as typically specified on an invoice (bill) that the suppliers issue to the business. If sports equipment maker Spalding received leather for its footballs and the invoice has not yet been paid, that liability is part of accounts payable. accounts payable Money a business owes to its suppliers for goods and services received. Short-term debt is debt that is due within a year, such as a short-term bank loan taken out to cover immediate needs for cash. Current payments on long-term debt are the portion of long-term debt that must be paid within a year. For example, a business with a five-year bank loan typically must make payments every month, so the monthly payments to be made over the next year are considered current payments on long-term debt. short-term debt Debt that is due within a year, such as a short-term bank loan taken out to cover immediate needs for cash. current payments on long-term debt The portion of long-term debt that must be paid within a year.

TMP-1171.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1171.text: Accrued expenses are expenses incurred by the company for which no payment has been made and no invoice has been received. These expenses are typically operating expenses such as wages, utilities, and rent. For example, suppose Spalding pays its employees on the first day of each month for work in the previous month. The company accrues wage expenses throughout the month that have not yet been paid. For an accurate snapshot of the business's financial situation, a balance sheet for, say, the last day of the month should include those unpaid but already accrued expenses. Because invoices do not exist for these items, the cost of accrued expenses such as utilities may be estimated. accrued expenses Expenses incurred by the company for which no payment has been made and no invoice has been received. EXAM TIP Don't confuse accounts payable and accrued expenses. Although they are similar concepts, accounts payable are generally purchases made from suppliers for which an invoice specifies the amount due. Accrued expenses are typically for operating expenses for which there is no invoice.

TMP-1172.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1172.text: Long-term Liabilities. Long-term liabilities are obligations due to be repaid in more than one year. Examples include long-term bank loans and long-term bonds. Long-term liabilities also include mortgages, which are loans for homes or business properties that give the lender a claim on the property (the lender keeps the property) if the borrower does not pay back the loan. It is common for mortgage loans to last as long as 30 years. Many families purchase homes using a mortgage loan. Businesses often use commercial mortgages to purchase office buildings, retail stores, and production facilities. long-term liabilities Obligations due to be repaid in more than one year. mortgages Loans for homes or business properties that give the lender a claim on the property if the borrower does not pay back the loan. OWNERS' EQUITY As the difference between the value of assets the business owns and the debts it owes, owners' equity is the net worth of the business. There are two main components of

TMP-1173.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1173.text: owners' equity: stock and retained earnings. Module 325 explained that investors can buy shares of ownership in a business by purchasing its stock. The amount the business initially received for those shares of stock — not the current market value that investors would have to pay now for those shares — is listed in the owners' equity section of the balance sheet. The second component of owners' equity, retained earnings, is profit reinvested in the company. Recall from Module that a business can distribute its profit directly to owners (shareholders) as dividends, or it can reinvest profit back into the business. The source of retained earnings is the accumulation of those reinvested profits over the life of the business. Retained earnings can increase with new profit that is not distributed as dividend payments. If cumulative losses and dividend payouts exceed the company's previous earnings, the retained earnings will be negative. retained earnings Profit that is reinvested in the company rather than distributed as dividends. Owners' equity increases when the company makes a profit that is reinvested as retained earnings, and when it sells new stock. If the company takes a loss or pays a dividend, retained earnings decrease, and so does owners' equity.

TMP-1174.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting

TMP-1175.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1175.text: Interpreting a Balance Sheet LG How should we interpret the information in a balance sheet? Having learned the elements of a business's balance sheet, you can probably appreciate its importance to people making decisions about the business. Internal stakeholders such as managers and owners, along with external stakeholders such as suppliers and banks, study a business's assets, liabilities, and owners' equity at a recent point in time — typically the end of the previous quarter or year — to inform strategies that put money and jobs at stake. As with an income statement, it is common for a balance sheet to include two or more periods of data for the purpose of comparison. In some cases, the balance sheet signals the need to seek legal remedies or close the business to prevent further losses. In this section, we will examine the numbers in a balance sheet to learn how stakeholders interpret their implications.

TMP-1176.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1176.navLabel: Net Worth, Working Capital, and Debt
TMP-1176.text: Net Worth, Working Capital, and Debt The financial position of every business and individual is reflected in their net worth. The information in a balance sheet reveals whether a business has a positive net worth, meaning that it has more assets than liabilities. Owners are among the stakeholders who care a lot about this, because a business's net worth, as we learned earlier, is also its owners' equity. That is, Net worth Assets — Liabilities Owners' equity If a business's liabilities equal its assets, the net worth is zero, as is the owners' equity that represents their stake in the business. Ifthe business's liabilities exceed its assets, its net worth is negative, meaning that what it owns cannot cover what it owes. If that business shut down and its legal structure lacked limited liability for its owners (as is the case for a sole proprietorship or partnership), the owners might be liable for the remaining debts. Let's examine a balance sheet to learn how these and other important determinations are made. Suppose a manufacturer of chocolate sprinkles called Sprinkles City has the

headings.text: Net Worth, Working Capital, and Debt

TMP-1177.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1177.navLabel: Net Worth, Working Capital, and Debt
TMP-1177.text: balance sheet shown in Table 3.7-1. Net worth is found by subtracting the total liabilities from the total assets: . That positive net worth of $435,000 is also the owners' equity. Sprinkles City has plenty of assets to cover its liabilities and leave a sizable stake for its owners. TMP-1178.text: Intangible assets $51,000 Total Long-term Liabilities $200,000 Total Long-Term Assets $601,000 Total Assets $816,000 Total Liabilities $381,000 OWNERS’ EQUITY Stock $100,000 Retained earnings $335,000 Total Owners’ Equity $435,000 Total Liabilities and Owners’ Equity $816,000 A positive net worth is desirable, but it does not indicate whether the business has enough cash on hand to pay its debts when they are due. That is, some assets might not offer the liquidity needed to cover upcoming payments because it would take too long to sell them and obtain cash. However, we can look elsewhere on the balance sheet to learn whether there are sufficient liquid assets to cover short-term debts. Working capital is the difference between current assets and current liabilities: Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities

TMP-1179.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1179.navLabel: Net Worth, Working Capital, and Debt
TMP-1179.text: working capital The difference between current assets and current liabilities (Working capital Current assets — Current liabilities). Working capital is a measure of the business's short-term financial health. If it is positive, current assets exceed liabilities, and there is enough liquidity to cover payments that are coming up soon. If it is negative, payments due for liabilities in the coming year exceed the value of cash and assets expected to be converted to cash in the coming year, so the business will have trouble paying its bills. Sprinkles City has working capital of $215,000 — $181,000 $34,000, so it has enough working capital to fund its day-to-day operations. We can also learn the business's overall level of debt from the balance sheet. The sum of current liabilities and long-term liabilities is total liabilities. This represents the total amount that the business owes in the coming year and beyond. We've learned that one way to assess whether liabilities are at a reasonable level is to compare them with assets to determine net worth. It is also common to compare the level of total liabilities across similar businesses to find out whether the studied business has a particularly high or low level of debt. SKILLS TIP One of the skills for this course involves presenting data from financial statements that is targeted for a specific audience. As you discuss balance sheet data, consider the interests of the group you are addressing. For example, when presenting balance sheet data externally to potential investors, emphasize key strengths of the business that signal high profitability and investor returns, such as low levels of debt, considerable assets, and ample cash reserves. When presenting to managers, tailor the focus for internal reporting needs, such as a detailed breakdown of debts and expenses to identify needs for cost control, or an analysis of cash and short-term investments to inform discussions of budgeting and liquidity needs.

TMP-1182.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1182.navLabel: Net Worth, Working Capital, and Debt
TMP-1182.text: Redbox filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in 2024. The next step was to liquidate its assets, which included some 24,000 red DVD rental kiosks. Proceeds from the sales went to the company's creditors. Bankruptcy When profits are lacking, liabilities are hovering above assets, and there is little hope for turning things around in the near future, a business's owners may decide to shut down the business. Another last-resort option is to file for bankruptcy_, which is a legal process businesses and individuals use to seek relief from their debts. There are six types of bankruptcy in the United States, each named after the chapter of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code that defines them. Three types of bankruptcy are particularly relevant to businesses: bankruptcy A legal process businesses and individuals use to seek relief from their debts. Chapter 7 bankruptcy is for liquidation, meaning that the business will shut down operations and sell most of its assets. A court-appointed trustee oversees the sale of

TMP-1183.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1183.navLabel: Net Worth, Working Capital, and Debt
TMP-1183.text: assets and the payment of creditors, to the extent possible, using the proceeds. In the end, the business ceases operations and is officially dissolved (closed). That was the fate of movie rental company Redbox and electronics retailer Circuit City. Chapter 11 bankruptcy is for reorganization, meaning that the business will continue to operate with a plan to pay creditors over time. The business restructures its debts, which often involves missing original deadlines but making payments on an extended schedule. Although Chapter 11 bankruptcy is available to smaller businesses, the complexity and expense of negotiating reorganization arrangements makes it more attractive to large companies. Big Lots, Forever 21, and Marvel Entertainment are among the companies that have filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. If successful, the business can emerge from bankruptcy with a manageable load of debt and an opportunity for a fresh start, as did General Motors and AMR Corporation, the parent company of American Airlines. Chapter 13 bankruptcy is for adjustments in debts. This is similar to Chapter 11 bankruptcy — the business plans to stay open and repay its debts over time — except Chapter 13 is only available to individuals, which include sole proprietors. The sole

TMP-1184.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1184.navLabel: Net Worth, Working Capital, and Debt
TMP-1184.text: proprietor wants to keep their business but restructure the timing of payments. Debts are typically repaid over a 3- to 5-year period under court supervision. Many individuals also file for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. For businesses and individuals alike, bankruptcy can provide a roadmap for getting finances back in order, and there may be opportunities to avoid some unaffordable debts. That said, due to its many downsides, bankruptcy is generally regarded as a last resort. Filing for bankruptcy is likely to damage a business's reputation and harm the filer's ability to receive credit in the future. The process typically involves the owners' or individual's loss of control over finances. There are court filing fees and, in many cases, legal advisors to be paid. And the whole process can be a complicated and time-consuming ordeal. For an individual, one way to avoid bankruptcy is to maintain a healthy net worth.

TMP-1187.text: If you complete a Free Application for Student Aid (FAFSA) form as you prepare for college, your household's net worth will help to determine your eligibility for federal student aid. Just as a business has a net worth, you have a personal net worth. Individuals don't need to create balance sheets like corporations do, but you might need to calculate your net worth when you apply for a loan, insurance, or financial aid for college. Knowing your net worth will also help you understand your financial situation and make informed decisions about expenditures, employment, and investments. And you, or your financial advisor, will want to consider your net worth when it comes time to decide whether you have enough savings to retire. This section explains how to find your personal net worth, which is a lot like finding a business's net worth. Personal net worth is typically calculated for a household, meaning one or more people who live in a housing unit, such as an apartment or a house. The formula for personal net worth is the same as for a business: Net worth Assets Liabilities. A household's assets might include a house, a car, investments, bank accounts, and retirement accounts. A household's liabilities often include the balance on a mortgage

TMP-1190.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1190.text: Module 3.7 Review Learning Goals What are the components of a business's balance sheet? • The balance sheet is a financial statement that shows a business's assets, liabilities, and owners' equity at a particular point in time. The balance sheet reveals a business's net worth — its assets minus its liabilities. The difference between a business's assets and liabilities is also called owners' equity. This represents the net value of the business that belongs to the owners. The balance sheet equation captures the relationship between assets, liabilities, and owners' equity: Assets Liabilities + Owners' equity. • The balance sheet starts with assets, which are grouped according to liquidity, meaning the ease with which they can be converted to cash. The most liquid, and

TMP-1191.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1191.text: thus first, asset category is current assets, which are highly liquid assets used to pay for the daily operations of the business. Cash is currency (bills and coins) and immediately accessible bank deposits, such as money held in checking accounts. Following cash on many balance sheets are short-term investments, which are investments that can easily be sold for cash and are expected to be sold within a year. Accounts receivable refers to money owed to the business for goods or services already provided to customers. Inventory is what the business has available to sell, as well as materials used to make goods. • Noncurrent or long-term assets help the business generate revenue over time and have a useful life that exceeds one year. Among the long-term assets are fixed assets, which are tangible (physical, able to be seen or touched) assets such as production plants, land, vehicles, machinery, and equipment. Long-term assets include long-term investments, which are investments expected to be held for more than one year. Long-term assets also include intangible assets, which are nonphysical items with the potential to provide future financial benefits. • Liabilities are financial obligations of the business, such as money it owes to lenders, suppliers, employees, or the government.

TMP-1192.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1192.text: • Current liabilities are obligations due within one year of the date of the balance sheet. Current liabilities include accounts payable, accrued expenses, short-term debt, and current payments on long-term debt. Accounts payable is money a business owes to its suppliers for goods and services received, as typically specified on an invoice (bill) that the suppliers issue to the business. Short-term debt is debt that is due within a year, such as a short-term bank loan taken out to cover immediate needs for cash. Current payments on long-term debt are the portion of long-term debt that must be paid within a year. Accrued expenses are expenses incurred by the company for which no payment has been made and no invoice has been received. • Long-term liabilities are obligations due to be repaid in more than one year. Examples include long-term bank loans and long-term bonds. Long-term liabilities also include mortgages, which are loans for homes or business properties that give the lender a claim on the property (the lender keeps the property) if the borrower does not pay back the loan. • There are two main components of owners' equity: stock and retained earnings. Retained earnings is profit reinvested in the company. The source of retained earnings is the accumulation of those reinvested profits over the life of the

TMP-1193.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1193.text: business. If the cumulative losses and dividend payouts exceed the company's previous earnings, the retained earnings will be negative. LG How should we interpret the information in a balance sheet? • The financial position of every business and individual is reflected in their net worth. Working capital is the difference between current assets and current liabilities. If working capital is positive, current assets exceed liabilities, and there is enough liquidity to cover payments that are coming up soon. • A last-resort option for business or individuals struggling with liabilities is to file for bankruptcy, which is a legal process used to seek relief from debts. Through bankruptcy, debts are sometimes paid off by liquidating (selling) assets, or debt payments are extended over a longer period of time. Bankruptcy has negative repercussions that include loss of control over finances and damage to the filer's ability to borrow money in the future.

TMP-1209.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1209.text: The Anatomy of a Cash Flow Statement LG What information is included on a business’s cash flow statement? We’ve learned that a business’s income statement summarizes its revenues, costs, and profit for a given period, and that a balance sheet is a snapshot of the business’s assets, liabilities, and net worth at one point in time. For a better picture of a business’s financial health, stakeholders also examine a statement showing the sources and uses of cash — the lifeblood of a business’s daily operations. Regardless of profits and net worth, if a business lacks the cash to cover recurring expenses such as payroll and rent, handle unexpected expenses, and repay lenders, there are big problems. In this section, we’ll investigate the elements of a cash flow statement that reveal where the money came from, and where the money went.

TMP-1210.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1210.text: Cash In, Cash Out A cash flow statement tracks the movement of cash in and out of a business over a specified financial reporting period. Those inflows and outflows of cash determine the cash balance a business can use to cover its invoices and pay its employees. Cash inflows bring money into the business and increase its cash balance. Money comes in from sales, returns on investments, proceeds from the sale of assets such as property or equipment, and financing such as a new bank loan. Cash outflows take money out of the business and decrease its cash balance. Examples include cash used for payments to employees and suppliers, debt repayments, interest paid on loans, tax expenses, purchases of assets such as buildings, and dividends paid to shareholders. Table 3.8-1 summarizes these and other common cash inflows and cash outflows. cash flow statement A financial statement that tracks the movement of cash in and out of a business over a specified financial reporting period. cash inflows Inflows of money into a business that increase its cash balance. cash outflows Outflows of money out of a business that decrease its cash balance.

TMP-1211.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1211.navLabel: A Tour of the Cash Flow Statement
TMP-1211.text: Table 3.8-1 Common Cash Inflows and Cash Outflows Cash Inflows Cash Outflows Payments for Products (Sales Revenue) Payments to Suppliers Loans Received Loan Interest and Debt Repayments Interest and Dividends from Investments Wage and Salary Payments to Employees Purchases of Stock by Investors Dividends to Shareholders Proceeds from Sales of Business Assets Payments for New Asset Purchases Tax Refunds Taxes on Profits A Tour of the Cash Flow Statement The cash flow statement is like a cash register for the company. It shows the cash available at the beginning of the period, which is like cash already in the register. It also shows cash received during the period — the cash inflows already mentioned, such as for sales, investments, or loans. The cash coming in is reduced by the cash paid out during the period. These are the cash outflows, such as for wages, debts, and dividends. Credit transactions — those that involve an agreement to make or receive a payment at a later date — do not affect the cash flow statement.

TMP-1215.text: AP ® EXAM TIP The financial statements are interconnected. If you’re asked about the effects of a change on the key financial statements, note that a change in one statement might cause a change in another statement. For example, net income in the cash flow statement is equivalent to net profit or loss on the income statement. Cash on hand at end of period on the cash flow statement feeds into cash and cash equivalents on the balance sheet. And changes in assets and liabilities on the balance sheet explain cash inflows and outflows on the cash flow statement. Line 3 shows that a $50,000 expenditure on inventory reduces cash by that amount. Accounts payable represents payments owed to suppliers or other creditors, so the $70,000 increase in accounts payable shown in Line 4 indicates an amount not yet paid. Remember that the net income figure at the top incorporates all expenses, but cash has not yet flowed out for accounts payable, even though those expenses are reflected in net income. To adjust for this, the positive $70,000 represents the cash that is still being held by the company. After those adjustments, the net cash from operations was $350,000 − $100,000 − $50,000 + $70,000 = $270,000, as shown in Line 5. If the business paid a supplier for goods purchased in a previous period, the transaction would appear as a decrease in accounts payable. For example, suppose the

TMP-1216.navLabel: A Tour of the Cash Flow Statement
TMP-1216.text: $70,000 in accounts payable accumulated this period were repaid the following period. That payment would be recorded under Cash Flows from Operating Activities as: “Decrease in accounts payable: ($70,000)” in the cash flow statement for that period. Since cash would leave the business for a payment that was not part of the calculation of that period’s net income, this adjustment would be needed to determine the business’s cash holdings. On the cash flow statement, “investments” is the catchall term that incorporates assets such as property, plants and equipment, long-term investments such as stocks and bonds, and even subsidiaries or divisions of the company, which sometimes are sold. The cash flows from investing activities in Table 3.8-2 include a $90,000 outflow for the purchase of equipment (Line 6) and a $20,000 inflow for the sale of investments (Line 7). When investments are sold, the amount received for the sale adds to the company’s cash on hand. For this business, the net cash from investments was −$90,000 + $20,000 = −$70,000, as shown in Line 8.

TMP-1217.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1217.navLabel: A Tour of the Cash Flow Statement
TMP-1217.text: Mario Tama/Getty Images Multinational finance and insurance corporation AIG sold billions of dollars’ worth of assets between 2010 and 2025, including its Alico insurance unit. Many of these sales were needed to provide cash flow, in some cases to repay government loans received during the Great Recession of 2007–2009. These sales of assets show up as cash inflows from investing activities in the cash flow statement.

TMP-1218.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1218.navLabel: A Tour of the Cash Flow Statement
TMP-1218.text: The cash flows from financing activities include $100,000 in proceeds from a bank loan (Line 9). Borrowing from a bank increases the amount of cash on hand. On the cash flow statement, loan “proceeds” describe the money received from a loan after paying any costs and fees associated with the loan. Cash gained by issuing new shares of stock would be listed as “proceeds from the sale of stock.” The $60,000 payment of dividends recorded in Line 10 was a cash outflow for the distribution of some of the business’s profits to shareholders. The net cash from financing was $100,000 − $60,000 = $40,000, as shown in Line 11. Adding the cash flows from operating, investing, and financing activities may leave the business with a cash increase or decrease for the period. Line 12 indicates that for this business, the net cash flow was $270,000 − $70,000 + $40,000 = $240,000. At the start of the period, there was $80,000 in cash on hand (Line 13), so the cash on hand at the end of the period was $240,000 + $80,000 = $320,000, as shown in Line 14. The cash flow statement shows that this business had a positive cash flow of $240,000, which means more cash came in than went out. It is also possible for the cash flow to be negative, meaning the business spent more cash than it brought in during that period. A negative cash flow can signal problems with the business’s financial health, or it can be

TMP-1219.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1219.navLabel: A Tour of the Cash Flow Statement
TMP-1219.text: an expected and short-lived result of the company’s growth process, as we’ll discuss next.

TMP-1220.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1220.text: Interpreting the Cash Flow Statement LG How do stakeholders use the information on the cash flow statement? A business’s stakeholders use the cash flow statement to inform their decisions and strategies. Managers use it as they plan their budgets and determine whether new financing (loans, bonds, stock sales) is needed to cover upcoming expenses. Suppliers use the cash flow statement to assess the business’s ability to pay its invoices. Lenders want evidence the business has enough cash to make loan payments on time. Shareholders know that cash helps the business survive tough times, grow, and pay dividends. And cash matters to employees who want their wages to be paid and their jobs to be secure. Although a positive cash flow is a good sign, a period or two with a negative cash flow may not be a problem. This can occur when a rapidly growing business spends large

TMP-1221.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1221.text: amounts of cash to expand its inventories and assets. A new business faces a timing challenge, because it must spend heavily on employees, facilities, advertising, and other startup costs long before sales revenues provide much cash. The initial delay between expenses and revenues might cause a year or so of negative cash flows. If the business has sufficient access to cash — perhaps from savings or loans — it may be able to withstand negative cash flows in the short run.

TMP-1222.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1222.text: South_agency/Getty Images A big investment in renovations can lead to a negative cash flow in the short term, but bring rewards in the long run. For a mature business, consistently negative cash flows may signal a problem with its ability to cover current expenses. The result could be bankruptcy or shut down, even if

TMP-1223.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1223.text: the business has a positive net income, because the business cannot pay its operating expenses and meet its other financial obligations. A business with cash flow problems like this may need to pursue new sources of financing, which might mean issuing new stock, selling bonds, or taking out loans. The business may also be able to collect money owed by customers (accounts receivable) more quickly by using electronic invoicing, making due dates sooner, enforcing late fees, or developing stronger customer relationships. And it may be possible to negotiate an extension on payments to suppliers and lenders as a way to stay open. The cash flows for operating, investing, and financing activities can also hold valuable information. A positive cash flow from operations is a good sign that the business’s core activities of selling goods or services provide enough cash to cover its expenses. A consistently negative cash flow from operations is cause for concern that, despite what the income statement may say about profits, the business may have trouble paying its bills.

TMP-1224.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1224.text: Tim Boyle/Getty Images When Hostess Brands was in financial trouble, it sold its snack cake business to obtain needed cash. That showed up on its cash flow statement as a large cash inflow from the sale of assets. Large outflows in the cash flows from investing activities often mean that the business is investing in growth by purchasing assets such as property and equipment. That can

TMP-1225.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1225.text: be a good sign, as long as the investments aren’t too risky. Large inflows can mean the company is selling off assets to obtain cash. That could be fine if the assets are no longer needed, but it may signal that the business is in financial distress and urgently needs cash. For example, Hostess Brands, famous for sponge cakes called Twinkies among other goodies, sold off its snack cake business as it entered bankruptcy in 2013. After a brief absence from store shelves and several changes in ownership, Twinkies and other Hostess products are now offered by the J.M. Smucker Company. AP ® Skills TIP One of the skills for this course is the ability to interpret quantitative data. If you are asked to interpret numbers in a cash flow statement, be alert to findings that could be interpreted as good or bad, depending on the circumstances. For example, a negative cash flow is often a bad sign, but not if the business is new or growing rapidly. And large cash flows from investing activities can be good if the business is selling assets or other investments it doesn’t need, but bad if it is selling assets out of desperation. Pay attention to the details of the situation to make the right interpretation. The cash flows from financing activities reveal whether the business is relying on borrowed money or stock sales to survive and grow. Large loans may indicate efforts to expand, but it may also signal desperation to cover expenses despite losses. Constant

TMP-1226.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1226.text: borrowing is generally a reason for concern. Sizable outflows to pay off debt or buy back stock can indicate financial strength, especially if there is a pattern of such outflows over time.

TMP-1227.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1227.text: Module 3.8 Review Learning Goals LG What information is included on a business’s cash flow statement? • A cash flow statement tracks the movement of cash in and out of a business over a specified financial reporting period. Cash inflows bring money into the business and increase its cash balance. Cash outflows take money out of the business and decrease its cash balance. • Accounts receivable represents sales for which cash payments have not yet been made. Accounts payable represents payments owed to suppliers or other creditors. LG How do stakeholders use the information on the cash flow statement?

TMP-1228.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1228.text: • A business’s stakeholders use the cash flow statement to inform their decisions and strategies. Managers use it as they plan their budgets and determine whether new financing is needed to cover upcoming expenses. Suppliers use the cash flow statement to assess the business’s ability to pay its invoices. Lenders want evidence that the business has enough cash to make loan payments on time. Shareholders know that cash helps the business survive tough times, grow, and pay dividends. Cash matters to employees because it allows their wages to be paid and helps make their jobs secure. • A positive cash flow is a good sign, although a period or two with a negative cash flow may not be a problem. A new business faces a timing challenge because of the delay between when startup costs must be paid and when sales revenues are received. A business with sufficient access to cash — perhaps from savings or loans — may be able to withstand negative cash flows in the short run. • For a mature business, consistently negative cash flows may signal a problem with its ability to cover current expenses. The result could be bankruptcy or shut down, even if the business has a positive net income, because the business cannot pay its operating expenses and cover its other financial obligations. A business with cash

TMP-1229.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1229.text: flow problems may need to pursue new sources of financing and try to collect money owed by customers (accounts receivable) more quickly.
