TMP-1233.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1233.text: CASE STUDY Home Depot Arina Habich/Alamy Stock Photo Home Depot addressed its cash flow problems in part by finding ways to reduce spending on inventory. The solutions involved better systems for tracking products and reductions in the amount of inventory kept in storage, rather than on store shelves where it could generate sales.

TMP-1234.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1234.text: The Home Depot was the brainchild of Bernie Marcus and Arthur Blank, two do-it-yourselfers who sat in a coffee shop in 1978 and dreamed of building a store that had everything like-minded people would need. They brought on board several talented entrepreneurs to handle finances and merchandising, and made plans to fill the store with highly skilled staff who could advise customers on their projects. The new company opened two Home Depot stores in the Atlanta area the following year. To demonstrate its commitment to a “whatever it takes” philosophy, Home Depot adopted a “customer bill of rights” stating that customers could expect the best assortment, quality, and price in its stores. The company also provided service from trained sales associates who could not just “sell or tell,” but actually show customers how to use tools and make home repairs. The company’s values include the principle to “put customers and associates first, and the rest will take care of itself.” 1 The business model worked, and the company grew. To raise financial capital, Home Depot issued shares of stock to the public in 1981. Despite that financial infusion, the company’s growth was so rapid that it ran into cash flow problems. In 1985, Home Depot was spending $4 million more in a typical month on operating expenses than it was collecting from customers. On top of that,

TMP-1235.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1235.text: it was spending an average of $8 million per month building or acquiring new stores. As the company burned through $12 million in cash per month that year, it borrowed $92 million to help cover its expenses, adding to the $120 million it had borrowed the previous year. Home Depot was able to turn its cash flow situation around with a multipronged approach. It became more proactive about collecting accounts receivable by securing timely payments. At the same time, it slowed its payments to suppliers, allowing it to hold on to more cash for longer periods. The company improved its inventory management system so that inventory didn’t sit idle in warehouses, and less inventory was needed for the same volume of sales. And it reduced overhead expenses needed to keep stores running, such as utilities, rent, and administrative costs. Home Depot’s efforts to restructure operations and improve cash flow were successful. Today, the company operates more than 2,300 stores in the United States, Mexico, Canada, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. As the world’s largest home improvement retailer, Home Depot offers more than one

TMP-1236.text: million products, truly living the dream of providing virtually everything a do-it-yourselfer would need. The company’s cash flow statement for 2023–2024 is provided in Table 3.8-3 . TMP-1240.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1240.text: MODULE 3.9 Ethics and Financial Reporting LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 3.9.A Explain the incentives behind unethical financial management and reporting 3.9.B Discuss the laws and codes of conduct designed to promote ethical financial management and reporting

TMP-1241.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1241.text: SOPA Images/Getty Images Cryptocurrency trading platform FTX was reportedly worth $25 billion before it went bankrupt in 2022. The company’s downfall was financial mismanagement and embezzlement that cost customers billions of dollars. Some victims pointed to a lack of transparency, inadequate audits of financial statements, and insufficient regulations that permitted company leaders to engage in unethical behavior.

TMP-1242.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1242.text: Incentives for Unethical Reporting LG Why do some individuals and businesses engage in unethical business practices? Unethical financial management stems from incentives for misconduct. Those incentives grow when opportunity tempts wrongful behavior. Working against those incentives (hopefully) are personal standards for ethical behavior, professional codes of conduct, and legal policies with threats of punishment. But all too often, those deterrents leave room for breaches of ethics. This section explores the incentives to engage in unethical financial reporting. The following sections examine the repercussions of those actions and the efforts to prevent them. Temptations for Wrongdoing Most of the legal and ethical paths to financial security involve patience and hard work. It can be tempting to seek easy money by breaking the rules. A small business

TMP-1243.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1243.text: owner can try to reduce the burden of income taxes by not reporting some sales. And some employers may avoid payroll taxes by paying employees “under the table” in cash or misclassifying them as independent contractors for whom payroll taxes do not apply. Leaders at a public company may misstate earnings to keep the business’s stock price up even though earnings are down. Accountants could misstate the company’s cash flow situation to improve opportunities for loans. And temptation may lead employees with access to large sums of corporate cash to find ways to take home some of that money. In Modules 3.6–3.8 , we learned that stakeholders judge the health of a business using numbers from financial reports. With decisions by investors, creditors, suppliers, and corporate leaders resting on the information in their reports, businesses face incentives to stretch the truth. These incentives may be particularly tempting for the accounting and finance teams, which generate the reports meant to reveal their company’s financial situation. By falsifying numbers, or by simply failing to report an asset or a liability, employees can alter financial reports to misrepresent the truth and benefit the business — but seldom for long.

TMP-1244.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1244.text: The payroll process of providing employee compensation creates its own temptations to falsify information for personal gain. Employees may be able to exaggerate their work hours to receive higher wage payments than they have earned. There is also a threat of ghost employees who are listed in a company’s payroll system, but who do not really work at the organization. A ghost employee could result from the accidental failure to remove a former worker from the system. Ghost employees might also be created to generate payments that end up in a real employee’s bank account. A human resources manager in China allegedly created 22 ghost employees who existed in the payroll system for eight years and collected over $2 million in compensation. 1 The incentives for business-related misdeeds give rise to a host of unethical and deceptive behaviors. Next we’ll examine several problems that arise all too often. Unethical Practices The tangled web of bad business behavior is woven by a multiplicity of misdeeds. Many unethical practices involve ways to steal money; others are ways to cover up the theft. In this section, we explore some of the most common forms of wrongdoing and deception.

TMP-1245.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1245.text: Misuse of funds is the unauthorized or inappropriate use of money that is not your own. For example, Sam Bankman-Fried, the CEO of FTX, reportedly used more than $8 billion of his customers’ money for personal spending, investments, political contributions, and loan repayments for his other company. But crime doesn’t pay, of course, and he was sentenced to 25 years in prison and fined $11 billion in 2024. 2 Of course, individuals can spend their own money in inappropriate ways, too — but that is described as wasteful spending, squandering money, or poor financial management. misuse of funds The unauthorized or inappropriate use of money that is not one’s own.

TMP-1246.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1246.text: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images As Sam Bankman-Fried learned, the misuse of funds has serious consequences. In cases like Sam Bankman-Fried’s, the misuse of funds may also involve embezzlement , which is the intentional theft of money or other assets that have been entrusted to an individual. Embezzlement is a type of misuse of funds that is always

TMP-1247.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1247.text: illegal and deliberate. If a manager uses company funds to travel to a conference that she mistakenly thought was approved by her business, that misuse of funds was unintentional, so it would generally not be considered embezzlement. Classic examples of embezzlement are accountants, cashiers, or treasurers deliberately diverting cash from their organization into their own pockets. embezzlement The intentional theft of money or other assets that have been entrusted to an individual.

TMP-1248.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1248.text: Kayla Bartkowski/Getty Images In the United States, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) collects federal taxes from businesses and individuals. Some businesses try to evade taxes by misreporting their profits. To address this and related problems, the IRS has its own Criminal Investigation division that targets tax evasion by businesses and individuals.

TMP-1249.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1249.text: As discussed in Module 3.6 , all businesses are obligated to comply with tax laws. Tax evasion is an illegal attempt to avoid or reduce tax payments. Businesses are required to pay taxes on their profit, so tax evasion often involves reporting inaccurately high costs or low revenues to reduce the apparent profit. In the United States, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) collects the federal taxes paid by compliant businesses and individuals. The IRS estimates that tens of billions of dollars go unpaid by corporations in a typical year as a result of tax evasion. Law enforcement actions by the IRS Criminal Investigation division recover only around one-fifth of those unpaid taxes. 3 tax evasion An illegal attempt to avoid or reduce tax payments. Other unethical (and illegal) behaviors involve paying for favors. Bribery is offering, giving, receiving, or requesting any item of value (money, gifts, services) for the purpose of influencing an action or decision. A construction company might be tempted to bribe regulators to overlook safety violations. A technology company might try to bribe government officials to award it contracts for services. And a pharmaceutical company might try to bribe a supplier to establish an exclusive supply agreement for a rare

TMP-1250.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1250.text: ingredient needed to make a profitable drug. Bribes can also arise within a business, such as to influence decisions about employee promotions. bribery Offering, giving, receiving, or requesting any item of value (money, gifts, services) for the purpose of influencing an action or decision.

TMP-1251.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1251.text: Andriy Popov/Alamy Stock Photo Bribes often involve unrecorded cash payments to influence decision makers, secure deals, or avoid penalties. Another unethical behavior is hiding the truth or keeping important information secret. There is transparency when information is openly, honestly, and clearly shared with stakeholders. A lack of transparency can prevent stakeholders from understanding

TMP-1252.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1252.text: the financial health of the business and making appropriate decisions. It can also erode trust in the organization and remove accountability that would otherwise create incentives for ethical behavior. Examples include a business not disclosing that a product under development has failed performance tests, or a government agency holding closed-door meetings on public policy decisions. transparency Sharing information openly, honestly, and clearly. When information is distorted, it can sometimes cross the line into fraud, which is a more serious form of deception. Fraud is the act of intentionally deceiving someone for unfair or unlawful gain. Falsifying information in financial statements is one of the common types of fraud. Other types include identity theft, unauthorized uses of credit cards, insurance fraud, tax fraud, fake job postings, fake charities, and investment fraud such as the Ponzi schemes discussed in this module’s case study. fraud The act of intentionally deceiving someone for unfair or unlawful gain.

TMP-1253.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1253.text: The many possible practices with harmful effects on businesses and their stakeholders — and the sizable incentives to engage in them — motivate strong efforts to prevent them. We’ll examine those countermeasures next. AP ® Exam TIP As you prepare for the exam, prioritize material that could easily become part of an exam question. For example, a question could predictably ask you to explain an appropriate remedy for a particular case of business-related misconduct. With an understanding of the four ways to motivate ethical business practices explained in this module, you’ll be prepared to address many possible variations of a question about deterring financial misdeeds.

TMP-1254.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1254.text: Motivations for Ethical Business Practices LG How do laws and professional codes of conduct guide accounting and financial managers to act ethically? Most accountants and financial managers who oversee budgeting, financial reporting, and investment decisions for firms are upstanding citizens. Sadly, the subset of these and other employees who engage in misconduct cause billions of dollars’ worth of harm every year. The vulnerability of businesses and their stakeholders to unethical behavior makes countermeasures crucial. Governments, professional organizations, and businesses themselves do what they can to deter the damaging misdeeds. This section explores the rules and policies designed to encourage ethical behavior.

TMP-1255.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1255.text: Laws and Punishments The importance of ethical business practices spurs countries around the world to enact laws against fraud, tax evasion, embezzlement, bribery, and the misuse of funds. Legal policies vary, and punishments can be severe. In the United States, bank fraud is punishable with fines up to $1 million and prison sentences up to 30 years. Financial scammer Bernie Madoff, featured in this module’s case study, received a sentence of 150 years for multiple types of fraud. In France, accounting fraud is punishable with up to five years in prison and a fine of €375,000 (roughly $425,000). In China and Vietnam, large-scale cases of financial fraud are punishable by death. For tempted individuals who understand the likelihood of getting caught and the severity of the punishments, these repercussions provide strong disincentives. Unfortunately, many people do not think they will be caught or are unaware of the consequences. 4 Financial Reporting Requirements Having more eyes on financial reports helps to encourage accuracy. Most countries have financial reporting regulations intended to promote transparency in business activities. In the United States, regulations by the Securities and Exchange Commission

TMP-1256.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1256.text: (SEC) require public companies (those whose stock is traded on a stock exchange) to give investors access to financial reports. The income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement are among the financial documents submitted to the SEC each quarter and made available to the public. These reports are also subject to thorough examinations called audits by independent accounting firms each year. Financial reporting requirements make the companies’ financial health more transparent and help to protect investors and other stakeholders from fraud. Professional Ethics Codes Motivation for ethical behavior can come from a code of ethics or a similar outline of standards and expectations for people in a particular profession. Accountants and financial managers have professional organizations with codes of ethics for their members. For example, the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute for Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) says that members should “serve the public interest,” “honor the public trust,” and “act with integrity.” Similarly, the Association for Finance Professionals has standards of ethical conduct that require members to “refrain from abusing the financial system and markets” and “disclose fully all relevant information that could reasonably be expected to influence business dealings.” 5 These

TMP-1257.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1257.text: and other professional ethics codes promote honesty and integrity and establish guard rails for ethical behavior that include transparency, objectivity, and confidentiality. Hum Images/Alamy Stock Photo A code of ethics can motivate good behavior if it is taken seriously by leaders and employees alike. A major accounting scandal at former energy giant Enron showed that dismissal of ethical standards by top executives can lead to the downfall of a company. Both Enron and its accounting firm shut down after findings of questionable accounting practices.

TMP-1258.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1258.text: Internal Mechanisms Because the repercussions of financial misconduct can be devastating to the business itself, many leaders devise their own means of promoting ethical behavior within their company. One example is a code of conduct, which details rules, expectations, and standards for conduct within an organization, as discussed in Module 1.6 . Businesses can also adopt a variety of processes and internal controls to monitor their finances and limit temptations for wrongdoing. The separation of duties is a method for discouraging financial misconduct by splitting tasks among multiple people. For instance, one person may record an invoice, which is passed on to another person for review and approval, before being passed to a third person to make the payment. By involving several people in the process, there is less chance for one person to conceal fraud, such as payments to nonexistent suppliers. Even when duties are separated, tight control of access to accounting and finance systems is common to limit the number of employees with the passwords and keys needed to manipulate data. With fewer people who could conceivably falsify

TMP-1259.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1259.text: information, the odds of one of them being a bad actor is lower, and it is easier to determine what happened when problems arise. An internal audit is an independent review of a business’s own financial activities, processes, and policies to ensure legal compliance, efficiency, and integrity. The team conducting the audit reviews financial records, systems, and operations and may interview employees and observe work processes. The team verifies that the business is obeying its own policies, government regulations, and legal requirements. It also assesses the checks and balances meant to prevent errors and fraud, such as supervision, security systems, the separation of duties, control of access, and safe cash-handling processes to limit the misuse of funds. A smaller, less formalized version of an internal audit can be achieved with surprise counts of inventory or cash to determine whether any theft has taken place. Misuse of funds is the unauthorized or inappropriate use of money that is not your own. Embezzlement is the intentional theft of money or other assets that have been entrusted to an individual. TMP-1267.text: CASE STUDY Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities, LLC. Hiroko Masuike/Getty Images Bernie Madoff used unethical financial reporting to cover up fraud that caused victims to lose an estimated $18 billion.

TMP-1268.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1268.text: One of the biggest financial fraud cases in history was orchestrated by Bernard “Bernie” Madoff, whose company falsified financial records to keep a massive Ponzi scheme alive. Before we learn more about Madoff, let’s set the stage with the story of how Ponzi schemes originated. Charles Ponzi was a Boston resident in the 1920s who promised investors a 50% profit in 45 days. Ponzi’s plan was to buy and sell coupons for international postage, which could be purchased for a lower price in Europe than they were worth in the United States. In theory, if he were able to buy and sell a tremendous volume of these coupons, Ponzi could make a handsome profit. In reality, Ponzi was unable to pull off the coupon plan at the scale necessary for it to be worthwhile. Nonetheless, he continued to promise amazing profits and obtained more than $8 million in investments (more than $130 million in today’s dollars). He was able to pay early investors high returns using the money from later investors. That trick could not be maintained, however, because only an ever-growing number of investors could finance the promised financial growth. Only so many people were willing and able to put money into such a scheme, so it was destined to fail. When it did, most of his investors lost their money, and Ponzi found himself in prison.

TMP-1269.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1269.text: Forty years later, Bernie Madoff began following the Charles Ponzi playbook, but it was a Ponzi scheme on steroids. Madoff eventually had thousands of clients, and his fraud involved roughly $65 billion in investments. Like Ponzi, Madoff’s plan was to find risk-free opportunities to buy something for a low price and sell it for a high price, a practice called arbitrage . Madoff’s arbitrage involved buying and selling corporate bonds that came with the option to be exchanged for shares of the issuing company’s stock. By finding bonds that were priced lower than the associated stocks, his company could buy the bonds and convert them to the stocks for certain profit. But as with Ponzi, such arbitrage opportunities were not available at the scale needed to sustain his investment scheme. Madoff found coworkers who were willing to help him falsify financial statements and lie to clients as they used money from new investors to provide high returns to existing investors — while keeping a substantial portion for themselves. To bolster the questionable story of arbitrage, the company studied past stock returns to find high-performing stocks and then claimed it had purchased those winning stocks for its clients. No stocks had actually been traded, but the purported high returns drew more investments, along with scrutiny from the media and the

TMP-1270.groupTitle: Unit 3 / Part 2 Business Finance and Accounting
TMP-1270.text: Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Using falsified documents, Madoff’s company passed a series of SEC audits in the mid-2000s, but his luck did not last. When the stock market crashed in 2008, many investors wanted their money. This defeated Madoff’s practice of claiming he was investing clients’ money, when he was actually giving it to other investors or keeping it for himself. When he lacked the liquidity to return investors’ request for $1.5 billion in withdrawals, the jig was up. Madoff was sent to prison for life, and investors lost an estimated $18 billion. The U.S. Department of Justice set up a Madoff Victim Fund with money collected from legal actions against Madoff, his coconspirators, and some of his investors. Over 40,800 victims received partial compensation for their losses. 6 Unfortunately, new cases of financial fraud occur daily. 7 As Ponzi and Madoff remind us: If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is! Often, there is no perfect

Decision making is the process by which an entrepreneur, manager, or business unit identifies opportunities or problems and recommends one or more solutions to address them. UNDERSTAND DECISION MAKING In order to make effective business decisions, entrepreneurs should be able to describe the various factors (market, internal, external) that may impact their business. They should be able to explain the ways in which these factors create opportunities or problems for stakeholders. One example of establishing decision-making criteria is use of the PACED model, which consists of identifying the problem; listing the alternatives; naming the criteria used to evaluate the alternatives; evaluating the alternatives; and making a decision. Often, business leaders will use financial statements to help guide decision making. Let’s consider an example. Suppose Cate Ruiz starts a pet-boarding facility, Cate’s Doggy Day Care, for dogs in her town. In the business’s sixth year of operations, Cate finds that she has outgrown the space and considers opening a second location in a neighboring town to handle increased demand. Answer: One advantage of a second location is the opportunity to generate an additional revenue stream. After having run the first location for over five years, Cate likely has a stronger understanding of the business and of her customers’ needs. This experience will help her to make strategic decisions about space, amenities, equipment, and the design of her facility. One disadvantage of a second location is the risk that Cate will overextend herself. If she is managing one location full time, Cate may find it difficult to manage two locations on her own. This means that she might have to hire additional managers, which would reduce her cash flow due to the expenses of payroll and benefits for the new staff. Another disadvantage is that if the locations are in the same area, the new location might cannibalize sales from the original. Explain the distinction between a cash flow statement and an income statement. Answer: A cash flow statement shows the amount of cash moving into and out of a business over a particular period of time (such as a month, quarter, or year). These cash flows come from operating, investing, and financing activities. A positive cash flow shows that a company’s liquid assets are increasing. TMP-1301.text: MODULES 4.1 Management and Leadership 4.2 Evaluating Performance Using KPIs 4.3 Strategy and Decision Making 4.4 Strategic Frameworks: Porter’s Five Forces and SWOT Analysis What a Difference Leadership Makes: AMD About one in four PCs run on chips from Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), a multinational technology company headquartered in Santa Clara, California. Founded in 1969, AMD took on Intel and other rivals in the microprocessor market starting in 1975. But after decades of growth and success, the company began to struggle in the face of strong competition and inconsistent product quality. By 2010, AMD’s share of the global microprocessor market was 11% — compared with Intel’s 81% — and the company’s stock price was a dismal $3 per share. Stakeholders feared the worst. But then, their fortunes changed.

TMP-1302.text: Lisa Su became the CEO of AMD in 2014. After earning her PhD in electrical engineering, Su held leadership roles at IBM and Freescale Semiconductor, where she built a reputation for technical expertise and strategic innovation. With its new leadership, AMD’s freefall turned into flight. Within a decade, the stock price exceeded $200 per share, and AMD’s profit was higher than ever before. Su’s strategies not only saved the company but also enabled it to challenge Intel in several segments of the chip market, and to ride the growing wave of demand for chips to support artificial intelligence (AI). Su’s leadership approach began with a focus on people. She invested in talented workers with a strong work ethic and built a culture of dedication to the company, modeled by her own long workdays and high performance standards. She then turned to repairing relationships with stakeholders. Su gained confidence among customers, investors, and partners by prioritizing transparency, consistency, and communication. And she restored trust by setting achievable goals and meeting or exceeding expectations. Su moved boldly into the uncharted territory of AI, which required large investments in technology at a time when AI’s trajectory was unclear. This strategy paid off, as AI

TMP-1303.text: data centers around the world proceeded to clamor for the chips AMD could provide. Meanwhile, Su helped her industry lobby against tariffs and other trade restrictions that would hinder the export of chips to overseas markets. AP ® SKILLS Concept Application (1.A, 1.C) Entrepreneurship (2.C) Decision Making (3.A, 3.B, 3.C, 3.D) Communication (4.A) By motivating employees to succeed, evaluating performance with key indicators, defining clear and effective strategies, and responding to threats and weaknesses, Su was able to reshape an ailing corporation. Under Su’s leadership, AMD rebuilt its reputation, productivity, and financial health. Using 44,000 of its chips, the company was also proud to help build the most powerful supercomputer in the world, El Capitan, in Livermore, California.

Strong management reversed the fate of chipmaker AMD.

TMP-1307.text: MODULE 4.1 Management and Leadership LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 4.1.A Explain what managers do 4.1.B Identify effective leadership and business communication skills 4.1.C Discuss core competencies that businesses seek in employees and ways those competencies can be improved 4.1.D Describe how businesses compensate employees, motivate good work, and retain top performers

TMP-1308.text: Houston Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images The planning, organizing, leading, and evaluating activities of managers help businesses run smoothly and meet their goals.

TMP-1309.text: What Managers Do LG What is the role of managers? You’ve probably seen managers in action, taking charge of stores, restaurants, and other businesses. You’ve also observed leaders in nonbusiness settings, such as teachers, coaches, camp counselors, clergy, caregivers, and others with responsibilities for guiding people and achieving goals. Many successful leaders have contagious energy, commitment, and social skills built from years of practice. Beyond internal drive and the fruits of experience, there are keys to strong leadership that are easier to pin down and study in a great high school course. In this module, we will dive into the roles, skills, and best practices of effective management and leadership. Management is the process of planning, organizing resources, leading people, and evaluating outcomes to achieve a business’s goals. All business leaders, from the

TMP-1310.text: supervisor of front-line workers to the chief executive officer, are involved in management. Their actions, strategies, and decisions influence internal factors such as worker motivation as well as external factors such as the company’s public image. management The process of planning, organizing resources, leading people, and evaluating outcomes to achieve a business’s goals. Organizations are typically divided into specialized departments that include finance, operations, marketing, and human resources, as discussed in Module 1.7 . Each department needs managers with the right skills to guide the business forward in that area. Those managers are responsible for aligning the work of their teams with that of the larger institution and its broader purpose and vision. Next, we’ll examine the planning, organizing, leading, and evaluating functions of management, as summarized in Figure 4.1-1 .

TMP-1311.text: Planning Setting goals Designing strategies Acquiring resources Organizing Developing employees Ensuring resources are in place Designing the organizational structure Leading Guiding and motivating employees Communicating clearly to ensure goals are achieved Evaluating Measuring performance Comparing performance with goals Taking corrective action as needed Functions of management Copyright © BFW Publishers Extended description for Figure 4.1-1 Four Functions of Management The center of the flowchart reads: Functions of management. The flowchart is circular, with each heading pointing to the next, and reads as follows: Planning Setting goals Designing strategies Acquiring resources Organizing Developing employees Ensuring resources are in place Designing the organizational structure Leading Guiding and motivating employees Communicating clearly to ensure goals are achieved Evaluating Measuring performance Comparing performance with goals Taking corrective action as needed

TMP-1313.text: Figure 4.1-1 Four Functions of Management Planning Planning is the process of setting goals and determining how best to achieve those goals. This management function begins well before the launch of a business. Early planning culminates in a business plan, as discussed in Module 3.5 , which includes the goals, value proposition, marketing strategy, and financial projections. Next, planning involves developing appropriate strategies and acquiring the right resources to achieve the goals and objectives of the business. Planning is an essential part of management because the other functions are unlikely to succeed without it. Some of the most important planning is for potential future problems. Even an established business should have contingency plans to prepare for challenging times ahead. When a

TMP-1314.text: hurricane, flood, earthquake, or financial crisis hits, the businesses with a plan for how to cope will come out ahead. planning The process of setting goals and determining how best to achieve those goals. Organizing Organizing is the process of orchestrating people, resources, and activities in a structured way to achieve goals efficiently. Organizing involves deciding what is going to be done, how it is going to be done, and by whom. In a hardware store, the managers help things run smoothly by assigning employees to specialized departments such as tools, paint, and customer service. They schedule work shifts to ensure adequate staff at all times. Managers have their teams organize stockrooms in logical ways that allow for quicker restocking. And they group products on shelves so that customers and employees can find them easily. organizing The process of orchestrating people, resources, and activities in a structured way to achieve goals efficiently.

TMP-1315.text: Hispanolistic/Getty Images Managers keep departments, schedules, and inventory organized so that everything runs smoothly.

TMP-1316.text: Leading Leading is the process of motivating, inspiring, and guiding people to achieve common goals. Strong leaders provide the direction and support needed to help workers reach their potential. Understanding what influences employee behavior and communicating effectively with a diverse team are critical leadership skills for managers, as discussed later in this module. A shortage of effective leaders can wound a business — a problem some businesses avoid by cultivating leaders from within. Bank of America, technology giant IBM, and consulting company McKinsey & Company are among the businesses known not only for great leadership, but also for leadership development programs that nurture future generations of successful leaders. For example, programs at Bank of America include an eight-week Student Leader paid internship program for high school juniors and seniors, and The Academy at Bank of America, a training program that helps current employees develop new leadership skills and advance their careers. leading The process of motivating, inspiring, and guiding people to achieve common goals.

TMP-1317.text: Evaluating The last of the four management functions, evaluating , is the process of measuring results, comparing them with goals, and correcting performance when necessary. The main aim of evaluation is to ensure that performance meets the planned objectives. For example, many companies track the time it takes to address customer questions or problems. Ride-hailing service Uber aims to respond to customer queries within 24 hours. Managers at Uber can evaluate performance in this area by measuring the response times, comparing them to the 24-hour goal, and making changes if the goal is not being met. evaluating The process of measuring results, comparing them with goals, and correcting performance when necessary.

TMP-1318.text: FatCamera/Getty Images To complete projects on time and keep people safe, construction site supervisors must set goals, organize people and materials, give workers direction and support, and ensure objectives are being met.

TMP-1319.text: Effective Leadership and Communication LG What are the qualities of effective business leaders? Managers must navigate uncertainty, adapt to rapid change, challenge established practices, and learn new skills to meet the demands of an evolving workplace. To be effective leaders, managers must also motivate and inspire workers. And a good manager is a good collaborator because every business is a group project — even a sole proprietor benefits from working well with suppliers, banks, accountants, legal advisers, and community groups. All of this means that management encompasses a multifaceted set of skills and behaviors, which are the subject of this section.

TMP-1320.text: Leadership Skills Just 18 years after its launch, the technology company Google became the most valuable company in the world. * A lot of things had gone right at Google, and leadership was one of them. With an eye on future success, the company studied what makes its managers great. Table 4.1-1 summarizes the behaviors that stood out. Managers in most businesses would do well to develop the skills that underlie these behaviors. Table 4.1-1 Ten Behaviors that Make a Manager Great at Google 1. Is a good coach 2. Empowers team and does not micromanage 3. Creates an inclusive team environment, showing concern for success and well-being 4. Is productive and results oriented 5. Is a good communicator — listens and shares information 6. Supports career development and discusses performance 7. Has a clear vision/strategy for the team 8. Has key technical skills to help advise the team 9. Collaborates across Google 10. Is a strong decision maker

TMP-1321.text: Information from: Google, “Identify what makes a great manager,” https://rework.withgoogle.com/en/guides/managers-identify-what-makes-a-great-manager#introduction RONNY HARTMANN/Getty Images Team-building skills are essential for managers because production is a team effort.

TMP-1322.text: The research at Google revealed that great managers borrow from the playbook of great coaches. For instance, team building is a key skill for managers because collaboration fuels productivity. Teamwork is crucial everywhere in a business — from the boardroom to the stockroom. On the factory floor, a product is likely to be made on an assembly line, thanks to contributions from a team of employees. That line can only move as rapidly as the slowest worker, so a manager who can empower and motivate people will bring the most productivity out of the team. Motivated employees are also more likely to develop healthy relationships with customers and coworkers, and to remain loyal to the business for a long and productive career. And when conflicts arise among team members, a strong manager draws on coaching skills to listen actively, mediate disputes, and guide employees toward solutions. More broadly, managers convey the mission and vision of the organization to get everyone focused on common goals. An admirable mission can inspire and align work efforts. Confusion about the strategic direction of a company can lead to wasted time and money. For example, in the early 2000s, Yahoo transitioned from a simple web directory into a broad platform of online services. A lack of clarity on the company’s mission and priorities led to a scattershot strategy of overlapping products. Was it

TMP-1323.text: primarily a media company? A technology platform? A search engine? Ambiguities at Yahoo led to investments in news, finance, shopping, email, and social networking that diluted the brand’s identity and may have prevented the company from reaching its potential in any of these areas. To build and maintain teams and keep them focused on the company’s mission, a good manager must listen empathetically, express ideas clearly, offer advice, and collaborate well — all of which require strong communication skills. Communication Skills The IBM Institute for Business Value surveyed executives around the world to learn more about the skills needed to execute business strategies. After flexibility, time management, and the ability to work effectively on a team, the most critical skill was effective communication. 1 Communication is the act of exchanging information (facts, thoughts, ideas, or feelings) between individuals or groups. A skilled communicator writes and speaks clearly and uses body language, eye contact, and tone of voice effectively.

TMP-1324.text: communication The act of exchanging information (facts, thoughts, ideas, or feelings) between individuals or groups. You’ve probably suffered through conversations with people who pretend to listen, or who don’t even pretend. A skilled communicator listens actively, paying full attention to others, asking clarifying questions, and responding thoughtfully with verbal or nonverbal cues (such as nodding) to signal their engagement in the conversation. They empathize with others, showing understanding and respect for people’s feelings and points of view. And they give and receive constructive feedback politely, without condescension or taking offense. Communication skills are valuable to everyone in the workplace. Employees with the ability to express themselves verbally and in writing, in formal and informal settings, will get their message across to the people who should receive it. For a manager, those people include customers, colleagues, employees, lenders, investors, and community members. Complaints from customers about shoddy products, rude service, and cold restaurant meals quickly find their way to the manager. A manager skilled at handling customer

TMP-1325.text: complaints will stay calm, listen carefully, validate feelings, take responsibility when appropriate, and offer fair and timely solutions. Managers’ other troubleshooting responsibilities may include handling failed projects, disgruntled employees, and contract negotiations with suppliers. Skills in problem solving, conflict resolution, and negotiation help managers address those situations in an effective, professional manner. Much of a manager’s most important communication is for the purpose of persuasion. Human resources managers try to persuade the best workers to join their team. Sales managers try to persuade customers to choose their product. And purchasing managers try to persuade suppliers to provide the best possible prices and delivery times. The persuasive communication skills you may practice to pursue an extension on a homework assignment, a later curfew, or a better price at the flea market will come in handy if you decide to go into management.

TMP-1326.text: Visual Art Agency/Getty Images Good communication means listening actively, trying to understand someone else’s perspective, and responding thoughtfully — both verbally and through body language.

TMP-1327.text: AP® SKILL TIP The skills of communication and collaboration are improved with active listening. Practice this in your next few conversations. Give the speaker your undivided attention, ask clarifying questions to ensure you fully understand their message, respond verbally and nonverbally, and show understanding and concern for the speaker’s feelings. This skill development will serve you well in this course, and throughout your career!

TMP-1328.navLabel: What Businesses Look for in Employees
TMP-1328.text: Core Competencies for Employees LG What core competencies do businesses seek, and how can these be improved? We’ve discussed what makes a good leader, but what are leaders looking for in their employees? Module 1.5 explained that core competencies are capabilities or strengths that enable an individual or business to stand out among rivals and deliver value in unique ways. This section focuses on the core competencies that businesses try to find, or develop, in their workers. What Businesses Look for in Employees One of the roles of business leaders is to hire employees to perform the day-to-day functions of the organization, such as producing, marketing, and selling products. When a business hires for an entry-level position, some core competencies are almost universally sought. An employee who is hardworking, dependable, honest, cooperative,

headings.text: What Businesses Look for in Employees

TMP-1329.navLabel: What Businesses Look for in Employees
TMP-1329.text: and good at problem solving would be a dream for many businesses. Workers with skills in communication, teamwork, adaptability, time management, organization, and AI are highly sought after as well. 2 Within most businesses, there are needs for more specialized core competencies that vary depending on the role. Consider banks, which hire workers for many positions that demand an assortment of core competencies. A bank needs tellers with interpersonal skills, loan officers with skills in risk assessment, managers with leadership skills, accountants with attention to detail, information technology workers with computer skills, and customer service specialists with skills in dispute resolution. Businesses generally benefit from workers with diverse experiences, skills, and backgrounds because ideation, problem solving, and community building are enriched by a wide variety of perspectives. Outsourcing is common for businesses whose employees lack the core competencies to complete certain tasks efficiently or effectively. For example, a bank might outsource its marketing to another business with expertise in persuasive communication, and its security needs to a business with core competencies in strength and surveillance.

TMP-1330.text: Skill Development Hiring involves an interview process that helps to reveal which candidates have the core competencies a business needs. However, a perfect match between an employer’s desires and job candidates’ abilities is rare. Rather than letting skill deficiencies lead to flawed products or services, businesses protect their customers, reputation, and profits by implementing programs to improve the skills of their workforce. Skill development programs are common, both to improve general core competencies such as creativity and to build skills specific to a particular business. If you get a job at a zoo, you may bring skills in time management and teamwork, but penguin care is one of those rare skills that will require some training to pick up. Zoos are among the businesses with apprentice programs that pair new employees with experts to provide hands-on experience and develop needed capabilities.

TMP-1331.text: picture alliance/Getty Images Many businesses can’t expect new employees to arrive with all the skills necessary for success. Skill development programs include apprenticeships, on-the-job training, and online training programs. Many companies also provide tuition assistance with post-secondary education , such as college or vocational school, to help employees gain new skills. For example, Chipotle

TMP-1332.text: has a “Cultivate Education” program that helps eligible employees pay for select undergraduate and master’s degrees, as well as high school completion and preparation for college. Many employers use on-the-job training to teach employees new competencies while they perform their work duties. Online training programs offer videos or live tutorials to enhance workers’ knowledge. And teachers, physical therapists, and accountants are among the workers who complete continuing education programs , such as classes or weekend workshops, that offer new learning opportunities to people who have already completed their formal education. AP® EXAM TIP It’s a good idea to learn several of the core competencies that are useful in most jobs. Then, if a question asks what you would look for as a leader when hiring for a particular role, you can provide specific answers that are likely to be applicable.

TMP-1333.text: Compensation and Motivation LG How do businesses compensate, motivate, and retain employees? High-quality workers are an asset to any business, and a good manager knows how to use incentives to attract, develop, and retain the best workers. An employee’s starting pay is usually based on the type of job, the availability of workers, and individual factors such as education, experience, and core competencies. For existing workers, leaders typically factor productivity into the basis for pay to motivate skill development and work performance. In this section, we explore several compensation strategies aimed at incentivizing the efforts that lead to productivity. Compensation Schemes Hopefully you will find a job that you love — but no matter what, you will need to pay the bills. The necessities of life place compensation high on the list of interests and

TMP-1334.text: motivations for most workers. Compensation schemes are plans for how employees will be rewarded for their work. The right compensation scheme can help a business encourage its employees to do their best. It can also improve employee retention, which is a priority because it typically costs more to recruit and train a new employee than it does to incentivize an existing employee to stay. compensation schemes Plans for how employees will be rewarded for their work. An hourly wage provides a set amount of money for each hour worked. If the number of work hours is flexible, this provides an incentive to work more hours, although many jobs involve working for a set number of hours. For example, a full-time worker at a Sonic restaurant typically works 40 hours per week. hourly wage A set amount of money paid to an employee for each hour worked. Managers, professors, and engineers are among the workers who typically receive an annual salary , meaning they are paid a set amount per year. Many jobs with an annual salary also offer opportunities to earn more, such as after a promotion, raise, or

TMP-1335.text: performance-based bonus. For example, the manager at a Sonic might earn $60,000 as an annual salary, with opportunities for bonuses (extra money) for achieving targets for sales, customer satisfaction, or cost control. annual salary A set amount of money paid to an employee every year. Employees involved in sales, such as real estate agents, car dealers, and department store sales associates, often work on commission , which is compensation based on a percentage of sales revenue. Real estate agents typically earn between 5% and 6% of a property’s sale price, although that commission is often split if other agents are involved, such as an agent working for the buyer of the property. Commission payments provide an incentive to maximize sales. If you’ve been in some clothing stores where the sales associates are aggressive about making sales and others where it is difficult to get their attention, the difference might be the commission-based compensation scheme in the store with aggressive sellers. commission Compensation based on a percentage of sales revenue.

TMP-1336.text: Manufacturers, farms, and construction companies are among the employers that sometimes offer workers piece rate pay , meaning payment that depends on the number of items produced (or harvested or constructed). For example, apple pickers can be paid per bushel, which encourages fast picking. This compensation scheme works well in industries where work results are easily quantifiable and rapid work is desired. Piece rate pay would not work so well for police or healthcare workers because incentives to rush would compromise safety. piece rate pay Payment that depends on the number of items produced (or harvested or constructed). Profit sharing is the distribution of a portion of a company’s profit to employees in addition to the employees’ wages or salaries. A company may set aside a portion of profit — at Delta Airlines it is 10% or more, depending on the level of profit — to share with employees. That money can be split evenly among the employees, or divided based on levels of salary, seniority, or performance. Profit sharing helps employees feel a sense of ownership in the business. The company’s success now provides payoffs to the employees, boosting their motivation for productivity, teamwork, and cost saving. Profit sharing can aid recruiting because job candidates are drawn to the possibility of added

TMP-1337.text: income. And this strategy can improve employee retention by providing an incentive to stay and collect the rewards in periods of strong profit. Profit sharing The distribution of a portion of a company’s profit to employees in addition to the employees’ wages or salaries. The appropriate compensation scheme depends on the industry, the role of employees, the level of competition with other businesses for high-quality employees, and the legal guidelines in place. For instance, farms with piece rate pay must ensure that workers are receiving at least the federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour. It is important to remember that compensation is not just money. When job candidates consider an offer, they take note of other benefits in the compensation package beyond the pay, such as health, life, and disability insurance; retirement savings plans; health savings plans; educational reimbursement programs; and paid time off. There are also legally required benefits such as Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment insurance, and in some cases supplemental pay such as bonuses and overtime pay. Figure 4.1-2 breaks down the compensation package for a typical civilian (nonmilitary) worker in the United States.

TMP-1338.text: Wages and salaries 68% Insurance 10% Paid leave 7% Retirement and savings 4% Supplemental pay 3% Legally required benefits 8% Copyright © BFW Publishers Extended description for Figure 4.1-2 Components of Compensation The pie chart reads as follows: Wages and salaries: 68 percent Insurance: 10 percent Legally required benefits: 8 percent

TMP-1339.text: Paid leave: 7 percent Retirement and savings: 4 percent Supplemental pay: 3 percent Figure 4.1-2 Components of Compensation Beyond wages and salaries, compensation packages include legally required benefits such as Social Security and Medicare. Many also include various types of insurance, retirement and health savings plans, and paid time off. This pie chart illustrates components of compensation for a typical civilian worker in the United States. Data from U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Workers also care about the working conditions at a business. Will they have autonomy , meaning the freedom to make their own choices? Are the work hours flexible? Are there options among multiple locations? Is achievement recognized and rewarded? Is there a positive workplace culture, or do people at that company do a lot of grumbling? Leaders with an attractive combination of pay, benefits, and working conditions are in a good position to attract and retain the best workers.

TMP-1340.text: Employee Motivation Gorodenkoff/Shutterstock Compensation schemes such as commission payments and profit sharing can motivate workers to put in extra hours. The importance employees place on compensation makes it an effective incentive that businesses use to motivate high levels of performance. We’ve seen how hourly

TMP-1341.text: wages can motivate more work time, commissions can incentivize aggressive sales efforts, piece rate pay can encourage a fast work pace, and profit sharing can encourage productivity and cost saving. The best strategies for motivation often depend on the type of employees involved. Full-time workers typically work at least 35 hours per week and are relatively likely to be with that employer for many years. Those workers are influenced by incentives with long-term repercussions, like profit sharing, impressive job titles, or generous comprehensive benefits packages. Part-time workers work fewer than 35 hours per week. Because part-time workers are typically not employed by the same company for as long as full-time workers, they are particularly motivated by incentives with value in the short run. These can include bonuses or awards for specific achievements, flexible scheduling options, and public acknowledgments such as an “employee of the month” program. Contract workers are hired for a specific project or period, typically under a contract that indicates the work to be completed and the resulting compensation. Temporary workers are generally hired for one year or less to cover short-term needs, such as an

TMP-1342.text: employee’s parental leave following the birth or adoption of a child. Like part-time workers, contract and temporary workers can be motivated by short-run incentives. They may also respond well to inclusion in meetings and events held primarily for long- term employees, and to the possibility of being retained as a long-term employee if the company is pleased with their performance.

TMP-1343.text: Module 4.1 Review Learning Goals LG What is the role of managers? Management is the process of planning, organizing resources, leading people, and evaluating outcomes to achieve a business’s goals. All business leaders, from the supervisor of front-line workers to the chief executive officer, are involved in management. Organizing is the process of orchestrating people, resources, and activities in a structured way to achieve goals efficiently. Planning is the process of setting goals and determining how best to achieve those goals. Leading is the process of motivating, inspiring, and guiding people to achieve common goals. Evaluating is the process of measuring results, comparing them with goals, and correcting performance when necessary.

TMP-1344.text: Managers must navigate uncertainty, adapt to rapid change, challenge established practices, and learn new skills to meet the demands of an evolving workplace. To be effective leaders, managers must also motivate and inspire workers, collaborate well, and engage in effective team building. Skills in problem solving, conflict resolution, and negotiation help managers troubleshoot and resolve disputes in an effective, professional manner. What are the qualities of effective business leaders? LG Valuable skills for business leaders include flexibility, time management, the ability to work effectively on a team, and effective communication. Communication is the act of exchanging information (facts, thoughts, ideas, or feelings) between individuals or groups. A skilled communicator writes and speaks clearly and uses body language, eye contact, and tone of voice effectively. What core competencies do businesses seek, and how can these be improved? LG

TMP-1345.text: Core competencies are capabilities or strengths that enable an individual or business to stand out among rivals and deliver value in unique ways. When a business hires employees for an entry-level position, they seek people who are hardworking, dependable, honest, cooperative, and good at problem solving. Workers with skills in communication, teamwork, adaptability, time management, and organization are highly sought after as well. Within most businesses, there are needs for more specialized core competencies that vary depending on the role. To improve employees’ core competencies, businesses use apprentice programs, post-secondary education, on-the-job training, online training programs, and continuing education programs. How do businesses compensate, motivate, and retain employees? LG Compensation schemes are plans for how employees will be rewarded for their work. An hourly wage provides a set amount of money for each hour worked. An annual salary is a set amount of compensation that is paid over the course of a

TMP-1346.text: year. Commission is compensation based on a percentage of sales revenue. Piece rate pay is payment that depends on the number of items produced (or harvested or constructed). Profit sharing is the distribution of a portion of a company’s profit to employees in addition to the employees’ wages or salaries. This approach helps employees feel a sense of ownership in the business. In addition to money, compensation packages may include health, life, and disability insurance; retirement savings plans; health savings plans; educational reimbursement programs; and paid time off. There are also legally required benefits such as Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment insurance, and in some cases supplemental pay such as bonuses and overtime pay. Compensation is a key incentive that businesses use to motivate high levels of performance. Hourly wages can motivate more work time, commissions can incentivize aggressive sales efforts, piece rate pay can encourage a fast work pace, and profit sharing can encourage productivity and cost saving. Full-time workers are motivated by incentives with long-term repercussions, such as profit sharing and generous compensation packages. Part-time workers, contract workers, and temporary workers respond more to incentives with value in the short term, such as bonuses and public acknowledgments.

TMP-1347.text: Practice Your AP ® Skills Preparing for the AP ® Exam MULTIPLE-CHOICE QUESTIONS 1. Of the four functions of a good manager, which should come first and which should be last? a. planning; organizing b. leading; evaluating c. organizing; leading d. planning; evaluating 2. Your manager at work listens actively when you speak. Your manager is demonstrating an effective a. planning process.

TMP-1348.text: b. compensation scheme. c. communication skill. d. organizing skill. 3. You open a new clothing store, “Rags to Riches.” Which compensation scheme for your employees will most likely maximize your sales revenue? a. commission of 5% of the sales price b. hourly wage c. annual wage d. “piece rate” of $2 for every customer who makes a purchase of any type 4. According to Figure 4.1-2 in this module, wages and salaries in the United States make up only 68% of worker compensation. Which of the following is the next largest component of worker compensation provided by employers? a. paid leave b. insurance c. legally required benefits

TMP-1350.text: CASE STUDY The Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company Tibrina Hobson/Getty Images Extended description for South by Southwest A large screen shows Cuban to the audience in a packed auditorium. ⓘ

TMP-1351.text: Mark Cuban brought his successful leadership style to the Cost Plus Drug Company to disrupt the pharmaceutical industry. Mark Cuban’s success shows how strong leadership can turn problems into business opportunities. He worked his way through college teaching disco dancing lessons and selling stamps door to door. He cofounded video portal Broadcast.com and sold it to Yahoo for $5.7 billion. He gained considerable fame as a “shark” on Shark Tank , a reality television show that features entrepreneurs pitching their product ideas. But this businessman wasn’t done with his entrepreneurial adventures, because he continued to identify problems and opportunities too important to ignore. One of those was an opportunity to help people with health issues and financial needs. The solution, as he saw it, was the Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company. People across the United States face health problems that are treatable with medication — if they can afford it. Customers also face uncertainty about how drug prices are determined and whether that price is reasonable. Cost Plus’s mission is to dramatically reduce the cost of drugs and add transparency to drug pricing. Cost

TMP-1352.text: Plus sets prices by taking its own cost for the drug and adding 15%, plus the $5.00 cost of having a pharmacy prepare and provide the prescription. For example, it can cost over $200 for a bottle of difluprednate eye drops to treat pain and swelling after eye surgery. Cost Plus pays $44.10 for a bottle of difluprednate. Adding 15% plus $5.00, the price to customers becomes $55.72 plus tax and shipping. The problem of high drug prices has existed in the United States for a long time. The opportunity to offer lower prices has been there too, but it took the right business leader to bring the solution to the masses. Mark Cuban’s leadership style fits Cost Plus well. He is passionate about achieving goals and helping people in need, and he keeps employees focused on that mission. Cuban’s leadership style includes direct communication and generous compensation packages that often provide bonuses for loyal, successful employees. The transparent prices at Cost Plus mirror the transparency he prefers in the workplace; according to Cuban, “Open offices keep everyone in tune with what is going on and keep the energy up.” 3 Cuban also likes to disrupt industries with radical change. His disruption of the drug industry by changing the pricing model is consistent with his leadership

TMP-1353.text: practices elsewhere. He disrupted the media industry as the cofounder of Broadcast.com, the technology industry as the cofounder of MicroSolutions, and the professional sports industry as the owner of the Dallas Mavericks basketball team. Cuban’s new approaches in these industries challenged established businesses to evolve for the sake of survival. For example, Broadcast.com was one of the first platforms to bring streaming audio and video to the internet. MicroSolutions gave small businesses access to advanced computing systems before that was common. And after buying the Dallas Mavericks, Cuban created a winning culture by treating players like partners, investing heavily in skill development programs, and providing top-quality training and recovery facilities. If you watch Shark Tank reruns, you might notice Cuban’s embrace of up-and- coming businesses intent on disrupting industries in their own ways. You will also see strong communication skills on display as he negotiates deals with budding entrepreneurs. Cuban understands the value of hard work and notes that success is “not about money or connections — it’s the willingness to outwork and outlearn everyone.” 4 Inc. Magazine calls Cuban “one of today’s most inspiring and successful entrepreneurs.” 5 His success across multiple industries demonstrates how strong

TMP-1354.text: management skills are transferable, and that purposeful leadership can spark innovation and change. Apply Your AP ® Skills 1. Identify the four main functions of management and explain two ways in which Mark Cuban excels at any one of them. 2. Suppose you are a manager in charge of hiring employees for the Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company. What is a core competency you would prioritize when screening candidates? Explain your answer. 3. Other than low prices, what competitive advantage of the Cost Plus Drug Company do you believe will be the most important to its mission to disrupt the pharmaceutical industry? Explain your answer. 4. Would piece rate pay be an advisable compensation scheme for pharmacy workers? Explain why or why not.
