TMP-1358.navLabel: M O D U L E   4 . 2 Evaluating Performance Using KPIs
TMP-1358.text: How Businesses Use Key Performance Indicators LG How do businesses evaluate performance? There are goals, and then there are achievements. Sadly, a business’s achievements do not always live up to its goals. A business that accurately measures performance will know when it has gotten off track and can make adjustments to find a better path forward. A key performance indicator (KPI) is a measurable value used to evaluate how well a business is achieving its objectives. key performance indicator (KPI) A measurable value used to evaluate how well a business is achieving its objectives. KPIs help a business monitor the effectiveness of its strategy and the progress toward its short-term and long-term goals. For example, the telecommunications company

TMP-1359.text: AT&T has short-term goals such as subscription growth and worker safety, and long-term goals such as expansion of its fiber broadband network. KPIs related to these goals include net additions (new subscribers minus lost subscribers), worker injuries per 100 employees, and fiber locations passed (the number of homes or businesses with access to the AT&T Fiber network). Small businesses are big users of KPIs as well. Consider the millions of sellers on Amazon Marketplace. Their available KPIs include the order defect rate (the percentage of orders with problems that lead to a return or negative feedback), the conversion rate (the percentage of visitors to a product’s listing that make a purchase), and the average order value (the average amount customers spend per order). In this module, we examine how KPIs like these are chosen and how businesses make use of them. How KPIs Are Chosen Because they serve as gauges for progress, managers choose KPIs that align with their mission and goals. It is typical to have KPIs related to common aims such as profitability, competitiveness, and long-term viability. Other KPIs depend on the characteristics and goals of a particular business. For example, the KPIs tracked by

TMP-1360.text: managers at SeaWorld theme parks include standard measures such as the number of customers, gross revenue, employee satisfaction, and operating costs. But due to its mission and goals, SeaWorld also has KPIs that track how long visitors wait for shows and attractions, the number of animals rescued and rehabilitated, and the number of people reached through educational programs. KPI selection also depends on the industry involved. Social media platforms like Instagram and X measure the time spent on the platform and the amount of engagement (replies, reposts) per post. In the videogaming industry, companies measure the number of daily active users and the amount of in-game currency (money used within the game to make purchases) spent. In the space industry, companies such as Blue Origin have KPIs that include the turnaround time per launch (the time between one launch and another) and the payload mass (the total weight of everything on board) delivered. The value of a business’s data on its achievements depends on the business’s interpretation of that data, which we will turn to now.

TMP-1361.text: Miguel J. Rodriguez Carrillo/Getty Images KPI selection depends on the business’s mission and goals, and the industry in which it operates. In the space industry, KPIs include the launch success rate.

TMP-1362.text: Interpreting KPIs LG How do businesses use financial and nonfinancial KPIs to track their financial health and progress toward goals? KPIs can measure performance related to any goal. You might monitor your school performance using your GPA, your progress toward saving for college based on the growth of your bank account, and your goal to help others based on the hours you spend volunteering. Businesses commonly use KPIs to provide useful information about financial health, marketing, sales, and operations. Let’s examine specific KPIs for each of these categories and consider ways you could apply them in a business of your own. KPIs for Financial Health Because financial health is crucial to business viability, organizations have formulated KPIs to monitor every aspect of financial achievement. Here, we will review the

TMP-1363.text: meaning and interpretation of eight popular measures related to finance. All of these were introduced in previous modules, but their usefulness as KPIs makes them worth a closer examination. Revenue is the money received in exchange for goods or services, as discussed in Module 1.1 . Revenue should not be confused with profit, which is found by subtracting costs from revenue. But like profit, revenue can be an indicator of performance, because rising revenue indicates growing sales, the ability to charge higher prices, or both. During periods of significant inflation, a business should recognize that at least some of the increase in revenue results from rising overall price levels in the economy, and is not particular to one good or service. An increase in revenue is one of the sources of higher profit, the other being a decrease in costs. Because they work against revenue in the calculation of profit, it is critical to consider costs. As we learned in Module 3.4 , the cost of goods sold (COGS) is the total cost of producing the goods sold over some period. Many businesses calculate their COGS each month. This metric can be used to track input costs and identify issues with waste or theft.

TMP-1364.text: AP ® EXAM TIP A common pitfall is to confuse the cost of goods sold with the price or revenue. If you spend a total of $120 producing 10 potted plants that you sell for $20 each, your price is $20, your revenue is 10 × $20 = $200, and your cost of goods sold is the amount that you (not your customers) spent on those plants: $120. COGS is a useful metric on its own, but it also plays an important role in calculating several other KPIs. One such KPI is gross profit (introduced in Module 3.6 ), which is the profit earned after subtracting the cost of goods sold from total revenue (the revenue received from all goods and services). A large gross profit indicates that the company is able to charge prices well above its cost of goods sold. A low gross profit might signal a need to consider higher prices. By measuring the money a business retains after covering its cost of goods sold, gross profit indicates a business’s ability to generate profit from its core operations — its day-to-day sales — excluding the effects of overhead costs such as rent and utilities, and one-time activities such as legal settlements and the sale of assets. A related KPI is the gross profit margin , which Module 3.6 defined as the ratio of gross profit to total revenue (multiplied by 100 to express it as a percentage). This KPI shows

TMP-1365.text: what percentage of revenue is available to cover indirect costs such as marketing and product development, interest expenses, and tax expenses, and to provide profit. The gross profit margin rises as the per-unit cost falls relative to the price, making it a useful tool for tracking cost efficiency. A low gross profit margin can indicate the need to examine the performance of the supply chain and the costs of raw materials and labor. Kindamorphic/Getty Images Most businesses rely on software for data analysis. Price hikes for software programs raise operating expenses and lower operating profit. By tracking these KPIs, businesses can monitor operational efficiency and assess the need to adjust software purchases and other operational expenses.

TMP-1366.text: As we learned in Module 3.4 , operating expenses include the costs of running a business that are not tied to the production or delivery of a particular product. The cost of sales staff, administrative salaries, research and development, and marketing are all examples. Businesses track their operating expenses as a measure of efficiency. An increase in operating expenses may signal the need to consider alternatives in an area with rising costs. For example, many businesses use SAS or STATA software for data analysis. When a software provider raises its prices substantially, this will appear as an increase in operating expenses. Such price hikes lead some organizations to adopt alternative software such as R, which is free but may be harder to learn. Several other concepts from Module 3.6 also serve as important KPIs. Operating profit — gross profit after subtracting operating expenses — reveals the business’s earnings before accounting for interest and tax payments. This KPI is used to monitor the operational efficiency of a business in terms of its ability to control both COGS and operating expenses. Operating profit can be compared across time periods, products, and businesses. Recall from Module 3.6 that the operating profit margin indicates a business’s excess of revenue over COGS and operating expenses, expressed as a percentage of revenue. The

TMP-1367.text: operating profit margin signals a business’s ability to generate demand for its products while keeping operating expenses in check. The operating profit margin rises when the business is able to charge higher prices, spend less on COGS and operating expenses, or both. A falling operating profit margin can indicate the need for new pricing strategies and cost-cutting efforts to achieve a sustainable level of profit. Finally, every business should keep a close eye on cash flow . Module 3.8 explained that cash inflows and cash outflows are the movements of money into and out of a business, and how the cash flow statement tracks cash inflows and outflows over a specified period. Cash flow is a key indicator of liquidity, meaning the availability of cash to pay bills, repay debts, invest in growth, and survive economic downturns. A business with a negative cash flow — more cash going out than coming in — must find ways to reverse that unsustainable trend. That might entail increasing cash inflows by targeting new customer segments, requesting faster payments from customers, selling assets such as idle equipment, or taking out loans. Another option is to decrease cash outflows by cutting costs, negotiating more time to pay suppliers, holding less inventory, or postponing nonessential purchases or repairs.

TMP-1368.navLabel: KPIs for Marketing and Sales Goals
TMP-1368.text: KPIs for Marketing and Sales Goals Businesses thrive, barely survive, or fail, depending on sales. Marketing is the engine that fuels — or fails to fuel — those sales. The vital importance of marketing and sales drives businesses to monitor them closely. In this section, we will explore six KPIs that focus on marketing and sales performance. Again, these are familiar terms that happen to serve as KPIs. Customer acquisition cost (CAC) is the marketing cost of acquiring a new customer, as discussed in Module 2.1 . It is common for businesses to track trends in the CAC over time. A business with a high or rising CAC may be experiencing inefficiencies and should consider whether alternative marketing campaigns could accomplish the same goals at a lower cost. It is also possible that the CAC is rising because the market is becoming saturated with competitors. By studying the customer acquisition cost using differing marketing methods, such as email messages and ads on social media, a business can allocate its marketing dollars to the lowest-cost approach. Customer lifetime value (CLTV) is the total revenue received from a customer throughout their relationship with the businesses, as also discussed in Module 2.1 . A low

headings.text: KPIs for Marketing and Sales Goals

TMP-1369.navLabel: KPIs for Marketing and Sales Goals
TMP-1369.text: CLTV may signal customer dissatisfaction, low customer retention, and a need for more post-sale engagement. The business may want to implement follow-up emails, loyalty programs, and requests for feedback. An increase in CLTV will bring more revenue to the business even if the number of customers remains the same. If a successful marketing campaign by Hallmark Cards established a new tradition of exchanging greeting cards every Halloween, the company’s CLTV would increase by: the average price of a card × the average number of cards purchased per customer × the average lifetime of a Hallmark customer.

TMP-1370.navLabel: KPIs for Marketing and Sales Goals
TMP-1370.text: Roberto Machado Noa/Getty Images Extended description for Rate Your Satisfaction A digital screen reads: Your satisfaction with our customer service today? Two logos below the screen read "Happy or Not" and "The Source: I want that."

TMP-1371.navLabel: KPIs for Marketing and Sales Goals
TMP-1371.text: Below the screen is a board that shows four push buttons displaying faces. Two green buttons correspond to Very Satisfied and Satisfied. Two red buttons correspond to Unsatisfied and Very unsatisfied. The device board reads: The Source, I want that. Some KPIs come directly from you. When you rate your level of satisfaction as a customer, the business receives quantitative data for use in identifying problems, tracking progress, and prioritizing spending. Feedback from customers, often collected during the checkout process or with email surveys, yields valuable KPIs. Customer satisfaction ratings are measurements of how pleased customers are with a business’s product or shopping experience. These ratings are useful because they provide quantitative feedback that can be tracked over time to help the business spot early signs of declining service or product quality. For example, In-N-Out Burger uses customer satisfaction ratings to monitor its performance and identify areas to improve. The company reportedly excels at burger quality, staff friendliness, cleanliness, and order accuracy, among other areas. The quality of its fries, however, leaves room for improvement. 1 customer satisfaction ratings Measurements of how pleased customers are with a business’s product or shopping experience.

TMP-1372.navLabel: KPIs for Marketing and Sales Goals
TMP-1372.text: The number of returning customers is also telling. Customer retention data are measurements of a business’s ability to keep its customers over time. For instance, the retention rate is the percentage of customers who remain as customers over a specified period; the churn rate is the percentage of customers who are lost over a specified period; the repeat purchase rate is the percentage of customers who make a second purchase; and the renewal rate is the percentage of customers who renew a subscription or service. Netflix, for example, keeps close tabs on the renewal rate for its streaming services, especially after a price increase. Smaller companies can sometimes obtain customer retention data from online sales platforms such as Amazon, and delivery services such as DoorDash provide customer retention data to the merchants they serve. High retention levels suggest a good product-market fit and healthy customer relationships. Low or declining retention levels may signal customer dissatisfaction or intense competition. Retention is important, because it often costs less to retain a customer than to acquire a new one. And, because retained customers are loyal and have familiarity with the business, they tend to spend more than new customers. customer retention data Measurements of a business’s ability to keep its customers over time.

Some KPIs are conveniently available from online sales platforms such as Amazon or from delivery services such as DoorDash. Of course, how much you sell is also a useful KPI. Total sales is the quantity of units sold over a specified period, such as a month, quarter, or year. Rising total sales often indicates demand growth, which may signal successful marketing. For example, an increase in the total sales of Eggo frozen waffles confirmed the success of Kellanova’s product placement marketing on the show Stranger Things , in which Eggos were a character’s favorite food. 2 Total sales also increase when prices fall, even if consumers have not changed their level of interest in the product. For example, a drop in the price of Hershey’s bars is likely to increase the quantity sold, even if nothing has happened to

TMP-1375.navLabel: KPIs for Marketing and Sales Goals
TMP-1375.text: change consumers’ taste for chocolate. Declining sales can indicate problems with product-market fit, pricing strategies, rising competition, or customer satisfaction. A small business might break total sales down by product category to help guide inventory decisions. It is common for large businesses to use enterprise resource planning systems or other software to study sales by product, store, region, or sales team. This allows those businesses to track progress toward goals and compare performance against forecasts and historical data. total sales The quantity of units sold over a specified period, such as a month, quarter, or year. AP® EXAM TIP An exam question might ask you to suggest a KPI for a business seeking to monitor its financial health, marketing, or operations. Be prepared to explain not only the KPIs for each area, but also the interpretation of changes in their values. One measure of a business’s relevance and competitiveness is its market share — the portion of the total sales in a market made up by the sales of that business. For example, Kroger’s market share in the U.S. grocery market is around 9%. 3 This means that 9% of

TMP-1376.text: all expenditures on groceries in the United States were made at Kroger. Growth in market share can indicate strength and strategic effectiveness, and can result from successful products, pricing, marketing, and expansion into new locations. Shrinking market share may indicate falling consumer demand and the need for new strategies to invigorate competitiveness. market share The portion of the total sales in the market made up by the sales of the business. KPIs for Operations Goals When managing a business’s day-to-day operations, it helps to have KPIs that measure cost control and efficiency. Common operations goals involve faster speeds for production and delivery, greater accuracy for order fulfillment, and cost cutting in all areas of the business. In this section, we will examine four KPIs used to track progress toward such goals. In Module 2.5 , we introduced per-unit cost — the average cost of producing and distributing a product — which turns out to be a useful KPI. A lower per-unit cost

TMP-1377.text: typically means production is becoming more efficient, as could result from more productive workers, the use of cost-saving automation, or new methods that reduce input costs. For example, the Coca-Cola Company found ways to redesign soda bottles to reduce their plastic content by more than 31%, thereby reducing its cost of materials. The KPI of per-unit cost reveals the success of cost control initiatives and the progress toward production efficiency goals. A second KPI for operations goals is delivery cost — the expense of transporting goods from a business to its customer or between locations in the supply chain. This expense can include the costs of shipping, fuel, delivery workers, packaging, shipping insurance, and payments for outsourced delivery services. The many elements of delivery cost represent opportunities for efficiency gains or losses. By tracking this KPI, a business becomes aware of any cost increases that may warrant consideration of alternative delivery methods. After an increase in the cost of insuring delivery vehicles, a local sandwich shop may find it can save money by outsourcing delivery to a service such as Uber Eats or DoorDash. And an online luggage seller may discover cost-saving strategies such as having the U.S. Postal Service ship lightweight packages and Federal Express or United Parcel Service ship heavier packages.

TMP-1378.text: delivery cost The expense of transporting goods from a business to its customer or between locations in the supply chain.

TMP-1379.text: Ute Grabowsky/Getty Images Whether orders are picked (retrieved from inventory) by people or by robots as in this pharmacy, correct product picking can be crucial to a business and to customer safety. This helps to explain why order accuracy is a KPI.

TMP-1380.text: Most of us have received the wrong size or color of something, or had an order shipped to the wrong address. Errors are also expensive, because they trigger costly returns, refunds, and reshipments. Errors also damage the customer experience, trust in the brand, and customer retention. These potential problems motivate our third KPI for operational goals: Order accuracy is the percentage of customer orders filled without errors. The goal is for the right quantities of the right goods to be delivered to the right place, but errors are common. Low order accuracy may indicate problems with mislabeling, employee training, or warehouse organization. order accuracy The percentage of customer orders filled without errors. Since customers don’t pull items off store shelves when they shop online, e-commerce businesses are also vulnerable to errors in product picking (when a human or, increasingly, an AI-enabled robot retrieves items from inventory) and product packing (when items are boxed for shipment to the customer). For these processes, speed can be the enemy of accuracy. Accuracy improves when workers take their time. But faster order fulfillment lowers labor costs and makes customers happy — if they get what they want.

TMP-1381.text: To keep tabs on the dual interests of speed and accuracy, businesses track delivery time. The KPI on-time delivery rate is the percentage of deliveries received on time. This is calculated as the number of on-time deliveries divided by the total number of deliveries, multiplied by 100. If a business made 200 deliveries last month and 192 of them arrived on time, the on-time delivery rate was (192 ÷ 200) × 100 = 96%. This KPI indicates the reliability of the business’s promised delivery time. An unacceptable or falling percentage indicates the need to address issues such as low stock levels, production delays, unreliable shippers, or inadequate staffing. Like order inaccuracy, slow delivery can cause problems with the customer experience, trust, and retention, especially when customers can purchase the same products quickly in a nearby store. Figure 4.2-1 summarizes several important KPIs in each category. on-time delivery rate The percentage of deliveries received on time, calculated as the number of on-time deliveries divided by the total number of deliveries, multiplied by 100.

TMP-1385.text: Benchmarks LG What are benchmarks, and how do businesses use them? A KPI is of little use if it is unclear what a good number would be. What is the target? Is the business underperforming or overperforming? Ambiguous expectations for KPIs leave room not only for differing goals among company leaders, but also for adjustments in standards to fit performance levels. If there are no clearly defined expectations, a manager in a low-performing department can argue that their KPI values are satisfactory. As a remedy for these problems, businesses use benchmarks. A benchmark is a reference point that provides a standard for comparison. benchmark A reference point that provides a standard for comparison.

TMP-1386.text: Selecting Benchmarks A business selecting benchmarks for performance has options not unlike the ones you have when evaluating your grades. If you compare your grade on one exam to your grade on a past exam, you’re using an internal benchmark. Likewise, a business can use internal benchmarks by considering its own historical (past) performance levels. For example, if clothing retailer Hollister wants to know if it had a good year, one gauge would be to compare this year’s sales revenue to last year’s sales revenue. There are also external benchmarks. To gain perspective on your exam grade, you might compare it to the grade of a friend or to the class average. A business can similarly use the performance levels of rivals as external benchmarks. For instance, a coffee shop can use the average customer satisfaction rating of its closest competitor on Yelp or Tripadvisor as a benchmark for its own ratings. If a business has a primary rival to pursue, performance levels from that other business can provide ideal benchmarks. For a business that wants to learn how it stacks up against its broader group of peer organizations, average KPI values for whole industries are sometimes available as standards. For example, the stock investing

TMP-1387.text: research platform FullRatio reports that the average gross profit margin is about 42% for the retail apparel industry and 23% for the auto parts industry. 4 And First Page Sage estimates that the average customer acquisition cost is $720 for the software development industry and $533 for the business consulting industry. 5 Benchmarks such as these give every market participant a target to aim for. Applying Benchmarks Having identified benchmarks, a business can objectively assess its performance by comparing KPI outcomes with established standards. Figure 4.2-2 details eight steps you can use to apply benchmarks to a business project. By using KPIs to spot gaps in performance, setting realistic goals for improvement, implementing strategies to achieve those goals, tracking progress over time, and following up with new approaches as needed, businesses can recognize and remedy underperforming areas. In the next module, we will examine how businesses make the underlying decisions and develop the strategies that help them achieve success.

TMP-1388.text: Step 1 Define the objectives of interest (such as strong customer retention and low delivery cost). Step 2 Identify Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) that address the business’s objectives. Step 3 Choose KPI benchmarks for comparison. These might be based on: The business’s past performance The performance of rivals Industry averages Step 4 Compare KPIs against benchmarks to assess performance. If the business is meetings its benchmarks, it can consider raising its benchmarks for the next assessment period. If the business is underperforming, proceed to Step 5. Step 5 Set realistic goals for the timing of improvements to meet or surpass benchmarks. Step 6 Implement strategies to improve areas where performance is below benchmarks. Step 7 Track progress over time using the KPIs. Step 8 Revise strategies as needed to address areas of continued underperformance. Copyright © BFW Publishers

TMP-1392.text: Module 4.2 Review Learning Goals LG How do businesses evaluate performance? • A key performance indicator (KPI) is a measurable value used to evaluate how well a business is achieving its objectives. KPIs help a business monitor strategy effectiveness and progress toward both short-term and long-term goals. Managers choose KPIs that align with the mission and goals of the business. LG How do businesses use financial and nonfinancial KPIs to track their financial health and progress toward goals?

TMP-1393.text: • KPIs for financial health include revenue, the cost of goods sold, gross profit, gross profit margin, operating expenses, operating profit, operating profit margin, and cash flow. • KPIs for marketing and sales goals include the customer acquisition cost, customer lifetime value, customer satisfaction ratings (measurements of how pleased customers are with a business’s product or shopping experience), customer retention data (measurements of a business’s ability to keep its customers over time), total sales (the quantity of units sold over a specified period, such as a month, quarter, or year), and market share (the portion of the total sales in the market made up by the sales of the business). • KPIs for operations goals include the per-unit cost, delivery cost (the expense of transporting goods from a business to its customer or between locations in the supply chain), order accuracy (the percentage of customer orders filled without errors), and on-time delivery rate (the percentage of deliveries received on time). LG What are benchmarks, and how do businesses use them?

TMP-1394.text: • KPIs are difficult to interpret if there is uncertainty about what constitutes weak and strong performance. A benchmark is a reference point that provides a standard for comparison. Available benchmarks include historical performance levels for the business and for primary competitors. In some cases, averages for KPIs across an industry are available as standards. • Having identified benchmarks, a business can objectively assess its performance by comparing KPI outcomes with established standards. By using KPIs to spot gaps in performance, setting realistic goals for improvement, implementing strategies to achieve those goals, tracking progress over time, and following up with new approaches as needed, businesses can recognize and remedy underperforming areas.

This may be the reason why its churn rate is increasing and its repeat rate, while outperforming its rival and the industry, is diminishing. c. The company is thriving. There is no need for adjustments. d. The company should consider shutting down. Its order accuracy and on-time delivery rates are below the industry average, and its repeat purchase rate is falling.

TMP-1399.text: CASE STUDY Ford Motor Company ROBERTO PFEIL/Getty Images What is the best way to paint a car? Manufacturers are always searching for more-efficient production methods. Ford uses KPIs such as per-unit cost to reveal opportunities for improvement and progress toward goals. Henry Ford and a group of investors launched the Ford Motor Company in Detroit, Michigan, in 1903. The company introduced its first car that year, the Model

TMP-1400.text: A, for around $800 ($30,000 in today’s dollars). Five years later, Ford launched the Model T at about the same price as the Model A, but things soon changed. In 1913, Ford revolutionized production with the moving assembly line — a production system that carries a product from one workstation to another. At each workstation, a worker (or robot, in modern times) performs one specific, repetitive task, such as installing the steering wheel. The efficiency of this system lowered production costs dramatically. Despite raising the minimum wage for Ford employees to an impressive $5 per day (about $160 in today’s dollars) — double the normal wage for that industry — by 1924, Ford was still able to drop the price of the Model T to $290 (about $5,400 in today’s dollars). With a price tag that made car ownership available to middle-income customers, the Model T became the most popular car in the world. During World War II, Ford shifted its production to military vehicles, including jeeps, airplanes, and tanks. After the war, in 1945, Ford shifted back to passenger car production and had success with new models such as the Ford Thunderbird, introduced in 1955, and the Ford Mustang, introduced in 1964. But starting in the 1970s, the availability of affordable, reliable, and fuel-efficient imported cars

TMP-1401.text: challenged the viability of Ford and other U.S. automakers. The company had more turbulent years ahead, with spiking gas prices in the late 1970s, economic downturns that caused large losses in the 1980s and early 2000s, and global supply-chain disruptions in 2022 that slowed production. There were good years amid the turbulence, but the ups and downs made it important for Ford to track its progress carefully. For example, Ford’s inflation-adjusted annual revenue fell from $237 billion in 2007 to $174 billion in 2009, rose fairly steadily to $205 billion in 2018, fell to $159 billion in 2020, and rose to $190 billion in 2024. 6 Ford’s approach to KPIs resembles what is known as a balanced scorecard system, because it helps managers assess the interrelated elements of a successful business without creating information overload. Following this approach, a business focuses on four perspectives: the financial perspective of shareholders, the customer perspective, the internal perspective of what is important to the business, and the innovation and learning perspective of how the business can improve. 7 The balanced scorecard assures attention to the most important KPIs in each of these areas and prevents managers from being bogged down by excessive focus on, say,

TMP-1402.text: financial data while missing underlying problems in other areas, such as customer service or innovation. In Ford’s case, the company collects KPIs on all the areas discussed in this module — among others, including safety (such as the number of workplace injuries) and sustainability (such as fuel efficiency). To maintain a balanced perspective, the company’s reports divide their attention among KPIs from the financial, customer, internal, and innovation perspectives. For example, when Ford reported on its Ford+ strategy for the future, it discussed financial matters such as profit margins; customer experience issues, such as the length of price negotiations; internal interests, such as the number of parts per car (Ford eliminated 2,400 parts from the F-150 truck to reduce production complexity!); and innovations such as the number of new electric vehicle models. 8 When driving a car, you want to consider your speed, fuel supply, direction, and surroundings. Overlooking any one of those matters could bring your whole mission to an unfortunate end. With a similarly balanced perspective on KPIs, Ford has kept its cars on the road for over a century.

TMP-1403.text: APPLY YOUR AP ® SKILLS 1. Ford uses the number of workplace injuries per 100 full-time North American employees as a KPI. Explain two ways the company could establish a benchmark for this metric. 2. Ford Pro is the segment of Ford dedicated to providing vehicles for business customers. Suppose that as the president of Ford Pro, you could consider one additional KPI that is not discussed in the case but is covered in this module. Identify that KPI and explain why you chose it. 3. Ford is interested in both cost cutting and innovation, but there are tradeoffs between these objectives, because innovation costs money. Explain how Ford could use KPIs to avoid excessive focus on one or the other of these objectives.

TMP-1404.text: MODULE 4.3 Strategy and Decision Making LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 4.3.A Explain the reasons and methods for the use of business strategy 4.3.B Describe the use of a deliberative process for business decision making

TMP-1405.text: A B A clear strategy. A B A common strategy. Photo credit David Anderson Extended description for Strategies The clear strategy is represented as a horizontal arrow pointing from A to B . The common strategy is represented by an arrow that moves from A , loops around itself several times, going up and down and around and around, before reaching B .

TMP-1406.text: Too many business strategies are convoluted or poorly conveyed. A clear strategy helps a business make decisions and reach goals.

TMP-1407.text: Business Strategy LG What is a business strategy, and how do businesses use strategies to achieve goals? Whether you’re trying to win a chess match, cut down a tree, collect blood donations, or save money for college, strategy provides a roadmap and promotes focus on the path forward. Businesses, too, have much to gain from strategy. Business strategy outlines how a business plans to achieve its goals. A clear strategy helps to align employees with the mission of the business, guide decisions, and enhance the prospect of success. Like a sports team without a game plan, a business without a strategy is likely to be disorganized and uncompetitive. In this section, the plan is to examine the formation and application of business strategy. business strategy An outline for how a business plans to achieve its goals.

TMP-1408.text: Choosing a Strategy Strategy selection begins with consideration of the underlying goal. Common goals include achieving competitive advantage, growth, operational efficiency, innovation, employee development, image repair, profit, and customer satisfaction. After the health insurance company Humana identified the goal of improving customer satisfaction, it developed a strategy to improve the customer experience with its call centers. The company trained its call center agents to empathize with customers and make their interactions more personal. Humana empowered agents to take charge of customer issues and see them through to resolution. And Humana further supported its agents’ efforts by providing them with AI tools that could analyze their calls in real time and provide additional suggestions and solutions for their clients. The strategy worked: In 2024, Humana was ranked No. 1 among health insurers for customer experience for the fourth year in a row. Optimal strategy selection also depends on the industry, the competitive environment, and the skills of the employees. Data plays a key role in the identification of successful strategies. For example, the best pricing strategy depends on the price sensitivity of customers, which data analysis reveals is high in the grocery industry and

TMP-1409.text: low in the healthcare industry. Marketing strategies should be more ambitious in highly competitive industries. And to choose appropriate strategies for growth, managers must consider the existing gaps in the market, the strengths of the employees, and the unique capabilities of the company. The team at web software company 37signals is great at writing programs with a focus on simplicity and communication. The company first launched project-management software called Basecamp, which helps work teams organize and collaborate on projects. Drawing on its strengths, the company’s growth strategy was then to create other user-friendly communications software, such as the HEY email program and the Campfire online chat service. In contrast, when online megastore Amazon tried to expand with a strategy of opening small pop-up stores in malls, the project failed, showing that small-scale, in-person retail was outside Amazon’s area of expertise.

TMP-1410.text: Extended description for 37 Signals Seven talking heads surround the icons for fourteen different products, such as Teams, PowerPoint, Word, and others. The icons are marked out with a big black X. In clockwise order, the talking heads say the following: • Wait, who made that decision? • I don't know where to put that! • Wait, can the client see that?! • This is exhausting! I don't know where to look!

TMP-1411.text: • But no one told me that! • Wait, when is this due? • Did we get that done yet? The strategy adopted by 37signals, maker of Basecamp software for team projects, is to keep things simple. Using a Strategy With a strategy in place, a business has a guidepost for decision making. The business can develop tactics , which are specific actions taken to carry out the chosen strategy. Whereas the strategy is an overall plan to achieve the business’s goals, tactics are steps taken in the day-to-day execution of the plan. For example, a business that has the goal of gaining market share in the earbuds market might have a strategy of differentiating its product with superior noise cancellation. A tactic for that business could be to hire an audio engineer who can conduct research and development on noise-cancellation hardware. Another tactic could be to partner with a business that excels in noise-cancellation technology.

TMP-1412.text: tactics Specific actions taken to carry out a strategy. Like the formation of a strategy, the effectiveness of a strategy should be considered on the basis of data and KPIs as discussed in Module 4.2 . Are the tactics working? Is progress being made? Without monitoring efforts by gathering and tracking specific data, it is easy for business leaders to make incorrect assumptions about strategy success. After identifying and gathering the relevant data on financial performance, customer satisfaction, market share, and other objectives, the business can better understand what is working and what tactics should be modified. Consider Jabra, a brand owned by the Danish company GN Group. Jabra initially pursued its goal to “make life sound better” primarily as a maker of headsets and speakerphones for businesses. 1 After studying data from the consumer market, the company shifted its strategy to include a new venture into consumer products. The data from B2C sales led Jabra to restructure into two divisions: one for enterprise (business) products and another for consumer products. The expansion strategy into consumer audio involved several tactics. Jabra: • used competitive pricing to contend with rivals like Apple, Bose, and Sony;

TMP-1413.text: • differentiated its products with water and dust resistance for users on the go; • and broadened its distribution channels to include more online platforms and major retailers. By monitoring key performance indicators and adjusting its strategy in response to the data, Jabra built a strong reputation as a producer of high-quality earbuds and other consumer audio equipment. Quang NGUYEN DUC/Alamy Stock Photo Data on financial performance, customer preferences, competition, and market trends is an appropriate driver for strategy decisions. Jabra successfully modified its business strategy after studying data on trends in the consumer audio market.

TMP-1415.navLabel: A Deliberative Process for Decision Making
TMP-1415.text: The Decision-Making Process LG How do managers use a deliberative process to make business decisions? Business leaders face seemingly endless decisions about products, pricing, staffing, operations, marketing, growth, and related strategies. Decisions made swiftly or without careful analysis of all the options can lead a business down a dead-end road. In this section, we consider a structured process for making thoughtful and informed decisions, and we examine the criteria businesses often use for such decisions. A Deliberative Process for Decision Making Yahoo was a leading search engine, web portal, and purveyor of online services in the 1990s. In 1998, they decided to pass on the opportunity to purchase a small search engine company called Google for $1 million. Four years later, after Google had grown, Yahoo offered $3 billion for it, but decided not to pay Google’s reported asking price of

headings.text: A Deliberative Process for Decision Making

TMP-1416.navLabel: A Deliberative Process for Decision Making
TMP-1416.text: $5 billion. Flash forward to 2025, and Google held almost 90% of the worldwide search engine market, while Yahoo held just over 1%. With Alphabet, Google’s parent company, valued at over $2 trillion, it’s clear that Yahoo made some regrettable decisions.

TMP-1417.navLabel: A Deliberative Process for Decision Making
TMP-1417.text: Roberto Machado Noa/Getty Images A decision can make all the difference. When Google was up for sale, Yahoo — a dominant search engine company at the time — made the unfortunate decision not to buy it. Today, Google holds almost 90% of the search engine market, while Yahoo’s market share is around 1%.

TMP-1418.navLabel: A Deliberative Process for Decision Making
TMP-1418.text: AP ® EXAM TIP PACED is an acronym that will help you remember the Problem, Alternatives, Criteria, Evaluation, and Decision elements of this process. Acronyms are one of several memory aids known as mnemonic devices that can be a secret to success on the AP® Exam. Another is acrostics, which are sentences where the first letter of each word stands for another word you are trying to remember. For example, to come up with the stages of the product life cycle, it may help to remember, “I Grow Many Daisies,” where the first letters of these words represent “Introduction, Growth, Maturity, and Decline.” If there are other sets of words you have trouble remembering, create your own acrostic! To be fair, hindsight is 20-20. Decades ago, Yahoo didn’t know what we know now about growth in the search engine market and the success of Google’s brand. So how can business leaders make wise strategy decisions when they don’t know what the future holds? Despite limited or imperfect information, a business can make better decisions by adopting a deliberative process — a structured approach to decision making involving thoughtful consideration and evaluation of the options. In this process, it is common to establish criteria , which are standards used to evaluate alternatives and inform decisions. One such deliberative process is PACED , which involves defining the problem, developing alternatives, establishing criteria, evaluating

TMP-1419.navLabel: A Deliberative Process for Decision Making
TMP-1419.text: options, and then making the decision. Table 4.3-1 details the five steps of the PACED process. deliberative process A structured approach to decision making involving thoughtful consideration and evaluation of the options. criteria Standards used to evaluate alternatives and inform decisions. PACED A deliberative process that involves defining the problem, developing alternatives, establishing criteria, evaluating options, and making the decision. Table 4.3-1 The PACED Deliberative Process Problem The business defines the problem in terms of the decision(s) that must be made. The problem might be that the business must decide which product to offer, what price to charge, or which marketing strategy to adopt. Alternatives The business identifies existing alternatives and, if possible, develops new alternatives . For example, a business facing the decision of how to handle declining product sales might begin deliberations with the options of advertising more, offering discounts, or discontinuing the product. With focus on this step, the business might develop additional alternatives, such as redesigning the product or bundling the product with complementary products.

TMP-1420.navLabel: A Deliberative Process for Decision Making
TMP-1420.text: Criteria The business determines the criteria , or the standards it will use to evaluate the alternatives. Criteria might include the cost of each alternative, its alignment with the business’s mission, the time it would take, and the level of risk involved. (We will explore the selection of criteria in the next section.) Evaluation The business evaluates each alternative against the criteria. This might involve ranking the alternatives or developing a scoring system. Decision The business reaches a decision . The business chooses the best option based on careful evaluation using the selected criteria. Suppose a furniture store needs a new marketing strategy and has decided to address the associated decision with the PACED deliberative process. This store’s problem is that it must choose a new way to advertise its products. In the past, it has used an email campaign, social media advertisements, and radio commercials. At a meeting of the store’s managers, they develop additional alternatives of hiring an influencer to promote the company online and placing an advertising banner on the fence at the local high school’s soccer field. The criteria it considers most important are cost, reach (how many potential customers will encounter it), and impact (how much revenue it will generate). The store would then evaluate the alternatives based on the criteria and let the results

TMP-1421.text: inform the selection of the best type of advertising. Next, we’ll explore how decision-making criteria are chosen and applied. Decision-Making Criteria Business leadership demands a whole lot of decision making. A business may need to choose a strategy for which markets to enter, services to offer, or technologies to adopt. In the contemplation of criteria for such decisions, it is important to account for the tradeoffs that are inescapable in business and in life. This means considering the cons — risks, costs, expenditures of time, challenges in implementation — that accompany the pros . Any strategy option worth considering will offer benefits. With the proper criteria, those benefits can be weighed against the costs. Criteria should incorporate key costs and benefits, whether they are quantifiable or not. The financial costs, sales revenue, and profit expected to result from a decision are quantifiable — they are numbers that can be estimated. Suppose a retailer must decide whether to open a new store in New York City’s famous Times Square. The finance department could review the best available data from similar decisions — that business’s decision to open stores in other big cities, or other businesses’ decisions to open in

TMP-1422.text: Times Square — to project the quantifiable outcomes from that opening. There are also intangible (not directly measurable) impacts that must not be overlooked, such as the reputational effect of having a store in a prestigious location alongside the world’s most famous brands. In this section, we examine common criteria for decision making, practical ways to assess intangibles, and the option of employing strategic frameworks.

TMP-1423.text: Alexander Spatari/Getty Images Extended description for Times Square The buildings display numerous advertisements of varying sizes on electronic billboards.

TMP-1424.text: The costs and benefits of opening a store in New York City’s Times Square can be directly quantifiable, such as added profit, and intangible, such as improved brand image. Criteria for decision making should incorporate all costs and benefits. Key Considerations A business typically has several options for how to invest its money. Decisions are made easier by clear, measurable criteria. A common financial consideration is the return on investment (ROI) , which is the added (net) profit from an investment divided by the cost of that investment (multiplied by 100 to express the result as a percentage): ROI = Net Profit × 100 Investment Cost return on investment (ROI) The added (net) profit from an investment divided by the cost of that investment (multiplied by 100 to express the result as a percentage).

TMP-1425.text: For example, if a new marketing strategy would cost $20,000, increase revenue by $50,000, and increase production costs by $25,000, the net profit would be $50,000 − $25,000 − $20,000 = $5,000, and the ROI would be: ROI = $5,000 × 100 = 25 % $20,000 The business may also want criteria to evaluate market considerations such as competitiveness, operational considerations such as supply chain risks, and organizational considerations such as the effect on employee morale. For instance, suppose a hospital is considering new strategies to reduce employee absences, such as reductions in the number of paid sick days and vacation days. The hospital should include not only criteria that capture financial benefits from each policy, but also criteria that account for employee departures and difficulties recruiting workers due to less-appealing employment policies. Some of these impacts are intangible, as we will discuss next.

TMP-1426.text: Accounting for Intangibles A decision’s intangible costs and benefits related to reputation, brand image, employee morale, corporate mission, and core values should also be considered. Although these costs and benefits are not directly measurable in dollars, in some cases, there are ways to analyze them in quantitative terms. For example, suppose a clothing company is deciding whether to move the production of its jeans overseas. The effects of this move on brand image could be quantified in terms of the expected loss in sales due to customers who perceive brands with overseas production as being less authentic. The dollar value of that loss could be estimated based on the experience of other companies that moved production overseas, past experience with similar changes by the clothing company itself, or surveys of likely customers. In other cases, the evaluation of intangibles can be measured using rating scales , which are sets of categories that represent a range of possible perceptions. Perhaps you’ve been asked to rate your experience with an online purchase or a streaming service on a scale from 1 to 5 stars. Similarly, customers can be asked to rate the options a business is contemplating using scales such as:

TMP-1427.text: Low/Medium/High to indicate the degree or intensity of a perception Positive/Neutral/Negative to capture sentiments for or against an option 1 to 10 to rate the level of favorability, effectiveness, or importance of something These scales convert customer perceptions into data on intangible costs and benefits that can be analyzed to inform the decision-making process. This data can be collected from stakeholders using surveys, focus groups, employee feedback, and customer interviews, as discussed in Module 2.3 . As an example, a company considering the use of AI for customer support could survey customers and ask whether they would feel positive, neutral, or negative about interacting with an AI support agent.

TMP-1428.text: Francesco Carta fotografo/Getty Images Extended description for AI Purchasing The woman appears blurry in the background as her finger touches the screen. The top left corner of the screen shows a robot icon, while the top right

TMP-1429.text: corner shows three gears. Text reads: Hello! Can I do something for you? How do you feel about making purchases from businesses that use AI customer support? When decisions are made about AI strategies, businesses should consider both the cost savings on staff and the reaction of customers, who may or may not respond favorably. AP ® SKILLS TIP A skilled decision maker incorporates easily neglected factors. Be careful to consider tangible and intangible impacts. Adopt criteria that weigh both the benefits and the costs. Include internal and external factors. And evaluate not only the readily apparent alternatives, but those that can be developed with additional thought and research. Strategic Frameworks To guide planning and support careful choices, a business can employ a strategic framework as a structured approach to understanding a situation, setting priorities, and aligning decisions with long-term goals. Strategic frameworks help a business choose among alternative locations, investments, directions for growth, areas of specialization,

TMP-1430.text: or other courses of action. The PESTEL analysis discussed in Module 1.3 provides one such framework for assessing the political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal factors relevant to a business. In the next module, you will learn two more strategic frameworks that help a business systematically analyze internal and external factors relevant to important decisions. The first is Porter’s Five Forces, which allows a business to better understand the competitiveness of its industry, which in turn informs decisions such as whether to enter a market and how to position a brand relative to competitors. The second is SWOT analysis, which guides key strategy decisions by shedding light on internal strengths and weaknesses along with external opportunities and threats. strategic framework A structured approach to understanding a situation, setting priorities, and aligning decisions with long-term goals. It is important to acknowledge that decision making is risky business. Managers must select strategies and tactics based on imperfect or limited data. The many available criteria may have conflicting implications, forcing leaders to prioritize certain criteria as the bases for decisions. For example, celebrity endorsements score high for the benefit of likeability, but also high for risk, because celebrities often get enmeshed in

TMP-1431.text: scandals that could taint the image of the associated brand. Cost-saving production strategies — such as using cheaper material — often shine when evaluated using criteria such as per-unit cost, but cause business leaders to cringe when assessing criteria for quality and brand image. The need to prioritize conflicting criteria and contend with data limitations makes it all the more important to take the time needed for deliberative decision-making processes like PACED, and for strategic frameworks like those discussed in Module 4.4 .

TMP-1432.text: Module 4.3 Review Learning Goals LG What is a business strategy, and how do businesses use strategies to achieve goals? Business strategy outlines how a business plans to achieve its goals. A clear strategy helps to align employees with the mission of the business, guide decisions, and enhance the prospect of success. A business can develop tactics , which are specific actions taken to carry out the strategy. Whereas the strategy is an overall plan to achieve the business’s goals, tactics are steps taken in the day-to-day execution of the plan. LG How do managers use a deliberative process to make business decisions?

TMP-1433.text: A business can make better decisions by adopting a deliberative process — a structured approach to decision making involving thoughtful consideration and evaluation of the options. In this process, it is common to establish criteria , which are standards used to evaluate alternatives and inform decisions. One such deliberative process has the acronym-based title PACED, which is a good way to remember its focus on defining the problem , developing alternatives, establishing criteria , evaluating options, and then making the decision . Criteria should incorporate key costs and benefits, whether they are quantifiable or not. A common financial criterion is the return on investment (ROI) , which is the added (net) profit from an investment divided by the cost of that investment (multiplied by 100 to express the result as a percentage). Businesses may also want criteria to evaluate market considerations such as competitiveness, operational considerations such as supply chain risks, and organizational considerations such as the effect on employee morale. Intangible costs and benefits are not directly quantified, although numerical estimates can be made, for example, based on their effect on sales or advertising

TMP-1434.text: costs. In other cases, intangible costs can be evaluated using qualitative criteria, such as scales of Low/Medium/High or Positive/Neutral/Negative. To guide planning and support careful choices, a business can employ a strategic framework as a structured approach to understanding a situation, setting priorities, and aligning decisions with long-term goals. Practice Your AP ® Skills Preparing for the AP ® Exam Multiple-Choice Questions 1. PACED is an acronym for the deliberative process of decision-making that stands for a. Problem, Action, Creation, Evaluation, Deliberation b. Performance, Action, Continuation, Establishment, Decision c. Problem, Alternatives, Criteria, Evaluation, Decision

TMP-1435.text: d. Preparation, Alternatives, Critique, Evaluation, Determination 2. Jean owns a glass art studio and is considering investing in a waterjet laser cutting machine that costs $20,000. Jean estimates that this machine will cause her sales revenue to increase by $40,000 and production costs to increase by $10,000. What is the return on investment (ROI) for this machine? a. $10,000 b. 50% c. 100% d. 200% 3. Pat’s Pizza is considering two new pizza ovens. The first one is a wood-fired oven and costs $21,000. The second one is a natural gas-burning oven and costs $9,000. Pat believes that many customers will value the intangible benefits of the wood-fired oven, such as its authenticity, aroma, locally sourced fuel, and effects on flavor. What is a good way for Pat to choose the oven that will maximize his profit?

TMP-1436.text: a. Pat should choose the natural gas-burning oven because it minimizes costs. b. Pat should choose the oven that maximizes the ROI estimated based on equal sales from each oven. c. Before making a final decision, Pat should survey potential customers to find out how strongly they would favor pizza baked in a wood-fired oven. d. Pat should choose the wood-fired oven because it provides intangible benefits. 4. Which of the following would be considered an intangible cost for Karl’s Cat Training Corps as it decides whether to outsource customer service to a call center operated by another company? a. reduced wage costs b. reduced customer satisfaction c. increased profits from the reduction in costs d. increased stock price due to higher profits 5. Which of the following would be considered an intangible benefit for a professional sports team that is considering adding seats to its stadium?

TMP-1437.text: a. increased parking revenue b. increased ticket sales c. increased prestige from having a larger stadium d. increased food concession revenue

TMP-1438.text: CASE STUDY Microsoft JASON REDMOND/Getty Images Extended description for Windows AI Foundry The screen behind Nadella reads, Announcing Windows AI Foundry . Tools to optimize inbox models. Open source models. Bring your own Windows ML model.

TMP-1439.text: The leaders of the world’s most successful companies, such as Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, eat, sleep, and breathe strategy. Microsoft’s growth strategy is to invest heavily in business acquisitions, cloud computing, gaming, and AI. There are few companies as well known as Microsoft, one of the world’s largest technology companies. Headquartered in Redmond, Washington, Microsoft employs 181,000 people worldwide, with subsidiaries in over 100 countries. Today, the company operates in three segments of the technology industry: productivity and business processes, intelligent cloud, and personal computing. Microsoft was founded in 1975 by Bill Gates and Paul Allen, two friends who foresaw the power of putting computers into the hands of everyday users. Since its inception, Microsoft has remained a leader in the ever-changing technology industry, where former giants like Netscape and Compaq did not survive. Under the leadership of CEO Bill Gates, Microsoft’s suite of Windows and Office products became the standard for productivity software all over the world.

TMP-1440.text: When Gates stepped down in 2000, incoming CEO Steve Ballmer continued Gates’s vision for Microsoft’s dominance in the tech industry. Microsoft gained a reputation for being hostile to competitors — a trait that won Microsoft few friends in the highly collaborative, open-source culture of Silicon Valley. However, in the early 2000s, when other tech firms were focused on the internet, cloud computing, and smartphones, Microsoft concentrated on desktop computers. Though still very profitable, this decision to maintain its focus on PCs led to stagnating shareholder value. As Gates noted, “Sometimes we get taken by surprise. For example, when the Internet came along, we had it as a fifth or sixth priority.” 2 When Satya Nadella became CEO in 2014, he changed the strategic direction of the company. First, he refocused the company by revising its mission statement to “empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more.” 3 Next, he unveiled a three-tiered strategy to encourage innovation in the company: (1) invest in cloud computing and target Microsoft services to iPhone, Android, Linux, and Mac users; (2) focus on technological growth areas like AI, quantum computing (which uses the principles of quantum physics to speed information processing), and mixed reality (which blends real and virtual environments); and

TMP-1441.text: (3) promote a collaborative culture of empathy and inclusion that encourages risk taking. For example, in 2019, Microsoft took its collaborative culture outside of its Redmond campus by partnering with competitors like Oracle. With Microsoft’s Azure cloud computing service integrated with Oracle’s Cloud Infrastructure, customers enjoy a seamless experience of the two leading cloud service providers in tech. In another successful tech partnership, Microsoft integrated Adobe’s PDF capabilities into Microsoft 365 to bring customers the benefits of both types of software. Microsoft also partnered with companies like Topcoder and WiPro. These companies expanded the number of testers giving feedback on devices and documenting errors in Microsoft operating systems. Under Nadella’s leadership, most of Microsoft’s revenue has been tied to relationships with partners. Microsoft’s growth in market share is also a result of strategic acquisitions. In 1987, Microsoft made its first acquisition of the company Forethought, which had pioneered a presentation program that would later become PowerPoint. When Ballmer was CEO, Microsoft continued to make about 10 acquisitions deals annually. But under Nadella’s leadership, the acquisitions signaled Microsoft’s

TMP-1442.text: interest in taking bigger risks. For instance, compare Ballmer’s acquisition of cell phone company Nokia to Nadella’s acquisition of video game developer Activision Blizzard. One might characterize the 2013 Nokia acquisition as reactive, an attempt to catch up to Apple and Google in the smartphone market, whereas the Activision Blizzard acquisition in 2023 demonstrated Microsoft’s intention to be on the cutting edge of game development and “provide building blocks for the metaverse.” 4 The Activision Blizzard deal was Microsoft’s biggest investment yet, at $68.7 billion. Microsoft, from its entrepreneurial roots in 1975, continues to practice an entrepreneurial mindset. Nadella told Fortune , “Empathy makes you a better innovator. If I look at the most successful products we [at Microsoft] have created, it comes with that ability to meet the unmet, unarticulated needs of customers.” 5 This outlook led Microsoft to invest in AI tools that give more people access to technology. Key innovations in this area include Eye Gaze, which allows people with ALS to type by using just their gaze, and Seeing AI, an app that uses a phone camera to describe objects and text — including handwritten words — to visually impaired users.

TMP-1443.text: APPLY YOUR AP ® SKILLS 1. How did Microsoft’s strategy change when Satya Nadella took over for Steve Ballmer as CEO? 2. What are two tactics of Microsoft’s acquisition strategy? 3. Suppose you are the new CEO of Microsoft. You are challenged to address conflicts between rapid expansion of energy-intensive data centers to support growth in AI and cloud computing, on the one hand, and the company’s environmental goals on the other. You will use the PACED deliberative process to decide how to move forward. Identify the problem, two alternatives, and two criteria you would adopt for that decision. 4. Suppose Microsoft is deciding between two new advertising methods: sponsoring the Women’s World Cup soccer tournament, or flying Microsoft blimps over major cities from coast to coast. The soccer sponsorship would provide an estimated net profit of $8 million for an investment of $40 million. The blimps would provide an estimated net profit of $30 million for an investment of $90 million. Use the ROI criterion to evaluate these options.
