TMP-1446.navLabel:
MODULE 4.4 Strategic Frameworks: Porter’s Five Forces and SWOT
Analysis
TMP-1446.text: Maskot/Getty Images The competitive forces that limit profitability in most markets go beyond direct rivals. For example, as movie theaters raise their prices, they must consider the threat of entertainment seekers substituting comedy shows, concerts, or sporting events for movies.

TMP-1447.text: Porter’s Five Forces LG What are Porter’s Five Forces? A business’s giant step of entering a market puts the time, money, and reputation of everyone involved at risk. Module 4.3 advised care and deliberation for such decisions, and introduced strategic frameworks : structured approaches to understanding a situation, setting priorities, and aligning decisions with long-term goals. In this module, you will learn two strategic frameworks for business analysis. We begin with Michael Porter’s Five Forces , a framework for evaluating a market’s competitive environment. Later in this module, we will discuss how you can use SWOT analysis to evaluate a business’s strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats. Michael Porter’s Five Forces A framework for evaluating a market’s competitive environment by considering competitive rivalry, the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitute products, the bargaining power of customers, and the bargaining power of suppliers.

TMP-1448.text: Michael Porter identified five forces that shape the competitive landscape in any market. These forces interact to influence the attractiveness of entering a market and the best strategies to optimize business performance as part of that market. They are: 1. Competitive rivalry: the competition from existing businesses in the market. 2. Threat of new entrants: the risk that new businesses will enter the market and increase competition. 3. Threat of substitutes: the availability of alternative products that can meet the same needs. 4. Customer power: the ability of buyers to demand lower prices or better quality. 5. Supplier power: the ability of suppliers to negotiate higher prices or enforce policies more favorable to the supplier (such as a larger minimum order size or a stricter return policy). Analysis of Porter’s Five Forces helps a business understand the intensity of competition in the market and the prospects for a new entrant to succeed in the long term. The findings also inform decisions about pricing strategies, which depend similarly on the competitive threats of power held by rivals, customers, and suppliers.

TMP-1449.text: Figure 4.4-1 illustrates Porter’s Five Forces and how they interact. In this section we’ll examine the meaning and influence of each force.

TMP-1450.text: The Five Forces that Shape Industry Competition Threat of new entrants ↓ Bargaining power of suppliers → ↻ Rivalry among existing competitors ↻ ← Bargaining power of customers ↑ Threat of substitute products Copyright © BFW Publishers Extended description for Figure 4.4-1 Porter’s Five Forces ⓘ At the center of the flowchart is a circle comprised of rotating arrows. Text inside the circle reads: Rivalry among existing competitors . Four text boxes surround the circle. Each text box has an arrow that points toward the center circle. The text boxes read, in clockwise order, as follows: • Threat of new entrants • Bargaining power of customers • Threat of substitute products • Bargaining power of suppliers

TMP-1451.text: Figure 4.4-1 Porter’s Five Forces Source: Adapted from M. E. Porter, The Competitive Advantage: Creating and Sustaining Superior Performance (Free Press, 1985). Competitive Rivalry The strongest force of competition in a market is generally competitive rivalry , meaning the intensity of competition among existing businesses in the market. This rivalry increases with the number of direct competitors, the similarity of their products,

TMP-1452.text: and the absence of pricing power among competitors. Recall from Module 2.5 that pricing power is the ability to raise prices without losing sales to rivals. Businesses in a competitive market with little product differentiation have limited pricing power. competitive rivalry The intensity of competition among existing businesses in a market. The U.S. airline industry is fairly competitive, with several major carriers and dozens of smaller airlines competing on many of the same routes. In that environment, fierce competition for market share can result in price wars that cut into a company’s profit. In contrast, businesses with highly differentiated products, strong brand identity, loyal customers, few substitutes, or high costs of switching between products may have the power to raise their price substantially without a large loss of market share. That is the case for the aircraft manufacturing industry, in which Airbus and Boeing dominate the market for aircraft sold to U.S. airlines. Threat of New Entrants New market entrants place downward pressure on prices and upward pressure on marketing costs as competitors try to maintain their customer base. Businesses evaluate

TMP-1453.text: this threat based on the barriers to entering the market, such as high startup costs, patents, licensing requirements, limited access to essential resources, or economies of scale, as discussed in Module 1.2 . The easier it is for new competitors to enter a market, the greater the threat to existing firms. For example, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation studied the ease of entering the food truck market in 20 cities. 1 It found that the barriers to entry were the lowest in Portland, Oregon, where new food truck owners must pay an average of $5,410 in fees, make 7 trips to government agencies to obtain permits and licenses, and complete 7 procedures such as vehicle inspections. The barriers were highest in Boston, where it took an average of $37,907 in fees, 21 procedures, and 32 trips to government agencies to open a food truck. As a result, food truck owners in Boston may worry less about a lot of competitors rolling in after a moderate increase in the prices on their menus. Threat of Substitute Products Comedy clubs aren’t direct competitors with movie theaters, but if the price of movie tickets becomes very high, more people would satisfy their desire for entertainment by substituting a comedy show (or a basketball game or a concert) for a movie. The threat of substitute products depends on the ease with which consumers can meet their needs

TMP-1454.text: with alternative products that are not direct competitors. The threat of substitute products increases when there are many alternatives available or when substitutes are relatively inexpensive, of high quality, or easily accessible. For example, substitutes are a sizable threat in the sugar market because there are a large number of alternative food sweeteners (corn syrup, honey, agave nectar, maple syrup, monk fruit, and a handful of artificial sweeteners), and some of those substitutes are inexpensive, of high quality, and easy to access. The availability of substitute products limits the profits of producers of sugar beets and sugar cane (either of which might be in the white packet next to the blue, pink, and yellow packets on the table at your local diner).

TMP-1455.text: IAN LANGSDON/Getty Images Customers have more bargaining power when few customers exist, the customer acquisition cost is high, or the customer’s cost of switching to another business is low. You are in a good bargaining position at a flea market with many similar vendors — even if there are more than a few customers — because it is easy to switch to another vendor if one demands an unreasonable price.

TMP-1456.text: Bargaining Power of Customers In some markets, customers get a taste of power. Customer power depends in part on the switching cost , which is the financial and psychological burden of changing from one product or brand to another. When the switching cost is low and customers are price sensitive, buyers have more power. They can influence pricing merely with their ability and desire to switch products if prices aren’t competitive — even in markets with no explicit price negotiations. For example, the makers of your usual brand of ketchup feel your power as a customer through an understanding that, if they raise their price substantially, you can easily switch to another brand. In contrast, the switching cost for a transfer from one college to another is much higher, involving applications and fees and moving personal belongings large distances. The result is that colleges can, and often do, increase their tuition without losing many current students. switching cost The financial and psychological burden on customers of changing from one product or brand to another. The threat of customer bargaining power is high when there are few customers, which may lead the seller to accept prices they would turn down if customers were lined

TMP-1457.text: up to pay the asking price. Tutors, photographers, electricians, plumbers, and DJs are among the businesses that might accept lower prices when business is slow. Module 2.1 explained that the customer acquisition cost is the average marketing expense per customer gained. Customers have more bargaining power when the customer acquisition cost is high. For example, a car dealership may spend between $500 and $1,000 on advertising for every customer that visits the dealership. That cost makes the dealership more willing to come down a bit on the price rather than losing a customer. Some customers gain bargaining power by virtue of the volume of their spending. A customer whose purchases represent a significant portion of a business’s sales is in a strong bargaining position. This is common in B2B sales when the buyer is a business of considerable size. For example, big-box retailers such as Costco and Walmart buy in such massive volumes that they can negotiate with manufacturers to get rock-bottom prices for many of the goods they purchase.

TMP-1458.text: Bargaining Power of Suppliers Businesses need suppliers to provide resources, including inputs such as raw materials and component parts used to make final products. If a business needs a particular supplier, either because the resource market lacks competition or because the switching cost between suppliers is high, that supplier has bargaining power. For example, aerospace contractor Lockheed Martin uses a heat-resistant metal called samarium in its military hardware. There are no good substitutes for samarium. Fitech is among a small number of companies in China that control the worldwide supply of samarium, which gives them strong bargaining power in the sale of that resource. The appeal of a business environment is influenced by the strength of Porter’s Five Forces. A highly competitive market, strong threats of entrance or substitution, and notable bargaining power among customers or suppliers lower the prospects of profitability. Ideally, a business would enter a market in which all of these forces are weak, but such opportunities are rare. Next, we will examine the realities of a market under the lens of Porter’s Five Forces.

TMP-1459.text: Anadolu/Getty Images Extended description for Streaming Music A large screen in the background reads, Spotify.

TMP-1460.text: Suppose a popular music streaming service wanted to jack up its prices. Would rivals, customers, substitute products, or new entrants provide a sufficient threat to keep its prices in check?

TMP-1461.text: Evaluating a Market’s Competitiveness LG How do managers use Porter’s Five Forces framework to evaluate competition in a market? Let’s apply Porter’s Five Forces to the market for streaming music. The competitive forces in that market are relevant to participants, such as Spotify, as they make decisions about pricing, marketing, and growth. 1 This analysis is also important to potential new entrants into this market as they evaluate their potential for profitability. Assess the Competitive Rivalry The level of competitive rivalry in the streaming music market is fairly high. Direct competitors include Apple Music, Amazon Music, Deezer, Pandora, SoundCloud, Spotify, TIDAL, and YouTube Music. The financial strength of key players such as Apple, Amazon, and Alphabet (the parent company of Google, which owns YouTube) makes it

TMP-1462.navLabel: Assess the Threat of New Entrants
TMP-1462.text: difficult for any company to stand out for long before competitors can match their features and marketing efforts. The result is a low level of product differentiation and intense price competition. The competitive rivalry among these companies reduces potential profitability and makes this market less attractive for new businesses. Assess the Threat of New Entrants If barriers to entry are low, a new business can easily enter and compete in a market. In the market for streaming music services, the barriers to entry are moderate to high. It is feasible for many potential entrants to set up a streaming music platform. However, the need to secure rights to music from the various music labels is expensive and legally complex, which creates challenges for new companies. Another barrier is that Spotify, YouTube Music, Pandora, and Apple Music all enjoy a sizable market share, brand recognition, and loyalty from existing customers. Large companies in related markets could certainly overcome these barriers with sufficient effort, but small players would have a tough time putting together a viable contender.

headings.text: Assess the Threat of New Entrants

TMP-1463.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Customers
TMP-1463.text: Assess the Threat of Substitute Products When it comes to music streaming, the threat of substitute products is high. There are a fair number of alternative ways to obtain music, some of which are less expensive or easier to access than others. Free alternatives include music on the radio, YouTube videos, websites such as Free Music Archive, and apps such as Jamendo. There are TV stations with music videos. Live music may be an option, sometimes for free, sometimes for a high price. Some people own music collections, which might include digital downloads, CDs, or vinyl records. Music piracy — illegally downloading songs — was common in the past and remains a threat. And nonmusic alternatives — including audiobooks and podcasts — also compete in the market for listeners. These assorted alternatives limit the pricing power of music streaming businesses. Assess the Bargaining Power of Customers The bargaining power of customers is high in this market. Music streaming companies know that listeners can easily switch platforms. The product differentiation among these businesses is minimal, which adds to the temptation to switch. Brand loyalty does exist in this market, but even loyal customers have options: Many of these

headings.text: Assess the Threat of Substitute Products
Assess the Bargaining Power of Customers

TMP-1464.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1464.text: companies adopt a freemium pricing model with a basic version for free, usually supported by advertising, and a premium version that may be ad-free and offer perks such as offline playback. Price-sensitive customers can respond to price increases by switching to the free version, even if they don’t want to move to a cheaper competitor. The low switching costs and the many alternatives give customers substantial power to prevent unreasonable prices. Recall that the other sources of customer power are high customer acquisition costs and a small number of customers who represent a large share of sales. In this particular market, those sources are weak — the acquisition cost is relatively low and there are many customers. Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers The bargaining power of streaming music suppliers is moderate to high. Supplier power comes from a small number of suppliers or a high cost of switching to a new supplier in response to a price increase. The suppliers of most mainstream music are a limited number of major record labels such as Sony, Universal, and Warner. Those companies typically demand royalties and have exclusive control over their music, making it impossible to switch to a new supplier of a particular song. However, substitutes do exist. Music streaming services have the option to offer music from

headings.text: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers

TMP-1465.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1465.text: independent artists who have far less bargaining power than the major labels. SoundCloud, TIDAL, and Bandcamp are examples of services that focus attention on independent music. This approach can be a win-win for both music services and musicians: The services help the musicians get discovered, and the independent musicians provide lower-cost music to the services. Having sifted through the competitive forces in this market, a company like Spotify would have a better idea about the importance of competitive prices and investments to improve the user experience. Potential entrants would consider the limited prospects for long-term profits unless a company has a novel idea for product differentiation. Keep in mind that Porter’s Five Forces is just one analytical framework. It’s not perfect, and other analysis tools provide differing perspectives for important decision making, as you will learn next.

TMP-1466.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1466.text: SWOT Analysis What factors are considered in SWOT analysis? In job interviews, it is common for candidates to be asked about their strengths and weaknesses. This is more than a formality; these questions reveal self-awareness, and the follow-up discussion can reveal efforts to improve in areas that need work, or a lack of such efforts. Businesses ask themselves the same questions, and a couple more, in efforts to improve. This constitutes SWOT analysis , a framework for assessing internal and external factors relevant to achieving goals and remaining competitive (or viable ). SWOT analysis considers strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats, as illustrated in Figure 4.4-2 . The results of SWOT analysis help a business strategize about leading with strengths, tackling weaknesses, seizing opportunities, and addressing threats.

TMP-1467.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1467.text: SWOT analysis A framework for assessing internal strengths and weaknesses, and external opportunities and threats, relevant to achieving goals and remaining competitive. Let’s go through each of the factors considered in SWOT analysis.

TMP-1468.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1468.text: Internal Factors External Factors Copyright © BFW Publishers S Strengths W Weaknesses O Opportunities T Threats Extended description for Figure 4.4-2 SWOT Analysis The illustration outlines the meaning of the acronym SWOT, as follows: • Internal Factors ○ S: Strengths. An accompanying icon shows a barbell. ○ W: Weaknesses. An accompanying icon shows chains breaking. • External Factors

TMP-1469.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1469.text: ○ O: Opportunities. An accompanying icon shows a magnifying glass focusing on a bar graph that displays growth over time. ○ T: Threats. An accompanying icon shows the caution symbol of an exclamation mark inside a triangle. Figure 4.4-2 SWOT Analysis Strengths The evaluation of strengths digs into the business’s internal advantages and core competencies — those unique capabilities that enable the business to stand out and deliver value (as discussed in Module 1.5 ). Strengths may include financial health, supply chain efficiency, employees with special skills, exceptional customer service, high-quality products, brand recognition, and intellectual property such as copyrights and patents. When evaluating its strengths, a business might ask itself:

TMP-1470.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1470.text: • What are we known for? • What resources are available to us? • What do customers like most about our product(s) and brand? • Do we have strong relationships with customers? Suppliers? • How are we different from competitors? • What assets do we have in terms of people, technology, infrastructure? • Do our employees have specialized skills? • Does our location give us an advantage over competitors? Answering these questions helps a business adopt strategies that take full advantage of its strengths.

TMP-1471.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1471.text: picture alliance/Getty Images Extended description for John Deere Several additional tractors and heavy duty vehicles appear in the background. Men and women walk around the showroom floor.

TMP-1472.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1472.text: The strengths of John Deere include its widespread dealer network, loyal customers, and a global reputation for durability. Weaknesses The consideration of weaknesses explores internal disadvantages that hinder a business’s ability to meet its goals or compete successfully. Weaknesses may include poor financial health, supply chain vulnerabilities, unfilled needs for skilled employees, poor customer service, high defect rates for products, low brand recognition, outdated technology, and a lack of core competencies. A company evaluating its own weaknesses might ask: • What issues cause us persistent problems? • What complaints do we receive most often from customers? From employees? From other stakeholders? • What resources do we lack? • What skills are our employees missing?

TMP-1473.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1473.text: • Do we have enough employees? Do we have too many? • Does the size of our debt make it difficult to pay off? • Is any of our equipment or software outdated? Answering these questions helps a business better address its weaknesses and avoid strategies that would fail due to internal problems. AP ® SKILLS TIP You should be able to differentiate between internal and external factors that influence decision making. As you study strategic frameworks, be aware of the factors that are internal (influenced by the business) and external (not influenced by the business). For example, Porter’s Five Forces are external, as are the factors in PESTEL analysis. SWOT analysis considers internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats. Opportunities SWOT analysis also considers factors that are external to the business, meaning they are outside of the business’s control. Some of these factors are opportunities that benefit a business. The implementation of government policies, such as regulations that break

TMP-1474.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1474.text: up monopolies, can create opportunities for smaller businesses to enter a market. Other examples include steady growth in the market, technological advances that benefit the business, and a decline in competition, such as a major competitor going out of business. When evaluating potential opportunities, a company should ask: • What changes are occurring in the industry? • What are our customers asking for? • What types of opportunities are we seeking? • What opportunities are competitors ignoring that we should go after? • What are the weaknesses of our competitors? • Are there opportunities for geographic expansion? • What trends should we pay attention to? Careful attention to external factors helps a business avoid missed opportunities.

TMP-1475.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1475.text: Threats The threats in SWOT analysis are external factors that could harm the business. Possible threats include new government regulations that disfavor the business, a market in decline, natural disasters that hinder the business or its supply chain, rising wages or other input prices, and disruptive innovation that reduces the need for the business’s product. For example, businesses that provide online tutoring and help with homework (such as Chegg) experienced a steep decline in use after artificial intelligence chatbots like ChatGPT became widely available. When assessing threats, business leaders should ask: • Are any competitors adopting new strategies that we’re unaware of? • Is competition increasing in our market? • Are competitors growing faster than us? • Can we afford the technology and other resources needed to keep up with the competition? • Are we losing customers to competitors? If so, why? • Can new technology make us obsolete?

TMP-1476.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1476.text: • How can the current state of the economy hurt us? It is essential for a business to be aware of new threats and emerging trends so that it is not caught off guard.

TMP-1477.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1477.text: Elwood Inn Fine Teas Extended description for Fine Teas The cylinders from right to left read as follows: • Reiki Blend. Green Tea with Serene Herbs. Net Weight 3.5 ounces (99 grams).

TMP-1478.navLabel: Assess the Bargaining Power of Suppliers
TMP-1478.text: • Temple Garden. Green Tea with Soothing Herbs. Net Weight 3.5 ounces (99 grams). • Labyrinth Blend. Green Tea with Serene Herbs. Net Weight 3.5 ounces (99 grams). • Yoga Blend. Green Tea with Serene Herbs. Net Weight 3.5 ounces (99 grams). A tariff on imported metal could pose a threat for Elmwood Inn Fine Teas, which packages some of its products in metal cans. AP ® EXAM TIP Porter’s Five Forces and SWOT analysis are likely to be on the exam because they are important and easy to ask questions about. The factors of SWOT analysis are easy to remember from the lettering in the term. For Porter’s Five Forces, to remember the (abbreviated) factors of rivalry, customer power, entry, supplier power, and substitutes, consider thinking, “Really Could Eat Some Supper!” Or, make up your own mnemonic device!

TMP-1479.text: Applying SWOT Analysis How do managers use SWOT analysis?

TMP-1480.text: Newsday LLC/Getty Images SWOT analysis can help a diner find ways to stand out, troubleshoot, grow, and reduce vulnerabilities. Let’s apply SWOT analysis to the fictional Friendly Burgers diner in the real town of Sandwich, Massachusetts. Suppose Friendly Burgers is a new entry in the Sandwich market, with a location on Main Street and hopes to expand to additional locations. The diner distinguishes itself from competitors by serving beverages in round smiley-face mugs, showcasing the world’s largest gumball machine, which is “always half full and

TMP-1481.text: never half empty,” and selling meatless Beyond Burgers as discussed in the upcoming case study. In addition to animal-friendly burgers, the diner offers a variety of soups, smoothies, and fresh-squeezed juices. Friendly Burgers relies on tourists for much of its business. To appeal to customers who are heading to the beach, the diner offers reusable takeout bags that double as beach bags and contain a free Friendly Burgers flying disk. Table 4.4-1 outlines Friendly Burgers’ SWOT analysis. Table 4.4-1 SWOT Analysis: Friendly Burgers Strengths Weaknesses Opportunities Threats Location The downtown location will attract more traffic from visitors and shoppers. Lack of financial capital To date, the business’s limited funds have come from loans and investors. Growth in tourism Sandwich is reconstructing its wooden-plank boardwalk, which should attract more tourists and potential customers. Competition The Next Door Burger Bar also sells meatless burgers, has a rating of 4.3 stars (out of 5) on Yelp, and has an established customer base.

TMP-1482.text: Uniqueness Offerings such as the meatless burger are unusual alternatives to fast food and will appeal to customers who are seeking vegetarian options. Lack of reputation This is a new business that hasn’t yet established a great, widespread reputation. New gap in market Sadly, a fire recently destroyed Captain Scott’s Seafood Restaurant in Sandwich. Serving Captain Scott’s former customers could be an opportunity for Friendly Burgers. Difficulty scaling up As the tourist season begins and the diner has busy days, Friendly Burgers may be unprepared for the crowds. Insufficient staffing, inventory, and preparation could lead to bad service, which may aggravate customers and lead to bad ratings on social media. Strong management The team members have a variety of special skills that equip them to run this sort of business, from experience in running restaurants, to accountancy, to staff management. Skeptical customers It might be a challenge to convince some customers to change their dietary habits and try the meatless burgers at Friendly Burgers. Longer high season Promotions by the region’s tourism council have successfully extended the tourist season to include not just the summer months, but also April, May, September, and October. Labor challenges The region relies heavily on workers who visit the United States temporarily as part of a cultural exchange or to assist with peak-season employment needs. The availability of workers with the associated J-1 and H-2B visas is now less than half of the number needed.

TMP-1483.text: Having conducted its SWOT analysis, Friendly Burgers can incorporate its findings into strategy decisions. For example, the diner may want to take advantage of its strength in vegetarian offerings by advertising on social media platforms popular among vegetarians. It should address its weaknesses, perhaps by seeking investors to add to its sources of financial capital. It could seize opportunities, perhaps by adding seafood items to the menu to court former customers of Captain Scott’s Seafood Restaurant. And Friendly Burgers should be prepared for the threats it has identified. That could include bracing for crowds by having back-up inventory on hand. The business could also survey staff to determine who could come in for an extra shift in the event of an unexpected rush of hungry tourists, so that a contingency plan is in place. A business can use benchmarks to gain perspective on the information obtained from SWOT analysis. Several bases for comparison are available for internal strengths and weaknesses. Established businesses can use data from past performance to evaluate the value of profits and physical assets (buildings, machinery) and the number of employees, as well as intangible assets such as reputation, brand image, and intellectual property. For example, Friendly Burgers could make quarterly comparisons of the number of five-star ratings it receives on Yelp, the percentage of customers who say they

TMP-1484.text: would recommend the diner to others, and the number of new recipes it concocts. Other benchmarks include the performance of rivals and industry averages as discussed in Module 4.2. Using SWOT analysis, a business can gauge whether its own performance is where it needs to be. It can also consider external factors such as economic trends and customer preferences to determine the market’s potential for growth. The evaluation of opportunities and threats may incorporate strategic frameworks we have discussed previously for a more structured assessment of external factors. PESTEL analysis is a great way to examine the political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal factors, as discussed in Module 1.3. And consideration of Porter’s Five Forces helps a business determine whether the bargaining power of customers and suppliers and the competition in its environment represent opportunities or threats.

TMP-1485.text: Module 4.4 Review Learning Goals What are Porter’s Five Forces? • Michael Porter’s Five Forces is a framework for evaluating a market’s competitive environment. The five forces are competitive rivalry, the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitute products, the bargaining power of customers, and the bargaining power of suppliers. • Competitive rivalry is the intensity of competition among existing businesses in the market. • Businesses evaluate the threat of new entrants by considering the barriers to entering the market.

TMP-1486.text: • The threat of substitute products depends on the ease with which customers can meet their needs with noncompeting alternatives. • The bargaining power of customers depends in part on the switching cost , which is the financial and psychological burden of changing from one product or brand to another. Customers also have more bargaining power when there are fewer of them, when the customer acquisition cost is high, and when customers purchase in volume. • The bargaining power of suppliers is higher when a business needs a particular supplier, due either to a lack of competition or to a high switching cost between suppliers. How do managers use Porter’s Five Forces framework to evaluate competition in a market? • By evaluating the competitive forces in a market, a company gains a better understanding of the prospects for profitability and the advisability of competitive pricing strategies. Porter’s Five Forces is just one analytical framework. It’s not

TMP-1487.text: perfect, and other analysis tools provide differing perspectives for important decision making. What factors are considered in SWOT analysis? • SWOT analysis is a framework for assessing internal and external factors relevant to achieving goals and remaining competitive. This framework considers internal strengths such as core competencies, internal weaknesses such as poor financial health, external opportunities such as a growing market, and external threats such as supply chain bottlenecks. How do managers use SWOT analysis? • A business can use benchmarks to gain perspective on the findings obtained with SWOT analysis. For internal strengths and weaknesses, available benchmarks include the previous performance of the business and the performance of rivals

TMP-1488.text: and the industry as a whole. The evaluation of opportunities and threats can incorporate strategic frameworks for the analysis of external factors, including PESTEL analysis and Porter’s Five Forces. TMP-1492.text: CASE STUDY Beyond Meat ANGELA WEISS/AFP/Getty Images Extended description for Beyond Meat The top shelf displays Impossible brand products. The middle shelf displays Beyond Meat products. The bottom shelf displays both Light Life and No Evil products.

TMP-1493.text: Innovation has brought us new protein sources, but can Beyond Meat and its competitors move beyond consumer reluctance? Founded in 2009, Beyond Meat, Inc., is a producer of plant-based meat substitutes. The company’s mission is to “nourish and protect our bodies, heal earth and climate, and better share the planet with the miracle of life that surrounds us.” 2 In 2012, the company launched its first product, chicken-free Beyond Chicken Strips made from soy and pea protein, flour, seasonings, and other nonmeat ingredients. Beyond Meat now makes nonmeat ground beef, meatballs, sausage, steak, and chicken nuggets, among other meat substitutes. Between 2013 and 2016, Beyond Meat received funding from investors that included Bill Gates, the Humane Society, and Tyson Foods. The company grew rapidly in the late 2010s and went public (sold shares of stock to investors) in 2019. The company continued to grow until 2021 but then experienced several years of decreasing revenues. In that same year, rival Impossible Foods launched meat-free Impossible Chicken, adding to its Impossible Beef and Impossible Sausage

TMP-1494.text: offerings. While Impossible Foods was a relative newcomer, founded in 2011, the meatless meat market was nothing new: MorningStar Farms was founded in 1975, LightLife in 1979, Quorn in 1985, and Gardein in 2003. Beyond rivalry, makers of meat substitutes contend with customers who are reluctant to pay the companies’ premium prices. The industry also faces a communication challenge, because people may not know what they are eating when they bite into meatless meat. And while many consumers have an appetite for healthy alternatives to meat, findings on the benefits of meat substitutes are mixed. 3 Some research suggests that the health benefits of ultraprocessed foods resembling meat are limited, despite them being plant-based products. 4 And simple foods made with seeds, beans, nuts, and legumes provide healthy, protein-rich options. 5 Working in Beyond Meat’s favor, the health and environmental impacts of real meat are becoming increasingly well known. Relative to real U.S. beef, Beyond Burger requires less energy, land, and water, and it pollutes less. 6

TMP-1495.text: Meanwhile, the company is developing new products and improving its recipes to make them tastier and healthier. For example, in 2024, Beyond Meat switched from canola oil and coconut oil to avocado oil to reduce the saturated fats in its Beyond Beef and Beyond Burger. Beyond Meat’s other strategies include leveraging partnerships with retailers and restaurants, expanding into new international markets, and enhancing its product offerings. Like Beyond Meat and Impossible Foods, some supporters of the meat industry apparently felt the prospect of meat replacements showed promise: One interest group placed an ad during the 2020 Super Bowl that claimed plant-based meat contained laxatives. 7 Impossible Foods responded with a parody ad claiming that real ground beef contains “poop.” 8 Game on. It also comes after the company announced plans to cut 7,000 jobs over the next two years amid slowing worldwide sales growth. On July 28, P&G announced its chief operating officer, Shailesh Jejurikar, 58, will take over as CEO on Jan. 1 and [current CEO Jon] Moeller will become executive chairman of the board. Jejurikar will earn a $1.6 million salary and up to $3.2 million in annual incentives. The company’s board has also approved a long-term incentive award valued at $14 million for Jejurikar. How much of his long-term incentives he ultimately reaps will depend on his performance in the current fiscal year. The proxy suggests Jejurikar should get a healthy raise: In the latest year, his total compensation as COO was $9.2 million, including his long-term pay. Like most Fortune 500 companies, P&G pays senior executives a mix of cash and stock as well as some perks. Here’s a breakdown: Moeller’s salary increased 2.3% to $1.6 million.

TMP-1501.text: His bonus, paid in cash, was cut by more than half to $1.9 million, down from $4.1 million a year ago. Moeller got $18.1 million in stock and option awards, a 7% increase or extra $1.2 million from the previous year. Other compensation totalled nearly $303,000, down 19% or about $73,000. Managers are often described as “wearing many hats.” Being responsible for a team frequently requires multitasking and a full plate, causing even some of the most well-intentioned leaders to lose sight of their employees’ needs. This failure to engage

TMP-1509.text: employees transcends industries—in 2024, only 31% of employees at US-based companies were considered “actively engaged.” Today’s pace of business indeed makes it more challenging to set aside time to nurture employee engagement. With many teams being distributed globally, hybrid work becoming a standard, and the rise of AI, building a strong workplace culture and keeping employees engaged is harder than ever. Traditional methods that may have worked as [recently] as a decade ago may fall short in this new landscape.³ Chris Gallagher, “The Future of Employee Engagement: How Bonfyre Is Transforming Workplaces,” USA Today , March 21, 2025. TMP-1510.text: 6. Identify and explain two specific duties of managers common throughout many firms and industries. 7. Identify and explain one specific KPI that could be used by a manager to determine the strength of employee engagement at a particular firm. Refer to the case study below when answering Questions 8–11. Jennifer opened Hearts and Minds Bookstore in Chicago after spending 20 years immersed in the world of romance novels. As a lifelong book lover, Jennifer’s passion for the romance genre began in high school with Nicholas Sparks’s The Notebook . She went on to read hundreds of other romance titles, eagerly anticipating new releases from her favorite authors. A challenge for Jennifer was that her local bookstore had only one shelf in the entire store dedicated to romance. This was both personally frustrating and, Jennifer felt, something of a missed opportunity. Conducting some initial research, Jennifer learned that in 2022, sales of romance novels soared 52% even as the book market as a whole experienced a decline.⁴ Jennifer understood that with limited shelf space for romance,

TMP-1511.text: retailers were both inhibiting potential customers interested in romance fiction and limiting their own sales. She believed that romance fans were more dedicated, read more, and purchased more books than the general reader. After years of considering and researching the problem, Jennifer decided to open Hearts and Minds Bookstore. Her store would sell a wide variety of romance, from romantasy (a blend of fantasy and romance fiction) to paranormal and YA romance novels. To guide her decision and plan her business, Jennifer relied on the following data: Romance readers read more than double the number of books per year as the general reader. Romance readers read an average of 36 romance books per year. Romance readers read an average of 312 hours of romance per year. Romance readers are active and social, joining book clubs and supporting some of the most successful BookTok communities on social media platform TikTok. Surveyed romance readers reported that a typical reading session lasts just under an hour.

TMP-1512.text: Gen Z (58%), millennial (51%), and Gen X (46%) readers are most likely to take a romance book recommendation based on the plot. Of 2,000 romance readers surveyed, 63% of men considered themselves die-hard romance enthusiasts, compared to 60% of women.⁵ Jennifer believed that a large market like Chicago would strongly support a bookstore focusing on the genre fiction that was given short shrift at general bookstores. She found that one of the easiest ways to engage her potential customers was with an active social media presence on Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, and Goodreads. Within six months of opening, Hearts and Minds had 300 people a day coming in to browse, with half of them purchasing at least one book and one-third purchasing two or more books. Given her extensive knowledge of the romance genre and its subgenres, Jennifer was also able to create online communities well beyond Chicago’s reading base. Customers sometimes drove up to two hours to find titles in her store that were not available closer to home.

TMP-1513.text: AleksandarNakic/Getty Images Building an independent bookstore starts with knowing your customers and what they love to read. One of Hearts and Minds’s employees suggested creating a reader loyalty program: For every nine books purchased, one was given for free. On birthdays, readers could

TMP-1514.text: enjoy a buy-one-get-one deal on any sale book, and they would receive a branded reusable bag to hold those new books. To keep customers coming back, Hearts and Minds staff rotated the selection in the different sections rapidly. A shelf would often receive a dramatic update every two to three weeks, with new titles or paperback editions of popular titles from different series. After speaking with customers, Jennifer began to host author signings, in-store book clubs, and after-hours events with appetizers and beverages. All of these drove customer engagement through the roof, with some regulars stopping by weekly to chat about recent reads and examine new titles, which were marketed with signage at the Hearts and Minds entrance and throughout the store. Jennifer was thrilled with the store’s initial success. Now—armed with customer and staff suggestions, research, and her own ideas—she was faced with a decision about the direction in which to take it. She considered the following two possibilities:

TMP-1515.text: Decision 1. Jennifer could dedicate part of her store to merchandise based on popular romance authors and books—such as t-shirts, tote bags, greeting cards, and novelty items—as well as e-readers. This would reduce her floor space for books by 14%. Decision 2. Jennifer could continue focusing exclusively on sales of romance fiction, without creating space for merchandise, accessories, and e-readers. 8. TMP-1516.text: AP® Skills Workshop: Collaboration Preparing for the AP® Exam What are the five course skills for this AP® course? There are five skills you’ll need to build for this course. Two of them are Business Skills: Concept Application and Entrepreneurship . The other three are Professional and Leadership Skills: Decision Making , Collaboration , and Communication . You will find five AP® Skills Workshops in this text—one at the end of each of the five units, with each Workshop addressing one of the Course Skills. In this workshop, we will focus on Collaboration . Identify Collaboration Almost no one works alone. Even a sole proprietorship relies on contractors, suppliers, customers, and community members to stay in business. Collaboration is the process of working with and leading others to accomplish a shared goal or task. Effective collaboration requires developing team objectives, defining individual roles and responsibilities, keeping team members motivated, and working together to achieve the specified goals. Understand Collaboration Consider Larry Page and Sergey Brin, who were, in the mid-1990s, two graduate students in the computer science program at Stanford University. They worked together on a research project called Backrub—a search engine powered by a unique algorithm they had created. Backrub used links to determine a webpage’s importance relative to the search query. The more others linked to

TMP-1517.text: that page, the higher it would appear in the search results. This proprietary solution, which they called PageRank, made it easier for someone searching online to find relevant websites. Backrub was later renamed Google, after a very large number: a 1 followed by one hundred zeroes ( googol ). Google received $100,000 in seed money from Sun Microsystems cofounder Andy Bechtolsheim, and it was incorporated in 1998. Google was not the first internet search engine, but it soon became the most popular. While they initially did not get along, Page and Brin learned to respect each other’s gifts. Page was a bold visionary and deep thinker. Brin was a problem solver with tremendous skill as an engineer. These unique, high-level skillsets helped them to define their individual roles and collaborate effectively. Their shared passion for problem solving and data analytics—both critical for success in the technology space—kept them motivated. And their shared mission—“to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful”—kept them focused on a common goal.⁶

TMP-1518.text: Kim Kulish/Getty Images Larry Page (left) and Sergey Brin, shown here in 2003 in the server room at Google headquarters, began their collaboration in a garage. With Page and Brin’s collaboration in mind, consider these questions: Describe one way in which collaboration helps entrepreneurs to achieve their goals. Answer: Collaboration helps entrepreneurs to reach their goals by bringing together the skills and strengths of multiple people. Sergey Brin and Larry Page combined their talents to create and implement a better internet search engine. While each of them was highly skilled and capable independently, the ability to exchange ideas, challenge one another’s thinking, and divide responsibilities helped turn Google into one of the world’s most influential companies. Explain how defining roles and responsibilities makes for more effective collaboration.

TMP-1519.text: Answer: One challenge for entrepreneurs is that of limited time. Defining roles and responsibilities enables each team member to concentrate on tasks that match their skills, increasing efficiency and freeing others to focus on their own tasks. For example, suppose your teacher assigns a project to develop a new type of cookie. Your small group divides up the responsibilities: If one person is an experienced baker, they can create the recipe and bake. If another is a strong artist, they can focus on designing the logo and creating social media posts. A third member with solid financial skills might create a budget and a price point to ensure profitability. This division allows for more efficient work and a higher quality product. Build AP® Skills Here are two activities to help you build the skills you’ll need to succeed in this course. 1. Activity: Consider what you’ve learned in Unit 4 about evaluating performance with key performance indicators (KPIs). Develop a list of four or five KPIs that Google’s cofounders might have used to determine the success of their product. Your teacher may have you present to the class the significance of each KPI. 2. Activity: Apply what you’ve learned about return on investment (ROI) to a real company that focuses on one product or service. Research the ROI for the company and any of its chief rivals in the market for that product or service. Your teacher may have you develop a slideshow illustrating the concept of ROI to your classmates.

The more you know about the market, industry, potential customers, and rival firms, the better prepared you and your team will be to successfully launch the business.

TMP-1524.text: MODULES 5.1 Taxes, Net Income, and Budgeting 5.2 Managing Personal Risk 5.3 Saving and Investing for Education, Housing, and Retirement Goals Not-So-Easy Come, Easy Go: The Importance of Personal Finance The story of financial security may begin with earning plenty of money, but that’s not how it ends. There are so many ways for money to escape you that, if you’re not extremely careful, what you’ve earned won’t be around for long. Cautionary tales come from the likes of Nicholas Cage, whose acting earned him hundreds of millions of dollars. Unfortunately, spending on real estate, cars, motorcycles, and exotic collectibles landed him $6 million in debt.¹ Similar stories of financial woes are common, not only among millionaires such as basketball player Darius Miles and Peloton co-founder John Foley, but also for the less rich and famous among us.

TMP-1525.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1525.navLabel: U N I T 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1525.text: In the United States, there are roughly half a million personal bankruptcy filings each year.² The average credit card debt for people with an unpaid balance is around $7,000.³ Most undergraduate students at public universities take out loans to cover tuition expenses, and among those who do borrow, the average debt at graduation exceeds $27,000. When it comes time to retire, 76% of retirees say they wish they had saved more money.⁴ There are also many personal finance success stories. Singer, songwriter, and philanthropist Dolly Parton, with a net worth of nearly half a billion dollars, grew up with eleven siblings in a one-room cabin with no electricity or running water. Marvin Ellison, who now earns over $20 million a year as the CEO of Lowe’s, began his career working part time at Target for $4.35 an hour to help pay for college. And after filing for bankruptcy in 2002, singer Elton John learned from his mistakes and worked his way back to a net worth of over $600 million. Ideally, that type of learning comes before the mistakes, which is why we bring these lessons on personal finance to you now. In previous modules, you learned about many of the challenges and solutions that apply not only to business finance, but also to personal finance. For instance, Module 3.1 explained the importance of saving for the future. Module 3.2 discussed how loans can

TMP-1526.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1526.navLabel: U N I T 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1526.text: solve the puzzle of needing to spend money before you have earned it, which is the case for many buyers of cars, homes, and college educations. Module 3.3 highlighted the value of budgets to guide spending. And Module 3.7 explained the pains of bankruptcy as a last resort for dealing with debt. Clearly, it takes deliberate efforts to stay on course and meet financial goals. This final unit will help you navigate personal finance hurdles that include paying taxes, investing, budgeting, handling personal risk, and saving for education and retirement. We all have goals for the future, many of which may require sizable expenditures. This course aims to help you hold on to as much money as possible and put it to good use. In short, we want to make you a financial rock star. AP® SKILLS Concept Application (1.A, 1.B, 1.C) Decision Making (3.A, 3.B, 3.C, 3.D) Communication (4.A)

TMP-1529.text: Nora Carol Photography/Getty Images Understanding how taxes affect your personal finances is key to making smart money decisions.

TMP-1530.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1530.text: Understanding Taxes LG What taxes do individuals pay in the United States? Ben Franklin famously observed that only two things in life are certain: death and taxes. The tax payments that individuals and businesses must make to the government help pay for important services, including law enforcement, fire protection, highway construction, and public schools. All levels of government — federal, state, and local — use taxes to fund their programs and activities. We have already discussed the taxes that businesses must pay. In this module, we’ll explore the various taxes that individuals are responsible for paying, and how taxes can affect people’s everyday lives and finances. We’ll start with a brief explanation of the different types of taxes that are levied , or officially imposed, in the United States.

TMP-1531.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1531.text: Income Taxes The collection of a portion of most workers’ income provides the largest source of funding for government services at the federal level, from nutrition assistance to national defense. Both individuals and businesses are responsible for income tax , which is a percentage of income that is paid to the government. Most Americans with income must pay federal and state income taxes. When you work for a business, your employer will typically withhold income taxes from your paychecks and send the money to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), the federal agency responsible for tax collection. income tax A tax that individuals and businesses pay to the government, calculated as a percentage of income. By mid-April of each year, individuals or households with income beyond a certain threshold ($15,750 for single individuals under the age of 65 in 2025) must file an annual income tax return for the previous year. An annual income tax return is a form that details all income, taxes paid, and taxes owed. Married couples may file together on a joint return . Children are typically included on a parent’s tax return as dependents.

TMP-1532.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1532.text: annual income tax return A form filed each year to report a person’s income and the taxes already paid, and to determine whether additional taxes are owed or a refund is due. A dependent is someone you support financially, like a child or older family member who lives with you. The number of dependents a person claims affects how much income tax they owe. When you start a new job, your employer will ask you to fill out a form W-4 to report how many dependents you have (among other things). If your parents or anyone else claim you as their dependent, you don’t claim any dependents yourself. Employers use this and other information from your form W-4, along with your income level, to determine how much tax to withhold from each paycheck and send to the government. dependent Someone a person claims on their tax return to get a tax benefit, usually because they support that person financially. Tax withholding is an imprecise practice based on estimates of income and deductions. If too little tax was withheld during the year, the taxpayer must pay the difference between the amount owed and the amount withheld when they file their return. If too much tax was withheld, after reporting the overpayment on their tax

TMP-1533.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1533.text: return, the taxpayer will receive a tax refund — money returned by the government when a person has paid more in taxes than they actually owe. Even if a taxpayer neither owes any taxes nor meets the income threshold beyond which they have to file a tax return, it may be worthwhile to file a return in order to receive a refund of taxes that were automatically withheld by their employer. tax refund Money returned by the government when a person has paid more in taxes throughout the year than they actually owe. Someone who works for themselves, rather than being employed by a business or another individual, is self-employed. Self-employed people have additional responsibilities when it comes to paying income taxes. Being your own boss means you handle your own tax withholding. You must estimate how much tax you owe and send those payments to the government yourself. Most self-employed people must make estimated tax payments quarterly if they expect to owe at least $1,000 in taxes for the current tax year (as of 2025). This helps the government collect taxes throughout the year — and helps self-employed people avoid a large tax bill at the end of the year.

TMP-1534.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1534.text: Tempura/Getty Images Many gig workers — those who do short-term, flexible jobs or “gigs,” like making deliveries for companies such as Uber or DoorDash — are technically self-employed. This means they face unique personal finance challenges, including having to manage and pay their taxes without support from the companies they work with.

TMP-1535.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1535.text: Capital Gains Taxes While most individuals earn the majority of their income from working, people can also receive income from other sources. One typical example is the profit from the sale of an asset, such as a home or shares of stock. Capital gains tax is the tax on profit earned from selling an asset. For example, if someone buys a stock for $600 and sells it for $900, the $300 profit is called a capital gain . Conversely, if someone buys a stock for $600 and then sells it for $400, they incur a capital loss of $200. Capital losses can be used to offset capital gains and, in some cases, reduce the amount of taxes that must be paid. capital gains tax A tax paid on the profits (capital gains) earned from the sale of assets. Capital gains are reported on annual tax returns, but they may receive a special tax rate, depending on how long the assets were held before being sold. Capital gains on assets held for a year or less are taxed at the same rate as regular income. Capital gains on assets owned for more than a year are taxed at a rate that is generally lower and depends on the taxable income of the individual or household. The possibility of paying a lower rate makes it wise to consider the timing of asset sales carefully.

TMP-1536.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1536.text: Don Mason/Getty Images When this home is sold, the seller’s profit will be a capital gain, which is generally taxed at a lower rate than regular income if the home was owned by the seller for more than a year.

TMP-1537.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1537.text: Payroll Taxes Payroll taxes are mandatory payments made by both employers and employees to fund specific government programs. The most well-known payroll taxes go toward Social Security and Medicare, which provide retirement and health benefits for older Americans and support people with certain disabilities. Another, smaller payroll tax funds unemployment insurance, which provides temporary financial support to workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own. Employers and employees each pay half of these payroll taxes. For example, the tax rates are (as of 2025) 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare; employers withhold half of these amounts from the employee’s paycheck (6.2% for Social Security and 1.45% for Medicare) and pay the other half themselves. The entire amount is sent by the employer to the government. payroll taxes Taxes that employers are required to withhold from their workers’ wages and pay on their behalf to fund specific government programs; these taxes are paid by both the employer and the employee. People who are self-employed are responsible for paying the full amount of payroll taxes themselves. They do so by paying the self-employment tax , a tax that combines both the employer and employee shares of payroll taxes. This tax is an important

TMP-1538.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1538.text: financial consideration for anyone who is choosing between working for a company and being self-employed. There are benefits of being your own boss, but remember that you will pay twice as much in payroll taxes as you would if you were working for someone else! self-employment tax A tax that combines both the employer and employee shares of payroll taxes that people who work for themselves must pay. Property Taxes If you own real estate, such as a home or a piece of land, you will most likely have to pay taxes on that property. Property taxes are based on the assessed value of a piece of property, as determined by local officials. They can be paid annually or in installments over the course of the year. These are taxes charged by local governments to help fund community services like public schools, roads, police, and emergency services. property tax A tax based on the assessed value of a piece of property.

TMP-1539.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1539.text: Property taxes are a significant and ongoing cost of home ownership. Because property taxes depend on the value of the property, as real estate values go up, so do the property taxes. For example, if a home is valued at $300,000 and the property tax rate is 1%, the homeowner owes $3,000 in annual property taxes. If the value of that home rises to $500,000 the following year, the tax bill will increase to $5,000. Property taxes can affect you even if you’re not a homeowner. Landlords often pass the cost of tax increases along to renters by raising the rent. And in many U.S. states, people also pay property taxes on personal property such as vehicles. These taxes vary depending on the state: The owner of a Toyota Camry valued at $29,000 in 2025 would pay anywhere from $0 (in 25 states) to more than $1,100 (in Virginia). 5 Unlike real estate, cars tend to lose value over time, so the property tax would likely go down as the car gets older. Sales Taxes Even if you’ve never filed an income tax return, you may already pay a significant amount in taxes. In most U.S. states, governments collect a tax on the sale of goods (and in some cases, services). Sales taxes are based on the item’s price and are collected by

TMP-1540.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1540.text: the business, which must then submit the tax payment to the government. Because state and local taxes vary, where you live — and where you shop — can affect how much you pay. For example, an item purchased for $100 in Montana (which has no sales tax) might cost as much as $110 in Louisiana, where the average combined state and local tax is more than 10%. Figure 5.1-1 details state and local sales taxes across the United States. sales tax A tax on the sale of goods (and in some cases, services), imposed by state or local governments.

TMP-1547.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1547.text: How Income Taxes are Calculated LG Why do different people pay different amounts of federal income tax? As we’ve learned, not everyone pays the same tax rate, even though federal tax laws are the same across the country. In addition to different rates for different types of income, such as wages versus capital gains, people also pay different rates depending on how much total income they earn. The amount a person or household owes in annual taxes depends on their level of income and on any tax credits or deductions they qualify for. How Progressive Taxes Work The federal income tax — and some state income tax — is a progressive tax , meaning those with higher incomes are taxed at higher rates. Even for a particular taxpayer, the first dollars of income are generally taxed at a lower rate than the last dollars of income.

TMP-1548.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1548.text: The tax system is bracketed , meaning earnings up to a certain level fall into the lowest bracket and are taxed at the lowest rate, additional earnings up to another level fall into the second-lowest bracket and are taxed at a higher rate, and so on, as shown in the first two columns of Table 5.1-1 . Since only income that falls within each bracket is taxed at that bracket’s rate, the higher tax rates apply only to the income in the higher brackets, not to all of it. progressive tax A tax with rates that increase as income rises. Table 5.1-1 Progressive Taxes Income Tax rate Yelena’s Tax First $10,000 10% $1,000 Next $10,000 ($10,001–$20,000) 15% $1,500 Next $20,000 ($20,001–$40,000) 20% $4,000 $40,001 and up 30% $3,000 Yelena’s total tax bill: $9,500 Even though Yelena’s marginal tax rate was 30%, she did not pay that rate on her entire income.

TMP-1549.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1549.text: The rate that applies to your last dollar earned is called your marginal tax rate . For example, suppose Yelena received $50,000 in taxable income in a year (the next section explains what income is taxable), and the (simplified) set of tax brackets is: 10% on the first $10,000; 15% on the next $10,000; 20% on the next $20,000; and 30% on all income over $40,000. When Yelena earned her first dollar, her marginal tax rate was 10%. For her 17,000 th dollar, it was 15%. And for her 35,000 th dollar, it was 20%. marginal tax rate The rate applied to the last dollar earned. As shown in Table 5.1-1 , although Yelena eventually earned enough to pay a marginal tax rate of 30%, she did not pay that much on the entire $50,000. Instead, only the amount above $40,000 was taxed at the marginal tax rate of 30%. Yelena paid a total of $9,500 in income tax, making her average tax rate $9,500/$50,000 = 0.19 or 19%. Tax Deductions Yelena had $50,000 in taxable income, but she actually earned more than that. Taxable income refers to the portion of a taxpayer’s income that is subject to taxation by the government. Deductions of income that is not taxable make the taxable income

TMP-1550.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1550.text: lower than the total income. A tax deduction is an amount that is subtracted from total income before calculating how much tax is owed. Yelena claimed the standard deduction, which is an amount that every taxpayer can deduct from their income. The standard deduction varies by year and depends on the filing status (such as single, married filing jointly, or married filing separately). For example, in 2025, a single person with no dependents was entitled to a standard deduction of $15,000.⁶ Yelena’s actual income was $65,000, but after taking the standard deduction, her taxable income was $65,000 − $15,000 = $50,000. There are larger standard deductions for married couples filing a joint return, single working parents with dependent children, and others. Dependents who earn less than the standard deduction have a smaller standard deduction. taxable income The portion of a taxpayer’s income that is subject to taxation by the government. tax deduction An amount that is subtracted from income before calculating how much is owed.

TMP-1551.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1551.text: Bloomberg/Getty Images Extended description for H and R Block The window shows an advertisement of a man adjusting a bow tie. Text in the window reads, Get Your Billion Back America. H and R Block. H and R

TMP-1552.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1552.text: Block dot com. As finances grow more complex, a professional accountant can help uncover valuable tax breaks that might otherwise be missed. As an alternative to the standard deduction, the tax code allows taxpayers to claim a wide range of itemized deductions for specific expenses. These include mortgage interest, certain costs related to buying a home, contributions to qualifying retirement accounts, charitable donations, and eligible medical, educational, and job-related expenses. Taxpayers may also deduct certain state and local taxes — such as income or property taxes — up to the allowable limit. Taxpayers eligible for itemized deductions that exceed the standard deduction amount can benefit from itemizing, which may significantly reduce their taxable income and result in a lower overall tax bill. Tax Credits Some individuals and households may qualify for certain tax credits , which directly reduce the amount of tax owed. For example, a child tax credit helps with the cost of raising a child; a child or dependent care tax credit assists with daytime childcare costs to

TMP-1553.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1553.text: enable the qualifying individual to work or seek employment; an education tax credit helps with the expenses of higher education; and various other tax credits assist with the purchase of specific types of items such as energy-saving appliances. Unlike deductions — which lower the taxable income to which tax rates are applied — credits directly cut the tax bill, dollar for dollar. Because of this, a tax credit of a particular amount lowers taxes by more than a tax deduction of the same value. For instance, a $100 tax credit would lower Yelena’s tax bill by $100 — but given her 30% marginal tax rate, a $100 tax deduction would lower Yelena’s tax bill by $100 × 0.30 = $30. tax credit A credit that directly reduces the amount of taxes owed. The benefit a taxpayer receives from a tax credit may depend on whether the credit is nonrefundable or refundable. A nonrefundable tax credit can reduce a tax bill to zero, but will not lead to a refund if it makes the tax bill negative. For instance, the Lifetime Learning Credit — designed to help cover education and job training costs — can only be used to cancel out taxes owed. If a student owes $500 in taxes and qualifies for a $700 credit, their tax bill will be reduced to zero. They will not, however, receive the remaining $200 of the tax credit as a refund.

TMP-1554.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1554.text: Refundable tax credits , on the other hand, can not only eliminate a tax bill but also result in money back. One example is the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC). Designed to support low- to moderate-income workers, the EITC can create a refund even when no federal income tax is owed. For example, if someone qualifies for a $700 refundable credit and owes $500 in taxes, they will receive the remaining $200 as a refund. This key difference makes refundable credits especially valuable for those with lower incomes.

TMP-1555.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1555.text: 24K-Production/Alamy Stock Photo Extended description for United States Treasury Check The check shows the Statue of Liberty on the left side. Details for the check read, from top to bottom, as follows: United States Treasury. Kansas City,

Additional text toward the bottom of the check reads, Economic Impact Payment, President Donald J. Trump. Refundable tax credits don’t just reduce taxes — they can lead to a refund.

TMP-1557.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1557.text: Examining Income and Payroll Deductions LG What information is included on an individual’s pay stub? When an employee gets paid, their wages might come in the form of a check or a direct deposit into their bank account. Either way, they’ll usually receive a pay stub — a statement that shows exactly how their pay was calculated, how much was withheld, and how much they get to keep. A pay stub is more than just a receipt; it helps you understand how much money you’re earning, how much is automatically withdrawn for various purposes, and how much is available for you to save or spend. It’s an essential tool for budgeting and ensuring that your employer pays you correctly. Figure 5.1-2 shows a sample weekly pay stub.

TMP-1558.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1558.text: pay stub A statement that details how an individual’s pay was calculated, how much was withheld, and how much they get to keep.
