Figure 5.1-2 Sample Pay Stub A pay stub provides the details on how much you’ve earned, the deductions for taxes and other purposes, and the amount available for you to save or spend. As Figure 5.1-2 illustrates, a pay stub breaks down an employee’s earnings. Most pay stubs include information for both the current pay period (the period you’re being paid for now) and the year to date (values accumulated since January 1). You can think of a

TMP-1561.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1561.navLabel: Gross Income: How Much Was Earned
TMP-1561.text: pay stub like a school report card — it shows how you did in the current marking period and how you’re doing overall. In the same way, a pay stub gives you a snapshot of your current paycheck and a running total of your income and deductions for the year. We’ll break down each part in the sections that follow. Gross Income: How Much Was Earned Gross income is the full amount of money you earned during a specified period, such as a week or a month. If you get paid every two weeks and earn $1,200 each time, that $1,200 is your gross income. This income depends on how you are compensated by your employer: For example, you might receive an hourly wage for a certain number of hours worked, an annual salary, or an amount specified in an employment contract. It’s the total payment before any money is taken out. But gross income provides a misleading picture of the money available to you, because it does not reflect the inevitable deductions. gross income The total amount earned before deductions.

headings.text: Gross Income: How Much Was Earned

TMP-1562.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1562.navLabel: Payroll Deductions: What Was Taken Out
TMP-1562.text: Payroll Deductions: What Was Taken Out Your pay stub will detail any money that is deducted by your employer. There are two kinds of payroll deductions: mandatory (sometimes called statutory ) and voluntary. Mandatory deductions are amounts that an employer is legally required to withhold from an employee’s paycheck. These include federal, state, and local income taxes, as well as payroll taxes like Social Security and Medicare. (On some pay stubs, the latter two are referred to as FICA deductions, which stands for the Federal Insurance Contribution Act.) Employers must take this money out of your paycheck and send it to the government, as described earlier in this module. mandatory deductions The amount of money that an employer is legally required to withhold from an employee’s paycheck to cover payroll taxes such as Medicare and Social Security. Voluntary deductions are amounts that an employee chooses to have withheld from their paycheck to pay for optional benefits or services, such as health insurance, life insurance, a retirement savings plan, or union dues. These deductions help pay for things that can benefit you in the future or protect you from unexpected costs.

headings.text: Payroll Deductions: What Was Taken Out

TMP-1563.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1563.navLabel: Net Income: How Much Do You Keep?
TMP-1563.text: voluntary deductions Money that an employee chooses to have withheld from their paycheck to pay for optional benefits or services, such as health insurance or retirement plans. Some voluntary deductions are designated as pre-tax deductions , which means they’re taken out of your gross income before your taxes are calculated. Money you put into a tax-deferred retirement plan , for example, is deducted from this year’s income, lowering your tax bill. You may also be able to use pre-tax deductions to fund accounts used to pay for qualified medical and dental expenses or education. These plans create an incentive to save for the future by lowering your tax bill in the present. pre-tax deductions A type of voluntary payroll deduction that is taken out of an employee’s gross income before taxes are calculated, reducing the employee’s taxable income and lowering the amount of taxes owed. Net Income: How Much Do You Keep? After all deductions — both mandatory and voluntary — are subtracted from your gross income, the amount that’s left is your net income , also known as your take-home pay . This is the actual money you receive in your paycheck. Net income can be much

headings.text: Net Income: How Much Do You Keep?

TMP-1564.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1564.navLabel: Net Income: How Much Do You Keep?
TMP-1564.text: less than gross income — and it’s the number you should focus on when deciding how much to save or spend on things like rent or a monthly car payment. When creating a budget, you should focus on your take-home pay, not the total amount you earn. For example, in Figure 5.1-2 , an employee earned a gross income of $1,634.80 this pay period, but they only took home $1,156.82. The difference between their gross income and their take-home pay was $1,634.80 − $1,156.82 = $477.98 each week. That means a monthly budget based on their gross income would overstate the income available for spending by 4 × $477.98 = $1,911.92 or more (depending on the length of the month). net income The money an employee receives after all taxes and deductions; often referred to as take-home pay.

TMP-1565.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1565.text: Module 5.1 Review Learning Goals LG What taxes do individuals pay in the United States? • Taxes are payments individuals and businesses make to the government to fund services like law enforcement, fire protection, highway construction, and public schools. An income tax is based on how much money a person or business earns. Most people have income taxes automatically withheld from their paychecks by employers and must file an annual income tax return to report earnings, calculate taxes owed, and possibly receive a tax refund . Self-employed workers must handle their own tax withholding. People who support others financially, such as parents who support their children, may list eligible support recipients as dependents . The number of dependents you claim affects how much tax you owe.

TMP-1566.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1566.text: • Another tax is the capital gains tax , which applies to profits from selling assets like stocks or homes. These gains are taxed at a lower rate than income if the assets were held for more than a year. • In addition to income tax, payroll taxes fund programs like Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment insurance. Workers and employers share these taxes, but self-employed people pay the full amount themselves through the self-employment tax . • Other taxes include property taxes , which are levied by local governments on real estate and, in some cases, on personal property such as vehicles. These taxes fund public services, including schools and law enforcement, and vary depending on the value of the property and where it is located. Many states and local governments also charge a sales tax , which customers pay as a percentage of the price of goods and services purchased. LG Why do different people pay different amounts of federal income tax?

TMP-1567.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1567.text: • Federal tax laws apply nationwide, but people pay different amounts of federal income tax depending on their level of income, the type of income (such as wage income or capital gains), and the tax deductions and credits for which they qualify. • For a progressive tax , those with higher incomes are taxed at higher rates. An individual’s marginal tax rate — the rate applied to the last dollar earned — does not apply to all their income. Income that falls within lower tax brackets is taxed at a lower rate. • Tax deductions and tax credits affect the amount of taxes paid. A tax deduction is subtracted from income before calculating how much is owed, reducing taxable income . In contrast, a tax credit directly reduces the amount of taxes owed, dollar for dollar — making it generally more valuable than a deduction. A nonrefundable tax credit can reduce your tax bill to zero but not below it, while a refundable tax credit can not only eliminate your tax liability, but also result in a refund if the credit exceeds the amount owed. LG What information is included on an individual’s pay stub?

TMP-1568.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1568.text: • A pay stub provides important details about your earnings over time, how much is deducted from your income, and how much you take home. Gross income is the full amount you earn before any payroll deductions are made; it’s not the amount available for you to save or spend. • Mandatory deductions include required payroll taxes like Medicare, Social Security, and federal and state income taxes. Voluntary deductions are optional allocations for items such as healthcare, retirement savings, and union dues. Some of these are pre-tax deductions , meaning that they lower your taxable income (and your tax bill). After all these deductions, what’s left is your net income — the money you actually receive. This is the amount to consider when budgeting or making spending decisions.

TMP-1578.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1578.text: MODULE 5.2 Managing Personal Risk LG LEARNING GOALS In this module, you will learn to: 5.2.A Discuss the different insurable risks that people face 5.2.B Explain how people use different types of insurance 5.2.C Describe the factors that influence decisions about insurance coverage

TMP-1579.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1579.text: Anadolu/Getty Images We all face insurable risks, like weather disasters that damage our property. Insurance can help protect us from the financial losses associated with these risks.

TMP-1580.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1580.text: Understanding Insurable Risks LG What insurable risks do people face? Life has its share of risks. Some risks are purely financial, such as the risk that hail will cause expensive damage to the roof of a car. Other risks are both financial and physical, like the risk that an illness will require treatment and affect your ability to work, or the risk that a tree will fall on a house and hurt someone. Luckily, there are ways to protect yourself from many types of risk. Insurable risks involve the possibility of a loss due to a chance occurrence, like a hurricane or a car accident. To be considered insurable, a risk must meet two criteria in addition to being accidental. First, it must be quantifiable , meaning that an insurer can estimate the potential cost of the loss in dollars. Second, it must be statistically predictable , meaning that an insurer can estimate the likelihood of a loss occurring.

TMP-1581.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1581.text: insurable risks Situations in which a potential loss occurs by chance. To be insurable, a risk must be quantifiable and statistically predictable . quantifiable The ability to estimate the potential cost of a loss in dollars. statistically predictable The ability to estimate how likely a loss is to occur. Although risks involve uncertainty, estimates of losses and likelihoods are informed by historical data. For example, no one knows where the next traffic accident will occur or what damage will result. However, for decades, U.S. drivers have experienced between 5 and 7 million traffic accidents each year — and between 1.5 million and 2.3 million injuries have resulted from those accidents annually, as have between 29,000 and 40,000 fatalities. 1 Insurance companies can use that data to form useful estimates of how many accidents, injuries, and fatalities to expect in the coming year, and the size of the associated insurance claims. People face three main types of insurable risk: personal risk, property risk, and liability risk.

TMP-1582.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1582.text: Personal Risk Personal risk is the risk of experiencing injury or illness that impacts your health, well-being, or ability to earn income. Examples of personal risk include death or disability, and the loss of income or employment. Medical expenses are also a significant personal risk, as unexpected illnesses or injuries can lead to high costs for treatment and care. personal risk The risk of experiencing injury or illness that impacts a person’s health, well-being, and ability to earn income. Property Risk Property risk involves threats to the physical assets that a person (or a business) owns. This can include damage or loss caused by fire and explosions, which can destroy homes, buildings, or valuable belongings. Theft and vandalism are also common property risks, where possessions are stolen or deliberately damaged. Additionally, natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods, hurricanes, or tornadoes pose significant risks to property by causing widespread destruction and loss.

TMP-1583.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1583.text: property risk The risk of loss or damage to a person’s physical assets. Liability Risk Liability risk is the risk of being held legally responsible for causing injury to someone else or damaging their property. This can include situations where an individual or company is liable for bodily injury or property damage resulting from their actions or negligence. If you hit a parked car, for example, you will be responsible for the damage you cause. And if a person is injured on your property, you may be held liable. liability risk The risk of being held legally responsible for causing injury to someone else or damaging their property.

TMP-1584.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1584.text: PhotoAlto/Odilon Dimier/Getty Images Driving involves personal risk (you could get hurt in an accident), property risk (your car can be damaged or stolen), and liability risk (you could hurt someone else or damage their property).

TMP-1585.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1585.text: Types of Insurance LG How do different types of insurance protect people? Without insurance, unexpected events — like a medical emergency, car accident, or damage to a home — can cause major financial setbacks and even serious debt. Insurance helps us to manage these risks by replacing a small chance of a large expense at an unpredictable time with a certain, periodic payment of a relatively small amount to purchase the insurance. Insurance companies effectively spread the cost of insurable risks across large numbers of people by collecting payments from all of their customers and providing assistance to the subset of people who experience covered losses. When you buy insurance, you’re buying a policy — a contract that specifies the types of losses the insurer will cover, and under what circumstances. In return for your desired amount of coverage, you pay a premium — a fee that may be billed monthly,

TMP-1586.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1586.text: semi-annually, or annually. If an event covered by your policy occurs, you can file a claim, which is a request for the insurance company to reimburse your financial loss based on your policy terms. policy A contract specifying the types of losses an insurer will cover, and under what circumstances. premium A fee billed monthly, semi-annually, or annually by an insurer for a period of coverage. claim A request asking an insurer to reimburse a financial loss based on the policy terms. People can buy different types of insurance — including health, auto, homeowner’s, renter’s, and life insurance — to cover insurable risks and limit their financial consequences. As we will discuss later, some types of insurance are also required by law. Health Insurance Health insurance provides partial or full reimbursement for the cost of most medically necessary healthcare and some types of preventative care. Medically necessary

TMP-1587.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1587.text: healthcare includes services required to diagnose, manage, or treat health-related conditions. Treatment for illnesses such as diabetes, injuries such as a broken arm, and life events such as childbirth are all considered medically necessary healthcare. Preventive care is meant to detect issues early and prevent illness — think annual wellness visits and vaccines. A health insurance policy may offer the option to include a person’s relatives or dependents in its coverage, such as a spouse, children (up to age 26), or, sometimes, older dependents such as aging parents or adult children with disabilities. health insurance A type of insurance that reimburses people for medically necessary healthcare, and sometimes preventive care. You may have choices among plans when you sign up for health insurance. Two common types are HMO (Health Maintenance Organization) and PPO (Preferred Provider Organization) plans, which have different costs, rules for coverage, and guidelines for choosing healthcare providers. HMO plans tend to cost less, but members are required to visit in-network doctors and get referrals to visit specialists. PPO plans tend to have higher premiums, but they offer more freedom to choose doctors and visit specialists without referrals.

TMP-1588.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1588.text: Many people receive health insurance as a benefit from their employer. Others can purchase insurance through the Health Insurance Marketplace ( HealthCare.gov ), through a health insurance broker that works with multiple insurance companies, or directly from a health insurance company. Some people qualify for government- sponsored insurance programs such as Medicaid (for individuals and families below a certain income level) and Medicare (mainly for people 65 and older). And some colleges and universities offer health insurance plans for students. The importance of health insurance is underscored by the high cost of healthcare, the unpredictable nature of healthcare needs, and the frequency of healthcare-related bankruptcy. 2

TMP-1589.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1589.text: FatCamera/Getty Images Health insurance helps people cover the costs of diagnosing, managing, and treating a health condition or injury. Depending on the level of coverage, it may also cover preventive care.

TMP-1590.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1590.text: Auto Insurance If you own a vehicle or do much driving, another type of insurance is critical. Auto insurance helps to protect you from the risk of injury or property damage related to your vehicle. It generally covers injuries or property damage you cause in an accident, and depending on the type of coverage selected, it may cover damage to your own car as well. auto insurance A type of insurance that protects drivers if the vehicle they are driving is involved in an accident or an injury. People may choose among different types of auto insurance. Three of the most common are: Liability coverage , which covers costs like medical bills and legal fees if you injure someone in an accident, as well as the damage you cause to another person’s car or other property while driving. Most U.S. states require drivers to have at least this type of coverage.

TMP-1591.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1591.text: Collision coverage , which covers damage to your vehicle if you’re in an accident (no matter who’s at fault); it also covers collisions between your car and other objects, like a tree or a guardrail. Comprehensive coverage , which covers damage to your vehicle from other events — like theft, hail, or flooding. It’s wise to determine the cost of insuring a particular car before deciding to buy that car. When considering how much auto insurance you’ll need, weigh the value of your vehicle against the cost of the insurance premiums. A car that is newer or higher in value might justify the added cost of collision or comprehensive coverage. For a car that is lower in value, the premiums for that additional coverage might be greater than the value of the car.

TMP-1592.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1592.text: sturti/Getty Images Even a minor accident can mean a costly car repair. Auto insurance helps to offset these costs.

TMP-1593.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1593.text: Homeowner’s and Renter’s Insurance Homeowner’s insurance helps to protect people who own their home from financial losses due to specified types of incidents and events. With limitations, this insurance typically offers personal property coverage to protect the belongings inside your home from perils such as fire and theft; loss of use coverage that pays for hotel, meal, and other living expenses if you’re unable to live in your home for a covered reason (say, a gas leak or a roof collapse due to snow); and liability coverage that pays a visitor’s expenses if they’re injured in your home. Homeowner’s insurance also covers damage to a home’s physical structure, as could be caused by a fire or a falling tree. homeowner’s insurance A type of insurance that protects homeowners with personal property, loss of use, and liability coverage, as well as coverage for damage to a home’s structure. Renter’s insurance helps to protect people who are renting a home (which can also be an apartment, condo, or other living space) from losses due to specified types of incidents and events. Like homeowner’s insurance, renter’s insurance typically provides limited coverage of personal property losses, liability, and loss of use expenses caused by qualifying incidents and events. Renter’s insurance generally does not cover

TMP-1594.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1594.text: expenses related to building structures or the landlord’s property (such as appliances provided by the landlord). renter’s insurance A type of insurance that protects renters with personal property, loss of use, and liability coverage. Life Insurance Life insurance provides money to a chosen person or group of people, known as the beneficiaries, in the event that the insured person dies. This money, known as the death benefit, may cover immediate needs like funeral costs and other end-of-life expenses. It may also help fund the beneficiaries’ future needs, like college tuition, and help to replace the insured person’s lost income. life insurance A type of insurance that provides funds (the death benefit ) to beneficiaries if the insured person dies. beneficiaries The individual or group chosen by an insured person to receive funds when the person dies.

TMP-1595.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1595.text: You don’t have to buy life insurance, but it can be very helpful for people who have others depending on them. Life insurance can make a big difference for families who would have a hard time managing financially after losing someone who helped support them. Extended Warranties and Service Contracts Most vehicles, major appliances, and electronics — like new cars, refrigerators, and laptops — come with a warranty . This is a guarantee from the manufacturer or the seller that, if the product has a defect during the covered time period (usually one year), the company will provide a repair, replacement, or refund. Customers may also have the option to purchase an extended warranty or a service contract. An extended warranty lengthens the period of coverage beyond that of the original warranty. The original manufacturer’s warranty on a new laptop, for example, might cover hardware issues and other defects for one year; the extended warranty may cover those issues for two additional years. An extended warranty may also provide broader coverage than the original by covering additional components or types of problems. extended warranty An add-on option customers may purchase to lengthen the terms of a product’s original warranty.

TMP-1596.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1596.text: A service contract covers certain repairs and maintenance of the product, which can remedy problems beyond manufacturing defects, such as the effects of wear and tear and accidental damage. A service contract for that new laptop, for example, might include repairs or replacement if the owner drops it and shatters the screen. service contract An add-on option customers may purchase to obtain more comprehensive coverage for a product. By protecting you against future financial loss, these options serve as a form of insurance. When considering an extended warranty or service contract, be sure to read the contract carefully and familiarize yourself with its terms and conditions, including the claims process, exclusions, and limitations. That way, you can better weigh the cost of the warranty against the benefits you are likely to receive from its coverage.

TMP-1597.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1597.text: Bloomberg/Getty Images For big-ticket items, extended warranties and service contracts can mean extended peace of mind — but consider the cost and terms of the contract carefully. Table 5.2-1 outlines the types of insurance people buy to protect themselves from the unexpected.

TMP-1598.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1598.text: Table 5.2-1 Types of Insurance Insurance Type What Is Typically Covered? Is It Required? Who Needs It Most? Health Medically necessary healthcare; some types of preventive care Varies by U.S. state (legally required in CA, MA, NJ, RI, DC) Everyone Auto Damage to other vehicles, property, or people; may also cover your vehicle Yes, in 49 states (NH offers alternatives) All drivers who own or frequently operate a vehicle Homeowner’s/Renter’s Personal property, liability, and sometimes loss of use; for homeowners, structure of home Not legally required, but often required by lenders (homeowner’s insurance) or landlords (renter’s insurance) Anyone who owns or rents a home Life Death benefit to beneficiaries No People with dependents, or those wanting to leave financial support Extended Warranties/Service Contracts Repairs, replacement, or refund of items (such as cars or appliances) No People seeking additional or extended protection for expensive purchases

TMP-1599.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing

TMP-1600.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1600.text: Making Insurance Decisions LG What factors influence insurance decisions? Buying insurance is personal. The amount and type of coverage you require depend on your individual needs and circumstances. There may be legal requirements to purchase a certain type of insurance. Some people have dependents whose financial needs must be considered. And people differ in their levels of comfort with risk, which means they need different amounts of insurance for their own peace of mind. Suppose Bianca is 40 years old and lives with her four teenage children in a house on which she makes monthly mortgage loan payments. Three of her children drive the one- year-old family car, and all of her kids plan to attend college. Bianca thinks often of the future and how to ensure that her family is healthy, successful, and financially stable. She loses sleep worrying about the prospect of financial losses due to unexpected events

TMP-1601.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1601.text: such as accidents or storms. Across town, 25-year-old Benjamin lives in his mother’s home; he drives cautiously in an old, inexpensive car and has no dependents. Benjamin doesn’t worry much about unexpected financial losses, because he doesn’t own valuable material goods and has the support of his family. Bianca and Benjamin will need very different levels and types of insurance coverage. In this section, we discuss several factors that help people determine the right coverage for their situation. We also explain steps that may reduce premiums and make insurance more affordable, and we consider the potential for insurance fraud, which everyone buying or using insurance should be aware of. Legal Requirements State and federal laws require certain types of insurance. As we noted earlier, most U.S. states require car owners to have auto liability insurance. And while state laws don’t require homeowner’s or renter’s insurance, mortgage lenders will typically require borrowers to have homeowner’s insurance.

TMP-1602.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1602.text: Health insurance wasn’t required in the United States until 2010, when the Affordable Care Act, in an effort to expand healthcare access, established a penalty for people without health insurance. This penalty was reduced to $0 in 2019, effectively ending the federal mandate — but some states, as described in Table 5.2-1 , still require residents to have some health insurance coverage. Risk Tolerance Anyone making an insurance decision should weigh the cost of the insurance against the value of the protection it provides. A key factor in that analysis is a person’s risk tolerance — the level of financial risk someone is willing or able to accept. People with a lower risk tolerance generally prefer to buy insurance with more comprehensive protection, paying higher premiums now to safeguard against big, potentially catastrophic costs later. Bianca, whom we met in the earlier example, would likely consider all the possible events that could compromise her household’s stability — say, a car accident for one of her teenage drivers, a serious illness in the family, or her own death and the family’s resulting loss of income. Her large exposure to risk and her

TMP-1603.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1603.text: low risk tolerance would make her willing to pay higher premiums to avoid the hardships these scenarios could cause. Benjamin, on the other hand, has a higher risk tolerance. He would likely choose more basic coverage. He would probably also select a higher deductible , which is the amount an insured person agrees to pay out-of-pocket before insurance kicks in. For example, if the deductible on his health insurance is $3,000, Benjamin would pay the first $3,000 of his healthcare costs and the insurance would cover eligible costs beyond that amount. By accepting the risk of paying more out-of-pocket with a higher deductible, he would pay lower premiums each month. Because Benjamin has few financial obligations, less exposure to risk, and a high risk tolerance, he may reason that the potential benefits from more comprehensive coverage are not worth the additional cost. deductible The amount a person agrees to pay out-of-pocket before insurance takes over.

TMP-1604.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1604.text: Dependents Having dependents generally increases the need for various types of insurance. Someone like Bianca would probably want family health insurance, which covers the healthcare needs of multiple family members under a single policy. Life insurance is important when dependents rely on a parent or guardian to support their lifestyle, cover household debts, and pay for future expenses such as education. And when dependents are drivers, that affects the need for auto insurance — which will, unfortunately, be more expensive for younger drivers like Bianca’s teenage children.

TMP-1605.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1605.text: Sladic/Getty Images More dependents can mean more insurance to keep a household safe and supported. Making Insurance More Affordable There are several steps you can take to lower your insurance premiums. You could:

TMP-1606.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1606.text: Reduce your risk. As when seeking loans, being perceived as a lower risk usually means getting a better deal. The fewer incidents on your driving record, the lower your auto insurance rates are likely to be. Avoiding risky behavior such as smoking may get you lower life insurance premiums. And having safety features in your home, like a security system or fire sprinklers, might get you a better rate on your homeowner’s insurance. Being perceived as a higher risk, on the other hand, can make your premiums rise. A speeding ticket may raise the cost of your auto insurance. Adding a pool or a trampoline to your backyard might raise the cost of your homeowner’s insurance, because they increase the likelihood of injuries occurring on your property. And if you’ve recently used your insurance — say, by filing a claim for damage to your car or home — you may be perceived as a higher risk, resulting in higher premiums. Reduce your coverage. Insurance is critical in many cases, but it is possible to buy too much insurance. Consider Bianca, who needs life insurance with a sizable death benefit now, because her family relies on her to pay the mortgage loan and support their way of life. In 30 years, when her kids no longer rely on her financially, she may decide to reduce her insurance cost by lowering her coverage to just enough for end-of-life expenses.

TMP-1607.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1607.text: Raise your deductible. By choosing a higher deductible, you’re agreeing to take on more of the cost of an unforeseen event — to pay more of a hospital bill or cover more of a car repair before insurance takes over. Insurance companies typically charge lower premiums for insurance plans with higher deductibles. Use discounts. Many insurance companies offer discounts for setting up autopay, using an app that monitors your driving safety, paying your entire premium upfront rather than over time, or buying multiple kinds of insurance (such as home and auto) from the same company. Completing a driver’s education course, maintaining an accident-free driving record, or even being a good student can earn you additional savings. Taking advantage of these discounts can reduce your insurance premiums substantially.

TMP-1608.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1608.text: JulPo/Getty Images The cost of homeowner’s insurance can depend on the presence of trampolines, swimming pools, and other identifiable risks.

TMP-1609.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing

Insurance Fraud Honesty matters. Customers commit the crime of insurance fraud when they deliberately misrepresent information or falsify claims when purchasing or using insurance. This could include lying about or exaggerating a loss or an injury (say, the amount of property stolen in a burglary), filing more than one claim to cover the same loss, or failing to disclose certain health conditions when buying life insurance. This

TMP-1611.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1611.text: type of fraud may result in not only denied claims and canceled policies, but fines and jail time. insurance fraud A crime committed by insured people or insurance sellers who make false claims or misrepresent information. Insurance sellers — whether companies or individual agents — can also commit insurance fraud. This occurs when an agent or company sells fake policies, misrepresents the coverage a policy provides (for example, if an agent lies about what is covered in order to make a sale), or alters your application for insurance after you’ve signed it to make its approval more likely (such as by deleting a pre-existing health condition). Fraud by insurance sellers can leave people unprotected in ways they don’t realize until they seek coverage for an unexpected event. To protect yourself from this kind of fraud, it pays to verify an insurance agent’s license (your state’s insurance website will allow you to check their credentials). Consider buying from well-known, reputable insurance companies and the agents associated with them, and be sure you get the full policy in writing, with a clear explanation of what is and is not covered.

TMP-1612.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1612.text: Module 5.2 Review Learning Goals LG What insurable risks do people face? Insurable risks are situations in which a potential loss occurs by chance. To be considered insurable, a risk must also be quantifiable (an insurer can estimate the potential cost of the loss) and statistically predictable (an insurer can estimate the likelihood of the loss). People face three general types of insurable risk. Personal risk is the risk of experiencing injury or illness that impacts your health, well-being, or ability to earn income. Property risk is the risk of loss of, or damage to, your physical assets. Liability risk is the risk of causing injury to someone else or damaging their property.

TMP-1613.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1613.text: LG How do different types of insurance protect people? Anyone purchasing insurance is buying a policy — a contract that specifies the types of losses the insurer will cover, and under what circumstances. In return for coverage, the insured person pays a premium — a fee that may be billed monthly, semi-annually, or annually. If a covered event occurs, you can file a claim , which is a request for the insurance company to reimburse a financial loss based on policy terms. Health insurance reimburses people for medically necessary healthcare, and it may also cover preventive care. Auto insurance helps to protect you if your vehicle is involved in an accident or an injury. It may include liability coverage, which covers harm to another person or their property while you are driving; collision coverage, which covers damage to your vehicle if you’re in an accident; and comprehensive coverage, which covers damage to your vehicle from other noncollision events. Homeowner’s insurance protects homeowners with personal property, loss-of-use, and liability coverage, as well as coverage for damage to a home’s structure.

TMP-1614.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1614.text: Renter’s insurance protects renters with personal property, loss-of-use, and liability coverage, but it does not typically cover the physical structure of the home or the landlord’s property (such as appliances). Life insurance provides funds to beneficiaries — the individual or group chosen by an insured person to receive funds when the person dies. This money is known as the death benefit . Most vehicles, major appliances, and electronics come with a warranty . Extended warranties and service contracts act like insurance by protecting customers from future financial loss. Extended warranties lengthen the terms of the original warranty, while service contracts may include more comprehensive coverage. LG What factors influence insurance decisions? People may be legally required to purchase certain types of insurance. Most U.S. states require drivers to have auto liability insurance, and a handful require health insurance coverage. There are no legal requirements for renter’s, homeowner’s, or life insurance, but mortgage lenders will typically require borrowers to have

TMP-1615.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1615.text: homeowner’s insurance, and landlords may require a tenant to have renter’s insurance. A person’s risk tolerance — the level of financial risk they are willing or able to accept — is an important factor in making insurance decisions. People with a lower risk tolerance are generally more willing to pay higher premiums for more comprehensive coverage. People with a higher risk tolerance might prefer to pay less for more basic coverage or a higher deductible — the amount paid out-of-pocket before insurance takes over. The number of dependents an individual or household has is an important consideration in making insurance decisions. For example, the appropriate amount of life insurance depends largely on the expenses, debts, and future goals of dependents. People can make insurance more affordable by reducing risk, reducing coverage, choosing a higher deductible, or making use of discounts. The crime of insurance fraud occurs when insured people or insurance sellers make false claims or misrepresent information. Fraud by insurance sellers can leave customers unprotected.

TMP-1616.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1616.text: Insurance is highly personal; it’s not one-size-fits-all. When considering the types and levels of insurance someone needs in a hypothetical situation, be sure you take the specifics — legal requirements, risk tolerance, and dependents — into account. TMP-1619.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1619.text: CASE STUDY The Just-Right Amount of Insurance Coverage valentinrussanov/Getty Images Figuring out the right amount of insurance coverage is a personal process influenced by many aspects of the insured person’s life. Martine is 26 years old and recently finished her master’s degree in early education. A few months later, she was thrilled to land a job as Assistant Director of Bloom Academy, a big daycare center in a city several hours away. Martine lived with her parents during college and graduate school, but she’s just moved into a rental apartment closer to her new job. Her new neighborhood is pleasant, but

TMP-1620.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1620.text: there have recently been some break-ins in her building and nearby. She spent some of her small savings on a used car, since she has a thirty-minute commute to work and wants to be able to visit her family easily. She’s currently saving money to buy a new laptop, which she’ll need both for work and for personal tasks. Growing up, Martine’s household was financially unstable. Her parents, who often couldn’t find work in their small town, had to prioritize expenditures on basic necessities such as food and clothing over the purchase of adequate insurance to protect against the risk of unexpected events. They were underinsured — they had some insurance coverage, but not nearly enough to protect them from loss if something went wrong. This led to some financial catastrophes over the years, including several car accidents and medical emergencies that landed the family in serious debt. Martine wants to do things differently. She’s determined to leverage her education and her ability to relocate to a place with stable work opportunities, and she wants to protect herself from unforeseen events that could cause financial ruin. Martine soon finds herself overwhelmed by the available insurance options. Her new upstairs neighbor, an insurance agent, has tried aggressively to sell Martine an

TMP-1621.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1621.text: expensive life insurance policy. Bloom Academy offers its employees an HMO or a PPO option for health insurance. Martine isn’t sure which to choose. Her considerations include a chronic condition that her beloved primary care doctor and a particular specialist help her to manage. She can’t decide how much auto insurance to purchase for her car, which is 15 years old and worth a few thousand dollars. And while her new landlord strongly suggests renter’s insurance for tenants, she isn’t sure whether to buy it and, if so, how much coverage she’ll need. Martine wants to be sure she has the just-right amount of insurance coverage — enough to provide appropriate protection from future losses, but not more than she actually needs. She decides to make an appointment with an insurance advisor to discuss her options. Imagine that you’re this advisor, tasked with helping Martine determine her insurance needs and providing advice. APPLY YOUR AP ® SKILLS 1. Given Martine’s specific situation, what would you advise her to do regarding renter’s insurance and auto insurance? 2. What advice would you give Martine about health insurance?

TMP-1625.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1625.navLabel:
MODULE 5.3 Saving and Investing for Education, Housing, and
Retirement Goals
TMP-1625.text: What are your goals for your future? What are your dreams for your future? Careful financial planning can help you get there, and it’s never too early to start. In fact, the sooner you start, the more empowered you’ll be to make good choices and grow your wealth over time. If your goals include pursuing higher education, buying a home, or retiring comfortably, understanding how to save and invest can help you build a solid foundation — and live well at every stage of your life.

TMP-1626.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1626.text: Planning for Your Goals LG How does financial planning help people achieve their goals for post-secondary education, housing, and retirement? People’s long-term financial goals commonly include paying for post-secondary education (such as college or trade school) for themselves, or for their children; purchasing a home; and saving enough to enjoy a comfortable retirement. No matter where you’re starting from, you can work toward your future goals by learning the basics of money management and making smart choices along the way. Educational Goals Your decisions about post-secondary education are highly personal — what you want to study, which schools or training programs interest you, and how you might use your new skills and knowledge. These decisions are also guided by the costs of an education,

TMP-1627.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1627.text: which can be significant and may include tuition, fees, housing costs, and other expenses. To pay for educational costs, individuals or households often start with their personal savings. If a student has been awarded grants or scholarships, which don’t need to be repaid, these may provide a powerful incentive to attend school or to attend a particular school. Millions of students also finance their educations with student loans. When deciding how to pay for their education, students and their families may consider both the short-term affordability and the long-term impact of borrowing, because any loan means a future financial obligation. Federal student loans may offer lower interest rates and more flexible repayment terms than private student loans, and they may be government subsidized. Many students also participate in work-study programs, a type of financial aid that allows students to work part time while taking classes. In the United States, most work-study programs are funded through the Federal Work-Study (FWS) Program, which is managed by the U.S. Department of Education. Some colleges and universities also fund their own institutional work-study programs. Balancing work and academics requires

TMP-1628.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1628.text: discipline, commitment, and strong time management skills — but work-study programs can help students cover expenses while gaining valuable work experience. MediaNews Group/Boulder Daily Camera via Getty Images Work-study programs are an important part of many students’ financial aid packages.

TMP-1629.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1629.text: Housing Goals Decisions about housing — where to live, what type of space to live in, and whether it’s best to rent or buy — are also highly individual, determined by people’s location, lifestyle preferences, family needs, and financial situations. Most people finance a home purchase with a combination of personal savings and borrowing. Savings are typically used for a down payment — an upfront payment from the buyer that reduces the amount that must be borrowed — which lenders usually require (as discussed in Module 3.2 ). A common down payment is around 20% of the home’s selling price, but it can be much less. For the remainder of the home’s purchase price, buyers may qualify for a mortgage loan (also discussed in Module 3.2 ). Monthly mortgage payments are determined by several factors: the loan amount (smaller loans mean smaller payments), the repayment term (longer terms reduce monthly payments, but increase total interest), and the interest rate. As we learned in earlier modules, interest rates on loans are influenced by the lender, the loan type, the loan size, and the borrower’s credit history.

TMP-1630.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1630.text: The interest rate on a mortgage may be fixed or adjustable (variable). A fixed-rate mortgage has an interest rate that never changes during the term of the loan. An adjustable-rate mortgage has an interest rate that can vary over the term of the loan. The interest rate on an adjustable-rate mortgage typically starts out lower than the rate on fixed-rate mortgages and remains fixed for a certain period (say, for five years). After the fixed period ends, the rate is adjusted at regular intervals (such as every six months) based on how interest rates are changing in the economy. The interest rate and associated loan payments can increase significantly after the fixed period, making it harder to predict the future cost of the loan, although most adjustable-rate mortgages have limits on the size of rate increases. fixed-rate mortgage A mortgage with a rate that never changes during the term of the loan. adjustable-rate mortgage A mortgage that often begins with a lower fixed rate for a certain period, then changes — or adjusts — based on how interest rates are changing in the economy. A fixed-rate mortgage is a good option for those who prefer predictable payments and plan to remain in their home for a long time. Due to the relatively low initial interest rate on adjustable-rate mortgages, they can be a good option for people whose income is

TMP-1631.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1631.text: currently low but is expected to rise, and those who plan to sell their home before the rate adjusts. PeopleImages.com - Yuri A/Shutterstock When buying a home, homebuyers should consider how long they plan to live there. A fixed-rate mortgage provides interest-rate certainty over the long term, but an adjustable-rate mortgage can provide savings if the home is temporary.

TMP-1632.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1632.text: Retirement Goals Imagine your life in 50 or 60 years. If you’re retired, where are you living? What kind of lifestyle, location, and space do you think will suit you best? It’s hard to know how your preferences may change over the years, but saving for retirement is something you’ll need to start doing well in advance of that time. Deciding when and where to retire depends not only on your personal preferences, but also on your health and medical needs (for example, if you have mobility issues that would make certain environments difficult) and sources of funding. Retirees’ income usually comes from a combination of Social Security, employer-sponsored retirement plans, individual investments, and earnings from part-time or continued employment. When families share their finances, collaboration is key. Married or cohabiting partners should discuss their short- and long-term financial goals, their budgets, and their plans for savings, as well as any individual or shared debts they may have. A mutual understanding of priorities for major expenses, like home purchases, education, and retirement contributions, can help partners minimize conflict and improve financial stability.

TMP-1633.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1633.text: Modern financial technology provides useful tools when it comes to saving for retirement. As discussed in Module 3.2 , automated savings plans and payroll deductions for retirement accounts can help individuals and households overcome barriers to saving. Budgeting apps make it easier to track spending and progress toward savings goals.

TMP-1634.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1634.text: Halfpoint Images/Getty Images How do you envision your retirement? It’s never too early to think about it — and the sooner you start saving, the more you can make of your money.

TMP-1635.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1635.navLabel:
What Affects the Return on Financial
Assets?
TMP-1635.text: What Affects the Return on Financial Assets? LG What factors affect an investor’s return on financial assets? Smart saving and investing requires long-term financial planning. Whether you’re saving for a home purchase, education expenses, or retirement, you’ll likely put your money in financial assets that have the potential to grow. Some of these assets are savings vehicles — accounts that investors use to save and grow their money over time, like savings accounts and certificates of deposit (CDs) (discussed in Module 3.1 ). Other financial assets include stocks, bonds, and mutual funds. Mutual funds are a type of investment in which many people pool their money together and a professional manager invests that money in a mix of assets, like stocks and bonds. Each person owns a share of the fund and earns money if the investments perform well. In this section, we’ll examine key influences on the returns gained from financial assets such as these.

headings.text: What Affects the Return on Financial Assets?

TMP-1636.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1636.text: savings vehicles Accounts that investors use to save and grow their money over time, like savings accounts and certificates of deposit (CDs). mutual funds A type of investment in which many people pool their money together, and a professional manager invests that money in a mix of assets, like stocks and bonds. Time and Compounding It takes patience to earn money on financial assets, because the growth in their value generally takes time. The benefit to those who are willing to wait for that growth is called the return , which is the amount of money gained or lost over a certain period, such as a year. Suppose you invested $100 one year ago in shares of a mutual fund that are now worth $110. The amount of money you put into the investment, $100, is called the principal . Your return on the investment was what you got back from the investment minus the principal: $110 − $100 = $10. return The amount of money an investor gains or loses over a certain period.

TMP-1637.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1637.text: If your returns from a financial asset are reinvested back into the asset, you’ll earn returns on not only the principal, but also on the returns. For example, suppose you put $1,200 into a savings account that earned 5% interest per year. After one year you would have $60 in interest. If you kept the principal and interest in the account for another year, you would earn 5% interest on the larger $1,260 amount in the second year, and earn the larger return of $63. This snowball effect of earnings generating additional earnings is called compounding . The power of compounding is greater the earlier you begin saving and investing. compounding The process of earnings generating additional earnings over time. To illustrate the value of investing early, suppose Leroy invests $3,000 into a retirement account at the age of 20, while Lara invests that same amount at the age of 35. For simplicity, we will assume a 7% annual return, compounded annually. At the age of 65, Leroy’s original investment will be worth $63,007; Lara’s will be worth $22,837. Even with the same amount invested, Leroy’s earlier start will nearly triple the account’s value at retirement.

TMP-1638.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1638.text: Many people like to invest a little bit each month. Figure 5.3-1 shows the power of compounding applied to this sort of recurring investment. Suppose that for 25 years you deposited $20 at the beginning of each month into an account that earns 6% annual interest, compounded monthly. After 25 years you would have a total of $13,929 in your account. And over that period, thanks to earning interest not only on your principal but also on your interest, your total interest would be $7,929, exceeding your total deposits of $6,000.

Lower-risk financial assets include treasury bonds and savings accounts insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (as discussed in Module 3.1 ). These lower-risk assets generally have lower expected returns. Other financial assets, like individual stocks, are

headings.text: The Risks and Costs of Investing

TMP-1641.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1641.navLabel: The Risks and Costs of Investing
TMP-1641.text: riskier because the asset’s value depends on the success of a business. These riskier assets generally have higher expected returns. Buying, selling, and holding financial assets may involve transaction fees, management fees, and fees for any professional advice you may receive. Stocks and bonds must be purchased through a broker, who may charge brokerage fees. All such fees will decrease the return on your investment, which makes them important to consider when choosing investment vehicles. Some investors elect to work with discount brokerage firms, which provide fewer services than full-service firms but charge lower fees. Taxes on your investments will also decrease your return. Earnings from your financial assets may be subject to several types of taxation. Interest income — from savings and bonds, for example — is generally taxed as ordinary income. Dividends — which we learned in Module 3.5 are a company’s distributions of profits to its shareholders — may be taxed at lower rates, depending on how long the stock was held and whether the company qualifies for those lower rates. Capital gains — those profits on the sale of assets we learned about in Module 5.1 — may also be taxed at lower rates, depending on how long the asset was held.

TMP-1642.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1642.text: The Effect of Inflation Inflation reduces the amount of goods and services you can buy with your money over time. As a result, the real return on an investment — the purchasing power of that return in terms of what you can actually buy with that money — may be smaller than the investment’s nominal return , which is the number of dollars you’ve earned. Let’s say that Cory invests $1,000 in a bond with a 4% annual return. At the end of the year, Cory’s investment will be worth $1,040. But if inflation that year is 3%, then the cost of the goods and services that Cory buys rose by 3%. By subtracting the inflation rate from the nominal rate of return, we can approximate the real rate of return: 4% − 3% = 1%. So, while Cory earned a nominal return of $40 in interest, the real increase in his purchasing power was only about $10. When investing, it’s therefore important to consider real ( inflation-adjusted ) and nominal ( unadjusted ) returns. real return The increase in purchasing power earned from an investment — calculated by subtracting inflation from the nominal return . nominal return The dollar amount earned from an investment.

TMP-1643.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1643.text: Daniel Wischenbarth/Getty Images How far can your investment earnings take you? By considering real (inflation-adjusted) returns, you’ll have a more accurate sense of the increase in your purchasing power.

TMP-1644.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1644.text: Behaviors That Can Cost Us Sometimes the greatest threat to returns on your assets isn’t the market — it’s your behavior as an investor. We often believe we’re acting rationally, but our psychological and emotional states can play a big role in our decision making. Understanding the behavioral biases that impact our financial decisions can help us to think more objectively and make smarter choices. Two common behavioral biases that can adversely affect investment returns are overconfidence and loss aversion. Overconfidence is an investor’s belief that they possess greater knowledge or predictive abilities than they actually do. This inflated confidence may lead to reckless behavior — for example, investing in risky assets without weighing possible negative outcomes, or disregarding evidence suggesting that a particular investment is a poor choice. overconfidence An investor’s belief that they possess greater knowledge or predictive abilities than they actually do.

TMP-1645.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1645.text: Loss aversion , on the other hand, is the tendency to prefer avoiding losses more strongly than achieving gains of the same amount. A person with loss aversion would experience the loss of $100 with more intensity than the pleasure of gaining $100. In the world of investing, this means that if the market dips, an investor with loss aversion may panic and sell their investments prematurely — often losing money — to avoid further declines in value. Fear can prevent us from thinking rationally and strategically. Often, the better move is to stick with the long-term investment plan and give the market time to recover. As shown in Figure 5.3-2 , the value of stocks in the Standard and Poor’s 500 (S&P 500) stock market index (which tracks the performance of 500 companies’ stocks, as discussed later in this module) rise and fall dramatically over short time intervals, but have generally risen over the longer term. loss aversion The tendency to prefer avoiding loss more strongly than achieving gains of the same amount.

AP ® SKILL TIP Overconfidence and loss aversion are behavioral biases that affect us not only in the world of investing, but in our everyday lives. Can you think of a time when you’ve felt overconfident and made a poor judgment? How about a time when you were so worried about losing something that you acted too soon? Becoming aware of such biases is the first step toward overcoming them. This is an important skill that can help us make better, more objective decisions.

TMP-1648.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing

TMP-1649.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1649.navLabel: Creating a Saving and Investment Plan
TMP-1649.text: Creating a Saving and Investment Plan LG How can investors create a saving and investment plan tailored to their goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance? Many factors influence how we save and invest our money. When considering how to allocate our funds among different assets, we need to take into account the amount of funding needed to meet our goals; how much we can realistically save; the amount of time we have to save and invest; what rate of return we can expect from each asset; and our individual and household risk tolerance. If you were advising a client or a friend who wished to make a saving and investment plan — or if you wanted to create such a plan for yourself — how would you take these various factors into account?

headings.text: Creating a Saving and Investment Plan

TMP-1650.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1650.text: Time Horizon When it comes to saving and investing, time horizon and risk go hand-in-hand. Individuals or households with a longer time horizon may choose higher-risk, higher-return investments, like stocks, because those people can better cope with downturns and wait for assets to regain their value. A 25-year-old saving for retirement, for example, has time to ride out market fluctuations and a better chance to reap the benefit of higher returns from riskier investments. A shorter time horizon makes safer assets relatively attractive. If the investor may need to liquidate assets such as stocks in the short run, that may necessitate a stock sale during an economic downturn, resulting in a loss or a lower-than-expected return. An 18-year-old saving for college might choose to keep their money in a lower-risk, lower-return option like a savings account, which ensures they’ll have access to their money in the short run when they need it, without worrying about losses due to fluctuations in the economy. And older adults, who may need money from their investments for near-term living expenses, typically prefer safer investments so they don’t have to wait for the market to recover in the event of a downturn.

TMP-1651.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1651.text: Risk and Diversification As we discussed in Module 3.5 , individuals and households exhibit varying degrees of risk tolerance — the amount of risk someone is willing or able to accept. Those with a lower risk tolerance tend to prefer stable, low-risk assets like CDs and federally insured savings accounts, despite the lower returns. Those with a higher risk tolerance are willing to accept more volatility in exchange for potentially higher returns, and are more likely to invest in riskier assets like stocks and mutual funds. Financial assets don’t need to be all high-risk or low-risk, however. Financial advisers will often suggest a diversification strategy to clients — that is, spreading money across diverse assets with different risk levels and expected rates of return. This collection of financial assets is called a portfolio . Strategically investing in a variety of assets with different risk levels can allow investors to enjoy both the stability of lower-risk assets and the better returns of higher-risk assets. This might mean placing some money in stocks that are relatively risky but have high expected (average) returns; bonds with moderate risk and moderate average returns; and savings accounts or CDs with lower risks but lower returns.

TMP-1652.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1652.text: diversification The strategy of spreading money across diverse assets with different risk levels and expected rates of return. Since everyone’s situation is different, your preferred portfolio might be weighted more heavily toward higher-risk or lower-risk investments, or it might be a balanced mix of each type. And the best portfolio can change over time as your circumstances change. Someone’s portfolio as a single 25-year-old may be very different from their portfolio as a 50-year-old homeowner with several dependents. AI-driven robo-advisers can help investors build diversified portfolios based on data collected from online questionnaires, taking into account factors like time and risk tolerance. Like humans, robo-advisers can make mistakes, and it’s important to remember that stock and bond investments always involve the risk of loss.

TMP-1654.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1654.text: Seeking Professional Advice Some people may seek advice from financial professionals to weigh their options and build a saving and investment plan that works for their unique circumstances — their goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance. In choosing a financial adviser, it is important to consider their licensing and certifications, their education, and their experience. For example, a Certified Financial Planner ® (CFP ® ) has a college degree with specific coursework in financial planning and has passed a comprehensive exam on finance-related topics. The cost of financial planning assistance varies, with some planners charging a flat fee and others taking a percentage of your assets. If you work for a large employer, they may offer financial education programs or opportunities to consult with financial planners at no cost. Tracking Your Investments As we’ve learned, managing your financial portfolio is a long-term activity — and that portfolio should evolve as your life evolves. When circumstances change, it’s wise to step back and consider your portfolio. Are your assets working for you? Should you reallocate any funds — say, to take on more or less risk?

TMP-1655.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1655.text: It’s also important to review your investments periodically and keep track of how they’re performing. To inform investment decisions, many investors use a stock or bond index — a measurement that tracks the performance of a representative group of stocks or bonds. Investors use these indexes as benchmarks (discussed in Module 4.2 ), against which they can assess the performance of their own investments. For example, the S&P 500 is a stock index that tracks 500 of the biggest publicly traded U.S. companies to provide a solid snapshot of the U.S. stock market. A bond index, like the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index, tracks a wide selection of corporate and government bonds. stock or bond index A measurement that tracks the performance of a representative group of stocks or bonds. Using stock and bond indexes, investors can learn whether their investments are underperforming, outperforming, or keeping pace with the market, and they can make adjustments to their portfolios as needed. Let’s say you want to assess the performance of one of your stocks over the past year. You know that, over that time period, the value of your stock grew by 10%. Examining the percentage change in the index with stocks that most resemble your own — the S&P 500 — you learn that the index grew by 7%. This

TMP-1656.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1656.text: means your stock outperformed the index, an indication that it is doing well. But if your stock only grew by 5%, it would have underperformed the index, indicating that this investment is doing worse than the broader collection of stocks. In this case, you might consider adjusting your portfolio — acting rationally, of course, without excessive influence from loss aversion!

TMP-1657.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1657.text: Module 5.3 Review Learning Goals LG How does financial planning help people achieve their goals for post-secondary education, housing, and retirement? People’s long-term financial goals commonly include paying for post-secondary education (for themselves, or for their children), purchasing a home, and saving enough to enjoy a comfortable retirement. To pay educational costs, individuals or households often turn to personal savings; grants and scholarships (which don’t need to be repaid); student loans (which do need to be repaid); and work-study programs. People typically finance a home purchase with a combination of personal savings and borrowing. They may have a fixed-rate mortgage (with an interest rate that

TMP-1658.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1658.text: never changes during the term of the loan) or an adjustable-rate mortgage (with an interest rate that is initially lower, but then varies based on how interest rates are changing in the economy). Retirees’ income usually comes from a combination of Social Security, employer-sponsored retirement plans, individual investments, and earnings from part-time or continued employment. LG What factors affect an investor’s return on financial assets? Most investors put their money in financial assets that have the potential to grow. Some of these assets are savings vehicles — accounts that investors use to save and grow their money over time, like savings accounts and certificates of deposit (CDs). Other assets include stocks, bonds, and mutual funds — a type of investment in which many people pool their money together, and a professional manager invests that money in a mix of assets, like stocks and bonds. Time is a key factor affecting investment returns — the amount of money an investor gains or loses over a certain period. If an investment does well, you’ll earn

TMP-1659.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1659.text: returns on the amount you originally invested (the principal). If your returns from an asset are reinvested back into the asset, you’ll earn returns on not only the principal, but also on the returns. This snowball effect of your earnings generating additional earnings, known as compounding , becomes more powerful the earlier you begin saving and investing. Every financial asset has some level of risk. Lower-risk assets include FDIC-insured savings accounts and treasury bonds, which generally have relatively low expected returns. Other assets, like individual stocks, are riskier, but have higher expected returns. Buying, selling, and holding financial assets may involve transaction fees, management fees, and advisory fees if you work with a financial professional. You may pay brokerage fees if you buy stocks or bonds. Taxes on your investments will also decrease your return. Inflation reduces the amount of goods and services you can buy with your money over time. So, the real return on an investment — the purchasing power of that return in terms of what you can actually buy with that money — may be lower than the investment’s nominal return (the dollar amount you’ve earned). Investors should consider both real ( inflation-adjusted ) and nominal ( unadjusted ) returns.

TMP-1660.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1660.text: Two common behavioral biases that adversely affect investment returns are overconfidence — an investor’s belief that they possess greater knowledge or predictive abilities than they actually do — and loss aversion , the tendency to prefer avoiding loss more strongly than achieving gains of the same amount. LG How can investors create a saving and investment plan tailored to their goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance? Investors with a longer time horizon may choose higher-risk, higher-return investments, because they can better cope with economic downturns and wait for assets to regain their value. A shorter time horizon often prompts investors to choose safer assets. Individuals and households exhibit varying degrees of risk tolerance — the amount of risk someone is willing or able to accept. Those with a lower risk tolerance tend to prefer stable, low-risk assets, despite the lower returns. Those with a higher risk tolerance are willing to accept more volatility in exchange for potentially higher returns.

TMP-1661.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1661.text: Financial advisers will often suggest a diversification strategy to clients — spreading money across diverse assets with different risk levels and expected rates of return. In choosing a financial adviser, it is important to consider their licensing and certifications, their education, their experience, and any costs. To ensure they’re making the most of their money, investors often use a stock or bond index — a measurement that tracks the performance of a representative group of stocks or bonds. Investors use these indexes as a benchmark for comparing the performance of their investments to that of the broader market. AP ® Skills Workshop: Communication Preparing for the AP ® Exam WHAT ARE THE FIVE COURSE SKILLS FOR THIS AP ® COURSE? There are five skills you’ll need to build for this course. Two of them are Business Skills: Concept Application and Entrepreneurship . The other three are Professional and Leadership Skills: Decision Making, Collaboration, and Communication . You will find five AP ® Skills Workshops in this text—one at the end of each of the five units, with each Workshop addressing one of the Course Skills. In this workshop, we will focus on Communication . IDENTIFY COMMUNICATION Communication is the imparting or exchanging of information. Employers consistently rate strong communication as among the top skills needed in the workplace. Business communication may include setting expectations for employees, discussing performance and promotion, presenting data effectively, and developing materials such as surveys, pitches, and presentations. Effective communication is key when interacting with coworkers, customers, suppliers, and community members.

TMP-1689.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1689.text: UNDERSTAND COMMUNICATION Bailey has been working at the Wanderlust Wonders Furniture and Antique Shop for two years. She is interested in applying for an assistant manager role that the store just advertised. This would involve making decisions regarding staff scheduling, hiring, and training. In Bailey’s two years at the shop, she has made many suggestions to her boss. One was to change the merchandise organization, placing higher-demand items at the ends of the store so that customers would have to walk through more of the store to get to them. In doing so, customers discovered more new items to purchase for their home. Partly as a result of such efforts, as Table U5-3 shows, sales revenue increased 18% year over year. TMP-1690.text: Bailey decides to bring up the assistant manager position in a one-on-one meeting with the store manager, Imani. When she considers how best to communicate her goal, Bailey feels that Imani will appreciate a direct approach. She arrives at their meeting prepared with the relevant data and presents her case to Imani: “I’m interested in the assistant manager position. I feel that I’ve grown a lot with this company in the past two years. If you look at my record, you’ll see that sales in the store have gone up 18%, and I’m the most productive salesperson on the floor. The layout suggestions I made have also been implemented successfully: Customers can find items they need quickly, and they can discover new ones.” Impressed, Imani begins to consider Bailey’s value to the company. She is an excellent salesperson, often upselling customers with other items that they had not considered, but appreciate. Bailey also trained several new employees on all aspects of the floor. While the advertisement requested two years of prior management experience, Bailey’s proven competence and skillset are major assets even without a title. With Bailey’s example in mind, let’s test your understanding of communication.
