TMP-1691.text: Maskot/Getty Images Strong communication helps build trust, and can open doors to career opportunities. Describe the concept of communication in the workplace with regard to hiring, training, supervising, and evaluating employees. Answer: Communication is key in all aspects of the workplace. During the hiring process, applicants who communicate well can present themselves effectively, and employers can convey their expectations. Communicating well during training ensures that employees understand their responsibilities. Supervisors need to maintain good communication with employees to provide feedback and address issues. During evaluations, employers can discuss performance, and employees can communicate their value to the company. Explain how good communication skills can influence the development of a person’s career.

TMP-1692.groupTitle: Unit 5 Personal Goals, Budgeting, and Investing
TMP-1692.text: Answer: Communicating well can influence a person’s career beginning with the hiring process, as the Bailey example demonstrates: Knowing how to communicate your strengths to an employer can help you secure the position you want. Once you are employed, effective communication remains essential for building strong relationships, performing your role well, and demonstrating leadership potential. Over time, these skills can translate to greater responsibilities, promotions, and professional growth. Using a slide show presentation with data and charts, educate your classmates on the benefits of saving or investing a set portion of their income each month. 2. Activity: Apply what you’ve learned about communication to create signage in an employee break room to motivate stronger sales performance.

TMP-1695.text: The Business Model Canvas alexey_ds/Getty Images A Business Model Canvas helps everyone from new entrepreneurs to corporate leaders paint a picture of how a business provides value to customers and earns profit.

TMP-1696.text: The Building Blocks of Your Business In the AP ® Business with Personal Finance course, you will apply the business concepts you’ve learned to an entrepreneurial project. You will illustrate the building blocks of that project with a tool that helps entrepreneurs and executives describe, visualize, and experiment with their business plans on a single page. This strategic management tool— a Business Model Canvas (BMC) —is a simple overview of how a business creates, delivers, and captures value. This appendix will familiarize you with a typical Business Model Canvas, a modified version of which you will apply to your project. Business Model Canvas (BMC) An overview of how a business creates, delivers, and captures value. The more general term business model refers to a plan for the operation and profitability of a business. A business model comprises four main elements: the offering (what is sold), the customers (to whom it is sold), the infrastructure (how the product is made and delivered), and the financial viability (how the business makes money). Swiss business theorist Alexander Osterwalder proposed the BMC as a one-page plan that breaks down the four main elements of the business model into nine smaller

TMP-1697.text: components to further explore how the business pursues its goals. Those nine components are 1. Key Partnerships: The strategic collaborations with suppliers, other companies, and individuals (such as investors) that help the business succeed. 2. Key Activities: The essential tasks the business performs to operate, such as innovating, manufacturing, marketing, and selling. 3. Value Proposition: The products offered and their unique benefits to customers, such as being affordable or easy to use. 4. Customer Relationship: The strategies that build strong ties with targeted customer segments, which might include personalized service, focus on product quality, the convenience of self-service, or close attention to customer feedback. 5. Customer Segment: The targeted group(s) of people or organizations the business aims to serve, such as high school students, country music lovers, or restaurants. 6. Key Resources: The assets needed to operate the business and deliver its value proposition, such as skilled workers, manufacturing systems, cash, and intellectual property such as patents and brands.

TMP-1698.text: 7. Distribution Channels: How the business delivers its product and communicates with customers, such as with an app, retail stores, or direct sales. 8. Cost Structure: The major costs of operating the business, such as payroll, research, production, or marketing. 9. Revenue Streams: How the business earns money, such as with subscriptions, sales, rentals, or memberships. You can think of the offering, customers, infrastructure, and financial viability elements of a business model as being mapped into the nine components of a BMC in this way: The offering is central to the value proposition. Customers relate to customer segments, distribution channels, and customer relationships. Infrastructure includes key activities, key resources, and key partners. Financial viability is tied to cost structure and revenue streams. Figure A.1 illustrates the BMC’s nine components using ride-sharing company Uber. The business’s key partners include payment processors, companies that provide digital

TMP-1699.text: map technology, and investors who enable Uber to adapt and grow. Uber’s key activities include refining the Uber platform, marketing and advertising, recruiting drivers, and operating the business. Uber’s main value proposition is to connect riders with drivers. It fosters customer relationships through a rating system that builds trust and loyalty. Uber’s customer segments are people who need a ride and people who want to earn money providing rides. The company’s key resources include its talented employee pool and its network of self-employed drivers. The Uber app is the business’s channel for distributing its services and communications. The cost structure involves the major expenses of paying employees, drivers, legal fees, marketing and advertising, and technology costs. Uber’s revenue streams include a share of the fares, which increase with surge pricing—their strategy of charging higher fares in times of peak demand. Uber also offers UberEATS—an app that allows people to order food from restaurants remotely for either pickup or delivery. For the purposes of this example, we have focused solely on the original, ride-sharing side of the business.

TMP-1704.text: Figure A.1 The Business Model Canvas Uber Adapted from J. Lokitz, How to Use the Business Model Canvas for Innovation , Design a Better Business (November 2, 2017), https://designabetterbusiness.com/2017/11/02/how-to-use-the-business-model-canvas-for-innovation/ . Using the BMC for Ideation and Innovation The BMC is a useful tool for visualizing the business model, assessing the key elements, and refining business strategies. Study of the BMC can also inspire creativity, ideation, and innovation. In this section, we explain several ways the BMC can help a business kickstart the ideation process when applied to an existing business model. Freshwatching Examining the business models of other businesses can promote deep thinking about how your own company operates and lead to new ideas about how to improve your business. Freshwatching is the ideation technique of overlaying the business model of an unrelated business onto your own to ignite new ideas. In other words, you will examine your company through the lens of another company to gain a fresh perspective and

TMP-1705.text: learn new approaches. Suppose you operated a traditional house-cleaning business. You could consider each of the elements of Uber’s BMC to see if there are ideas you could borrow. Uber’s BMC might inspire you to expand your business by offering an app that matches customers who need cleaning services with people who want to provide cleaning services. On the face of it, a cleaning business has nothing to do with a ride-sharing business; yet examining both together can reveal some interesting opportunities and inspire new ideas. Remove the Core Removing the core is an ideation technique that encourages businesses to think beyond their main or “core” sources of value. 1 The idea is to take the core value proposition out of your business model and consider how else the business could deliver value. For example, in the Business Model Canvas for high-end car manufacturer BMW shown in Figure A.2 , the core value proposition is to offer customers the “ultimate driving experience.” What happens if you remove this value proposition? How else could BMW deliver value? What other customer needs come to mind? Perhaps BMW could disrupt the industry by being the first automaker to offer free maintenance for the life

TMP-1706.text: of the car. Or BMW could become the automaker known for superior technology integration or carbon-neutral manufacturing.

The market research prompted by this exercise may reveal that customers really want reliability, better gas mileage, and lots of cup holders. For businesses new and old, thinking outside the box of existing value propositions can lead to new ideas of great worth. After ideating, of course, the core can be restored, but the insights gained from removing the core may lead to new value propositions or new directions for the company.

TMP-1712.text: Epicenters The Business Model Canvas is made up of interdependent blocks. Changing a component in one block, or epicenter , is likely to influence components in other blocks. With epicenter-based ideation , the change is more radical than just removing the core, and can lead to a larger pivot in the business’s direction. With this technique, every component except one is removed, and the exercise is to imagine what else could be done with that remaining epicenter. Using the BMW example, the thought experiment would be to imagine what would happen if the company removed everything in the Business Model Canvas except, say, BMW’s key resources. All else would be gone, but the company would still have the BMW brand name, a sophisticated manufacturing system, and a pool of talented employees. What else could the company do with those key resources? In the past, the company has used its resources to make aircraft engines, railway brakes, and farm equipment. Going forward, perhaps they could consider applying their talent for precision engineering to the development of satellites, medical equipment, or wind turbines. For more ideation, the retained epicenter could be customer relationships, key activities, or key partners, leading to more answers to the question, “What else could the company do with this?” Some of the answers could then be incorporated into the original Business Model Canvas.

TMP-1713.text: Ask Trigger Questions Each block of the Business Model Canvas can be the subject of trigger questions to stir up new, creative ideas. 2 With your leadership team assembled, you can pose “what if?” questions and make a list of the promising ideas that follow. In the case of Uber, examples from the first three blocks might include, “What if Uber chose an entirely new partner?” “What if we started providing a different mode of transportation other than cars (and in some cases boats and bikes)?” and “What if safety became our primary value proposition?” Answers might include “We could partner with Macy’s for the rapid delivery of clothing for people with last-minute wardrobe needs,” “We could consider air transportation, light rail, and space travel,” and “We could capture the segment of people with serious concerns about the safety of transportation services.” Some ideas may be gems and others far-fetched, but even bad ideas often lead to good ones. Conclusion The techniques highlighted here exemplify opportunities for fruitful ideation and innovation based on the BMC. Expect plenty of your ideas to end up in the scrap heap, but others could shift your perspective and help you to view your Business Model Canvas in an entirely new light. A business model portrays how a business captures and delivers

TMP-1714.text: value, and sometimes the business model itself can be a game-changer. With fresh ideas, businesses can create or update business models to capture and deliver value in new ways, and perhaps even disrupt existing markets by displacing big, established companies whose ideas have become stale.

TMP-1735.text: Glossary A/B testing A type of experiment in which researchers compare responses to two or more versions of a product, promotion, or pricing strategy. ( p. 140 ) accounting The process of recording, organizing, and reporting financial data. ( p. 239 ) accounting department The department that records all financial transactions, summarizes those transactions in reports and statements, and ensures compliance with tax laws and regulations. ( pp. 85, 242 ) accounts payable Money a business owes to its suppliers for goods and services received. ( p. 297 )

TMP-1736.text: accounts receivable Money owed to a business for goods or services already provided to customers. ( p. 295 ) accrued expenses Expenses incurred by the company for which no payment has been made and no invoice has been received. ( p. 297 ) adjustable-rate mortgage A mortgage that often begins with a lower fixed rate for a certain period, then changes—or adjusts—based on how interest rates are changing in the economy. ( p. 417 ) alternative financial services Services such as payday loans, check-cashing services, and instant tax refunds, which can be accessed without a credit check or banking history and may provide quick access to cash (at a high fee). ( p. 224 ) annual income tax return A form filed each year to report a person’s income and the taxes already paid, and to determine whether additional taxes are owed or a refund is due. ( p. 389 ) annual salary A set amount of money paid to an employee every year. ( p. 339 )

TMP-1737.text: artisan processes Production processes involving skilled craftspeople who employ traditional, nonmechanized methods to make goods in limited quantities. ( p. 91 ) auto insurance A type of insurance that protects drivers if the vehicle they are driving is involved in an accident or an injury. ( p. 404 ) automated savings plan A system that transfers a portion of your income directly into a savings account on a regular schedule. ( p. 206 ) balance sheet A financial statement that shows a business’s assets, liabilities, and owners’ equity at a particular point in time. ( p. 293 ) balance sheet equation An equation showing the relationship between a business’s assets and the combined total of its liabilities and owners’ equity (Assets = Liabilities + Owners’ equity). (Also known as the fundamental accounting equation.) ( p. 294 )

TMP-1738.text: bankruptcy A legal process businesses and individuals use to seek relief from their debts. ( p. 300 ) bar chart A data display for multiple categories, using rectangular bars whose heights or lengths indicate values for a single measure. ( p. 142 ) barriers to entry Obstacles that deter new competitors from entering a market. ( p. 20 ) benchmark A reference point that provides a standard for comparison. ( p. 354 ) beneficiaries The individual or group chosen by an insured person to receive funds when the person dies. ( p. 406 ) big data Large, complex datasets that accumulate rapidly and often require advanced analytical techniques for processing. ( p. 197 )

TMP-1739.text: board of directors A group of people elected by company shareholders to oversee the organization’s leadership and strategy. ( p. 81 ) bond A loan from an investor; the investor buys the bond from a borrower who issues (sells) the bond. ( p. 266 ) bootstrapping Self-funding of a business by drawing on the founders’ own resources. ( p. 262 ) brainstorming The technique of encouraging participants to think freely and propose ideas without fear of criticism. ( p. 46 ) brand The identity of a product or business that distinguishes it from its competitors. ( p. 154 ) break even When a business’s total revenue equals its total cost. ( p. 264 )

TMP-1740.text: bribery Offering, giving, receiving, or requesting any item of value (money, gifts, services) for the purpose of influencing an action or decision. ( p. 321 ) budget A plan for how to allocate available income across expenses and savings over a period of time. ( p. 286 ) business An organization that produces or purchases goods or services and then sells them; most businesses seek profit by selling their products for more than the cost of obtaining them. ( p. 5 ) business ethics The application of ethical standards to all aspects of a business. ( p. 62 ) business hypotheses A set of assumptions about products, customers, or markets. ( p. 138 ) Business Model Canvas (BMC) An overview of how a business creates, delivers, and captures value. ( p. 430 )

TMP-1741.text: business plan An outline of a business’s goals, value proposition, market research, marketing strategies, and financial projections. ( p. 273 ) business strategy An outline for how a business plans to achieve its goals. ( p. 359 ) business-to-business (B2B) Companies that sell their goods and services primarily to other businesses. ( p. 180 ) business-to-consumer (B2C) Companies that sell their goods and services primarily to consumers for personal use. ( p. 180 ) capital gain The profit earned from an asset that is sold for more than the purchase price. ( p. 271 ) capital gains tax A tax paid on the profits (capital gains) earned from the sale of assets. ( p. 390 ) cash Currency and immediately accessible bank deposits, such as money held in checking accounts. ( p. 295 )

TMP-1742.text: cash flow statement A financial statement that tracks the movement of cash in and out of a business over a specified financial reporting period. ( p. 309 ) cash inflows Inflows of money into a business that increase its cash balance. ( p. 309 ) cash outflows Outflows of money out of a business that decrease its cash balance. ( p. 309 ) certificate of deposit (CD) An account that offers a higher interest rate in exchange for keeping money deposited for a fixed period. ( p. 214 ) checking account A deposit account used for everyday transactions like paying bills, making purchases, or withdrawing cash. ( p. 213 ) chief executive officer (CEO) The highest-ranking executive in a corporation. ( p. 81 )

TMP-1743.text: claim A request asking an insurer to reimburse a financial loss based on the policy terms. ( p. 403 ) code of conduct A document that details the rules, expectations, and standards for conduct within an organization. ( p. 62 ) collateral Something of value that the borrower will forfeit to the lender if the loan is not repaid. ( p. 222 ) collusion Secretive cooperation between businesses to hinder competition. ( p. 170 ) commercial bank A for-profit financial institution that offers services like checking and savings accounts, loans, and credit cards. ( p. 212 ) commission Compensation based on a percentage of sales revenue. ( p. 339 )

TMP-1744.text: communication The act of exchanging information (facts, thoughts, ideas, or feelings) between individuals or groups. ( p. 335 ) compensation schemes Plans for how employees will be rewarded for their work. ( p. 338 ) competitive advantage A firm’s position of superiority over competitors. ( p. 16 ) competitive pricing A strategy in which a business bases its prices on competitors’ prices. ( p. 165 ) competitive rivalry The intensity of competition among existing businesses in a market. ( p. 372 ) compounding The process of earnings generating additional earnings over time. ( p. 419 ) consumer The user of a good or service. ( p.5 )

TMP-1745.text: consumer behavior A set of selection, purchase, and consumption activities consumers use to address their needs and wants. ( p. 121 ) consumer psychology The study of how and why consumers make purchasing decisions. ( p. 126 ) core competencies Capabilities or strengths that enable an individual or a business to stand out among rivals and deliver value in unique ways. ( p. 53 ) core values Underlying principles and beliefs that shape decision making for companies and individuals. ( p. 52 ) corporation A business owned by shareholders that is a legal entity apart from its owners. ( p. 78 ) cost of goods sold (COGS) The total cost of producing goods sold over some period.
